The food was fairly decent—I chose a simple burger and enjoyed a flavorful berry sangria. The atmosphere was inviting, cozy, and had a pleasant energy. Initially, I expected this to be just another average spot—not outstanding, but not bad—and I was ready to move on with that impression.

That said, some problems came up. Before arriving, I checked their website to plan my meal since I try to avoid overly calorie-heavy options. Their site advertises “skinny drinks.” When I asked the waiter about them, he said it was possible but not a usual practice because it’s a hassle for the bartenders, and he actually discouraged it. So why advertise it if it’s not commonly offered?

Also, we had confirmed in advance—when booking our reservation—that we could bring a birthday cake and light candles. Unfortunately, communication broke down. We never received the candles we requested, and the waiter struggled to find a lighter before realizing there were no candles available at all. This was clearly not the waiter’s fault, and we made sure to thank him and tip well for doing his best despite the situation.

One more thing: this is one of those places where ordering a medium rare burger means it ends up overcooked. I now order medium rare on purpose just to get a medium-cooked burger instead of medium well or well done.

In short: if you’re coming for the beers, go for it; the food is decent enough. Honestly, I left feeling a bit underwhelmed.

Visiting Rock Bottom on Father’s Day brought to mind familiar spots like Applebee’s, Chili’s, or Fridays—where sticking to classic bar fare like burgers, sandwiches, pizza, wings, and salads is the safest bet. This was our second Father’s Day attempt here; nearly ten years ago, we showed up early afternoon only to find they’d already run out of steaks. How does that happen on Father’s Day? This time, arriving around noon allowed us to avoid the rush.

My wife ordered the Berry Bash Sangria and enjoyed it, though she felt it had too much ice. Our daughter loved her root beer float. I started with a Mango Iced Tea but found it lacking in sweetness, so I switched to a Raspberry Iced Tea.

We began with the Kobe beef sliders as an appetizer, which took about 15 minutes to arrive. Once they did, the three sliders were very good. My wife started her meal with a small greenhouse salad dressed in jalapeño ranch, which she liked, followed by the lobster and shrimp enchiladas. She found the enchiladas overly salty and was disappointed to discover there was no lobster in them at all.

Our daughter went with the kids’ burger and fries—no surprises there. I ordered the New York Strip with mashed potatoes and green beans. The steak was cooked perfectly and tasted decent, though Longhorn offers steaks of noticeably better quality. The green beans were good, but the mashed potatoes were bland and unremarkable.

The kitchen was a whirlwind, sounding like a live episode of Hell’s Kitchen. Servers had to ask for our orders repeatedly—at least five or six times—and the kitchen stayed backed up throughout our meal.

On the bright side, our waitress Susan was excellent. Overall, I’d recommend coming here for drinks and bar food, but skipping everything else.

My maid of honor arranged a charming banquet room that was nicely separated from the main dining area. Both she and my mother spoke highly of the reservation coordinator, describing them as exceptional and very easy to reach. The shower itself was delightful—the waitstaff stayed attentive and kept everyone’s glasses filled throughout. When a sudden downpour started, they kindly allowed us to stay a bit longer so my gifts wouldn’t get soaked while being carried out to the car.

The only reason I’m giving this venue 4 stars instead of 5 is because we weren’t allowed to take home any leftover buffet food. There was salmon, chicken, potatoes, and mac and cheese left, but they refused to let us pack it up. I don’t understand why—since the food can’t be reused, it just ended up going to waste.

On a separate note, unrelated to the shower, their trivia night is a lot of fun!

When we arrived, the place was quite packed, so we wandered around the bar area for several minutes until a kind couple mentioned they were about to leave and offered us their bar table. While their generosity was appreciated, it felt a bit awkward standing nearby as they finished their drinks, paid their bill, and left.

Once seated, I scanned the drink menu. As a devoted IPA fan, I chose one—and it was a great pick. My husband went with the Red Ale, which he also enjoyed.

The service was average—not remarkable, but not terrible either. Now, onto the food, which fell far short. I ordered the mini street fish tacos—four small tacos with lime-marinated fish and tomatillo salsa. Sadly, they were nearly inedible. I love fish tacos; they’re such a simple dish, so why is it so hard to get right? The shells were tough and literally cracked at the bottom when I picked them up. The sour cream splattered messily across the plate, and the fish was severely overcooked. If I hadn’t been so hungry, I wouldn’t have eaten them at all. Lesson learned.

My husband ordered the BBQ Chicken Pizza, topped with beans, corn, roasted red pepper, and sour cream. Usually, he strips specialty pizzas down to just chicken, BBQ sauce, and cheese, but this time I insisted he try it as is because I was curious about the unusual combination. When it arrived, I was jealous—it completely outshone my disappointing tacos. I really should have gone with something simpler.

Would I return? Honestly, I couldn’t care less. The beers were good, but you can find a solid IPA almost anywhere these days. The underwhelming food sealed the deal for me. Yes, it’s a chain, but that doesn’t mean it has to be so disappointing.

I ordered the Veggie Burger for $8.50 and absolutely loved it! The homemade patty, made from beans, rolled oats, and vegetables, gave it a truly unique flavor. The chipotle mayo added a perfect kick that really boosted the taste. The portion was more than enough for me, and I felt it was well worth the price.

As for drinks, I’m new to beer, but my friend ordered a draft. Even from a small sip, I could tell it was high quality—well balanced between bitterness and sweetness, with a subtle tang. I rarely drink beer, but if I do, I’d want it to be fresh and microbrewed, just like this one.

A quick note for vegetarians: the options are somewhat limited. Besides the veggie burger, there are veggie tacos, a few appetizers, and some salads. Still, I’d definitely recommend the veggie burger.

I’ve never actually paid full price for a ticket at this venue. The two-item minimum can be somewhat frustrating—not because of the rule itself, but because the quality doesn’t match the hefty prices. We spent about $30 on four items—two appetizers and two beers—and honestly, the appetizers were quite disappointing. To make matters worse, the servers didn’t seem very welcoming.

There are several rules to keep in mind. They won’t seat your group until everyone has arrived, and if you have dinner reservations, every person must order a meal. Plus, an automatic gratuity is added to the bill, along with other policies.

The "box office" setup is also unusual. You pick up your tickets at a window with a microphone and a slide-under slot, but once inside the club, the box office is completely open with staff just sitting there. This makes the whole window process feel unnecessary.

Despite these issues, the seats are cozy, the atmosphere is pleasant, and the performances are generally good.

Some performances at this venue have truly stood out—Jim Breuer being a prime example—while others, surprisingly, have fallen short, like Tracy Morgan. Still, the overall experience has always been enjoyable. The intimate setting ensures every seat has a great view and sound, so there really isn’t a bad spot. Just a heads-up: if you’re in the very front row, you know exactly what’s coming!

That said, there are a couple of drawbacks. Waiting outside in the dead of winter can be harsh since the lobby is so small you have no choice but to queue outdoors until the show starts or the previous one ends. If you want a good seat, be prepared to wait in line for a while—brr!

The two-drink minimum is another downside. While understandable from a business perspective, it means inflated prices for watered-down drinks. My advice? Stick to beer and wine—skip the fancy cocktails.

As for the food, don’t expect much. Ideally, venues serving food would offer something exceptional, but that’s rarely the case. I’ve never had anything memorable here—for example, the nacho platter had too many refried beans and not enough chips.

So, what’s the bottom line? This is a solid venue. Focus on the talent, come with realistic expectations, enjoy beer or wine, eat somewhere better beforehand, and have a great time!

That Saturday night was exactly what we needed! My husband and I went to the comedy club to see Tammy Pescatelli live. Having enjoyed her routines on TV and the occasional DVE morning show, we expected a fun night—and she definitely delivered plenty of laughs. The surprise highlight was the opener, Gene Collier, the well-known Post-Gazette sports columnist. He was a fantastic choice to start the evening, with his sharp humor about being 58 and a baby boomer resonating deeply with us.

However, the sightlines were less than ideal. A woman with a massive Pittsburgh BIG HAIR sat right in front of us. I found myself constantly bobbing my head from side to side, trying to actually see the stage instead of just listening, as she repeatedly reached for her table overflowing with snacks.

As for drinks, there was a two-drink minimum. My first drink was quite weak, but the second was strong enough to balance it out. Still, the drinks aren’t really the main attraction, are they? All in all, it was a very enjoyable evening!

At that time, only a few well-known comedians were listed as Special Events on the Improv’s website, clearly indicating that Groupons could be used for any shows not marked as such—something that seemed fair. On the very day the Groupons were purchased, my friend Katrina called and successfully reserved two tickets for Jim Jeffries on March 30th at 10 pm. They accepted her Groupon and even gave her a confirmation code. However, shortly after, the Improv suddenly reclassified many comedians, including Jim Jeffries, as Special Events. When I called to redeem my Groupon, I was told it was no longer valid. Many of my friends encountered the same problem. It felt like a classic bait-and-switch since these performers were not labeled Special Events when we bought the Groupons.

In addition, new restrictions appeared unexpectedly—such as prohibiting Groupon use on Saturdays and requiring four vouchers to be redeemed for a single show—none of which were disclosed at the time of purchase. Tonight, my friends and I had mostly accepted that we wouldn’t be able to use our Groupons at the Improv. But when I went with Katrina to the Will Call window to pick up her tickets, we were shocked to find her reservation missing from their system. They refused to hand over the tickets. This whole situation is a complete joke. How is anyone supposed to use their Groupons by September if every show is suddenly labeled a Special Event?

To make matters worse, no one at the Improv answers phone calls or responds to emails. About ten of us are now pursuing refunds through Groupon or our credit card companies, and we’re reporting the Improv to the Better Business Bureau and other agencies. The Pittsburgh Improv’s conduct is extremely shady, and it’s clear they have zero regard for their customers.

The food was honestly quite uninspiring. First, if you’re attending a show, keep in mind there’s a two-item minimum per person, meaning you must order two items each from their expensive bar food and drink menu. Also, sodas don’t come with free refills—I found that out the hard way, so I’d suggest sticking with water. Another thing: before tipping, double-check that your server hasn’t already taken their cut. Even after paying for two bland, overpriced meals and way too many Diet Cokes, my bill felt unusually high. Upon closer inspection, I realized my server had already added an 18% gratuity. The menu states automatic gratuity applies only to parties of six or more, yet there were just two of us, and we weren’t even drunk. I found that assumption quite presumptuous. Normally, I tip well over 20%, but this time I left exactly 18%. Overall, I dislike being forced to buy food just to watch a comedy show. I understand their reasoning, but if I had to buy mediocre popcorn and overpriced soda every time I went to the movies, I’d be far less likely to go—and that’s exactly how I feel about returning to the Improv.

This venue is a reliable spot if you’re looking to kick off or spend an evening surrounded by laughter. Comedy nights here are genuinely enjoyable, especially with acts like Owen Benjamin and Pablo Francisco—both of whom are hilarious. On the other hand, Tammy Pescatelli didn’t quite connect with me.

Be aware, though, that the staff is firm about the two-drink minimum, so expect to pay for their fairly pricey food and beverages. I also find myself wishing the menu offered more variety. Service tends to be unpredictable; after many visits, I’ve had both attentive and inattentive waitstaff. On my most recent trip, our waitress was rude, skipped basic pleasantries, and barely interacted with us. Another thing to note: gratuity is added automatically. While I’m usually fine with that when service is good, this time I wasn’t willing to go along with it.

On the bright side, redeeming my Groupon went smoothly with no issues.

For my bachelorette party, my friends surprised me with tickets to see John Witherspoon, and we were all eagerly anticipating the night. The show was absolutely hilarious, and John was outstanding. The servers were excellent, consistently checking on us to ensure we had plenty of food and drinks. I highly recommend trying the Pink Cadillac cocktail along with the cheesecake and chocolate cake for dessert.

The only reason I can’t give a perfect 5 stars is the long wait before the show started. We were scheduled for the 9 pm performance, with doors opening at 8:45 pm. Unfortunately, we had to stand outside in 28-degree weather for an entire hour because the previous show ran late. We were finally let in at 9:20 pm, and after ordering drinks, the show didn’t begin until 9:45 pm. While the host did offer a general apology, it hardly made up for the nearly hour-long delay.

This venue is an excellent pick for a date night—I suggest choosing a later show and having dinner beforehand. I got lucky with $5 tickets for John Heffron through an online promo code, so it’s definitely worth hunting for discounts before paying full price for any event here. We showed up early to pick up our tickets at the box office, only to find a line forming outside about an hour before the show in freezing weather. Instead of standing out in the cold, we headed across the street to Rock Bottom for a beer. When the doors opened just 15 minutes before the show, the line moved quickly, and even at the very end, we still secured a table in the back. The venue is fairly small, so there really aren’t any bad seats. Usually, there’s an MC who warms up the crowd, and this one was genuinely funny, as was the opening act before John Heffron took the stage. My only gripe is the two-drink minimum combined with steep prices—$9.50 for a mixed well drink, $7 for draft beer, and $3.50 for soda. Ouch! At least we saved by not paying full price for the tickets.

The renovation at this store is seriously driving me up the wall! Honestly, I don’t mind change—I really don’t. I probably should have expected it, considering all the clues. First, they moved the pharmacy to the far end where the now-closed Iggle video used to be. That didn’t bother me since I never used the pharmacy anyway.

But then things got worse. They relocated the entire toiletries section over there too. To add to my frustration, my beloved spaghetti and “ethnic food” aisle (and yes, I love that spaghetti counts as ethnic food) was shifted to where the Tylenol used to be. Now, my kitty food is in the spot where the spaghetti once was. Can you feel my irritation?

Did I mention I don’t mind change? The real issue is, I hate grocery shopping. Partly my fault—I have to read every label to avoid anything with 25 grams of fat and 5000 calories, although ice cream sometimes sneaks into my cart. I used to enjoy shopping here because I KNEW exactly where everything was. Now, I’m totally lost... wahhh!

Alright, enough complaining. I know I’ll come back eventually. Hopefully (??), the shopping experience will be even better and more magical once the remodel is done. But for now, I just can’t handle it. I’ll be stuck at the Ghetto Bird down in the Southside until my favorite store is shiny and new again.

I enjoy visiting Barnes & Noble, but sometimes finding something as simple as a calendar can be quite frustrating. After a dinner with neighbors, I stopped by and was surprised by how crowded the store was. We had to wait about 10 minutes just to gather enough chairs for the four of us, eventually having to take them from other tables. Meanwhile, my husband stood in line for 15 minutes just to get an iced tea lemonade.

The store includes an audio and video section among the books, newspapers, and magazines, but the prices there aren’t very appealing. I can get the same movies online for much less, though that means waiting. Occasionally, I do shop their discount books and have found some great recipe and mystery titles for under $5, which is a decent deal. Still, with a half-priced bookstore nearby offering a wide selection at literally half the price of typical retailers, those bargains are tough to beat.

Barnes & Noble feels more like a place to hang out, with books available if you want to buy one on the spot. The layout can be confusing, and you often need to ask for help finding items. For anything I really want, I prefer shopping online since buying in-store just doesn’t seem worth it.

The restaurant was nearly empty, with three waitresses on duty. We were seated and immediately attended to. We ordered drinks—just two waters and an iced tea—but it took a full 15 minutes for them to arrive. That should have been a warning sign, but we went ahead and placed our food order.

After 20 minutes passed with no food, we flagged down our waitress to mention we had a movie in 45 minutes. She assured us our meal would be out shortly. Another 20 minutes went by, still no food, and our waitress had vanished. We caught the attention of another waitress, who promised to find our server. Meanwhile, we noticed our waitress chatting with a coworker instead of checking on us. After finishing, she finally came over about five minutes later and claimed she hadn’t realized our food hadn’t arrived—hard to believe since she never checked in. After consulting the kitchen, she insisted she “definitely” placed our order but it “must have been given to someone else by mistake.” Seriously? Wouldn’t the other table have noticed the wrong dish?

She offered to pack our food for takeout, and since we were starving, we reluctantly agreed. Ten minutes later, our food and bill arrived. The only concession was the iced tea, plus some complimentary utensils and wet wipes—how generous! We hurriedly ate what we could, left no tip (thankfully, we avoided the extra gratuity John had), and rushed to the movie where we discreetly finished our smuggled meal. To top it off, when I opened the wet wipe, it was completely dry. Of course.

Despite everything, I gave the place two stars instead of one because when I finally received my food, it was perfect. I ordered the Greek burger, which was huge, cooked exactly how I like it, and topped with delicious ingredients. I really wish I could come back for the food, but under these circumstances? Absolutely not.

There was a time when visiting Bar Louie guaranteed delicious food, attentive service, and an overall pleasant experience—returning months later to find it just as enjoyable. Unfortunately, that’s no longer the case. On my recent visit, something felt off in a way I couldn’t quite explain; the place no longer felt familiar.

The food itself wasn’t awful. I ordered the pretzel sticks as an appetizer, but the cinnamon sauce was watery, and the pretzels tasted stale. I still ate them, so that’s on me. The highlight was my sandwich, the Mario, which remained as flavorful as ever.

Now, the disappointments:

First, fruit flies were swarming everywhere, making it feel like we were dining on a garbage heap. At one point, a fly landed right in my beer, forcing me to get a fresh drink. I understand the indoor/outdoor setup, but having about 15 fruit flies buzzing around my table is simply unacceptable.

Second, despite the venue’s large size, there was only one server working. She was very kind but clearly overwhelmed, moving nonstop as if on the verge of collapse.

Third, because of this, the overall service suffered. I can’t entirely blame the server—she did the best she could under the circumstances. Having played Diner Dash on my iPad, I know exactly what happens when a place fills up fast and only one person is managing everything.

It’s truly disheartening when a place you once loved becomes one you no longer want to visit. I’m being generous giving it two stars, but because I used to enjoy it so much, I can’t bring myself to rate it any lower. Part of me hopes it improves, but like an absentee father, I fear it will only disappoint me again.

My companion and I arrived at Bar Louie around 8:30 and decided to sit outside. It took nearly 30 minutes before our server finally came to take our order. When I tried to catch the attention of a waitress, she said, “this isn’t my table.” Eventually, our waiter took our order: one bottle of Sam Adams Light and one pineapple juice with vodka.

About 15 minutes later, another staff member—possibly the manager—checked in to ask if we had been served. We confirmed we had but explained we were still waiting. He left, and shortly after, a different waitress brought our drinks—but they were incorrect. My date received vodka on the rocks, and I got a Sam Adams. They took the drinks back, and after another 10 minutes, the correct order finally arrived.

We asked for another round and the check, but it took 20 minutes for them to return—and they forgot the check. By then, we needed to leave to make it to a movie on time. My date requested the check again, and they eventually brought it. I handed over my card, signed the receipt when the waiter returned, and we hurried out.

For two bottled beers and two pineapple juice with vodka cocktails, I was charged $31.03. I didn’t have time to complain or ask questions, but I definitely won’t be coming back.

I can’t provide a full review because the service was so poor that I left before ordering. We initially sat at the bar behind the taps, but after five minutes without any acknowledgment, we assumed the staff hadn’t noticed us. We moved to another pair of seats in the middle of the bar, picking up menus along the way to be ready to order. Although it was fairly busy, no one was standing at the bar trying to get drinks—everyone was seated—and I’m sure they handle much busier times. We waited nearly 15 minutes in our new seats (I timed it; this is not an exaggeration) without a single acknowledgment. At the very least, the bartender should have acknowledged us and let us know he’d be with us shortly. But despite watching him closely most of the time, we couldn’t even make eye contact. I hope this was just a rare incident, but I probably won’t return to find out.

Bar Louie is somewhat pricey for what it offers, and our server didn’t leave much of an impression. So, why the 3-star rating? It mainly comes down to the Happy Hour and the inviting patio vibe.

Happy Hour runs Monday through Friday from 4 to 7 pm, featuring a solid range of specials: $3 drafts, $4 wines, $5 martinis, plus half-price select appetizers and flatbreads. My friend and I split four martinis and three appetizers, and our total came to under $40—a good value.

I ordered the Strawberry Peach Bellini and the S'Mores Martini, both flavorful choices. We also shared Bruschetta Pomodoro, Spinach & Artichoke Dip, and Roasted Vegetable Flatbread. The food was satisfying, and I’d happily order all three again.

My recommendation? Stick to Bar Louie’s strengths—Happy Hour—and plan your visits accordingly.

My friends and I came here for happy hour, which starts at 5 pm. They advertised $1 drafts, $5 mixed drinks, and half-off appetizers, but when we arrived, we found the deals only applied to select items, making the discounts almost meaningless. As a result, we ended up spending a lot on beer and rather uninspiring appetizers.

I only sampled the appetizers, so I can’t comment on the entrees, but here’s my experience with the food and drinks. I ordered the spinach artichoke dip, which was somewhat runny and had a disappointing chip-to-dip ratio. The texture was off, especially the artichoke, which was very fibrous and felt like chewing on grass.

Overall, I wouldn’t recommend this place unless you’re ready to spend freely without much reward. The food was far too average for the prices they charge.

This restaurant thrives thanks to its prime spot near the Waterfront, attracting plenty of workers who stop in after their shifts. It’s always busy, likely because it’s right next to the AMC theater, which brings in steady crowds before and after movies.

The food, though, is just average, and the prices are pretty high. For example, I had the BBQ ranch chicken salad—without the chicken. The BBQ ranch dressing tasted good, but it’s easy to make at home: just mix ranch dressing with KC Masterpiece hickory BBQ sauce, add a little Worcestershire, and a splash of Frank’s hot sauce.

They do offer dollar burgers on Tuesdays from 5 p.m. to midnight, plus daily drink specials and happy hour deals, but even those aren’t enough to make me want to come back. Honestly, I’d skip this place.

One thing in its favor is the free parking, which is much better than Station Square where you have to pay to park. I’m interested to see if business drops off once Burgatory opens across the street.

This venue urgently needs significant improvement. We stopped by on a Friday evening before a show at the Improv, hoping to catch up with friends over drinks and a quick snack. Unfortunately, we never made it to the food due to disappointing service. We arrived between 6:40 and 6:45, just as Happy Hour was ending, yet the bar was far from busy—less than three-quarters full with plenty of empty tables. That should have been our first sign to leave, but we decided to stay and grabbed a table.

Although I’m not one to constantly watch the clock, it took at least 5 to 7 minutes before a server approached us. Our drinks didn’t arrive until 7:04, and I only know this because I was checking my phone. My husband and I had hoped to order appetizers before Happy Hour ended, but that plan fell apart. When our friends arrived, they ordered drinks, we finished ours, and then left.

The server was friendly—this wasn’t the issue. The real problem was how severely understaffed the place was. There appeared to be only two bartenders and far too few cocktail servers. The server apologized for the delay but explained it as the bar getting overwhelmed at the end of Happy Hour. To me, that clearly indicates a need for more staff. I’ve never experienced such a wait at any other bar.

We skipped food not because we didn’t want Happy Hour prices, but because we were concerned about timing. Even though we were ready to order around 7:50 to 7:55, I believe they should have honored Happy Hour pricing. Instead, we left and got food at the Improv. Due to their staffing problems, Bar Louie lost a significant amount of my business, and they won’t be receiving any of mine—or my friends’—in Pittsburgh again.

Over the years, I’ve stopped by this place a few times for both food and drinks, but it’s never really left a strong impression. The food is decent—years ago, I treated myself to a massive fried chicken sandwich that I genuinely enjoyed—but neither the entrees nor the appetizers have ever stood out. I do like their cocktails and might consider coming just for drinks more often, but the prices are simply too high. Even during happy hour, drinks remain expensive, and most of the cocktails I prefer aren’t eligible for the discount, which is disappointing. Once, after a movie with friends, I paid $10 for a single drink—not even a large one! That felt pretty ridiculous, especially with cheaper options nearby.

The food and drinks are fine, if overpriced, so I’d give this place three stars—if only I could hear myself think while eating here. It’s always so loud that I leave with a sore throat from having to shout to be heard. Not cool, Bar Louie. Not cool.

All in all, the food and drinks are passable, but the noisy atmosphere and steep prices keep this from being a favorite. With other options at the Waterfront, I don’t expect to return anytime soon.

You can snag a "burger"—beef, chicken, portabella, or turkey—for just a dollar, served on a bun with lettuce. After that, it’s easy to build your own by adding toppings for a small extra fee: cheese is 75 cents, veggies are 50 cents, “Artery Cloggers” run 75 cents, and sauces are 25 cents. Each topping category offers several choices, including nine different cheeses. Sides like tots or fries are also available at a budget-friendly price.

My burger, with toppings, came to $2.25. Is it the best burger I’ve ever had? No. But for $2.25, it’s definitely the best I’ve found. The cooking is a bit inconsistent—mine was well done, but one of my son’s burgers was pink in the middle. We could have asked for a different one, but a little pink doesn’t bother us.

The tater tots are excellent: crisp and nicely salted. Delicious! Our server was great, and we’re looking forward to coming back.

I usually visit Sandcastle about once a year, but when my friend Catherine from Chicago came for a weekend, we decided to drop by after a day at the zoo. While the main park closes in the evening, the Sandbar, along with the Sandbar Pool and Hot Tub, remains open exclusively for guests 21 and older. The Sandbar offers a great variety of food and drinks, though there is a $6 cover charge to enter. Occasionally, live entertainment adds to the experience.

It’s impressive to think that this lovely spot used to be the railroad yard for the Homestead Works steel mill. After thorough cleanup and redevelopment, it has been transformed into a beautiful place to enjoy a warm day or a relaxing evening. The view across the Monongahela River is stunning, with a wooded hillside on the far side providing a picturesque backdrop. For those interested, there’s even a boat dock, allowing visitors to arrive by river.

Reconnecting with Sandcastle was a pleasure, and I look forward to visiting again soon.

Sandcastle offers a variety of waterslides and pools that are ideal for younger visitors. However, like many urban amusement parks, it also draws a considerable number of high school kids eager to break free from their parents and assert their independence. Unfortunately, these teens often don’t hold back their language around younger children, and in the Mon Tsunami wave pool, personal space is frequently ignored. The wave pool can sometimes resemble a mosh pit, with pushing, shoving, and showboating to impress the opposite sex, which can be unsettling and even dangerous for smaller kids.

Despite these issues, a day at Sandcastle can still be enjoyable—indulging in cheese fries, taking a refreshing dip on a hot day, and riding some exciting slides. To fairly evaluate the park, it’s essential to consider its environment. Supervision isn’t particularly strict, so parents of young children need to stay alert, watching out for groups of teenagers who might “accidentally” bump into others just to provoke a reaction.

Overall, most visits to Sandcastle are a good time—mostly.

Nni planned our trip just a day ahead for me and Bobby—his first time at the park. Although the forecast promised good weather, it shifted two weeks before our visit. Still, we picked a decent time to go. Since rain was expected all day, there were no lines, and we managed to ride every water slide within an hour. However, when we tried the lazy river, it was closed. Staff said it was due to low attendance, which was frustrating since we paid $70 for two people and had already gone through everything so quickly. Keeping the lazy river open would’ve been a perfect way to pass the time! The Cliff Hanger was also closed, as usual.

We ended up riding everything again. The Dragon’s Den is fantastic, and the Blue Tubaluba is a lot of fun too. Bobby had a blast on the speed slides. I have to admit, I do miss the regular body slide. Another reason I chose August 3rd was because the park was supposed to stay open until 7 p.m., instead of the usual 5 or 6. But at 4:45, we got a “15-minute warning” that the park would close at 5 due to rain. A bit more notice would’ve helped.

Nni missed the announcement and asked an employee, who explained they were closing in ten minutes because of the weather and understaffing, so staying open until 7 wasn’t possible. It started raining at 5, but by 5:20, the rain had stopped. The park could’ve paused the rides until the rain passed, but since they were understaffed, they chose to hand out rain checks instead. That’s fine for us since we get another full day, but it would be a major inconvenience for out-of-town visitors planning a family outing.

In the end, the smile on Bobby’s face was priceless, but I truly wish we could’ve enjoyed the lazy river and stayed until 7. Hopefully, next time, everything will go as planned.

This venue seems to cater mainly to children rather than adults or families, since there isn’t much here for anyone over 16. The water slides were underwhelming—there weren’t many, and most lacked excitement. On my last visit, I noticed there weren’t any modern slides, like a tornado slide, so the park is definitely in need of updates.

The "adult pool" and bar area exist, but they were so overcrowded that it was almost impossible to enjoy them. The pool itself is small, similar to what you’d find at a hotel, and the hot tub only fits about eight adults. People were constantly trying to squeeze in, which made the whole area less enjoyable.

I typically like lazy rivers, but this one was packed to the point of discomfort. People kept bumping into me, and the close contact was unpleasant.

The wave pool was the highlight for me. It was crowded, but large enough for everyone to have space. The water was clean, and the waves were strong, which made it a fun experience. I could have spent my entire visit there.

Overall, I found the place mediocre. It didn’t impress me much. Still, if you’re local and have kids, it’s a decent spot for summer fun outside of the mall.

I’m not fond of having to try things before buying, especially something as important as a mattress. I usually start my reviews by sharing a bit about myself. That said, I was quite anxious about purchasing a mattress because if it turned out to be bad, I’d have to endure discomfort for a large part of my life until I fixed the issue. Who wants that? Especially given how costly mattresses can be.

The team here was fantastic. They patiently answered all my mattress questions and made me feel genuinely valued as a customer. Both times I called, the man on the phone remembered not just my name but also my number, and he took great care of me. When I mistakenly decided against buying a box spring (why did I think I could manage without one?), they handled everything over the phone and arranged for a box spring to be delivered the same day—within just a few hours. What truly impressed me was that they even helped me set up a mattress I hadn’t purchased from them.

Their professionalism and friendliness are outstanding. I will gladly recommend them to anyone shopping for a mattress, especially students, since their student deals are excellent.

We rented a limo/bus for a bachelor party, but the whole experience turned into a disaster. Our driver, Scott, was completely clueless about navigating the city. Even though we gave him very clear directions, he kept making wrong turns and missing exits. Because of his incompetence, every stop took three to four times longer than expected, forcing us to skip some of our planned destinations.

After one stop, when we got back on the bus, Scott told us the police had boarded and searched the vehicle with dogs. We were stunned—why did this happen? How was it even allowed? Our bags had been thoroughly rummaged through, leaving us feeling violated and confused. At that point, we decided to call it a night. More than half of our group refused to get back on the bus and took cabs home instead.

Just when we thought the nightmare was over, it got worse. As we entered the highway, Scott drove the wrong way up the ramp and onto the highway! He then started slowly reversing down the ramp while cars honked and swerved around us. It was terrifying. After that, we were upset and just wanted to get home. Despite several more wrong turns, we finally made it back.

In short, it was an absolutely awful night. If you want a party bus with a driver who’s hopelessly lost, unwanted police searches, a near-death highway incident, and a whole lot of frustration and panic, then these are your people. Otherwise, I strongly advise you to stay far, far away!

Since there’s no Chinese delivery in Homestead, I decided to walk to the nearest Chinese restaurant near my home. The family running the place is very warm and welcoming. I even saw a Google review claiming the mom looks like she might want to cook you alive—don’t believe that!

On this visit, I ordered the Steamed Dumplings (a recommendation from a Google reviewer... what a fib) and the Vegetable Chow Fun. Usually, I enjoy steamed dumplings, but these were disappointing—too much wrapper and barely any filling. They’ll probably be sitting in my mini fridge tomorrow, and I’ll only eat them when I’m starving or have the munchies. The Vegetable Chow Fun, however, was incredibly tasty and definitely a must-have next time someone stops by.

Overall, it’s your typical Chinese takeout spot. *taps menu on the fridge*

Friday's is considered a "fine dining chain" by many Pittsburgh locals. We were seated surprisingly quickly, which caught me off guard since the place is often packed—I never quite understand the draw, but I appreciated the prompt seating. I ordered a blackberry "skinny margarita," which was a decent size, though at $6 each, it made up half of my entire food bill.

Our server began attentive but disappeared once the food arrived. I ordered a turkey burger with only lettuce, mustard, and a pickle on the side, plus loaded mashed potatoes—because I was feeling daring with my heartburn. When the meal came, the burger had only lettuce on it. The waitress was supposed to bring our next round of drinks but never returned, so I had to ask for my pickle myself.

The loaded mashed potatoes were a disappointment—rubbery instead of creamy, far from what I expected. After that, the waitress vanished completely and only came back to drop off the check.

I won’t be dining at Friday's again, though I might stop by if there’s a happy hour special.

A standout deep dish pizza should have a thick crust that’s crispy on the outside and soft inside, paired with a fiery, peppery sauce that can scorch your tongue, and a mix of toppings that slide down your chin as the bubbling pie melts in your mouth. Yet, I remain baffled by the draw of Pizzeria Uno. This place has done to deep dish pizza what McDonald's did to hamburgers, Pizza Hut to pan pizza, Domino’s to hand-tossed pizza, and Taco Bell to Tex-Mex—making it nearly inedible.

Our order included French onion, chicken bites, and a pizza topped with pepperoni, hamburger, and romano. Beyond the mediocre service and the fact that the food arrived undercooked and lukewarm, the quality was simply lacking. While this isn’t the worst pizza I’ve ever had, it perfectly illustrates what happens when a dish becomes so overprocessed, overanalyzed, and formulaic that it no longer resembles the original masterpiece that once delighted the palate.

I genuinely have no desire to return.

After reading other critiques, I approached this visit with tempered expectations typical of a chain restaurant: decent food at fair prices. It’s not a gourmet destination, but it meets basic standards.

We were greeted promptly upon arrival. While the hostess fetched menus, another server checked in to ensure we were being attended to. Service stayed consistently attentive, with drinks refilled promptly. I chose soup and two appetizers instead of a full entrée, and the server kindly asked how I wanted them served.

My fiancé ordered the deep-dish pizza. Although it took a bit longer, it arrived sooner than expected, and he really enjoyed it. I had the potato skins appetizer, which immediately brought to mind a “baked potato pizza” I loved in Buffalo. With a dash of hot sauce, it was excellent.

Would I trade this for the original Uno’s in Chicago? Absolutely not—nothing beats the authentic hometown experience. Still, for a reliable deep-dish fix without the cost of traveling, this place works well. It won’t become a regular in our dining rotation, but it’s a solid fallback when that deep-dish craving hits.

I was seated right away, which was definitely a plus, and enjoyed a solid selection of Pennsylvania craft beers. I ordered the classic deep dish pizza, making sure to specify no onions. Unfortunately, things went downhill after that. The waitress never offered another beer and just refilled my water instead. When my pizza arrived, it still had onions on it. I made it clear immediately that I didn’t blame the person who took my order—I know from my own years as a cook that mistakes happen since cooks don’t always catch every detail. The manager handled the situation by removing the pizza from my bill, which I appreciated. I still ate the pizza and thought it was tasty, just not with onions.

Regarding the bill, the server kept apologizing for the onion mistake and insisted she had told the kitchen not to add them. I reassured her it had already been taken care of and there was no need to worry. Then she mentioned that her birthday was the next day and hinted that if I wanted to leave all my money as a tip, it wouldn’t go unnoticed. I took it as a joke since I had told her earlier that I worked in the industry. When I handed over my gift card, she came back and repeated the request, adding that cash tips were preferred because she didn’t have to report them at night. She said again that if I left her all my money, she’d be “so freaking happy.” Let me be perfectly clear: no server anywhere should ever ask a guest for a tip—not once, let alone twice. Still, out of kindness, even though I felt I shouldn’t have, I left a generous tip based on the cost of the food I actually paid for.

In short, the food was good for the price, but the service from this particular server was just terrible. I can’t speak for the others, but my experience with her was very disappointing.

PF Chang’s has been a longtime favorite of mine in the Chicago area, so my wife and I have given this Pittsburgh location multiple chances. Unfortunately, over the past year, every visit has been plagued by the same frustrating problem: a 90- to 120-minute wait for dinner, no matter when we arrived. Whether early or late, the wait remained unchanged, and the front-of-house staff was consistently discourteous.

For a special date tonight, we made a reservation a week ahead. We showed up right on time, waited in line to check in, and were immediately handed a pager—without any clue about how long we’d have to wait.

Expecting a short delay, we stepped outside and waited inside a nearby store since the entrance was so crowded that waiting at the bar or in the limited seating was impossible. After 20 minutes, we returned only to find the staff still unable to provide an estimated seating time, despite several empty tables clearly in sight.

It’s baffling why they take reservations if they don’t intend to honor them. The food is decent but hardly remarkable. We ended up at a local Thai restaurant where we were seated within five minutes, enjoyed far better food, attentive service, and much more reasonable prices—even though it was just as busy.

We will definitely not be coming back to PF Chang’s.

I arrived at 8 pm on a Saturday, expecting about an hour’s wait, but we were seated in just 30 minutes, which was a nice surprise. We started with the lettuce wraps—something I used to enjoy but now find rather bland (for reference, I’m a big fan of the Cheesecake Factory’s version). I ordered the Singapore rice noodles, which were fairly average; I immediately thought Lu Lu Noodles and Asian Cafe do a better job. The fried rice was disappointing, and the vegetables tasted undercooked. On the plus side, the Dynamite shrimp was plump, juicy, tangy, and had a pleasant kick. The sweet and sour chicken was similar but missing that same spark.

The service was frustrating. Although we were there for less than 45 minutes, our waiter seemed eager to rush us out, repeatedly asking if he could clear my plate. I had to firmly tell him I’d let him know when I was finished. That felt rude, especially since there was no line waiting.

In the end, I think we’ll pick a different spot after a movie next time. The experience didn’t quite live up to my expectations.

There’s nothing fundamentally wrong with this place. The portions are generous, the food is adequate, and the atmosphere attempts to suggest fine dining. Yet, the flavors are surprisingly flat. Everything on P.F. Chang’s menu can be found elsewhere in Pittsburgh for less money, prepared with more precision and richer taste. Take the honey chicken—it was so uninspired that I kept thinking about heading over to Wai Wai in Bloomfield for a far better dish at just eight dollars.

Our last visit was marred by poor service. I’ve never felt so awkward in a restaurant. The server brought unsweetened tea to my girlfriend’s father, Don, then said he hadn’t brought sugar because Don had requested it sweetened. He didn’t seem to understand that Don could sweeten it himself and became visibly annoyed when Don kept asking for sugar, even seeming angry at us. When it was time to order, Don placed his and his wife’s order, but before Janey and I could speak, the server was already walking away. We had to call him back—not rudely, just to finish ordering. After that, he appeared to regard us as difficult diners, becoming silent and placing items down with passive-aggressive attitude. It was genuinely uncomfortable, and every time he approached, the conversation died.

Of course, one server’s bad mood doesn’t define the restaurant. But honestly, the food is just so bland! I’d recommend going elsewhere for Chinese food. Search Urbanspoon for local options—you’ll find plenty of great places with better flavors at half the price.

PF Chang’s features what I’d consider “elevated” Ameri-Chinese cuisine. If you’re looking for truly “authentic” Asian dishes, this isn’t the destination—most menu items have been adjusted for American preferences. Honestly, I’m fine with that. Do I know what “authentic” Chinese food tastes like? Somewhat, yes. And no, I won’t stop putting quotes around “everything” any time soon!

Our group of six arrived about 45 minutes before closing on a weeknight. We were seated right away, ordered, and ate without ever feeling rushed by the staff. At this Homestead Waterfront location, service was quick and friendly, although our server did forget our asparagus.

We sampled several dishes, including Szechuan shrimp, Mongolian beef, and Dan Dan Noodles. The flavors were enjoyable, but none really stood out. I don’t come to PF Chang’s often, but when I do, I always leave satisfied and full.

My boyfriend and I found ourselves at Dave & Busters, but we weren’t craving the American dishes all around us. So, I decided to give P.F. Chang’s a try. Since we arrived on a Saturday night without a reservation, we had to wait about 45 minutes. Fortunately, the wait went by quickly as I browsed Yelp reviews on my phone. Once we were seated, we ordered right away, and our server was genuinely friendly and welcoming.

We started with the salt and pepper calamari as an appetizer, followed by the Dan Dan noodles and Shanghai shrimp with garlic sauce. The food arrived swiftly, which was impressive given how busy the restaurant was. The calamari was only okay—I felt the strips were sliced too thin, and the portion could have been larger. In contrast, the Dan Dan noodles were bursting with flavor and very satisfying; I would definitely recommend them. The shrimp was cooked perfectly and tasted great too.

Overall, I was happy with my first experience at P.F. Chang’s and would consider returning whenever I’m in the mood for Chinese-American cuisine.

PFC stands out from the average non-franchise restaurant because of its presentation and overall atmosphere. Sadly, my visit was disappointing due to a clear lack of presentation.

Our party arrived about 15 minutes early for our 5:30 reservation, but by 6:11, we were told our table had been given to another group. This was an obvious mistake.

When we asked for silverware, the waitress blamed the hostess. While the hostess should have provided it, the waitress’s deflection felt unprofessional. As a customer, I don’t care who’s at fault—I just want the problem fixed. This definitely detracted from my experience at PFC.

Additionally, my hot and sour soup usually comes with those little "noodley" bits I like to add, but they were missing this time. I’m not trying to be difficult, but PFC is about more than just food—they’re selling an experience. And it’s that experience that makes the restaurant special.

We took a seat at the bar, where the female bartender clearly seemed unhappy. When we ordered drinks, she appeared irritated by the request. Over the course of an hour, she spent about 20 minutes texting and stepped out for three smoke breaks, leaving our drinks untouched. We also ordered appetizers, but they never arrived. Shockingly, she brought us the check before any food was served—even though we were the only customers at the bar. After paying, a busboy finally brought our food because we assumed our table was ready.

Once we were seated by the windows, the area was uncomfortably cold, so I wouldn’t recommend sitting there. We ordered dinner and drinks again, but once more, our drinks never came. When our food arrived, we asked about the drinks, and the waiter admitted he had forgotten them. No compensation was offered, and no manager was available.

PF Chang’s is in desperate need of new management. The food was the only bright spot, earning two stars, but the staff—from hostess to bartenders to servers—were all clearly miserable. We won’t be returning and suggest avoiding this place until major improvements are made. It’s simply not worth the frustration.

A colleague recommended this place to me, although I was initially hesitant due to some negative reviews I had read. Despite that, my first visit was quite positive. The reception staff were welcoming and helped me navigate the process of licensing my dog. The atmosphere felt warm and lively, with everyone seeming cheerful and engaged.

Dr. Bezak was genuinely kind and kept a smile on his face throughout the appointment. He quickly provided detailed information about my dog, which made the experience reassuring. Overall, I had a pleasant first visit and definitely plan to return.

The only reason I didn’t give a full five-star rating was the timing of my appointment at 12:15 pm. Since the staff takes their lunch break at 1 pm, there was a noticeable rush to finish the visit promptly. While I didn’t mind the brief appointment, I would have liked more time to ask questions. For a more relaxed consultation with the doctor, it’s best to schedule your appointment after their lunch break.

Target boasts a wide array of products, but it's important to be discerning and resist the temptation to buy everything simply for convenience. While their merchandise often looks attractive and is a good option for students, it generally doesn’t stand up to long-term use. For instance, the zipper on a skirt I purchased broke the very first time I wore it. I’ve also heard disturbing stories about comforters falling apart after just one wash.

On the plus side, their store-brand toiletries and miscellaneous items are quite affordable, and their selection exceeds that of Giant Eagle or CVS. They also offer a handy partnership with Flickr.com—allowing you to upload photos online, order prints through Target’s One-Hour Photo kiosk, and pay by credit card when you pick them up.

I especially love their inexpensive accessories—glasses, bags, and jewelry. Along with Claire’s and Filene’s, Target is one of my favorite places to shop for these kinds of items.

The service at this location is painfully slow. Every visit, we wait at least ten minutes before a server even acknowledges us. Since we live near the Waterfront, we’ve given this place multiple chances, hoping previous visits were just exceptions—perhaps due to new staff or other issues. Unfortunately, that’s never been the case. No matter when we arrive, we’re overlooked for several minutes, and when service finally arrives, it’s mediocre at best. Rarely, we experience excellent service, but those moments are few and far between.

Today was particularly frustrating. After sitting for fifteen minutes without any attention, I got up and found a server in another section, only to be told our table was in a “closed” area. The server kindly offered to help, but by then, we chose to leave. When I informed the hostess who seated us about the mix-up, she responded with a blank stare. I’ve never encountered this issue at any other EnP location.

We ended up driving to the Squirrel Hill branch, where our orders were taken in less time than we wasted waiting at the Waterfront. Management—you have a beautiful, prime location here. Please get your hosts and servers coordinated!

The cocktails here truly stand out—the Ketel One extra dirty blue cheese olive martini was exceptional. The atmosphere is also quite welcoming. However, when it comes to the food, I find myself placing this review in my “disappointing but hopeful” category.

Our server was warm and attentive throughout the meal. I did mention the gritty texture in the mashed potatoes. Trusting her recommendations, we ordered the appetizers, but unfortunately, they missed the mark.

The seared ahi tuna was a major disappointment. The flavors clashed badly with the seasoning and preparation, the tuna wasn’t properly chilled inside, the chips were uninspired, and there was no soy sauce—only wasabi. It simply didn’t work. I strongly urge the chef to compare this dish to Outback’s ahi tuna appetizer—there’s no contest. I hope the chef, who seems like a decent guy, takes this feedback seriously.

The BBQ shrimp was another letdown. For comparison, try Redstone’s buffalo shrimp appetizer in Philly—it’s served chilled and tastes fantastic. This BBQ shrimp, despite being recommended, was terrible. The barbecue sauce was overpowering and left an unpleasant aftertaste for both me and my client. It reminded me of a generic Gordon Food Service or Sysco BBQ sauce—a definite dish to avoid.

The cod entrée was just passable. The skillet beans were overly firm and mature; petite green beans would be a better choice. The potato skin again contained gritty mashed potatoes.

Why only one star? The prices were nearly as steep as Capital Grille, yet the cuisine falls far short. I genuinely hope they improve their food because the venue itself is quite nice.

Initially, I assumed this place would be another Red Lobster clone. But after asking a friend who was familiar with it—and actually liked it—I decided to give it a shot. Upon entering, I was pleasantly surprised by the warm, cozy, and unexpectedly upscale atmosphere that surpassed my expectations. The staff delivered excellent service, and the menu offered a wide variety of choices.

Prices were somewhat higher than I expected, with most entrees ranging from $17 to $30, but considering it’s seafood in Pittsburgh, that felt reasonable. We started with delicious sourdough bread, and I appreciated that the butter was perfectly soft.

Our meals arrived promptly. I ordered a seafood sampler featuring blackened tilapia, grilled sea scallops, and salmon cooked on a plank. The scallops were cooked to a typical doneness, though I prefer mine a bit more done. Everything else was tasty. My partner had the crab cakes and really enjoyed them.

We’ll likely return, though we plan to try different dishes next time. Overall, we had a good experience.

I attended a meeting with a large group and was given a private room where two servers efficiently and attentively took care of us—kudos to them. For starters, I had the crab dip and calamari, both quite good. The servers kindly brought extra chips with the dip as we needed them, though I’m always surprised more chips aren’t included from the beginning. The dip was flavorful, and the calamari was well-cooked. I preferred the shrimp cocktail sauce over the Asian-style soy sauce served alongside it.

The wedge salad with bleu cheese, however, was overloaded with cheese—far too much, even for a bleu cheese fan like me. For my main dish, I chose the blackened tuna with mashed potatoes and seasonal vegetables. Unfortunately, the carrots were barely cooked, dry sticks; the green beans were overdone, and the broccoli looked less than fresh. Simple green beans would have been a better choice. The tuna had the right blackening spices but lacked a good sear; it wasn’t overcooked, and the potatoes were as expected.

I also noticed other dishes like the fisherman’s platter, which looked greasy—typical for a fully fried meal—but it would be nice if a broiled option were offered. The crab cakes and filet appeared decent. Overall, I consistently leave feeling underwhelmed and overcharged. Maybe that’s typical for chain restaurants, but when I’m paying $25 for tuna that’s barely seared, I expect a lot more.

A definite highlight was being able to choose your fish and cooking style. I went with a trio of Jamaican jerk tilapia, salmon, and scallops. While all were flavorful, the scallops were smothered in too much sauce. My husband had the surf and turf special; the snow crab legs were tasty but smaller than I anticipated. I appreciated that raw oysters were available, but it was disappointing not to know their origin—especially at $2.50 each, that information should be provided. The staff were friendly and welcoming but clearly inexperienced with wine service—we even ended up showing two of them how to open a champagne bottle.

The outing was enjoyable overall, but I had two main complaints. First, when I used my phone’s flashlight to look for a floor outlet, I found a surprising amount of debris: crumbs, napkins stuck between the booth and wall, gum, and dirt. For the price, I expected a much cleaner setting. Second, our waiter kept saying “Thank you” after every sentence, often when it felt unnecessary. Though a minor annoyance, it became so frequent that it felt less like genuine politeness and more like a thinly veiled request for a tip.

Out of all the Dick’s locations I’ve been to, this one is the least impressive. The soccer gear selection is quite limited, likely reflecting the local community’s low interest in the sport. Most of the items available are basic youth equipment, which doesn’t serve adults or many older teens well. On the bright side, the staff is always friendly. Since it’s the closest store to our home, I visit frequently for running gear and apparel—though we often leave empty-handed because they simply don’t carry what we need. If you’re looking for fan merchandise for Pittsburgh teams, this store offers a fairly wide range. Still, overall, the inventory falls short of what I expect from a quality Dick’s location.

After months of searching for my very first road bike—and feeling quite overwhelmed by the process—I finally stopped by Big Bang. As a student with a limited budget, I didn’t expect much, but from the moment I walked in, I was warmly welcomed. I tend to be reserved when uncertain, yet the staff never pressured me or made me uncomfortable. Despite my modest price range, they genuinely worked hard to find a bike that fit me perfectly and offered me an *excellent* deal.

They paid close attention to ensuring the bike’s fit was just right, which I truly appreciated. What really set this shop apart was their enthusiastic encouragement of test rides—unlike other stores where it’s grudgingly allowed. They even said, “You haven’t tested it enough, go climb that hill on it!” Their priority is clearly matching the rider with the perfect bike, not rushing to close a sale.

I would wholeheartedly recommend Big Bang to anyone seeking a road bike, whether you’re a seasoned racer or a complete beginner like me.

Glen undoubtedly has a wealth of knowledge, but his style can feel overwhelming, sometimes even irritating and pushy. He can be quite helpful for the average customer, but if you visit his shop, it’s essential to come well-prepared. This isn’t a Walmart-style shop; the products are mid to high-end. I would recommend getting fitted and even buying a bike there, but the service side is a different matter entirely.

Same-day service is unheard of, even for simple adjustments, and there is no weekend service available. The first time I brought my bike in to have a rear derailleur hanger replaced and adjusted—I had already purchased the hanger myself—it took 11 days before I was contacted to pick it up. I assumed this was a one-off and gave them the benefit of the doubt.

Unfortunately, the second time was just as disappointing. I brought in a bike to have a damaged shift lever replaced with a new 7800 pair. After 9 days, I called and was told it would take two more days. When I arrived two days later, it still wasn’t done. It took another two days beyond that—13 days total. My advice: steer clear of their service department.

While exploring McKees Rocks, I came across Marge's Place. I hadn’t heard much about it before, but after reading a few reviews, I decided to give it a shot. Inside, the space was larger than I expected, yet it still had that warm, homey diner feel. Most of the customers seemed like regulars, and although the wait staff clearly knew them well, they welcomed me warmly as a newcomer.

I picked a corner table to take in what I imagined was a typical Sunday morning scene. I ordered the breakfast special: two scrambled eggs, bacon, potatoes, and toast. Any place serving Mancini’s Italian toast automatically earns points with me, and here in McKees Rocks, it felt like a natural choice. The potatoes were thinly sliced with onions and packed with flavor. Describing the bacon is tough—maybe “porkier” fits? I’m not sure if that’s a real word, but it captures the taste perfectly. The portions were generous, and all for under five dollars.

One small detail I appreciated was the tables and chairs. They were comfortable not only for sipping coffee and reading the paper but also for sitting down to eat. The spacing between table and chairs was just right. It might seem minor, but I’ve been to places where booths are either too cramped or too wide, and that can really affect the experience.

I’ll definitely return to Marge’s Place and recommend it to anyone nearby. It was a pleasantly surprising find, and I enjoy neighborhood spots like this where everyone feels like they belong.

I’ve ordered from this place twice, and neither time left me particularly impressed. Just to be clear, I haven’t tried their pizza yet. Their steak hoagie is decent—middling-good at best. It’s a pretty standard example of what you’d expect from a typical Pittsburgh pizza spot: nothing special, but not bad either.

The seafood calzone was a different story altogether. It had a bitter flavor that made it almost inedible. I suspect it was either the garlic or some burnt residue from the oven. Whatever it was, it was definitely unpleasant. The shrimp didn’t fare any better, carrying that distinct “iodine” taste that really put me off.

On the plus side, R&B stays open fairly late, which is convenient given their location. However, their phone service can be quite surly, and delivery always takes over an hour. That might be fine if I lived farther away, but I’m only a block from the place. Normally, I’d just walk over to pick up my order, but for the sake of fellow Yelpers, I endure the frustration of waiting on my couch for my food to arrive.

My fiancé, a friend, and I set out to try pizza from three different places, with Luigi’s included. Although I had driven past Luigi’s many times before, I never stopped in, so it stood out as a fresh option when searching for a new pizza spot in Bellevue. When I called to place my order, I was told it would be ready in about 15 minutes. However, when I arrived nearly 30 minutes later, I was immediately confused.

To the left was a spacious dining room packed with patrons, but I couldn’t quickly find where to pick up my pizza. After walking further inside, I finally realized the entire back section was designated for pickup. My pizza was ready, I paid promptly, and just as I was leaving, the cashier said, “Stay out of trouble.” I sincerely hope that was meant kindly and not based on my appearance or anything else.

The pizza itself had a medium-thick crust and a sauce that was surprisingly bland, despite visible green herbs mixed in. The cheese was mediocre at best, and the pizza had a faintly sour taste that I didn’t enjoy. Compared to the other two pizzas we sampled that night, this one was by far our least favorite, as shown by the fact that three-quarters of it remained uneaten.

In the end, I likely won’t return to Luigi’s. Between the somewhat odd experience inside (not unpleasant, just unusual) and the many superior pizza options nearby, I don’t see a reason to make another visit.

Luigi’s is a charming, family-run spot offering straightforward Italian dishes in a cozy, slightly kitschy setting decorated with red, white, and green accents. Soft Dino and Frankie tunes play in the background, creating a relaxed atmosphere. I’ve been several times for dinner with various friends, and the food has consistently been enjoyable and satisfying. It’s not fancy or pretentious—just a reliable place for a casual night out with pasta or lasagna, accompanied by a side salad, garlic bread, and good conversation.

Portions are generous, and prices are reasonable. While the flavors won’t amaze you or transport you straight to Sicily, they’re far from disappointing or reminiscent of mass-produced meals. Service is straightforward—neither unfriendly nor overly warm, simply adequate.

The crowd varies widely, from “Oh my gosh, I’m surrounded by hillbillies” to a local Mayberry-style gathering, which seems typical for many Pittsburgh spots. I haven’t tried the pizza, which reportedly gets rave reviews, mostly because I usually think of pizza as a delivery option when I’m too lazy to cook. However, I have sampled three or four pasta dishes, all served in hearty portions with a side salad and garlic toast. They taste satisfying, fill you up, and won’t break the bank.

For a neighborhood joint, that’s exactly what I want—a dependable, reasonably priced meal I can enjoy regularly in a cozy, no-frills environment. And that’s precisely what Luigi’s offers.

What a huge letdown. Since moving here, my large family has been excited to try the local food scene. Having sampled Chinese cuisine at numerous spots across a dozen cities, I can say this was easily the worst experience. The food arrived cold, tough, gelatinous, and completely flavorless—there’s just no other way to describe it. I won’t be ordering from here again.

The fact that I took time away from my kids to write this review shows just how bad it was. Sadly, my complaints were ignored. They seemed genuinely surprised that someone would liken their food to low-grade dog food. I understand that restaurants sometimes mess up—it happens. But when it does, you go out of your way to fix it. Not here. I was told the person I spoke with had to check with the owner before helping me. It felt like a way to pass the blame onto absent owners and leave me even more frustrated.

It’s unfortunate because we’ll be turning to a competitor from now on. This family of seven won’t be coming back to China Sea. And seriously, why isn’t there an option to give zero stars?

I ordered the General Tso tofu, one of my favorite dishes, while my husband went with the beef Mei Fun noodles. We also always add some egg rolls to our order. The woman on the phone wasn’t exactly rude, but she wasn’t very helpful either—she avoided directly answering several of my questions. My husband wanted to switch the sauce on his noodles, and I had to ask multiple times before she finally told me the size of the tofu dish. Still, I was in a good mood, so her attitude didn’t bother me. The prices were reasonable, typical for takeout. A plus is that they accept credit card payments over the phone, which is convenient if you don’t carry cash like me. She gave an estimated delivery time of 45 minutes.

Since we live just half a mile away, the food arrived in about 20 minutes. It was hot and smelled great. My husband’s Mei Fun looked fairly standard, but he was disappointed that they didn’t swap the white sauce for brown as he requested. The beef was mushy and lacked flavor. On the bright side, the vegetables were fresh and stayed crisp despite soaking in the sauce. The noodles were okay, nothing special. My General Tso tofu was excellent—exactly what I wanted. The tofu was fried perfectly, cut into perfect pieces, and coated in a fantastic sauce. The broccoli was fresh and tasty. This dish only comes in one size, which is quite large, so my husband and I shared it along with some mediocre egg rolls.

In short, the woman on the phone was a bit frustrating, but delivery was quick and the food fresh. Depending on what you order, the quality ranges from so-so to great. If you want a quick Chinese food fix, this place is a decent option, though I’ll probably stick with Uncle Chen before trying China Sea again.

Eager to try a new spot in my Brighton Heights neighborhood, I checked Yelp and chose Star Nails. The salon was bright and spotless, with modern, well-kept pedicure stations, and the staff greeted us warmly. Unfortunately, the good first impression didn’t last. My mom and I each picked a color and sat with our technicians. Mine was friendly and chatty but lacked attention to detail. I received no hand or arm massage, minimal shaping, and the polish was applied thickly and messily. Despite her efforts, the polish around my cuticles stayed untidy. Their method also seemed odd—both technicians had us dry our nails right after the first coat. When we left, my mom and I almost simultaneously agreed it was the worst manicure we’d ever had. At least the price was fair—$13 plus tip each. Maybe their other services are better, but next time I’ll be trying other nail salons nearby.

From the moment you step inside, this place makes you feel unwelcome. They advertise a variety of services, but when I asked, they snapped that they only do hair—it was uncomfortable and downright strange. After hearing warnings about getting my hair done there, I opted to use a gift certificate for a pedicure instead. That’s when I was told their employees only accept cash if they have to touch a client’s feet.

I might return just to get my bangs trimmed since I don’t want to waste the certificate entirely, but honestly, this place gives me the creeps. It feels dirty and offers absolutely terrible customer service. It’s clear they have no clue how to run a business, which explains why they’re struggling. Sue and Kristi keep passing the phone back and forth because no one wants to answer it. She even admitted the business is failing and needs more clients. I’ve never dealt with a ruder salon—or should I say, a deadbeat dive.

I was all set to become a new client with a 12:30 appointment, but when I arrived right on time, the place was locked, dark, and completely empty. I stood outside in the rain for five minutes, yet no one showed up. I called and left a voicemail, explaining that I was still willing to wait and understood if there had been some confusion. I asked them to call my cell, which I provided since I had initially given my home number when making the appointment.

After waiting nearby at a coffee shop, I returned five minutes later, only to find the place still locked and no call from them. I wasn’t guessing the time—I was carefully watching my phone to make sure I wasn’t calling or leaving too soon. Eventually, I gave up and moved on with my day. Later, when I got home, I found a voicemail on my HOME PHONE—despite my clear request not to be contacted there. The message said, “Oh hi. Sorry you missed me, but I was MAYBE two minutes late at the most. I hope you haven’t left, but you should just call back to reschedule.” Seriously?

While I was waiting, another woman showed up at the door. I assumed she worked there, but she was actually another client, also trying to get in! When I shared this story at another local business, the women there said I was probably the fourth person to have had this same experience at this place. I couldn’t believe it. This place is awful, and I haven’t even stepped inside!

I was desperate for a haircut and walked in hoping for a major trim and some reshaping of my layers. At the front desk, the girl mentioned my hair might be "challenging" to cut because of its length—it was almost long enough to sit on—and said I would probably have to stand while getting it cut. That seemed strange, but I accepted it. When I asked about donating my hair to "Locks of Love," no one there knew anything about it, which surprised me since I think salons should be familiar with such programs. Still, I went ahead with the cut because I needed it.

While waiting, I watched the two stylists at work. One told her client she was going to do something different than what they had originally planned because it "wasn't looking right," which felt off to me. The other stylist was so distracted by her phone, checking it every few seconds, that she yanked on her client’s hair with the comb hard enough to cause what looked like whiplash. At that point, I pretended to receive an urgent text, apologized, and quickly left the salon.

I have naturally curly type 3b hair that’s completely grey, which I dye dark and often experiment with myself—usually with mixed results. If you want a great haircut, ask someone with hair like mine. Since I started going to Mane Attractions about four years ago, I’ve genuinely loved my hair. Kristi even managed to shape my curls into a short reverse bob without making me look like I was wearing a helmet—any curly-haired person knows exactly what I mean! I’ve received nothing but compliments, and even my mom, who’s always brutally honest, is impressed.

The only downside is that sometimes I’ve dropped in spontaneously during the week, only to find the salon closed. Now, I make sure to call ahead and book an appointment. It’s a small business, and I totally get it. Plus, kids’ haircuts are just $10—my daughter absolutely loves going there!

Here’s how my visit went. The store is spacious and reasonably clean, and the parking lot is definitely convenient. Clothing racks are packed so tightly that moving hangers around is difficult. Whether this abundance is a plus or a drawback really depends on your taste, but for me, it was frustrating. The clothes are sorted only by type—like dresses or blouses—but not by size. In a store this big, the lack of size organization means you spend a lot of time just searching for what you want.

Even so, I’m always up for a bargain and don’t mind putting in some effort—that’s part of the fun for me. I spent about 30 to 45 minutes looking through the racks and picked out a few items to try on. Normally, I’d take my time and browse for hours, but I was trying to be considerate of a friend who isn’t as enthusiastic about thrift shopping. With my selections ready, I went to look for a fitting room and, to my surprise, discovered after asking the staff that there isn’t one. I was honestly stunned and found it hard to believe. I had planned to check out some household goods as well, but my disappointment was enough to make me leave early. While I can see how this might work for RWB, I personally think it’s unacceptable—especially since there’s no warning about the lack of fitting rooms before you spend all that time searching for clothes you can’t even try on.

I’d still recommend this store if you’re looking for specific secondhand items like dishes, older electronics, or beauty products. At one point, I saw a used Nikon SLR with a wide-angle lens for $200. But if you’re shopping for clothing, like a sundress, and aren’t comfortable trying things on in the open, you’ll need to be sure about your choices. RWB doesn’t offer returns or exchanges, so if something doesn’t fit, you’re out the money and the item.

This thrift store stands out in ways many others don’t. First, the lighting is excellent, letting you clearly inspect garments and spot any flaws, so you’re never caught off guard by what you bring home. The cleanliness is impressive too—there’s no unpleasant odor, which indicates everything has been thoroughly cleaned. The selection features quality brands like Ann Taylor and Kenneth Cole regularly. You’ll mostly find timeless pieces such as twinsets rather than flashy clubbing tops, which is a definite bonus if you’re over your early twenties. 

They also excel at discounts and keeping fresh stock flowing. The store is always busy, with daily specials that keep the inventory turning over quickly. Because the merchandise changes so often, it’s easy to get hooked—you never know what treasures you’ll find.

To give you an idea of what I’ve picked up: a $6 designer knit dress, several silk twinsets priced between $2 and $5, countless heels, two pairs each of Birkenstocks and Doc Martens for $4 to $8, a dressmaker’s bust for $5, and even a pressure cooker for $7. The prices aren’t quite rock bottom, but they’re close, and the quality more than makes up for paying a little extra. I can’t recommend this place enough!

The 3 1/2 hour drive from my hometown to this store was absolutely worth it. The biggest draw? EVERYTHING is always half off! Just a heads-up: bring cash, as credit cards are not accepted.

The store is packed with fantastic clothing, neatly arranged by color and style—though unfortunately not by size. I found an impressive range, from casual wear to upscale business attire, plus trendy teen fashions. What really stood out was the QUALITY; nearly every item was flawless.
