A few pieces showed signs of wear or fading, but their prices reflected that. The brand selection was abundant, including Banana Republic, Ralph Lauren, Chico's, Jones New York, Ann Taylor, American Eagle, and H&M. On top of that, there were some amazing vintage 80s finds with bright colors and bold shoulder pads—perfect for anyone with a daring fashion sense.

The clothes smelled fresh and clean, not musty or grimy like in some thrift stores. There was even a large, carefully curated section for plus-sized clothing. I went to Red White & Blue looking for business attire for my new job and came away with two stunning, flawless statement blazers from Ann Taylor Loft and Banana Republic—for just $7 total!

Trust me, once you shop here, all other stores will feel unnecessary!

Every day features a half-price deal that really helps stretch your budget. The used book selection is quite decent—though you’ll have to wade through plenty of self-help books and Patterson mass-market paperbacks, finding a T.C. Boyle for just two bucks is definitely a win.

In the home goods area, I’ve found large, solid wood picture frames for only a few dollars. The artwork inside was awful, so I tossed it, refinished the frames to my liking, cut new mats, and added fresh art. Getting each piece professionally framed at a big fabric store would have cost nearly $360, but I managed to do it all for under $30.

They also have a fair variety of lamps ready for rewiring, lots of furniture, occasional hidden gems in the clothing racks, and plenty of quirky items that make browsing fun. Keep in mind it’s CASH ONLY, and the cashiers can be somewhat rude or lazy—though that’s never bothered me.

As a bonus, they offer free donation pickups right from your porch. Just visit http://www.pickupplease.org/—it’s super easy.

This place is truly amazing—a thrift lover’s dream come true. Each visit yields something unique, making every trip memorable. I always plan my visits on days off because it’s easy to spend hours browsing without noticing the time. This isn’t a spot for a quick stop; it encourages you to take your time and explore thoroughly.

One important thing to remember: there are no fitting rooms. You’ll often find people trying on clothes right in the aisles, which is unavoidable given the mirrors placed throughout the store. It’s just part of the store’s distinctive atmosphere.

The selection is vast, covering everything from clothing and electronics to furniture, bedding, books, and movies. If you want it, chances are you’ll find it here.

Also, note that it’s cash only, though an ATM is available on-site for convenience.

Shopping here definitely comes with its challenges, mostly due to its popularity. Parking is difficult right from the start—there are only a few spots in front and two overflow lots that fill up quickly. Leaving can be frustrating, especially when heading back toward the city like I usually do. To reach the traffic light, you have to drive the wrong way through a narrow parking area, then cross three lanes on 51 without a traffic signal, which doesn’t feel very safe.

Inside, be ready for the weekend crowd. I’ve dealt with some aggressive shoppers who practically wield their carts as weapons. It’s irritating when people block entire aisles just to browse at their leisure.

A couple more things to keep in mind: there are no fitting rooms, so I usually try clothes on over what I’m already wearing in front of a mirror—typical thrift store practice. Also, they only accept cash.

Despite these drawbacks, I keep coming back every few months. I’ve found some fantastic treasures here, from dresses to plates. Every visit feels like a little adventure worth taking.

Their breakfast menu offers a wide variety, yet none of the specials combined eggs, meat, potatoes, and toast in one dish. I opted for the eggs, bacon, and toast special, adding a side of potatoes. The portions were fairly typical, except for the potatoes, which I genuinely enjoyed—they were deep fried and flavorful. My dining companion ordered the French toast with ham and was quite pleased.

Since we visited on a weekday morning, the restaurant wasn’t crowded, and the service was reliable. Although nothing about the meal was bad, my two-star rating sums it up well: "Meh, I’ve experienced better." With so many breakfast choices in Bellevue, this probably won’t be my first pick if I find myself back on Lincoln Avenue.

Having passed by this spot many times, I was genuinely excited to finally step inside. We arrived fairly early, which worked in our favor since a line quickly formed after we were seated. The Rusty Nail manages the wait smartly by keeping a sign-up list outside and offering coffee to enjoy while you wait.

For my entrée, I chose one of the daily specials—the Rusty Nail omelet. My girlfriend went with another special: a mushroom, spinach, and feta junior omelet. Hers was straightforward, while mine included salami, cheese, and three slices of pepperoni on top. The pepperoni was clearly superior to the usual cheap kind found on most pizzas, with a richer and more flavorful taste. Both omelets came with home fries and toast, and we both selected deli rye.

Her junior omelet was flavorful, with the tangy feta perfectly balancing the earthy mushrooms, and the spinach adding a fresh, wholesome note. My omelet was just as enjoyable—if not more so—thanks to the blend of cheese and meats that gave it a pizza-like character. Some of my hash browns were a bit overcooked and had more onions than I preferred, but they still made a decent side to the main dish.

Overall, I would definitely return here. Everything I tried was delicious, and I wouldn’t hesitate to bring friends for breakfast.

They completely shaved my dog’s fur, claiming it was matted and that they had no other choice. This simply isn’t true—I brush my dog every morning myself. When I expressed my concerns, the owner responded, “But we did inform you we’d cut the dog’s fur short.” While they did mention a short cut, I assumed it meant a lighter trim suitable for the hot August weather. I never expected them to shave my dog down to the skin.

To me, this reflects a troubling level of carelessness. They charged $70 for this rough, thoughtless job, yet failed to trim the dog’s ears and tail. As a result, the hair on the ears and tail looks disproportionately long compared to the rest of the coat.

I have been a customer of Animal Elegance for over ten years, well before the current management took over. Over time, I tolerated occasional dips in quality and paid their steep prices without complaint. However, this blatant neglect, along with their complete disregard for my loyalty as a longtime client, is unacceptable. I will not be returning and strongly advise others to reconsider before choosing this place.

What a disappointing choice. My companion and I began with two appetizers: greens & beans and "Italian frites." Despite the menu’s claim of "fresh cut, twice cooked, fresh herbs & roasted garlic," the frites were just ordinary french fries—mediocre at best and hardly worth the $6 price. The greens and beans were even more underwhelming: a small bowl of bland produce that cost an outrageous $8. That’s quite a steep profit margin!

For our main course, we shared a flatbread topped with goat cheese, caramelized onions, and roasted red pepper. It was decent, but my enjoyment quickly faded due to the FM radio blasting car commercials through the speakers. Who wants that kind of noise in a supposedly "upscale" restaurant? It felt completely out of place.

In short, I’d much rather wait 45 minutes for a table at Point Brugge than be seated right away at Pino’s.

Upon returning to Pino’s after their renovation, I was immediately struck by the beautifully transformed interior. Although we had reserved a table, it seemed unnecessary since only a few other parties were dining when we arrived.

My two girlfriends and I are notoriously indecisive when it comes to ordering, so naturally, we chose everything that caught our eye. We began with the Charcuterie platter, which offered a delightful combination of prosciutto, capicola, and soppressata, accompanied by vegetables and mozzarella. It was a fantastic way to kick off the meal.

The seasonal pumpkin ravioli was irresistible to the three of us—certified pumpkin lovers—so we shared an appetizer portion. This ravioli stood out for being distinctly pumpkin-forward compared to others I’ve tried. While tasty, we all agreed that a full order would have been too much, as the dish leaned heavily on sweet spices, and I personally wished for a bit more savory balance.

For my main course, I chose the grilled sausage pizza. It was enjoyable, though pizza rarely excites me, and this one didn’t change that—it was satisfying but not something I found myself craving later. Overall, I’d rate the food between a 3 and 4.

Where Pino’s truly excelled was in service. Our waiter was warm and knowledgeable, making us feel welcome throughout. When my friends ordered dessert, the chef—likely Chef Pino—came by to check on them. After my friend jokingly suggested the dessert would be perfect with some sauce, the chef promptly took both desserts back, added fresh strawberries and sauce, and declared he’d serve it that way going forward. That level of care was impressive; the service easily earns a 5.

As a final highlight, the beer selection was excellent, featuring several brews I hadn’t encountered before. I was especially excited to find East End Homewood Reserve on tap—a first for me—and it was delicious.

There were only two tables occupied, yet multiple staff members appeared repeatedly during our meal. Our waitress was polite and attentive, but that couldn’t make up for the disappointing food. The meal started with what I assume was meant to be focaccia, but it was just long, stale, flavorless pieces resembling bricks or bark.

The vegetable board was probably the highlight—fresh, vibrant vegetables cooked perfectly and served with two tasty sauces. Then came the octopus, which was cold and bland; the citrus completely masked its natural flavor.

The Tuscan wings were decent, mainly ordered for my husband, who seemed to enjoy them. However, the diver scallops were utterly inedible. They were severely overcooked, and the pea purée was so minty I couldn’t eat it. We sent the dish back, and although we didn’t expect anything, they took half the price off our bill.

After that, we chose to skip dessert and left. I doubt I’ll return.

Here’s the summary: overall, the experience was fairly average. We had a 7:15 reservation and were seated right on time, which was fine—except we were placed outside. Once the sun went down, it got quite cold. With only three tables outdoors, it seemed like an attempt to fit in extra guests. Our server was friendly but noticeably inattentive; we waited 10 to 20 minutes between each course. Being right on the sidewalk meant a steady stream of pedestrians, animals, and cars passing by. The waiter had to dodge foot traffic multiple times just to take our meal order, needing three tries due to constant interruptions.

The wine was enjoyable, but the food was disappointing. We ordered the mussel and clam appetizer, and about half of it was inedible. The innards had fallen into the sauce, which gave off a strong, unpleasant odor like stinky cheese. Dinner for both my husband and me was acceptable—no major complaints there. For dessert, we had espresso and a S’more cupcake. The bill came to $134 before tip, and frankly, it didn’t feel worth it.

The highlight of the evening? Leaving. The low point? Having this place forever tied to our anniversary.

We chose one dish from each course on the very limited Restaurant Week menu. I started with the baked eggplant caprese, moved on to the Lazy Man lasagna Florentine, and finished with panna cotta for dessert.

Unfortunately, the baked eggplant caprese was a disappointment—the breaded eggplant was soggy and unappealing. The Lazy Man lasagna Florentine was essentially two enormous lasagna noodles sandwiching a massive, three-inch-high pile of spinach, with a few mushrooms scattered in. The spinach overwhelmed the dish, and after just a few bites, I couldn’t continue. The panna cotta was the only item that was even somewhat acceptable.

My friend ordered from the regular menu, which she later advised against because her dishes arrived at different times—though we never understood why. She tried the Italian Fries appetizer, described as similar to the excellent fries at Point Brugge, but instead, we were served a bowl of plain French fries that were bland and misleading. Her house soup with chickpeas looked like Spaghetti-O’s and tasted even worse.

I honestly can’t figure out where all the glowing reviews come from. Nothing we ate was impressive; everything was overpriced and well below average. I wasted my money and will never go back.

In hindsight, I definitely should have checked the reviews here first, as many others have shared the same frustrations I encountered. When my mother returned her steak for being heavily oversalted, the chef came out to “apologize,” but instead of a genuine apology, he humiliated her by criticizing her for not enjoying the dish. As he walked away, he sarcastically remarked that he would “never salt his steak again.” It was completely inappropriate for him to speak so disrespectfully to my mother, who was polite about sending the meal back and certainly didn’t deserve such attitude.

We had an event to attend, which we clearly communicated to our waitress. When my mother reordered a salad, it took an additional twenty minutes to arrive, so she asked for it to be wrapped up immediately. Then the chef reappeared, deliberately chewing to make a point, sneering that the steak she refused to eat was actually quite good. I have never felt more mortified. When I confronted him about his rudeness toward my mother, a paying customer, he defensively insisted it wasn’t his responsibility to please people. He added that everyone else seemed to enjoy their meals and that we just needed to get to the center of the steak to appreciate it.

The ordeal didn’t end there. The chef claimed he didn’t have change for a $100 bill on a $57 tab. Seriously—how do you not have $33 in change? To top it all off, he ended the night by tossing our crumpled bill onto the floor and walking away.

Overall, it was an utterly embarrassing experience for anyone witnessing it. I highly recommend taking the negative feedback on this site seriously—I certainly wish I had.

After waiting thirty minutes, my meal finally arrived, and we were told my friend’s dish would be served shortly. The whole situation felt quite uncomfortable. The salad was unimpressive—the beets had a canned taste, and the chicken was soaked in a dark, oily residue that seemed to come from a burnt pan.

Things took a turn for the worse when the chef came out to confront a customer who had returned her food. He openly humiliated her, insisting her returned steak was perfectly fine and even bragging that he was enjoying it himself. Watching him eat from a customer’s plate was a major turn-off—one can only wonder what else might be going on behind the scenes.

The awkwardness continued when it was time to pay. The chef didn’t have change for a $100 bill given by the woman who returned her steak. It was uncomfortable to watch the elderly customer and her young companion struggle with the situation. The chef loudly demanded she pay by credit card, which she didn’t have. Thankfully, another patron stepped in to provide change while the chef crumpled up the check. Honestly, I would have just walked out without paying. I truly admire that woman for tolerating such absurd behavior.

In short, if you want below-average food and a chef who loses his temper, this is definitely the place for you!

After my visit last night, I have no intention of ever returning. Although I don’t know the owner, Joe, personally, he stopped by our table several times, complimenting the presentation by saying the dish looked beautiful. He seemed very confident in his cooking, which would be great if the food consistently matched that confidence—usually, it does.

At the table next to us sat a mother and daughter. The mother asked the server for a replacement steak because hers was too salty—something I haven’t experienced myself as a vegetarian, but my guests have often noted the excessive salt. The server apologized and went back to the kitchen. Then the owner came out and gave what felt like a fake apology, insisting his steaks are perfect. The entire restaurant was listening—it was unbelievable. The strangest moment came when he returned again, saying, “I really enjoyed the steak you sent back,” while actually chewing it! I couldn’t make this up.

Everyone clearly felt sorry for the mother and daughter caught in that awkward situation. The owner became so unpleasant that the daughter tried to reason with him, only for him to snap, “It’s not my job to make people happy.” That’s odd, considering he clearly wants our business. When the mother tried to pay the bill with a $100 bill and leave, he claimed they couldn’t make change. Eventually, another customer stepped in to help with the change, and they left.

I was so angry I couldn’t finish my meal. Maybe Joe was having a bad day, but there’s no excuse for how he treated those customers. Sorry, but we will never step foot in this place again.

Honestly, that’s pretty much the only benefit this place offers! While you can usually find what you need, it also means facing huge crowds no matter when you shop. This store is nothing like the experience at Macy’s or Boscov’s—it’s just a large, impersonal chain focused solely on function. Giving it five stars is difficult because it lacks anything beyond basic utility.

You’d think a store like this could manage crowds more effectively. Waiting half an hour just to grab one item is ridiculous. That’s exactly what happened to me yesterday. I would have been better off going to Cogo’s or 7-11—maybe paying a bit more, but definitely getting in and out within five minutes. I definitely prefer the Giant Eagle in Squirrel Hill.

The moment you step inside, it hits you like a sharp blow to the head, leaving you confused and disoriented throughout your visit. The store’s layout is completely illogical. Who wants to start by wandering through the freezer section, then squeeze through a cramped passage at the end of an aisle, only to find the meat department hidden away in a corner? They could have easily removed a wall to make access simpler instead of forcing this awkward detour. The aisles feel excessively long, clearly a result of trying to make the most of the limited space. It’s the kind of place where, halfway down an aisle, you realize it’s just as far to the end as it is back to the start—and you seriously consider giving up and sitting down because it feels like you’ve been walking forever. Honestly, the only reason I shopped here was because I was already at Target and didn’t want to go anywhere else to finish my shopping.

As soon as you walk in, you’re ready to leave. This Giant Eagle is not the place for a full grocery run—prices are high, and the selection is lacking. If you need more than the basics, you’ll end up having to visit another store, which is inconvenient.

Produce here is often subpar. Unlike the fresh, fragrant selection at the Giant Eagle Market District nearby, the Shakespeare location regularly has fruits and vegetables that are wrinkled, blemished, moldy, and sometimes even attracting fruit flies, all while charging premium prices. Trader Joe’s consistently offers better quality produce for less.

The self-checkout setup is another hassle. There are two express lanes for fewer than 12 items and one belt lane for larger orders, but customers typically form a single, lengthy line that slows everything down. Staff rarely step in to organize the process.

Customer service is mediocre, and I don’t expect it to improve. I only come here when I need one or two things in a hurry. The best times to shop are early in the morning or late at night, when it’s less crowded.

Unfortunately, with Kelly, Melissa, and Jen unavailable, I had to settle for whoever was free—and it ended up being the worst haircut I’ve ever had. The stylist cut off more than an inch beyond just the dead or split ends. Despite my initial explanation and repeated instructions during the cut, she ignored my requests, cutting straight across instead of curving the back as I asked—something that does not suit my curly hair at all. When I tried to clarify again, she dismissed my concerns by comparing my frustration to coping with the deaths of family and friends, telling me to just get over it.

The long, beautiful layers I once had and hoped to restore are now choppy, uneven medium layers. The left side is especially more jagged than the right, and I’m worried I’ll have to straighten my hair just to hide the unevenness. I regret tipping her because, although I understand the service industry, my usual 20% minimum tip was not earned by such poor work.

I want to stress that the only competent stylists there were Kelly (now relocated to Philly), Melissa, and Jen. If they aren’t available, I strongly advise against taking the risk. Also, the Supercuts in Oakland is terrible at eyebrow waxing unless you’re lucky enough to get the only woman of color working there.

Although the cut was only $20 (plus the 20% tip), I ended up buying biotin to help my hair grow faster, which made the overall cost higher for me. I hope this review helps anyone considering this salon!

We've ordered takeout from this place multiple times because it's nearby. While nothing we've tried has been bad, nothing has really stood out either. Our top picks so far are the General Tso's tofu and the Moo Shu vegetables. Unfortunately, the eggplant was soggy and unappealing. Portions are generous, but even dishes marked as spicy on the menu don’t deliver much heat.

The prices are budget-friendly, making it an affordable choice for decent food. They don’t offer drinks. The atmosphere is typical for a Chinese takeout spot, with photos of every dish lining the walls. It’s located in a plaza next to Pizza Parma, which is convenient for that part of Shadyside.

The staff speak limited English but usually understand your order without much trouble. Food is generally ready for pickup within 10 to 15 minutes.

On the plus side, there’s a wide variety of options, low prices, and quick service. On the downside, the food isn’t particularly memorable. Would I go back? Only if I’m feeling too lazy or on a tight budget to try elsewhere.

Before diving into the details, I’ll admit the food was somewhat tough—especially the eggroll, as I had been warned. The rice had some dark spots, which I assume came from the bottom of the cooking pot. That said, I partly blame myself since I mistakenly thought they closed half an hour later and ordered about 10 minutes before closing. So, Tasty, I’m willing to forgive the rice this time.

I went with a vegetable eggroll ($1.50) and General Tso’s tofu ($8.25)—a guilty indulgence I’ve come to accept. I asked for the General Tso’s extra spicy, but it definitely lacked heat. The tofu was served in large chunks, which seems to be my unlucky trend lately. I prefer more surface area and don’t want to struggle cutting my food with chopsticks. On the plus side, the sauce was flavorful enough to make me want to order here again.

As for the eggroll, it was tough. It tasted good but was small and chewy, so it likely won’t be part of my future orders. However, with the $10 minimum, I need to add something alongside my tofu. Hopefully, the soup will be better.

The woman behind the counter was friendly and courteous on the phone and never mentioned they were about to close when I placed my order. The portion size was ample, and for the $10.44 I spent, I’m confident I’ll have enough left over for lunch.

I didn’t come in with high hopes, so the place met my expectations exactly. The best way I can describe their food is like a cafeteria-style pasta meal you might have had as a kid at summer camp. It was entirely edible but incredibly bland—nothing I’d be excited to pay for. There was nothing off-putting, just very uninspiring. I only tried the pasta, bread, salad, soup, and calamari, so maybe their pizza is better, but judging by what I had, that seems unlikely. On the plus side, the staff were friendly, and even at peak dinner time, plenty of tables were empty. If you’re hungry, you’ll definitely leave feeling full.

One morning, I found a note on my windshield letting me know I’d been the victim of a hit-and-run. The damage was minor, and after reporting it to my insurance company, they directed me here. Almost immediately after I ended the call, Mike’s called to schedule an appointment for an estimate. I picked a time that worked for me and carried on with my day.

When I arrived for the vehicle inspection, the process was refreshingly simple. My wait was short, the staff were polite and professional, and I didn’t feel like I was being misled or given the runaround. Within about five minutes of assessing my car, I was on my way back home.

They haven’t done any repairs yet because the police are still investigating the person who hit my vehicle. But if it comes to that, I’m confident they’ll handle everything with honesty and skill. Based on their customer service alone, I believe their bodywork is among the best in the city.

Yes, this isn’t the most upscale neighborhood, but honestly, that doesn’t bother me.

I used the Geico express service for my vehicle repairs, booking both the estimate and repair online for the next day. When I dropped off my car, the staff was ready and expecting me. The check-in took less than 30 minutes, and every employee I met was personable and genuinely attentive to my situation. The damage was minor, and the repairs were completed in under 48 hours. Since my policy included rental car coverage, Enterprise was conveniently on-site during check-in, making the rental process quick and effortless. Picking up my repaired vehicle was just as smooth and welcoming. While dealing with an accident is naturally stressful, inconvenient, and costly, Mike’s Auto Body turned the repair process into a notably positive experience. I sincerely hope more businesses treat their customers with the same dedication and professionalism that Mike’s Auto Body showed me.

From start to finish, the adoption experience was characterized by warmth and genuine enthusiasm from the staff. Shortly after bringing my dog home, a volunteer reached out via email to see how we were adjusting. Several months later, it became clear that my dog was struggling with significant anxiety and behavioral issues—problems the shelter understandably could not have identified while the dog was in their care.

When I asked for help, the shelter went above and beyond to support me. My dog and I attended two behavioral training sessions, during which Lacey’s dedication never faltered. We also consulted with veterinary professionals, and I consistently received emails from the shelter offering helpful advice and checking in on our progress. Over time, I learned to manage my dog’s behaviors, and my bond with him grew stronger.

Even nine months later, the shelter continues to stay in touch, offering guidance and asking about my dog’s well-being. I fully recommend adopting from this shelter. While my dog represents a particularly challenging case, the shelter is committed to ensuring your satisfaction with the adoption and will do everything possible to support both you and your pet. Their staff truly care about the welfare of both animals and their new owners.

He was clearly in distress, and after much anguish, we concluded that euthanasia was the most compassionate option. When we arrived at the ARL, we asked the receptionist if there were any alternatives. Her reply was cold and indifferent: "Well, basically the only thing you can do is sign him over for euthanasia." We were devastated. She then told us to wait by a door, saying someone would meet us there. After a few minutes, another woman came out, took the carrier, and said, "I'll bring your carrier back out in a minute." We declined, telling her to keep it, and she accepted, taking our cat to the back. That was the end of it. No comforting words, no sympathy, no offer to give us a moment to say goodbye, no apology—nothing at all. For us, this was one of the most painful days we've ever faced, yet no one at the ARL showed any sign of care or even made an effort to appear empathetic. They earn a few stars for providing a necessary service, but beyond that, this place only added to the heartbreak of an already terrible day through their complete lack of compassion.

My husband and I stopped by this CVS a couple of times to pick up prescriptions, and from the moment we arrived, the experience felt off. Parking is in a lot behind the store, which isn’t easily visible from the front. Since it’s a pharmacy, there are no back doors or windows facing that lot, creating an oddly isolated and somewhat unsafe feeling.

Inside, the store’s atmosphere clearly reflects its location in a rough neighborhood. The shelves are only about 4’6” tall, likely so staff can keep a close watch on customers. Strangely, common items like regular shampoo brands were locked behind clear cabinets. As someone who’s passionate about nail polish, I noticed the beauty section was seriously outdated, with products from past seasons and many polishes scattered and disorganized. Overall, the store felt cramped, with merchandise jammed onto shelves that seemed too short and inadequate for the inventory.

If you have the time and gas, I’d suggest heading to the CVS on Center Avenue, about a mile away, or the Walgreens at Penn Circle South and Trade Street, or even the Rite Aid at Baum and Negley—both within half a mile.

I’m not particularly fond of this place; convenience is really the only reason I keep coming back. Their greeting card selection is quite disappointing—I honestly can’t recall ever finding a decent card here. Every holiday or birthday, I give it another try, but each section is just full of duds. What frustrates me even more is that many items, like razor blades and, surprisingly, body wash, are locked behind panels that require an employee to unlock. Yes, body wash! Having to ask someone to open that shelf every time drives me crazy—it just doesn’t make any sense.

The staff’s friendliness is hit-or-miss. Some are cheerful and welcoming, while others seem like they’d rather you leave. On the bright side, I really appreciate their coupon rewards. I know it’s a CVS-wide thing, but those coupons keep me coming back since I snag good deals almost every other visit. I also had a positive experience getting a walk-in flu shot from the pharmacy—the pharmacist was friendly and quite attractive, which was a nice bonus.

All in all, the vibe here isn’t great. The locked merchandise and the small, somewhat uninspiring store layout make it feel a bit depressing. I’d prefer to shop at other pharmacies, but for me, this one wins out on convenience. Plus, they do have a parking lot, which could be a helpful perk for some.

Rockwel Realty insists on performing repairs strictly according to their own schedule and repeatedly refuses to give advance notice before entering your apartment, despite multiple requests. When I asked them to clean mildew, they used bleach but carelessly spilled it on my sheets, ruining them. After reporting both the damage and the mildew’s return, they blamed me for not turning up the heat and insisted that tenants must accept any damage caused during service, offering no solution. Instead of properly insulating the unit to prevent mildew, their response was for me to clean it myself.

In addition, the entire building experiences serious electrical issues that require lights to be replaced twice a month. Rather than making permanent repairs, management focuses on continuous construction to expand the aging building, seemingly prioritizing increased rent revenue over tenant comfort.

It took me much longer than it should have to warm up to Tazza D’Oro, mostly because a bad ex of mine was obsessed with the place and that definitely put me off for a while. Looking back, I really regret all the time I avoided it. The dark wood inside creates a comforting, cozy atmosphere, and the small outdoor tables are perfect for enjoying the summer weather.

Tazza D’Oro serves Batdorf and Bronson beans, which are excellent, and offers Enrico pastries, free Wi-Fi, and a staff that’s both incredibly friendly and highly skilled. Everyone working there is not just nice—they’re also really good at what they do.

Their menu, though small, features local and fresh options that always look great, though I haven’t tried any of the food yet. What I can say is their espresso consistently beats what I’ve had at Batdorf and Bronson locations in Olympia, WA. I mentioned this to a barista at Tazza D’Oro, and they seemed a little offended, telling me, “We calibrate our machines the same, use the same beans, blends, and milk—it shouldn’t be any different.” Still, Tazza D’Oro comes out ahead.

Weekend mornings can get busy, but the lines move quickly. Located just off Highland Park’s main street, between Bryant Street and the reservoir, Tazza D’Oro feels like a true community hub. It’s where you pick up your CSA, where weekly bike rides begin, and where discussion groups meet almost every day. There aren’t many students here. Like the rest of Pittsburgh, you’re bound to see someone you know, but here, I usually run into people I actually like and miss, which is a nice change from my usual experiences in the city.

The espresso here is undeniably the best I’ve ever had, even outshining those I enjoyed on my limited trips to Italy. Each shot is robust, velvety, and intense, never sour or bitter. While subtle nuances shift slightly with each pour and the weather, the quality remains consistently excellent.

The coffee itself is outstanding, made from Batdorf & Bronson beans—the finest I’ve found for grinding at home. They also offer a tempting variety of pastries and cookies, along with a wide selection of flavorful sandwiches served with a satisfying side salad.

Their tea selection is just as impressive. Though I’m no expert and don’t know their tea sources, every one of the half-dozen blends I’ve tried has been memorably rich and flavorful.

Beyond the drinks and food, Tazza D’Oro is a wonderful community space. Whether you come with a laptop, a book, or a friend, you can comfortably stay for hours. There’s no rush to leave, and there almost always seems to be room for studying or conversation.

Enrico's Tazza D'oro Cafe stands out as a fantastic spot, and I truly appreciate its location in Highland Park. The early morning crowd was both friendly and diverse. During our visit, my girlfriend and I unexpectedly ran into a friend, which led to a pleasant conversation. We ordered lattes that were excellent, and the interior had a warm, inviting atmosphere. While the pastry selection was somewhat limited, the choices looked quite appealing. I did wish there was more outdoor seating, as the current amount felt rather sparse.

Finding coffee shops that earn a spot on my “I’m a fan” list isn’t easy, but I plan to return here and might revise my opinion in the future.

On a different note, regarding Highland Park, I want to join others in expressing disappointment over the recent hit and run involving two cyclists. Accidents, no matter how tragic, do happen, so my frustration isn’t with the accident itself. What’s truly appalling is the decision to flee and leave those seriously injured by the roadside. To whoever is responsible, I hope you dedicate yourself to making amends for this awful act. It’s never too late to change.

What I genuinely appreciated was the cappuccino—it was flawless, topped with a charming foam leaf that truly enhanced the experience. That said, here’s where I ran into a problem: sometimes I like my cappuccino plain; other times, I prefer adding a shot of syrup. This time, I asked for amaretto syrup, which they did have. However, the barista responded firmly with a “No, you can’t.” He explained that their cappuccinos are only served plain, and if I wanted something sweet, he could make a special drink—but I’d have to trust his judgment.

The issue is, I’m not into overly sweet drinks—I don’t have much of a sweet tooth. I just wanted a subtle touch of sweetness, so trusting an unknown concoction didn’t appeal to me. In the end, I settled for a plain cappuccino.

I’m not a fan of coffee shop elitism, and this barista seemed to assume I was a Starbucks-loving yuppie who needed a lesson on what a “REAL” cappuccino tastes like. For context, I’ve lived in Italy and have enjoyed authentic cappuccinos. But at that moment, I simply wanted a flavor shot in mine. I still tipped because I wasn’t sure if this was the barista’s personal attitude or a store policy, and he did offer to make me something different. Still, it baffles me why they offer flavor syrups if you’re not “allowed” to add them to your drink.

The cappuccino itself unquestionably deserves five stars—but I docked one due to the attitude.

Oh, and did I mention I left my water bottle behind during my ride? By the time I finished, I was genuinely parched. Once I got home and cooled off, I headed to Enrico’s, motivated by a Yelp review praising their iced caffe mocha as the best. Parking was easy right out front, and I liked that the café is tucked away in a quiet neighborhood rather than on a busy, noisy street. Inside, the tables provided plenty of space to work, with people on laptops enjoying the free Wi-Fi, while outside, groups of friends chatted around the tables.

So, why just 3 stars? The iced caffe mocha didn’t quite deliver. The syrup had all settled at the bottom, leaving my first few sips watery and lacking flavor. It definitely needed a better mix. Would I try it again? Yes—next time, I’ll be sure to ask for a strong shake before taking a sip.

That said, my favorite iced coffee spot remains the café at Walnut Mall in Shadyside. If you’re shopping Shady-style, you’ve got to try their iced or blended Ghirardelli mocha—it’s truly AWESOME!

La Prima Espresso ranks at the top of my favorite spots in town. The coffee is fantastic, and the baristas skillfully combine warmth with expertise. Sam, the owner, is almost always around, welcoming both regulars and newcomers with genuine hospitality. For me, the perfect Saturday morning involves savoring a dopio (double) cappuccino alongside a slice of pizza from Colangelo’s next door.

What truly distinguishes this café is its lively energy. On Saturdays, the place buzzes with activity as guests fill the indoor space and spill out onto the outdoor patio. Above the coffee machines in the upper left corner, a television remains tuned to REI, the Italian channel, often airing a futbol match or Italian news. In another corner, elderly Italian men are frequently seen engrossed in a classic card game.

If you’re seeking expertly crafted coffee paired with the authentic atmosphere of a genuine Italian café, La Prima Espresso is unmatched.

The club was fairly empty, with mostly young men in attendance. I had a funny encounter when a guy got confused in the ladies' room—there were no "men" or "women" signs, only Greek symbols indicating the entrances. The vibe was lively yet relaxed, and the crowd was friendly and easy-going. Drinks were pricey, and since I handle alcohol well, my "date" gladly paid extra to get me my birthday buzz. The DJ played techno, with a Lady Gaga track every fourth song—no joke! That night also featured a male stripper who performed twice, stripping down to his provocative underwear. While it’s not the best spot to pick up a date, it’s great for dancing and having fun. As a proud ally of the LGBTQ+ community, my stance is firm—so please, no hate mail. Thanks!

Would I return? Absolutely! And I’m definitely thankful to have these insider tips now.

Before the event, they offer food that all looked quite appealing, with prices that seemed reasonable. Drinks are available both at the front bar and through table service. However, once the show starts, table service ends. So if you want a drink later during the performance, you’ll need to plan ahead or get up and head to the bar yourself.

Seating comes in two styles: tables and rows. I found the tables quite comfortable and enjoyed the raised platform area, although the chairs there lacked armrests, unlike the floor seats. Next time, I’d probably opt for the raised bar tables on either side.

After the show, they circulate the checks. To avoid a long wait, it’s wise to request your check early—before the show—or bring cash.

I’m giving four stars instead of five because the will call staff was genuinely rude. I thought I had won multiple free tickets, but at will call, only one was available. When I inquired, the staff member was unhelpful. I ended up buying another ticket at a different table since she refused to transfer my complimentary ticket. Lesson learned: avoid the will call window.

Buon Giorno’s menu features three daily specials—usually a salad, sandwich, and pasta—alongside their regular offerings. While the food is generally dependable, it rarely makes a lasting impression. Many of the sandwiches and pastas, especially those with ricotta, feel somewhat bland. Instead of mixing ricotta with a sharper, saltier cheese as is typical in lasagna or stuffed pastas, they simply spoon it over penne with marinara, resulting in an uninspired dish.

On the positive side, their Italian tuna salad (the mayo-free kind) and wedding soup truly stand out. Each salad and soup comes with a few slices of Manini’s bread, which never disappoints. Sandwiches are served with a side of risotto—usually spinach, portabello mushroom, or spinach and feta. The spinach and feta risotto is so addictive that my coworkers have nicknamed it “crack rice” because you can’t get enough.

Breakfast is another strong point at Buon Giorno, with their breakfast sandwiches and frittatas delivering genuine flavor. Overall, the small plates and sides shine, while the main entrees tend to be just average. For a downtown cafe open only during breakfast and lunch, this level of quality is sufficient. However, if you’re looking for an exceptional Italian meal, Buon Giorno may fall short of your expectations.

Whether I’m in the mood for a quick snack or a more relaxed meal, Buon Giorno Cafe is my preferred lunch spot. They also serve breakfast, and if you’re searching for a more flavorful egg, meat, and cheese sandwich than what Dunkin’ or McDonald’s typically offer, this place truly hits the mark.

What I value most is the swift service—food arrives promptly, respecting the constraints of a busy schedule. During the weekday lunch rush, the cafe is especially bustling. Their signature dishes are the salads and sandwiches, known for their inventive Italian and Greek influences, often featuring feta or red peppers in almost every item.

A personal favorite is the pasta de la Sandra—a penne pasta with mushrooms, sausage, and peppers in a balsamic glaze that’s simply delicious. I also enjoy their Italian soup and the turkey, feta, hummus, and pepper sandwich served alongside risotto.

If you’re seeking fresh, flavorful meals at reasonable prices with attentive service, Buon Giorno Cafe is an excellent choice for your next lunch break!

Finding this place was such a relief—a genuine little piece of home! They stock essential Chinese vegetables, snacks, and frozen foods that are rarely available in typical grocery stores. They also offer dried Chinese herbs, the kind your mom or grandma would traditionally add to soups. While some of the pre-packaged Chinese vegetables look impressively fresh, a few fruits and other veggies don’t seem as fresh, so I usually avoid those.

That said, I missed the usual tofu varieties found at Ranch 99, and common produce like tomatoes, carrots, or bell peppers weren’t stocked. Fresh meat was also absent.

Here’s what I ended up buying: dried fish, miso, lily bulb, bok choy, baby napa cabbage, cilantro, green onion, garlic, shiitake mushrooms, rice, a couple of bags of frozen dumplings, shao bing, frozen lotus buns, frozen Shanghai veggie buns, soba noodles, mochi, red bean pancakes, hoisin sauce, soy sauce, soybeans, jasmine tea, and some canned goods. The total came to about $70.

This spacious market is carefully organized, making it easy to find what you need quickly. The fresh tofu is the standout item—it tastes noticeably better than typical store-bought varieties and is incredibly affordable at just $1 for three pieces, roughly equivalent to one and a half blocks of packaged tofu. Their extensive selection of Asian-style noodles, snacks, and sauces includes brands rarely found in regular supermarkets. Additionally, their fresh produce section offers unique items that are hard to come by elsewhere.

Keep in mind that many products don’t have English labels. This doesn’t mean beginners aren’t welcome, but expect some trial and error as you browse. The staff is often less helpful, mainly because the team is small, busy, and many employees have limited English skills. This lean staffing helps keep prices low, so a little patience is appreciated. Since this is a traditional Asian grocery, English isn’t the primary language, so communication challenges are to be expected.

I don’t see these aspects as drawbacks because the store perfectly fits my needs. It’s not intended for those seeking a guided introduction to Asian cuisine. But if you know what you want or are willing to explore and learn through experience, this place is definitely worth visiting.

Visiting the lovely LuLu was a real eye-opener, especially when it came to a charming vintage dress I’d purchased in Chicago last summer. The dress was too loose in all the wrong places, and I had kept putting off getting it altered. Even a seamstress friend was confused by the chest darts and unsure how to fix it properly.

At LuLu’s, she had me try the dress on, made a few simple markings, and I was ready to move forward. She suggested shortening the dress slightly, which I hesitated over at first, but after she pinned it up, I decided to go for it. Although she initially said it would take about a week, she called just a day or two later to say it was finished.

I have to say, LuLu truly knows her craft! She worked wonders on that dress, making it fit like a dream—it looked absolutely stunning. On closer inspection, I could see she had completely taken apart the bodice to reshape it for my chest, all while preserving the dress’s original style so the alteration was subtle and seamless.

Convinced by a salesman’s promise of a lifetime warranty, I spent nearly $300 on a suitcase that usually sells for about $100. He looked me squarely in the eye and assured me the company would always stand behind my purchase or replace it if necessary. With a charming smile and engaging manner, he spent 10 to 15 minutes entertaining me while extolling the craftsmanship and quality of their bags.

However, those assurances proved hollow. The suitcase deteriorated just like any typical bag you’d find elsewhere—only here, I paid extra because of their inflated “service” fees. When I returned with the “lifetime warranty” bag—now suffering from broken wheels and a zipper coming loose—he met me with a cold stare and accused me of having a “convenient” memory. He even laughed at the suggestion that he had ever promised a lifetime warranty.

I told him I was insulted by his misrepresentation of the bag’s quality and the excessive price I paid for such a substandard product. His response was a mere 10% discount on another suitcase, coupled with his claim that he was the one insulted. Stores like this are staffed by slick salespeople who twist the truth to push overpriced products that don’t justify the steep premiums they charge.

Matthew and his team continually impress us with their commitment to helping customers find exactly what they need every time we visit. They’re always straightforward if something isn’t in stock, and will make every effort to special order it—though, to be honest, if it’s not in their inventory, it probably doesn’t exist elsewhere. We’ve purchased a range of luggage and countless accessories over the years, and each one has been of excellent quality. When repairs have been necessary, the staff have managed them quickly and with genuine warmth, always giving us the benefit of the doubt if there was any question about warranty coverage. The prices are fair, and the customer service easily outshines anything you’d get from shopping online. Even browsing is enjoyable; we’ve come across plenty of useful products we never realized we needed and have been consistently happy with every purchase. Thanks to their wide selection, this store has become our top choice for holiday gifts.

For our lunch outing, a colleague who consistently raves about Madonna chose the new location, hyping the spices, flavors, and service. Unfortunately, only the service lived up to the expectations. Even during the busy lunch rush, the staff stayed friendly and efficient. I went with the chico chicken quesadilla, which cost $4.81 with tax and was fairly large. However, it contained just Monterrey jack cheese, chicken, and a soft tortilla—no spices, onions, or peppers at all. While it was passable for the price, I’m nearly certain the chicken was canned; I recognized it from when I’ve used the same canned chicken in quiches during hectic moments. It’s decent canned chicken, but seriously—c’mon! My lunchmates also thought their burritos were bland. I’m giving three stars because I believe Madonna’s can and will improve. And a quick note: it’s CASH ONLY!

This establishment has been around forever, which might explain why it often gets overlooked—I’m definitely guilty of that myself. It had been quite a while since I last dined here. The maroon bar stools, yellow walls, wood paneling, red drop-down ceiling, and green floor tiles create a setting that feels like a glimpse into another era. The menu stays true to the classics: beef sandwiches and beer, alongside longtime favorites like the Cobb Salad and Devonshire Sandwich.

Last night, I stopped by with some coworkers to celebrate a birthday. As I mentioned, it had been some time since my previous visit, and since I don’t drink, I can’t comment on the alcoholic beverages. However, everyone else seemed to be thoroughly enjoying their drinks. The atmosphere still carries that vintage charm that makes this place special. I’m definitely planning to return next week for lunch.

I'm glad to say the service here has improved compared to what some have experienced before—a definite plus. I visit a couple of times each month, mainly because of their Gas Crisis lunch menu. Their sandwiches consistently feature fresh ingredients and generous servings of meat and cheese. The fries always come hot and never soggy, although I usually prefer shoestring fries over their thicker-cut variety.

For ten dollars (tip included), I enjoyed a grilled cheese with bacon, a double order of fries, and a drink. I was in and out within about 35 minutes, which suited me well since I planned to take a walk afterward. The service was decent—not rude or dismissive, but they also don’t go out of their way to be overly friendly or attentive.

Overall, if you’re looking for a quick, solid meal at a fair price, this place is definitely worth considering.

The main appeal of this greasy spoon is its undeniable convenience. Would I go out of my way more than three blocks for it? Probably not. But would I take an elevator down and dash across the street in the middle of winter—without a coat—for it? Absolutely.

I’ve sampled every salad variation they offer, and each one stands as a dependable choice. They’re quite accommodating when it comes to adding or skipping ingredients, so don’t hesitate to ask. (If they truly wanted my input, I could write an entire dissertation on how to improve their salad options.)

On tough workdays when a salad simply won’t suffice, their hamburgers come through. They often mention having won an award—though none of the waitresses seem to know which one exactly. Still, no exaggeration: the burger and fries are excellent. There’s none of the flashy hype that new burger joints bring, but this is a genuinely solid burger.

The decor borders on shabby, but under the right dim lighting, it’s perfectly acceptable. After all, it’s a diner. The wait staff is a group of surly, no-nonsense women with about an 85% accuracy rate, but I like them. They mean well and always keep my Diet Coke glass filled to the brim.

Vintage tables, shelves, and hutches overflow with vibrant ferns and cacti—some prickly, others velvety—inviting you to touch and explore. Terrariums, filled with miniature worlds, seem to beckon you in, as if you could embark on a Tiny Alice adventure. As you move through the space, natural marvels greet you at every turn. The walls, adorned with wreaths and accents, offer a blend of bold colors and subtle elegance, creating a visually captivating atmosphere.

A glass-topped case catches your eye, packed with enormous jars of potpourri that tempt you to scoop generously and imagine your home filled with its heavenly fragrance. Passing this display, you come upon an open doorway that leads to a secluded garden, where lush greenery draws you outside. The gentle tinkling of wind chimes and the soothing murmur of water enhance the enchanting mood, and the plants themselves look as though they belong beneath the glass domes of Phipps Conservatory.

This shop is a true sanctuary, a welcome refuge from the constant bustle of the Strip. Roxanne, your work is outstanding. Thank you.

What could have been a dull wait becomes genuinely enjoyable when standing in line with Andy. His portions are impressively generous, offering exceptional value—two large pieces of toro for only $5 is almost unheard of. On top of that, he even included a third piece at no extra charge. While the presentation isn’t particularly polished—Andy’s knife skills aren’t the sharpest—he has to move quickly to keep the line flowing. Honestly, if you're grabbing sushi at a stand inside Wholey’s, sophisticated plating isn’t what you’re expecting.

His special sauce, with a sriracha-like heat, adds a nice flavor—just be sure to mention if you’d prefer your fish without it. I do think he uses a bit too much rice on the nigiri; halving it would improve the balance. Still, given the location next to Primanti’s in Pittsburgh, this style makes sense.

All in all, the value is unbeatable, and Andy is genuinely a wonderful person. I will definitely be back. Beyond his generosity with the fish, his kindness truly shines—today, for instance, he paused service to help a little girl find her mother.

Since Andy’s sushi stand is tucked away inside Wholeys, reviewing this place can be a bit challenging. Nonetheless, I can’t help but give him five shining stars for his outstanding sushi—prepared fresh right in front of you—and his memorable personality. Honestly, I’ve yet to meet anyone who doesn’t find Andy to be utterly charming.

When I worked on the Strip, this spot became my almost daily lunch refuge. After just two visits, Andy had memorized my go-to order and would start making it as soon as he saw me: spicy yellowtail with avocado. Sometimes it was simply yellowtail and avocado, maybe with a hint of cucumber. I have to admit, I’m obsessed with yellowtail—the buttery texture and delicate ocean flavor are utterly addictive. I could rave about yellowtail endlessly, though I know this isn’t a review solely dedicated to a single fish—despite Andy’s yellowtail being truly exceptional.

In addition to his classic offerings, Andy enjoys experimenting with new flavor combinations, often blending ingredients for customers to sample while they wait. I’ll never forget the maki roll he created—salmon, basil, cucumber, and mango—a brilliantly inventive fusion.

Wholeys itself is an excellent spot for people-watching, and it’s always amusing to see a diverse crowd of all ages and backgrounds walk in and shout, “ANDY!”

Lately, I’ve completely lost interest in ordering his sushi because, honestly, it doesn’t live up to the hype. It finally hit me: yes, the rolls are massive, but they seriously lack flavor. He rushes through making them so quickly that the moment you try to pick one up with chopsticks, it falls apart. The fish—the most essential element—doesn’t taste fresh at all, which is surprising given he’s supposedly in a prime area for fresh seafood. It’s nowhere near as fresh as the sushi you find on Penn Ave.

What really gets to me is that strange brown sauce he slathers on everything. Ugh, I just can’t stand it. I know I could ask to have it left off, but by the time I remember, it’s already been spread on again.

Sure, it might be cheap and fast, but to me, it’s just not worth it. Penn Ave is right down the street, and trust me, their sushi is fresh and delicious—you won’t regret going there!

When the weather turns sour, I usually head down to the Strip to avoid crowds, so long lines aren’t much of an issue. During our latest visit, while waiting for customers, Andy kindly offered us a freshly made spring roll to sample. The rolls here are notably large—some pieces have taken me two or even three bites to finish, which is bigger than what you typically find at other takeout sushi spots.

I often choose his specials because they highlight flavor combinations you rarely encounter at typical sushi places. For instance, I had never tried basil in sushi before, but it truly enhanced the roll’s flavor. Andy’s is a reliable spot for grabbing affordable sushi on the go. Everything I’ve tasted has been excellent, although the menu does include some unconventional options. If you’re a traditional sushi purist, this might not be the perfect place for you.

Sushi Kim makes a strong impression by offering both sushi and Korean cuisine, catering to American tastes and helping to overcome the general unfamiliarity with Korean food outside prominent Korean neighborhoods. Their name is clear and direct—they’re unmistakably and proudly Korean.

I’ve tried Korean BBQ on the upper level and sampled Korean dishes downstairs. While I wouldn’t travel from CMU just for their sushi, since there are plenty of other places for that, I would definitely make the trip for their Korean fare. Although people may have different opinions, my friends from Seoul believe Sushi Kim serves the best Korean food in Pittsburgh, at least by local standards. Prices are higher than Korea Garden, yet the atmosphere is a bit more upscale.

The soju selection stands out for Pittsburgh, with brands like Charm, Cheoeum cheo reom, and Jinro Chamisul—Chamisul is my personal favorite. Sushi Kim also offers Korean noraebang, which requires advance booking at $30 per hour. Only Korean songs are available, so reading Korean is necessary. As far as I know, it’s the only Korean noraebang in the city, though I haven’t tried it and can’t comment on the song selection.

The BBQ is a solid deal; while it’s not the best I’ve tasted, it may be the only Korean BBQ grill restaurant in town. The staff are attentive and quick to swap out the grills. I’d prefer a different sahm-jang and more variety in the non-BBQ buffet options. The BBQ setup is great for groups, with each grill seating four people.

This Korean-run restaurant features an extensive menu of both Korean and Japanese offerings. When we first arrived, the outside looked empty and uninviting, but inside was a different story: the dining area was open and energetic, with every table sporting mini barbecue grills and bento boxes. Although I had my doubts about the food quality, I decided to join my friends and ordered the 10-piece mixed nigiri set, a bowl of miso soup, and mango sorbet for dessert, which came to $41 including tax and tip.

The nigiri—specifically the sake, ikura, and uni—were fine, but not especially fresh or memorable. My miso soup was far too salty, and while the mango sorbet came as a generous double scoop, it didn’t stand out. Thanks to the wide-ranging menu and plenty of seating, the restaurant could work well for larger gatherings. Still, as someone from California who’s used to exceptional Asian cuisine, I found the sushi underwhelming considering the cost.

Here’s how I broke down my experience on a 1 to 5-star scale:

1) Quality and freshness: 3 stars – acceptable, but no excitement or wow factor.  
2) Creativity and presentation: 3 stars – generous portions and well-presented plates.  
3) Quantity and substance: 2.5 stars – flavors were mild, unremarkable, but still passable.  
4) Accessibility and affordability: 2 stars – expensive for what you get.  
5) Service and ambiance: 4 stars – service was sometimes inattentive, though the atmosphere was festive and clean.

In the end, I give this restaurant 3 stars, but without much enthusiasm. I won’t be coming back.

This restaurant offers plenty of seating, making it a dependable choice for groups. When my friend and I visited on a Friday evening, only about seven tables were occupied, so we ended up sitting alone at the sushi bar.

We came specifically craving sushi and rolls. In Pittsburgh, no place seems to truly specialize in rolls, and among the sushi spots near Shadyside and Oakland, this one appeared to have the largest variety (please let me know if you’re aware of any others nearby with a bigger selection!). We ordered a 12-piece combination sushi platter, Kim’s favorite roll—which actually felt like two separate rolls totaling 16 pieces—and a spider roll.

While the sushi and rolls were reasonably portioned, the fish was clearly not fresh. The spider roll was one of the most unappealing rolls I’ve had in quite some time. The soft shell crab was fried beyond recognition, making it tough to chew, with the crunching noise painfully echoing in my head.

We also shared a soon doo boo, served with a bowl of rice and a few small plates of banchan. The soon doo boo was passable, packed with tofu, but the banchan was disappointing—broccoli, weak kimchi, and bean sprouts.

Unfortunately, the bill was far too steep for a typical sushi dinner. After tax and tip, we each paid about $35. Although the service was friendly, I doubt I’ll be returning.

The kids clearly enjoyed the miso soup and edamame, both of which were promptly refilled when requested, while the sushi selections seemed to suit their tastes. Since I’m not particularly fond of Japanese cuisine, I stuck with the Korean dishes—after all, this is a Korean restaurant! I opted for the Mandu Guk, a satisfying bowl filled with meat dumplings and broth. My daughter chose the pork bulgogi, which she liked, although we’ve definitely had better. The pork was overly greasy and lacked the fire-grilled char marks, making the meat less flavorful.

Sushi Kim tends to be inconsistent. Occasionally, you receive a generous assortment of panchan (pickled or marinated vegetable side dishes), but other times it’s only kimchi—what’s going on with that? Judging by the clientele, I rarely see many Koreans dining here, which raises questions about its authenticity. The restaurant is spacious and roomy, yet overall, the experience leaves something to be desired.

When we arrived, we were warmly greeted and seated at a cozy corner table. The attentive staff quickly brought us water and green tea before we ordered. The menu offered a mix of Japanese and Korean dishes, so we decided to try a variety. My brother picked the Korean beef, my dad and sister shared a sushi platter, and my mom and I both chose beef bulogi.

Portion sizes were moderate—not the large American-style servings I expected. My brother liked his beef, although it came without rice. My dad and sister described the sushi as average, and while the beef bulogi was filling, I’ve had more flavorful versions elsewhere.

With entrees priced under $12 and the sushi platter around $15, the lunch prices seemed reasonable. Overall, if you’re on Penn Ave, this place is a fair option, though I’m curious to compare it with other Japanese and Korean restaurants in the area.

A quick heads-up: the BBQ option is only offered on weekends. Even with reservations, our visit started off rough when we arrived and were told a larger party had already booked the upstairs BBQ area, so they couldn’t seat us there. After some back-and-forth, they finally found us a table, and our experience began.

Having tried Korean BBQ in New York and San Francisco, I have to say this place fell short of those standards. The kimchi selection was limited to just pickled cabbage, missing the variety of flavorful kimchi plates I’m used to. If you’re looking for a good assortment of vegetables, this isn’t the place. The menu includes marinated bulgogi, kalbi, pork, chicken, and seafood options like calamari and shrimp. The chicken was truly flavorful, but the rest of the dishes were somewhat disappointing. One friend even joked that Trader Joe’s bulgogi tastes better than what we had here.

If you decide to visit, be sure to share the cooking duties with your tablemates. The communal aspect is where the real fun happens, especially when dining with friends. While the food didn’t impress me, we all had a great time and genuinely enjoyed ourselves. Just don’t expect this to be a standout culinary adventure.

After dining at Sushi Kim multiple times, I've started to think its reputation mostly hails from when it was nearly the only sushi spot in town. Just to be clear, this review only covers their sushi dinners—I haven’t tried their lunch menu or Korean dishes.

Each visit follows a familiar routine. The restaurant is nearly empty when I arrive, and while the service is attentive, it feels somewhat detached, as if guests are simply another task to complete.

The miso soup comes out first and is flavorful but consistently arrives cooler than it should be—almost cold, in fact. Unfortunately, this seems to be the norm here.

The biggest disappointment is the sushi itself. Although the prices are typical for sushi, the quality falls short. The sushi is served slightly too warm and lacks the freshness one would expect, especially given the raw fish involved. This is hard to overlook. Every variety I’ve tried has been equally underwhelming, ranging from “meh” to downright unappetizing.

With so many sushi options now available in Pittsburgh—even supermarket sushi from Giant Eagle in a pinch—I see little reason to return. After several visits driven by the restaurant’s reputation and hope for improvement, I’ve decided my latest trip to Sushi Kim will be my last.

Frankly, the food delivered to us was completely inedible. My husband and I ordered a selection of sushi for dinner, hoping to enjoy some tasty leftovers the next day. We spent about $60 on various rolls, expecting a satisfying meal. Instead, the presentation was disappointing: soggy nori that looked pre-made, unnaturally bright pink ginger drenched in MSG, and rice so sticky it formed a clumpy mass with no visible grains. The worst part, however, was the smell. When we lifted the tray lid, a strong, foul stench of spoiled fish hit us both—I actually gagged.

We sat there stunned, realizing we had wasted money on what was essentially a pile of rotten food. Reluctant to waste it all, I picked up a spider roll to inspect it more closely—and found a large hair tangled around the crab. Absolutely revolting. Meanwhile, my husband tried the inari, expecting plain tofu and rice, but it tasted like spoiled fish, having absorbed the putrid odor from the other rolls.

We had also ordered a vegetable and tofu soup, along with a green salad dressed with ginger. Shockingly, the salad leaves were brown and slimy at the edges—they somehow managed to ruin a simple green salad. The soup tasted metallic and burnt, as if cooked in an aluminum pot. It was all just dreadful. In the end, we discarded everything down the garbage disposal—a complete waste.

We tried calling to complain, but the restaurant was closed by the time our order arrived. We plan to call again today to request a refund. If they do the right thing and reimburse us, perhaps they’ll earn an additional star.

I’ve been to this place only a few times, and honestly, it doesn’t leave a strong impression. The ambiance feels a bit outdated and rather dim. One important piece of advice: avoid drinking the water. A friend of mine said it upset his stomach, and since Pittsburgh’s tap water isn’t known for its quality, I’ll be bringing my own bottle next time.

On my first visit with a friend, we sampled the kalbi and mandu. The dishes were decent but nothing exceptional. Although I’ve heard the kalbi is one of the better options, I’m not comfortable eating with my hands.

During my second visit, another friend introduced me to soondubu, a spicy tofu soup. I chose the vegetable-only version, while my friend went with the regular. Traditionally, soondubu contains vegetables and shellfish, but my friend was a bit disappointed since the regular had only shrimp. For me, the vegetable soondubu was just right—especially on a cold winter day, that spicy soup really hit the spot! It definitely makes me want to return.

I’ve also heard the BBQ dinner here is quite good!

I was genuinely excited to find a sushi spot within walking distance of my Pittsburgh apartment. That enthusiasm quickly faded, though, when I arrived on a Monday evening around 7 pm and realized I was the only patron in a surprisingly spacious restaurant.

Still, my craving for sushi kept me there. I ordered the Spicy Tuna and Salmon rolls, which arrived astonishingly fast—both within two minutes. While that seemed unusual, perhaps the chef was simply very efficient. Unfortunately, the rolls fell apart the moment I glanced at them, and the salmon tasted off. I ended up leaving it untouched on my plate, something I’ve never done before.

On the brighter side, the miso soup was acceptable, and the service was quite attentive—understandably so when you’re the sole customer. Since Pittsburgh has limited Korean dining options, I’d suggest trying the Korean BBQ, especially since Kim’s Korean dishes have fairly good Yelp reviews. But when it comes to the sushi here, I’d recommend skipping it.

Sushi Kim greets guests with a bright, immaculate setting and seating on both floors. The Korean BBQ buffet is set up upstairs and only operates on Friday and Saturday evenings from 5 p.m. onward. The staff throughout my visit were warm, attentive, and genuinely helpful, which made the meal all the more pleasant.

At the buffet, diners select raw proteins and vegetables from the stations and then grill them at their tables on hot plates. This interactive, self-serve format adds energy and engagement to the experience, which I truly enjoyed. Although the choices for proteins weren’t extensive, each option was flavorful—ranging from mussels and shrimp to pork, chicken, and beef. The bulgogi beef especially stood out for me.

However, a few things detracted from the experience. Butter or oil was not provided for grilling, and while I understand the health-conscious reasoning, the lack of grease meant food burned easily. Butter or oil should definitely be available. The hot plates themselves weren’t ideal either; the actual cooking surface was too small, which slowed down the grilling process a lot. I was also disappointed that there was no dessert bar. After all that grilled food, I really wanted something sweet and refreshing, but Sushi Kim didn’t offer any dessert options. Considering the $24 per person price, the addition of a dessert bar would make the meal feel much more complete.

Even with these drawbacks, I’m thankful Sushi Kim exists in Pittsburgh. As the only Korean BBQ buffet locally, it deserves recognition. I had a great experience overall and would happily recommend the Korean BBQ buffet—just keep in mind the higher price and budget accordingly.

Given the mixed reviews, I was a bit hesitant to try Sushi Kim, but my craving for BulGogi and my friend’s interest in sushi convinced us to go. I’ve only visited for lunch—not dinner—and there’s always plenty of seating during midday, which may actually be the best time to come. We went with the lunch specials: a sushi sampler, spicy pork BulGogi, and shrimp dumplings as an appetizer. The dumplings didn’t really win me over, but the pork was excellent—tender and well-seasoned—and the sushi offered a fresh and satisfying assortment. My friend chose green tea ice cream, and after sampling it, I found it quite enjoyable. We each had a glass of wine, and including tip, the bill came to about $50, which felt reasonable. The menu is pretty extensive, and I think what you order can really shape your experience. Personally, I’ve always enjoyed their BulGogi, Korean Pancake, Hot Pots, and sushi. Service was attentive, though arriving for a quiet late lunch probably made things easier. All in all, the food was tasty, the service reliable, and the price fair.

This theater truly stands out, infusing our local arts scene with a distinctive energy. Its programming mainly features plays, with the occasional musical, creating a thoughtful balance between innovative new works and beloved classics. For instance, they premiered The Chief—a creative production about Pittsburgh Steelers founder Art Rooney—alongside timeless favorites like A Midsummer Night’s Dream and The Importance of Being Earnest. They also regularly introduce fresh Broadway hits such as The Rabbit Hole and Superior Donuts. Every year, they host performances by Second City—a comedy troupe I greatly admire, especially since several of its alumni have gone on to become SNL stars.

I especially value their “in the round” theater layout, where the audience surrounds three sides of the stage. This setup fosters inventive staging, as seen when they built a real pool for Metamorphoses. My favorite production so far was the world premiere of The Secret Letters of Jackie and Marilyn, a captivating story imagining a correspondence between these two legendary women—a concept that truly ignited my imagination.

Beyond performances, the theater offers lively events like Mix at 6, designed for young professionals before shows. They understand that many of us under 26—and sometimes older—are budget-conscious, so they keep ticket prices affordable at just $15. And the best part? There’s not a bad seat in the entire house.

With such an exceptional theater district nearby, I highly recommend taking the opportunity to experience this gem—you won’t regret it!

It’s genuinely disheartening to see the City Paper fade away, replaced by a weekly filled mostly with ads, a few music reviews, and a lone restaurant critique. I deeply miss the days when In Pittsburgh and The City Paper fiercely competed for readers.

Where has the incisive, thought-provoking journalism gone—the kind that challenged readers and carried real weight? Has the editor lost his passion or grown complacent, abandoning that once-bold liberal spirit? Or have all the ambitious reporters left for New York City to join The Village Voice, a true alternative paper with a larger audience than the Times?

In a vibrant college town like Pittsburgh, a legitimate alternative weekly should cover college sports, local and national politics, pop culture, the music scene, technology, finances, and more. Instead, we get one uninspired weekly piece—lacking investigative rigor, nothing that would unsettle local politicians or catch the Post Gazette’s attention. Mostly, it’s feel-good fluff meant to avoid legal trouble.

Although I’m no fan of Mark Madden, his contributions to the City Paper were edgy, eye-opening, and generally accurate. The City Paper urgently needs fresh energy. It’s 2010—time to bring in hungrier reporters with meaningful stories to tell.

After biking along the north shore trail, I brought my boyfriend here without mentioning the negative reviews because I was eager to enjoy the river view. The scenery and atmosphere were still quite pleasant, but both of us were ultimately disappointed by the food and service. We each ordered the beer-battered cod sandwich—I convinced him to keep it simple after reading the poor feedback about the menu. While he liked his sandwich, I found the batter doughy and undercooked, and the tartar sauce had an unpleasant grainy texture; honestly, even a Giant Eagle brand tartar sauce would have been better. Our dissatisfaction wasn’t unique—a woman behind us was complaining that her meal wasn’t cooked properly and was asking for a refund. The beers were bottled and cold, which was a plus, but the service left much to be desired. We were rushed to pick our drinks and meals and then given barely any time to pay. Given all the reviews, I expected the staff to have improved by now. Overall, I’d return only for the beers and the nice riverside seating but would definitely eat somewhere else first.

I truly want to like this place and keep giving it chances, hoping it will finally impress me—but it never does. It’s like dating someone who’s stunningly attractive but utterly clueless; a good vibe can only stretch your patience so far.

One year, I took my dad here for his birthday. Normally, I don’t insult people, but our waitress was so hopelessly inept that we actually felt sorry for her. That’s the only reason we didn’t completely lose our cool. She forgot my dad’s order entirely. She served mine without noticing he was sitting there with no food. The manager came over and comped our drinks, but that barely helped since we had only managed to order one round in an hour—the waitress stopped by our table just twice. Then, when my dad’s steak finally arrived, she dropped it (I really did feel bad for her), and apparently, that was their last steak. So we paid and left for Eat n Park.

The second time I returned, the service was just as awful. To make matters worse, it was late summer, and our table was literally swarmed by wasps. Seriously, wasps everywhere, and my friend even got stung.

On another occasion, I made a reservation for a friend’s 30th birthday. They told me they don’t take reservations but could arrange tables together. When we showed up, it was as if I had never called.

My last visit was okay, but after the wasp attack, my friend and I chose to sit on the patio and only ordered burgers.

The service here really sucks. Being attacked by bees and then waiting forever for the server to bring ice (holding a cold beer bottle on the sting helps, by the way) just adds insult to injury. Honestly, this place isn’t worth the hassle.

That said, the atmosphere is fantastic! When your waitress finally shows up, just order a bunch of bottled beers, and you should be fine.

Redfin’s outdoor patio offers a stunning view of Washington’s Landing Marina, making it a frequent choice for us before heading out on the water—my parents’ boat is docked just below. Unfortunately, the service is consistently slow, even during the predictable weekend rush. You would expect better preparation for the Friday and Saturday evening crowds. Although we often wait quite a while, the welcoming outdoor ambiance helps make the delay more tolerable.
