The food is fairly average—nothing especially memorable, but not disappointing either. I mainly recommend this spot to marina visitors or anyone looking for a pleasant outdoor dining experience. Just be sure to allow plenty of time!

We arrived full of anticipation and were greeted by the host, who mentioned a 20-minute wait for cocktails—a wait list that, as it turned out, never existed. After thirty minutes of watching four parties who arrived after us being seated, I reminded the host that we were still waiting and was then directed to the bar. Another twenty minutes passed, during which two more parties were seated—one even seated themselves—so I approached a blonde woman who was seating guests and clearing tables to inform her we wanted to be removed from the “list.” Her response? “What list?” with no apology offered. No effort was made to help us find food or to make up for the inconvenience. Ironically, this entire fiasco led us to discover a new spot we now frequent. So, thanks for completely screwing it up.

Having grown up in a sunny coastal country and spent several years in California, I get a bit of that familiar vibe from this place. However, the restaurant’s atmosphere comes across as rather hectic; even with only a handful of patrons, the staff seem rushed. For instance, we ordered a dish that the menu said would be served with potato salad, but it came with fries instead. We also overheard nearby diners expressing frustration about their mixed-up orders.

While the food isn’t especially remarkable, it’s not disappointing either. I’m interested in trying more menu items and plan to visit again during the summer. However, I really think the owner should reconsider the management, since this spot has genuine potential to become a gold mine.

Not long ago, I joined a family member who had recently relocated to Pittsburgh’s North Shore for a visit to Redfin Blues. Although the restaurant isn’t new, it definitely comes alive when the weather is pleasant. On a lovely Sunday evening around 7 PM, the place was buzzing, but we only waited about 15 minutes for a table. During that time, we relaxed with Coronas and lime.

Once seated, we shared a couple of appetizers: chicken quesadillas and peel-n-eat shrimp. The shrimp were plentiful and paired with an outstanding cocktail sauce, while the quesadillas arrived hot, generously filled with cheese, meat, sour cream, and salsa. The deck is truly a highlight, making the visit worthwhile on its own. Sitting there, I found myself questioning if I was still in Pittsburgh, PA. I felt a deep sense of pride in my hometown, impressed by its ability to continually offer fresh experiences even to longtime residents.

If you're searching for truly one-of-a-kind and remarkable furniture near Pittsburgh, visiting Hot Haute Hot is a must. I went there with a friend who had been on a long quest for a new dining room table, and the selection we encountered was absolutely breathtaking—so stunning that I felt a twinge of envy. The shop offers an eclectic mix of items, from curio cabinets and eye-catching reclaimed ceiling tile mirrors to cozy plush chairs, striking lamps, a variety of side tables, wall hangings, and, naturally, dining room tables.

The customer service is exceptional. The friendly, knowledgeable staff are well-versed in every piece and genuinely enthusiastic about helping customers find the perfect fit. The store’s aesthetic and sense of style are truly impressive.

Adding to the charm, they also feature delightful, affordable jewelry ranging from delicate, subtle designs to bold, funky statement pieces. Take your time to explore and enjoy the experience—I certainly did!

When I arrived at the salon, my hair was long with fairly typical bangs that clearly needed trimming. The stylist told me he’d have to cut off a couple of inches due to damage, which I agreed to since I hadn’t requested any other changes. Yet somehow, I left with bangs covering most of my forehead, resembling a child’s haircut meant to keep hair out of their face. To make matters worse, he cut nearly five inches instead of the "couple" he originally mentioned. Now, my hair looks like a strange mix of a bowl cut, a female mullet, and Mia Wallace’s futuristic style from Pulp Fiction. While I’m usually open to trying new hairstyles, this one is genuinely awful. It’s also too short to pull back easily, making it more difficult to fix. Today, I’m heading to a salon in Shadyside to see if they can add extensions to fix the mullet or suggest a different cut to improve the look. It’s a real shame because this salon is downtown and very convenient for work, but I won’t be risking it again.

I’ll separate my review into two parts since my experiences with the service and the food were quite distinct.

The service was outstanding from the moment I arrived. I was promptly seated while waiting for my guest, and when the hostess learned it was a business lunch, she thoughtfully placed me in a quiet corner away from the lively main dining area. The staff were exceptionally polite, saying “thank you” and “you’re welcome” more times than I can recall. During the 30-minute wait for my delayed guest, they even shared some playful banter with me. (I used that time to browse Yelp reviews and decide on my order.) Honestly, I hope the service is consistently this impressive because, in my experience, it rarely gets better.

Unfortunately, the food didn’t quite live up to the stellar service. I chose the chicken parmesan after hearing the salads were underwhelming. If you prefer your chicken parm smothered in vegetables and cheese, this might suit your taste. Personally, I like my chicken parmesan to be mostly chicken. While it wasn’t terrible, I could easily make a better version at home—and I’m certainly no Italian chef. I can’t fully recommend the dish I had that day, though I do recall the lasagna I tried here once was quite flavorful.

To be honest, I find Olive Garden offers a better Italian experience despite its typical chain restaurant flaws. I’m willing to forgive poor service if the food is exceptional (thank goodness for tipping), but not the other way around. My search for a reliable Italian spot continues, though I wouldn’t hesitate to return if invited again.

We arrived early on a quiet Tuesday evening when the restaurant was nearly empty, though it gradually filled up. We began with the fried zucchini, which everyone agreed was a definite success. The bread, however, was fairly average and unremarkable.

For my main course, I ordered the veggie pasta and requested it without zucchini, but was told that wasn’t possible since it’s pre-prepared. The dish was just okay. My daughter chose the cheese ravioli and genuinely enjoyed them.

The other three in our group went with the seafood platter special, but their experience was disappointing. The shrimp and scallops were good, and the sole was acceptable, but all three sent back their lobster because it had a strong ammonia smell. Our waiter seemed somewhat overwhelmed by the situation and offered only a half-hearted apology. Later, two manicotti dinners were brought out, which were fine.

Overall, the service was only average at best. Given how long this place has been around, it’s disheartening, and I don’t anticipate returning anytime soon.

Friends who remember when this place might have been decent invited me along. However, the prices are *absurdly* steep considering both the quality and portion sizes of the food. I chose the Chicken Marsala, which was mediocre at best—similar to what you’d expect from a chafing dish at a funeral reception. It felt like a catered version of that, and frankly, the restaurant itself seems ready for its own funeral. Outdated and operating like an assembly line, it rushes patrons in and out so they can make it to their cultural events on time.

The waitress was friendly but appeared uneasy when she had to say “no” in response to my questions about the freshness of some dishes. Yet, she disappeared frequently and never offered dessert—something we likely would have ordered if asked.

While Downtown isn’t exactly bustling with dining options after hours, there are definitely other places I’ll choose over Tambellini’s next time.

At $30 a plate, you’d expect a bit more refinement, but when we asked for a bottle of Prosecco, the waiter gave us a blank stare and asked, “What is that?” We ordered gin and tonics and watched him prepare the drinks, only to be served cocktails completely without ice—who serves a drink without ice? Silverware was nowhere to be found until we repeatedly requested it. Our entrees, dessert, and coffee arrived at different times, and to top it off, we were handed the check before anyone even asked if we wanted dessert or coffee.

Putting aside the disappointing service, the food failed to live up to the Italian inspiration the restaurant claims. The stuffed banana pepper appetizer was so tough we couldn’t cut it with just a fork—and there were no knives available. The prime rib was fatty and cold, while the crab cakes were mostly filler with very little crab, leaving a mushy mess you had to work around. The pasta was simply plain—nothing special.

The atmosphere was dull and frankly depressing. The split plate fee was outrageously high, so we fibbed and shared plates anyway. Even so, our bill for five people was nearly $300.

Honestly, avoid this place unless you want a story to laugh about later. The only thing this overpriced meal gave us was a tale to tell. This was my second visit; the first time we had sandwiches in the basement, which was just as forgettable.

In short: AVOID!

It had been quite some time since my last visit, and although I’m not particularly fond of the downtown dining scene, I agreed to go. From the very beginning, the experience was disappointing—the hostess who seated us seemed completely disengaged, offering no warmth or enthusiasm. Then came the shock on the menu: simple bow tie pasta with meat sauce priced at $20! I expected something closer to $10 or $12, but instead, it was $20. Despite my irritation at the steep price, I felt awkward leaving after being seated, so we reluctantly stayed.

Looking back, I truly wish we hadn’t. Since I’m on a strict 1200-calorie-a-day diet, I asked if they could substitute marinara for the Alfredo sauce. The waitress reacted as if I’d requested something outrageous—she gave me attitude and then pretty much ignored us for the rest of the meal. When my food finally arrived, the steak was decent but clearly undercooked in places (some pieces were practically still mooing). The pasta, however, was completely bland. Paying $20 for tasteless pasta? That would have infuriated me.

I won’t be returning. This place was a major letdown, and I strongly recommend others avoid wasting their time or money here. The staff clearly needs an attitude adjustment, the prices are excessive given the current economic climate, and the dishes lack any real flavor. The only reason I gave two stars was because the steak was passable; otherwise, it would have been a one-star or even zero-star experience.

This establishment is basically unremarkable—just existing without any standout features. The food is adequate, and the service is acceptable, but nothing really grabs your attention or changes over time. Calling it “regular” feels appropriate, even if it does seem somewhat dull.

If you’re stopping by for lunch, expect to spend about $10 per meal, not including drinks, which could feel a bit pricey depending on your budget. I particularly enjoy their chicken parmigiana and also like their chopped salad. The complimentary Breadworks rolls add a nice touch that improves the overall experience.

I don’t anticipate any major changes here anytime soon, especially since a steady stream of business travelers keeps things running smoothly. They probably follow the mindset, “If it’s not broken, don’t fix it,” though I believe the outdated décor could use a refresh. Still, if the boss is covering the tab, there’s not much room to complain.

I’ve been to Caffe Amante twice in the last couple of months—most recently just yesterday—and both visits left me genuinely satisfied. Located on the second floor food court level of Fifth Avenue Place, home to HighMark Blue Cross Blue Shield, it clearly stands out among the otherwise uninspiring chain eateries nearby. It’s practically the only, or at least one of the very few, sit-down dining options in that area.

The service on both occasions was impressive: prompt and efficient even during busy periods, warmly personable, and patient enough to wait until I finished speaking before responding. The staff offered helpful menu recommendations and even acknowledged and corrected themselves when they initially provided inaccurate information.

So far, I’ve sampled two dishes. The Special Salmon topped with jumbo lump crab meat was flawlessly prepared, bursting with flavor, and generously portioned—a definite highlight. I also tried the Di Mare Amante, featuring shrimp and scallops in a white clam sauce served over capellini noodles (noting the menu spells it “cappellini” with two p’s). Both dishes were excellent, and I would happily order either again.

My impression and rating reflect what this place represents: an upscale lunch spot primarily catering to business clientele entertaining customers with a conveniently located meal. Although nestled among Chinese, Mexican burrito, and Philly cheesesteak outlets, it still manages to feel elevated. While I believe it would also be a solid dinner choice, it’s not the kind of venue I’d pick for a Friday or Saturday date night—there are more adventurous, exciting restaurants for those occasions.

This isn’t your typical $8 lunch spot; most entrées range from $12 to $16 and include bread, but the quality fully justifies the price. For lunch, I’d return without hesitation.

Seriouseats.com presents the "Pizza Cognition Theory," which suggests that the pizza we vividly remember from our youth shapes our lasting preferences. While our tastes may change over time, deep down, we all long to relive that first unforgettable slice. For me, that place is Villa Reale—yes, I know that might cause some raised eyebrows, but it’s true. Growing up in Latrobe, I was stuck with average chain pizzas until about age 12, when I finally tasted a pizza that was ultra-thin, floppy, generously cheesy, and greasier than usual. That was the pizza I dreamed of. My dad took me there before my first-ever Penguins game, and the spot holds special meaning for him too, thanks to the many post-work evenings he spent drinking beers and sharing pizza with friends.

Now, thirteen years later, I’m the one working downtown, enjoying post-work beers and pizza just like my dad did. Unfortunately, Villa Reale’s prices have risen so sharply that weekly visits feel impractical. The pizza remains that same thin, floppy, extra cheesy, greasy delight I love, but paying $15 for a pepperoni slice, a Coke, and a side salad is difficult to justify. On another occasion, when my dad wanted to thank me for helping him move, a medium calzone, a pepperoni slice, and two Cokes cost me $35.

Villa Reale, please reconsider your pricing. You played an important role in my childhood, but at these prices, you’re pricing yourself out of my adulthood.

Since their facade makeover and the addition of an ice cream machine—possibly even earlier—the prices have risen by about $2.00 per item on average. The pizza is generally flavorful, but ordering during busy times can lead to inconsistent quality and temperature. Hoagies tend to be dependable regardless of how crowded it is; the main drawback is the wait time between placing your order and finally enjoying your sandwich. Although I haven’t sampled their salads or other dishes, the feedback I’ve heard has been mostly positive. Personally, I’m not a fan of thin, delicate pizza crusts. While they can be enjoyable at times, I’m still searching for a thick slice to make my regular quick lunch spot in Downtown Pittsburgh.

I make it a habit to visit this place about four times a year. Before each visit, I prepare by avoiding red meat for several days. On the day of, I choose a normal but lighter breakfast—no bagels, as they take up too much room. I usually arrive a bit later than usual, feeling hungrier. The staff on duty are experienced regulars who recognize me but remain focused on making my visit worthwhile.

My usual order is a medium filet with mushrooms. I skip drinking because the beef is too exceptional to dull my senses. The plate and steak arrive quickly, the plate sizzling at a scorching 500 degrees. If the steak is too rare for my taste, I cut a piece and sear it right there on the plate.

Not long ago, I took the owner’s recommendation and tried the salmon, which was genuinely impressive. The panko crumbs and lemon added a fantastic touch. I always feel they go the extra mile for me, though with consistently excellent food and service, I suspect that’s simply their standard.

The steaks here are genuinely impressive in quality—my filet arrived perfectly cooked Pittsburgh rare, exactly as I requested. The sides, while fairly standard steakhouse fare and nothing remarkable, did have the plus of vegetables that weren’t overcooked.

On the downside, the interior is in urgent need of a refresh. Thick café curtains and shutters block the windows so thoroughly that you’d never guess half the restaurant is glass, lending the space an almost basement-like atmosphere. The oak details, patterned carpet, and banquette upholstery feel only marginally more current than what you might have seen at an Eat-n-Park over ten years ago.

This type of steakhouse will always appeal to a particular clientele, but I can’t help feeling that a bit of creative reinvention could push it beyond competitors like Morton’s. With so much innovation happening in American cuisine, Ruth’s Chris seems to be coasting.

That said, lunch is the wiser choice over dinner—the portions are more manageable, and you don’t need a group of six to tackle their family-style side dishes.

From the moment we arrived, the staff greeted us warmly and guided us into a room filled with the enticing aroma of steak. Our server was friendly and knowledgeable, creating a pleasant atmosphere—until the food was served, which proved disappointing.

I chose the special menu, which included corn chowder, a filet paired with lobster tail, creamed spinach, and dessert, all for about $55. My husband ordered the cowboy ribeye at $65, began with scallops, and had brussel sprouts on the side.

The corn chowder arrived lukewarm and was fairly average. Although the scallops came recommended, they fell short; the pesto sauce completely overpowered their delicate flavor, so we ended up using it as a dip for the bread instead. When the steaks came out, both were overcooked—my filet, requested medium rare, was well done, while his was closer to medium. We considered mentioning it but chose to eat without complaint, assuming the sizzling hot plates wouldn’t allow for less cooking. My husband enjoyed the brussel sprouts, but my creamed spinach was stringy and not properly warmed.

Overall, the food was mediocre, but the staff’s friendliness stood out. I had booked through OpenTable and noted it was my husband’s birthday; they kindly brought out a complimentary dessert. Still, I prefer Morton's, Ditka’s, and Peter Luger’s over this place.

Ullrich’s success is easy to understand, especially after their move to the current location a couple of years ago. This business has been operating in various forms for over 80 years.

They offer a wide range of services, from shoe and purse repairs to desalt and waterproofing treatments, as well as jacket and zipper restorations. If getting to the store isn’t convenient, you can even mail your shoes in for repair—really! Their mail-order service is available here: http://www.ullrichshoerepair.com/mailorder.htm.

Recently, my husband Rick asked me to drop off his shoes for resoling. I picked them up during lunch, and they look almost brand new. Last year, he had a tear in his leather jacket repaired there, and the work was exceptional. I’ve also had a purse fixed at Ullrich’s, and we’ve consistently been very satisfied with their craftsmanship.

It’s truly uplifting to see people choosing to repair and restore their belongings instead of discarding them. Rick and I have followed that philosophy for many years.

I can’t recommend this place enough—the craftsmanship and skill here are truly exceptional, and honestly, it might be the best spot on the planet. I only recently discovered the joy of repairing shoes instead of tossing them out. When I first arrived, my heels were so worn down I was practically walking on metal rods—no judgment, please. In about ten minutes, he had them fixed, and they looked as good as new.

Just yesterday, I brought in my favorite boots—a distinctive pair of Steve Madden cognac leather with rawhide ties running up the backs—hoping they could be restored. The heels were gradually falling apart. Not only did he completely replace the heels to look exactly like when I bought them, but he also polished them beautifully and recommended a cream to help them last forever. He confidently said they could endure for forty years. I smiled and said, “You, me, and these boots are going to be lifelong companions.”

Without a doubt, this is the best cobbler around!

Here’s the deal: the main point isn’t really about anything else. After Michelle—the genuine EYEBROW FAIRY—worked her magic on my eyebrows at Princess Nails, I realized I urgently needed a new set of keys. Apparently, keeping track of keys isn’t my strong suit, and I’m pretty sure my landlord isn’t thrilled about being woken up at 2 a.m. to let me back in.

I called locksmiths at 734-965-1474, but they outright refused to duplicate my keys—stooopid, right? Luckily, someone at Office Depot directed me to Ulrich’s Shoe Repair. Yes, a shoe repair shop that also cuts keys. When I walked in, the guy there—likely the owner—was extremely friendly and even a bit humorous, which was a pleasant surprise. I handed over my keys, and in literally 30 seconds, both copies were ready—and they worked perfectly.

Usually, places like Home Depot require multiple trips before keys fit properly. Not this time. The customer service was exceptional, the quality superb, and the price unbeatable—just $2 per key. If that isn’t a bargain, I don’t know what is!

I brought my boots in for salt removal, new heels, and a polish, clearly expressing that I wanted them to look sharp. However, when I picked them up, they appeared dull, with clumps of wax still stuck on. I pointed this out to the clerk, who took the boots back to the man in the back—likely the owner. He explained the wax hadn’t been buffed off and gave them a quick polish, deducting $5 from the price.

If he had returned the boots freshly polished and glossy, that would have resolved the issue. Instead, the shine was weak and insufficient. After sitting with dried wax for over three days, a quick polish barely improved the dullness. When I mentioned this, he insisted he had done the best he could. Honestly, if that’s truly his best effort, he shouldn’t be in the shoe repair business.

Eventually, I gave up trying to explain my dissatisfaction because it was clear he wasn’t going to help, and his attitude became rude and unprofessional. Since I had prepaid, he had my money and seemed indifferent to my concerns. I suspect if I still owed him, he might have taken my complaints more seriously instead of growing increasingly snarky and unpleasant.

Looking back, I wish I had paid more attention to another negative Yelp review about Ullirch’s, which included photos and closely mirrored my experience with both workmanship and customer service. The owner is charming when collecting your money if you prepay but decidedly unpleasant if you dare to complain about subpar work. I don’t mind mistakes as long as they’re acknowledged and corrected; what truly frustrates me is when someone becomes hostile over their own errors.

If you choose Ullirch’s, do NOT prepay.

Papa J’s truly distinguishes itself with remarkable cuisine, a distinctive ambiance, and, of course, Frank—the bartender who certainly deserves special recognition.

The atmosphere is anchored by the historic building, where dim lighting and dark wood set a slightly “dodgy” tone. This feeling is heightened by the headboard of Madame Dolly Cavanaugh displayed above the bar, a nod to the restaurant’s past as a brothel during Pittsburgh’s industrial peak. Yet, the quirky charm doesn’t stop there—rumors swirl that the place might be haunted! Honestly, it fits the setting perfectly. As you explore, you might half-expect the Mystery Inc. crew to slip behind secret walls. Jinkies!

The food is hearty, comforting, and generously portioned. The wedding soup is a perfect choice to warm you on a cold winter day. Entrées, ranging from $10 to $20, come with fresh Italian bread and dipping sauces. The menu offers a variety of pastas with an assortment of sauces and meats. The veal bolognese pasta, drenched in a rich tomato cream sauce, is a personal favorite—utterly delicious! Daily specials often feature seafood as well.

As for Frank, he’s a friendly, seasoned gentleman with a wealth of stories. While I usually stick to beer or wine, at Papa J’s I always trust Frank to pick my drink. Just share your preference—dry, fruity, bitter, or strong—and he’ll craft something tasty just for you.

I wholeheartedly recommend Papa J’s. It’s the ideal spot for those nights when you want to dine out but can’t quite decide where to go. If you’re tired of chain restaurants, not craving typical bar fare, and want to keep it affordable, head to Papa J’s Centro. Frank will make sure you’re well looked after!

I was looking forward to a pleasant evening of tapas and drinks with friends, so I brought a group of seven. The beverage selection was commendable, offering a solid variety of Champagnes and beers. Unfortunately, the experience was overshadowed by a disengaged waiter and a menu that felt outdated.

I ordered the Charcuterie, expecting torchon foie gras and duck rillettes, but neither was on the plate. Instead, it contained spicy sausage, prosciutto, and—surprisingly—a fresh tuna salad. When I pointed this out to the waiter, he offered no apology and simply asked if I wanted the dish removed, which significantly diminished the experience.

One friend chose the Croque Monsieur, a dish I enjoy, but it was only mediocre—more like something made by a novice staff member than an experienced chef. Another friend’s Pulled Pork Quesadilla also didn’t fully match the menu description, though it was acceptable.

Though the waiter checked on our drinks multiple times, twice he approached with his arms crossed, which I found quite off-putting. To add to the negatives, he requested a card to open a tab for our table, which was another considerable downside.

Overall, the place showed promise but fell short in execution. Perhaps it was an off night, but with these issues, I’m hesitant to return.

Whenever I drop in, the place is never busy. It has a distinct noir vibe, even in daylight—a place where you might imagine nervously watching horse races, betting everything on a long shot. You can almost see a regular at the far end of the bar who hasn’t been home in years, alongside a bartender guarding a Dark Secret best left undisturbed.

Despite this, the bartenders are warm and far from intimidating. They genuinely want to learn your favorite obscure cocktail recipes. One bartender, Frank, even keeps a small notebook filled with new recipes he’s picked up from customers, which I found truly charming. I also enjoy the appetizers here, especially the flatbreads and bruschetta—surprisingly light and inviting fare given the otherwise moody atmosphere.

So, don’t be misled by the eerie ambiance. While the entrees don’t leave a lasting impression, this spot is a solid choice for a quick stop if you have other plans for the evening.

Last week, a coworker recommended this spot, and I was genuinely excited to go back. However, the moment we sat down, dead fruit flies scattered across the table caught everyone’s attention—definitely not the best way to start. Our server was personable and attentive, though he did mix up one order. The person who received the wrong dish chose to eat it anyway.

I opted for the Chicken Piccata, a dish I truly enjoy. Since my boyfriend makes an excellent version, Papa J’s had high expectations to meet. Unfortunately, it was just average. The chicken was underseasoned, and the sauce was overwhelmed by lemon, leaving a strong citrus flavor that dominated the dish.

I also sampled a few bites of the Chicken Marsala. I’m not sure what was in the sauce, but it was excessively sweet—so much so that I’m relieved I didn’t order it myself, as I doubt I could have finished it.

Overall, this visit was quite disappointing, and we probably won’t be returning anytime soon.

We hit up three gay bars that evening, and this one quickly became our favorite—especially since we didn’t even bother with a drink at the second place. If you’re a woman searching for fellow female patrons, this probably isn’t the best spot. But if you’re hoping to relax in a cozy, welcoming space with great music, this bar is definitely the right choice.

We ended up sitting on Jeff’s side of the bar, where two bartenders were on duty. Both seemed competent, but Jeff made a real impression. He spent plenty of time chatting with us before things got busy, and even as the crowd picked up, he made sure we were looked after. Jeff was fantastic—and those eyebrows are unforgettable.

As the night went on, there was some commotion and fighting at the entrance and outside, though we didn’t witness any of it ourselves, and the bar didn’t clear out. For a downtown venue, a bit of drama isn’t unusual, but the staff handled everything quickly and efficiently, so no complaints there.

We stuck to beer, and the prices were very reasonable for the area. Happy hour apparently goes until midnight, which was a nice surprise! We enjoyed affordable drinks and good music, and we’ll definitely be coming back the next time we’re in town.

For chocolate lovers craving variety, this place offers both excitement and a bit of sensory overload. When the weather warms up, don’t miss the gelato tucked away in the back—it’s definitely worth a taste! The main draw is the impressive selection of chocolates sourced from nearly every corner of the globe, with little else competing for your attention.

That said, there are some drawbacks. Service can be inconsistent, and prices tend to be on the higher side. Many chocolates found here are available for much less at stores like Wegman’s—if you’re fortunate enough to live near one. We’ve knowingly paid a premium for certain treats, fully aware that cheaper options exist elsewhere. Still, sometimes the convenience justifies the extra cost.

Staff interactions are a mixed bag. Getting assistance while browsing the cases can be challenging, and the employees rarely seem particularly warm or welcoming. While they may feel they’re doing customers a favor by offering such a wide selection, it’s odd that they act as if they’re doing us a favor simply by being there. This somewhat arrogant attitude can be off-putting. Nevertheless, the treats themselves are unquestionably delicious!

I genuinely enjoyed browsing this store, though I found the prices somewhat steep—particularly since some of the same brands are more affordable at World Market. Because of this, I initially gave it 4 stars and chose several small sample sizes to try a broader range without overspending.

However, my rating dropped to 3 stars due to one employee’s unpleasant attitude. She wore a constant scowl, which made me wonder—how can someone be so unhappy working in such a charming place? At one point, she was sitting on the floor trying to move a box under a cabinet, loudly saying “excuse me” to a nearby customer who didn’t realize she was being addressed. When the customer finally noticed and apologized, the employee simply moved the box and walked away.

My husband and I were visiting from out of state while he attended a job interview, so I was exploring alone. I wanted to take a photo of the store to share with him and send to a friend relocating nearby. After making my purchase, I stood near the front door with my camera, only to have that same employee rudely shout from the back that photography wasn’t allowed. I hadn’t realized the store was so secretive—perhaps they’ve had their ideas copied before. I came in excited but left disappointed.

Thankfully, the other two older women working were very kind and helpful, which I sincerely appreciated.

The woman serving us eagerly pointed out that their gelato was “ranked in the top 5” nationwide, adding that it was “from Philadelphia.” To me, that just indicated it wasn’t freshly made in Pittsburgh. When we asked if we could mix flavors, she refused, saying it would be “too messy.” Realistically, she could have just explained the portions were too small to mix anyway. She then placed less than a full scoop carefully into our cup. Honestly, the gelato wasn’t worth such minimal servings, especially at a shop in the Strip District that claims to be upscale. Maybe they expect tourists won’t come back. If you’re at Mon Aimee Chocolat and thinking about gelato, I’d recommend leaving and heading to Mercurio’s on Walnut St. in Shadyside, where you’ll get better gelato, more mixable flavors, and genuinely friendly service.

Stan’s stands out with remarkably low produce prices—less than $20 for what would usually cost $40 to $50 at stores like Giant Eagle. Recently, I picked up 5 pounds of apples for just $2, bags of baby spinach for $1, a full flat of mangoes for $8, and red bell peppers for under $2 per pound. Honestly, some of these prices feel like a throwback to another era. The selection is fairly consistent too; you can almost always find the vegetables you need.

That said, two key issues keep Stan’s from being perfect. First, the market is poorly heated in winter, so unless you dress warmly, you’ll be quite cold. Second, you need to inspect your produce carefully before buying. Those $1 heads of cauliflower or quarts of strawberries come with a catch—often, about half are spoiled or past their prime. If you aren’t willing to thoroughly check your fruits and veggies, you might end up regretting your purchases.

For produce, this spot is a reliable option, but it doesn’t particularly stand out. The prices are appealing, though the quality isn’t always consistent. I’ve picked up some excellent bargains here, yet there have been times when the veggies were past their prime and not even worth the low price. The pre-packaging in Styrofoam trays doesn’t appeal to me either. On warmer days, with everything displayed out in the open, some items can look a little wilted. I wouldn’t make this my main destination for produce shopping; it’s really best for a quick pickup on your way home. When you need to stock up, Whole Foods, Market District, or real farmer’s markets in the summer are better choices. But if you just need a head of lettuce in a pinch, Stan’s is a perfectly fine stop on your way back from Penn Mac.

Klavon's keeps its menu focused on beloved classics, steering clear of any trendy or avant-garde options. What truly draws you in, though, is the nostalgic, inviting atmosphere that fills the place. As I walked in, I almost imagined myself in bobby socks and a poodle skirt—even though the shop’s history goes back to the 1920s—and half-expected to see someone in a letterman jacket. Even with those playful thoughts, I felt completely at ease in my casual Summer 2010 attire.

My friend and I took seats at the counter, enjoying our desserts while soaking in the retro surroundings. I picked the Chocolate Delight sundae, topped with chocolate whipped cream, and she went for an orange soda ice cream float. Normally, I’m hesitant to take photos in restaurants, but here I felt comfortable snapping pictures of the decorative vintage phone booths and the display cases full of nostalgic memorabilia. Klavon's also seems like a great spot for tracking down hard-to-find old-fashioned candies.

Klavon’s may not be everyone’s first choice, but for someone like me who adores mint chocolate chip and appreciates nostalgic ice cream parlors, it stands out remarkably. The establishment exudes a lively vintage charm that feels both timeless and fresh: amaretto-flavored whipped cream, vibrant red swivel stools, tall wooden booths, a man behind the counter sporting a flawless white handlebar mustache, a hammered tin ceiling, and those impressively large pecan balls.

Although classic flavors like chocolate and vanilla are always safe bets, I never pass up the chance to indulge in a pecan ball when it’s on offer. Imagine ice cream rolled in pecans, drenched in hot fudge or caramel, and topped with a generous swirl of whipped cream—a rich, nutty, fudgy delight. For those feeling adventurous and craving something regal, I recommend a scoop of coffee alongside a scoop of pecan, finished with that signature amaretto whipped cream. I sincerely hope they add this creation to the menu as the “Magic Magic Explosion.”

A charming photo of Joe Biden with the owners is taped to the mirror behind the bar. The owner shared a heartwarming story: “He was very thoughtful and left $20 for the next little girl in line to buy her ice cream.” Considering two scoops only cost five dollars, that’s an incredibly generous gesture. Mr. Biden, you are a genuine American hero in my eyes. It’s inspiring to see someone recognize how crucial it is for children to enjoy endless ice cream.

Kudos to you, sir. Truly, kudos.

If you find yourself wandering through the Strip District with an interest in Pittsburgh’s heritage, a desire to experience a classic soda fountain, a search for rare penny candy, or simply a craving for outstanding ice cream, Klavon’s is the place to go. I visited for all these reasons and left absolutely thrilled. Honestly, my excitement is through the roof—KLAVON’S RULES!! ! ! ! ! ! ! !

Here’s the scoop: The Strip District offers plenty of dining options, but Klavon’s is tucked just a few blocks away from the busiest spots (we started at Salem’s, which is fantastic too, but that’s another story). The walk is short, and with its bright neon signs, Klavon’s is impossible to miss.

Once inside, you’re immediately transported back in time. Pick a cozy booth or table and soak in the nostalgic atmosphere. You might notice an antique liniment bottle from when Klavon’s was a drugstore, spot the high-water mark from the 1936 flood near the ceiling, or admire the vintage penny scale and classic phone booths. This place truly embraces its rich history.

The menu isn’t large, but it’s packed with tempting options. Why not try a traditional phosphate, malted, or egg cream? If it pleased your great-grandfather, it will please you too. I indulged in a root beer float, hands down the best I’ve ever tasted, thanks to locally crafted root beer and ice cream. Before you leave, be sure to check out the penny candy racks—just a quarter lets you savor some rare treats.

I’d be remiss not to mention Mr. Klavon, who I believe is the original owner’s grandson and still runs the place. His iconic mustache alone makes the visit worthwhile, and he’s always eager to offer a tour. Friendly faces in friendly Pittsburgh—I’m already counting down the days until my next visit!

Entering Klavon's is like stepping through a doorway into another era, where vintage charm becomes a full sensory experience rather than just a visual theme. The antique furnishings do more than simply look old—they transport you to a time when everything seems to slow down. Their ice cream cones and milkshakes are delicious, and the shelves filled with nostalgic candies (with era-appropriate prices) amplify the retro ambiance. The staff’s genuine friendliness adds a welcoming touch to the whole visit.

I only found Klavon's because of a LivingSocial deal—without it, I probably never would have discovered this hidden spot. Tucked into a quiet, nearly forgotten stretch of the Strip District and surrounded by empty industrial buildings, Klavon's really does feel like a secret find. I tried the chocolate chip cookie dough cone, which was good, if not particularly memorable. However, the milkshake and those classic candies truly hit the mark.

If you’re looking for a cozy, sweet retreat into the past, Klavon's is absolutely worth checking out. And for the ultimate throwback, consider bringing a hot date—and maybe even a poodle skirt.

We were greeted by a cheerful ice cream technician, though her enthusiasm quickly began to feel overwhelming as our visit went on. The shop itself was nothing like the pictures online; the technician said it had just reopened after being closed for some time. The interior had a vintage parlor feel, but was almost empty and clearly needed some updating.

The menu was another challenge—it was small, tough to read, and only displayed above the counter. Being asked to sit down was actually a relief for me since I’m farsighted. The technician could only take one order at a time, so my guest got their ice cream first. When I ordered both chocolate and vanilla, the vanilla was completely overlooked. After waiting nearly half an hour and being pressed for time, I decided not to bring it up.

I gave two stars instead of one only because the ice cream itself—both chocolate and vanilla—was actually quite good. I added strawberries, but just got the standard topping; I’d expected a place like this to offer something homemade. The price also felt steep: $12 for two sundaes.

We might stop in again if we’re nearby, but we won’t be making a special trip.

In the past, stepping inside felt like entering a cozy piece of nostalgia, complete with whimsical antiques and the warmth of a family-run shop. The menu was impressively varied; while the ice cream itself never quite made my list of favorites, the inviting atmosphere made it a frequent stop for the occasional treat.

Since the original family sold the business, much of that special charm has faded. Now, aside from the building, the name, and the iconic old milkshake machine, very little remains of the original experience. My last visit left me genuinely disheartened, as though the soul of the place had vanished. The menu has been reduced to the basics, and the mostly new staff seemed inexperienced and unsure. I hope this is just a temporary phase, but I do question how they’ll bring back the unique atmosphere that once set this spot apart from other dessert shops.

There are a few positives. The new ice cream is a clear improvement over the Hershey’s they used to serve, and the shop now offers more consistent and extended hours, which is a definite plus. We’ll probably stop by again to see how things develop, but longtime fans of the old Klavon’s may find themselves missing what once was. Hopefully, the new owners will broaden the menu, help the staff grow in confidence and efficiency, and, most importantly, restore some of that historic charm. The staff is genuinely friendly, and I sincerely hope they succeed in bringing new energy to this beloved spot.

After spending a Saturday afternoon exploring the Strip District, we decided to stop by this spot. The place was busy, but there was no clear way to place an order. We sat at the bar and waited over five minutes to get any attention, even though employees were preparing ice cream just a few feet away. They kept their heads down and avoided eye contact entirely. Just as I was about to leave, a woman finally said, “I’ll be with you in a minute, thanks for your patience.” I stayed, only to overhear her complaining to a coworker about a customer who switched from a cake cone to a waffle cone. Maybe this kind of behavior is typical in Pittsburgh or at the places I visit, but it’s disappointing when staff openly gripe about customers within earshot.

My son ordered a single scoop of ice cream, and I had a one-scoop hot fudge sundae. Somehow, the total came to $7.38. The ice cream itself was icy, with a texture similar to what you’d find in gallon containers.

It’s unfortunate because this place should feel like a treat, not warrant a two-star rating. Those two stars are for the candy selection and the nostalgic, old-fashioned vibe.

Booking my appointment took a couple of days because Retta, who was managing the schedule, forgot her appointment book one day. When I arrived, I was surprised to find the space resembled a closet—right beside the elevator with no windows. Next door was an office that seemed to occupy most of the building’s right side. Giving it the benefit of the doubt, I tried the door, but it was locked. I assumed Retta was the only person there.

My appointment was at 5 PM, and since I arrived around 4:45, I waited patiently. At about 4:55, I knocked softly but got no response. I called Retta, but she didn’t answer. By then, I urgently needed to use the restroom. I waited until 5, then knocked more firmly to make sure I was heard and sent her a text asking for the bathroom code. At 5:05, I knocked again. Then at 5:12, I called once more and left a voicemail explaining I had been waiting and would wait three more minutes before leaving and contacting Amazon Local for a refund.

I asked several people if they had ever been there, and all said no. However, a few others I ran into knew the location and pointed it out to me. Around 5:15, the same men returned, and one knocked loudly on my behalf. They managed to get the bathroom code—thank goodness! I returned at 5:20 and knocked one last time. After that, I left and have not heard from Retta. It’s now 5:40, and I will definitely be reaching out to Amazon Local.

The customer service at this hotel is astonishingly poor. When my husband accidentally confused the weekends for our trip back to his hometown, we tried to resolve it by asking for a credit and even offered to extend our stay by another night. This would have meant zero financial loss for the hotel. Still, the corporate suits flat-out declined our request. As a result, they’ve lost a customer—a PLATINUM member, no less. After spending a substantial amount with Marriott over the years, it’s clear these greedy executives don’t care at all. A bit of goodwill wouldn’t have cost them a thing. Honestly, where has good customer service gone? It’s utterly pathetic. And to be fair, there’s nothing exceptional about this hotel anyway. The William Penn, the Doubletree, and several others are far superior. You’ll get better rates on Priceline, too. I’ll even shout out the Renaissance downtown, which isn’t managed by the Courtyard crew. Good luck! Go Steelers!

From the outset, I had the impression this hotel wouldn’t live up to expectations. I had booked two nights for a business trip but was stranded overnight at the airport due to canceled flights. When I called to explain my situation and request a reservation change, the receptionist was completely unsympathetic and insisted I pay for the night I wouldn’t be staying. It wasn’t until I involved my project manager that the issue was finally resolved.

The room and lobby were both quite small, which is somewhat understandable given the downtown location. What truly annoyed me, however, was the constant creaking of the floors throughout the hotel—no matter how softly I walked, the noise was amplified. Thankfully, I didn’t have noisy neighbors above me, but that didn’t matter because the AC unit was so loud that a good night’s sleep was impossible. I honestly can’t understand how a Marriott hotel could have an air conditioner louder than my grandmother’s from the 1980s.

If you’re considering staying here, I strongly advise against it. The room and service fell far below Marriott’s usual standards, and the only nearby parking option only adds to the already unreasonable cost of your stay.

I find it surprising this place hasn’t received any reviews yet—it really feels like one of Pittsburgh’s hidden gems. Our group of four sampled a variety of sandwiches: the classic Reuben, turkey and Swiss on a bagel, pastrami and Swiss on marble rye, and turkey and cheese on a bread I can’t quite place. Each sandwich impressed us, with quality ranging from very good to genuinely excellent. The lean meat was generously piled, complemented by fresh, crisp vegetables. Every sandwich came with a Kosher pickle spear, and we chose Snyder of Hanover chips—a nostalgic treat for me, as I haven’t enjoyed those since my Pittsburgh days.

The menu offered a wide selection of sandwiches, and the staff were both efficient and friendly, showcasing that distinctive Three Rivers warmth. I hadn’t realized they also serve Matzo ball soup, but I’ll definitely try it on my next visit to PGH. With my in-laws living nearby, I’m sure I’ll be back soon.

The moment you walk in, the restoration’s exquisite craftsmanship immediately draws your eye—it’s hard to settle on just one feature to admire, with a breathtaking ceiling, gleaming chandeliers, and intricate details at every turn. You may even end up with a stiff neck from trying to take it all in.

If legroom is a priority, main floor seats are the most comfortable option. Though the balcony offers an excellent view, the limited space there can make a noticeable difference in your comfort and overall enjoyment of the performance.

I’ve attended two Broadway touring productions at this theater, and both were exceptional. The sound and lighting exceeded my expectations, and the sets and staging for the traveling shows were truly impressive.

Restroom lines, a common frustration in older venues, are much less of an issue here. The lower level features a smart layout with plenty of facilities, so waiting is rarely a problem. There’s also a bar conveniently situated on that floor.

As for drawbacks, beverage prices are quite high—though that’s standard for venues of this type—and the lobby tends to get pretty cold in winter because of the constant flow of people. Theater doors generally open about 30 minutes before the performance, so keep that in mind when planning your arrival.

We were headed to "Les Mis," but traffic held us up and we missed out on experiencing the lobby before the show. We dashed up to the balcony and managed to slip into our seats just as the curtain rose. It wasn’t until after the performance, when everyone exited together, that we finally had a moment to soak in the lobby’s stunning atmosphere.

Our $50 seats in row N made the performers appear minuscule—almost ant-like from that distance. Looking back at the many rows behind us, I genuinely felt for those even further away. Being on the shorter side, my knees were nearly wedged against the seat in front. If you want a clear view, it’s definitely wise to pay extra for better seating.

The acoustics were outstanding, which is essential for a musical, and the cast delivered a lovely performance. During intermission, we had a chance to appreciate the theater’s impressive architecture. Nevertheless, despite the wonderful show, our seating fell short—especially for the price we paid.

Both times I arrived, I pulled up and waited at the entrance, but it took someone from the neighboring business rushing over to inform the staff that I was there. On my second visit, I was actually backing out of the driveway when a guy hurried after me to get my attention.

When you ask for your wheels to be cleaned, the attendants use brushes on them—brushes that are also used on the rest of the car’s exterior. Car enthusiasts often warn, "don’t use on your wheels what you use on your paint," but I’ll set that aside for this review. My main issue is that my wheels ended up scratched. Since my car isn’t anything fancy, I’m not overly concerned about paint damage, but if you have a newer or nicer vehicle, I would be cautious.

One thing I do appreciate, which earns them an extra star, is that your car is hand-dried at the end. The staff are friendly and straightforward, not trying to take advantage of customers. That said, the quality of the wash itself could definitely be better.

In short, come here, opt for the inexpensive wash, and leave with a clean, dry car.

The hostess and bartender left a memorable impression with their warm smiles and attentive service throughout our visit. When we arrived, the hostess estimated a wait of about 15 minutes. We asked if we could sit at the bar instead, and he was happy to accommodate us. We found a small booth at the bar, but on our way back, we noticed several empty tables, which felt unusual and influenced my decision to rate this place 3 stars.

Our bartender, who was both personable and quite attractive, handled a busy shift with ease, expertly pouring drinks and delivering food. He performed exceptionally well. I ordered tortilla soup and a salad with raspberry vinaigrette; both were flavorful, served promptly, and delivered with a friendly attitude. Throughout our meal, he kept our drinks topped up without us needing to ask.

In terms of ratings, I would give the service 5 stars and the food 3 stars. However, the restaurant’s large size seems mismatched with its staffing levels, which I would rate only 1 star. Overall, it’s a reliable spot for a quick lunch!

Located at 630 Stanwix Street in downtown Pittsburgh, Max & Erma’s offers a relaxed dining atmosphere with flavorful dishes and attentive, friendly service. During busy times, you can skip the waitlist by heading directly to the bar, where service tends to be faster. While their burgers are excellent, I often prefer the option of a half sandwich paired with soup or salad.

A standout feature is their frequent diner program, which awards a 5% discount after about five visits, with even greater savings the more frequently you dine there. They also send occasional special offers via email. On Wednesdays, you receive two complimentary, warm chocolate chip cookies with your meal, and during your birthday month, they generously offer six free cookies. These treats are always fresh from the kitchen and truly delicious.

In addition to the food, Max & Erma’s has a welcoming bar area. Conveniently located just across the river from PNC Park and Heinz Field, it’s about half a block from the T station. You can get off at the North Shore stop, situated between the two stadiums. Parking on the North Shore usually costs less than downtown parking, making it a convenient and affordable option.

If you’re looking for a one-stop shop that truly has everything, this is the place to go. Their selection is unmatched, featuring everything from Mardi Gras beads and tableware to Pittsburgh sports merchandise and quirky plastic babydolls. Honestly, if Stefon from SNL ever showcased a party store, this would be it!

The prices are excellent. During my most recent visit, I picked up supplies for gift bags for 70 people—all for just $70. That’s pretty impressive!

Whether you’re planning a Halloween party, a cowboy-themed gathering, or even a Hawaiian NASCAR bachelorette party on St. Patrick’s Day, Feinberg’s makes any theme completely doable.

If you can’t find exactly what you want, don’t worry—the staff is incredibly friendly and will go out of their way to help you track down the perfect items.

One thing to keep in mind: credit cards are accepted only for purchases over $10, so if you’re just grabbing a few things, bring cash. They’re open on Saturdays, making it a convenient stop during your usual Strip District stroll!

Wiener World unfortunately serves one of the most disappointing fish sandwiches I’ve ever had. In Pittsburgh, a poor fish sandwich feels as much like a betrayal as subpar BBQ in Texas or a lackluster cheesesteak in Philadelphia—an affront to the region’s pride and culinary tradition. I haven’t encountered a fish sandwich this dreadful anywhere else, even among greasy fast food spots, and at $10, this flavor disaster is far from affordable.

The sandwich missed the mark on every level: it was frozen, greasy, completely flavorless, buried under bland batter, and stingy with the fish itself. To make things worse, despite the spacious interior, there are no seats—just standing counters. They accept cash only (though there’s an ATM), and the dining area was uncomfortably cold—I was shivering inside at about 60 degrees, even though it was 80 degrees outside in July.

Why give two stars instead of one? Because my server was genuinely friendly, the fries served alongside the sandwich were freshly prepared and tasty, and I’ve heard from trustworthy sources that their ice cream is excellent. Still, I’ll be licking my wounds from this disappointment long before I’m ready to try their ice cream.

Curiosity got the better of me after the parade, so while exploring the cultural district, I decided to stop in—drawn by the authentic Irish name I’d noticed earlier. By late morning, the place was already crowded and full of energy, with people clearly gearing up for a day of festivities. Service was slow; the bartender was overwhelmed and not particularly friendly or enthusiastic.

When we finally got our Guinness, we only chatted for a bit, as the atmosphere didn’t really make me want to stay. We quickly took a shot of Jameson before heading to Market Square. The shots were reasonably priced, but the beers were definitely on the expensive side. I asked about green beer, but they had already run out. The bartender commented that this was unusual, especially since it was only noon. A band seemed to be scheduled for later, though we didn’t stick around for the performance. We also didn’t try the food, so I can’t comment on that. Ultimately, I’d say this spot is best suited for grabbing just one drink during a bar crawl.

We decided to try Mahoney's since it’s conveniently located just across the street and didn’t seem pricey or likely to disappoint. When you walk in, the bar area with TVs and stools immediately draws your attention. Further inside, a spacious dining area awaits, with tables arranged in a distinctive yet inviting layout.

The menu features traditional bar fare with a bit of added flair. I chose the half sandwich and soup combo, which was smaller than I anticipated. While the food was decent, it wasn’t particularly memorable. The French Onion soup was a bit too salty, and the mayo on my sandwich felt warm. I also sampled the fries—they were flavorful but somewhat greasier than I prefer.

On the other hand, my friend’s Greek salad was a highlight, offering a well-balanced mix of greens, feta, and even potatoes. The staff were friendly, and the prices were fair.

All in all, it’s a place I’d visit again, though not frequently. Maybe next time I’ll check out their happy hour.

If you work downtown, this place offers a dependable weekday lunch option, though it’s not worth making a special trip. The menu covers the essentials—sandwiches, burgers, salads—alongside homemade Italian favorites like Chicken Parm and classic diner dishes such as meatloaf. The Lamb burger stands out, delivering an Americanized gyro flavor with savory meat and fresh, crisp vegetables.

That said, happy hour falls short—not because of the selection, but due to the steep beer prices. It’s been about a year since I last visited during happy hour, and at that time, a bottle of Yuengling was priced over $5, possibly close to $6, which feels excessive for a widely available local brew. That experience firmly convinced me to keep this spot strictly for lunch.

In summary: tasty food, pricey beers, friendly staff, and décor that’s a bit rough around the edges—though its old-school Pittsburgh charm makes that easier to overlook. One final note: if you sit in a booth, be ready to be uncomfortably close to the person behind you. You’ll know exactly what I mean once you try it.

After leaving Fortunes, I felt like a complete fool and now genuinely hesitate to enter another authentic coffee shop. I went in with a couple of friends, utterly confused by the menu—nothing made sense to me. The only thing I knew was that I had tried a "macchiato" before and enjoyed it, so I thought, “Why not order a caramel macchiato?”

Here’s how my conversation with the barista went:

Me: Hi, I’d like a medium caramel macchiato.  
Barista: So, you want to order OUR macchiato?  
Me: Uhh... sure...?

Within minutes, I was handed a tiny cup with just a small amount of liquid. I glanced at my friends, confused, trying to figure out what I had done wrong. The barista noticed and called me over:

Barista: That’s why I asked if you wanted OUR macchiato.  
Me: Oh... okay...

Clearly annoyed, the barista took my cup, poured it out, and made me a caramel latte instead.

To all the coffee enthusiasts out there, feel free to laugh at me for not knowing there’s a difference between a Caffè macchiato (espresso macchiato) and the American version (Latte Macchiato??). Honestly, I’m not even sure I’m pronouncing it right.

As for the drink I ended up with, I can’t complain about the price—did I overpay or underpay for a caramel latte?—especially compared to Starbucks these days. Plus, the fact that I made such a silly mistake suggests this place must be a decent coffee spot. Beyond that, I can’t really judge, which is why I’ve given a modest rating. Maybe once I become more of a coffee drinker, I’ll revisit this review and bump up the score.

Why bring this gallery to light now? Because it deserves a broader audience. Spaces that engage both intellect and emotion are rare, especially in the Midwest, and this gallery’s meticulously curated exhibits fill that void with elegance.

We found the entrance discreetly tucked at the corner of Wood and Sixth, then took the elevator up to the gallery situated above the T-Station. There, a courteous gentleman sat quietly at a dimly lit table in a narrow hallway. He shared some background on the installation before leading us around the corner to Ryoji Ikeda’s audiovisual masterpiece, data.tron. The experience was breathtaking—fully immersive in both sight and sound, with ample room to stand or sit and truly absorb the projections.

For those who cherish installation art, leaving this gallery is a bittersweet moment. Wood Street satisfies your artistic cravings but still leaves you yearning for more.

We always choose the sleeper car when traveling with Amtrak because the trip can be genuinely pleasant if the train runs on time or is less than an hour late. However, delays are frequent since Amtrak relies on freight railroads that own the tracks. Last year, my husband, a dedicated train enthusiast, noted that trains often arrived in Chicago four to five hours late due to heavy freight congestion. We avoided traveling during that time, but since the track owner improved operations, reliability has greatly increased.

One benefit of Amtrak is that your meals travel with you, and you’re free to stand up and stretch your legs whenever you wish. Amtrak used to operate two trains daily to Chicago and two across Pennsylvania, but budget cuts a few years ago led to the cancellation of one, making schedules less convenient. Additionally, the train to Washington, DC departs from Pittsburgh in the early morning hours, which can be inconvenient.

I appreciate that Amtrak provides refrigeration or ice for my insulin if given 24 hours’ notice. They are generally accommodating to travelers with special needs when informed in advance. A helpful tip is to check your train’s on-time record on Amtrak’s website before traveling. You can see which routes tend to be punctual and which do not—my husband always emphasizes that punctuality varies significantly by route. Also, be sure to call 1-800-USA-RAIL before heading to the station to confirm whether your train is expected to be on time.

It’s impressive how much can change in just a few years. In the late 90s, I traveled regularly on the Pennsylvanian to Harrisburg several times a year. This past weekend, I took the train again for a meeting—departing Sunday morning and returning yesterday afternoon—and found the experience genuinely impressive.

Many reviews I’ve read focus heavily on the station, but honestly, that misses the point. Train stations are generally bleak and offer few amenities. The real focus should be on the journey itself.

What stood out most was the punctuality. Both trips left and arrived right on time, even arriving early in Harrisburg and Pittsburgh—a notable improvement from my past experiences. The onboard service also surpassed my expectations. The conductors and café staff were warm, friendly, and helpful—more like gracious hosts than just employees.

I chose to pay an extra $19 for business class, which provided a Metroliner car with extra legroom, power outlets at every row, and complimentary Wi-Fi for nearly the entire trip. Unlimited non-alcoholic beverages and a newspaper were included as well. I probably consumed more than $19 worth of drinks on each leg.

While driving would have taken about three hours compared to the train’s five, arriving in Harrisburg without the stress and fatigue of navigating the dreadful turnpike made it worthwhile. I even managed to get some work done, though I admit I spent more time admiring the beautiful scenery between Greensburg and Harrisburg than focusing on my tasks.

Amtrak’s Pennsylvanian offers a tranquil alternative for travelers aiming to avoid the stress of traffic. The route showcases beautiful scenery, especially between Greensburg and Harrisburg, but the highlight is undoubtedly the stretch from Johnstown to Altoona, where the Horseshoe Curve makes a lasting impression. Onboard, the atmosphere is typically welcoming, with courteous staff contributing to a comfortable journey.

That said, the westbound schedule presents a significant inconvenience. Arriving in Pittsburgh at 8 p.m. means missing dinner, leaving passengers to choose between the uninspired lounge car menu or their own packed meals. Those connecting to the westbound Capitol train face a lengthy four-hour wait in Amtrak’s basement waiting area. Eastbound travelers encounter similar frustrations, as delays on the incoming Capitol train directly delay the Pennsylvanian’s departure.

Fortunately, during our recent trip, the timing worked in our favor. Supervisor Susan and three colleagues had a one-day business trip to Altoona. Since the company car was already booked, we relied on the train’s schedule, which still allowed for a full workday. We anxiously awaited the departure—and thankfully, the train left right on time. That punctuality was essential for arriving at the Altoona jobsite exactly when needed.

I never once sat in the available chairs while waiting for my train. The walls were filthy, grimy, and dull, and the overpowering odor inside only made the already crowded station more uncomfortable. Overall, the atmosphere left me quite displeased.

The restroom was even more appalling. After witnessing its filth, I chose to walk down the street at 5 a.m. in freezing temperatures to use the cleaner facilities at the nearby Greyhound station.

There was no café or even a small convenience store inside the station to grab a quick snack. Although I found a coffee vending machine, the coffee it dispensed was weak and unsatisfactory.

This station desperately needs to be demolished and completely rebuilt from the ground up. My family and I ended up waiting at a different station down the street before returning to board our train.

I will definitely avoid this station in the future. It’s a dreadful reflection of the city—utterly terrible! The only reason I’m giving one star is because the train itself was comfortable and clean.

Living here, it’s really refreshing to have delivery choices beyond just pizza. My fiancé and I order from this place often enough that I’m fairly certain they almost recognize us by name. Everything we’ve tried has been consistently good—not outstanding, but reliably satisfying. The standout, though, is their peppered chicken. It’s generous, flavorful, and absolutely a must-try. Honestly, I think it’s the best dish on their entire menu.

I usually place orders online, but when I call, the person answering is always friendly and easy to understand. The delivery drivers are consistently cheerful and genuinely kind as well. Once, they forgot our steamed dumplings, but after I informed them, they came back within minutes to deliver the missing items, sincerely apologizing and handling the situation with genuine warmth.

I’m aware this place has received some negative reviews over time, but it’s common for people to skip leaving positive feedback when things go smoothly. So here’s my advice: give it a try—order the peppered chicken. It’s excellent! You’re welcome in advance, and if you’re satisfied, please consider leaving a positive review. :)

This shop offers a reliable selection of olives and a commendable variety of cheeses, along with flavorful ready-made dips and spreads. They also carry specialty items that can be hard to find elsewhere, such as rose water, pomegranate molasses, various grinds of bulgur wheat, and bulk fava beans. Additionally, packaged bulk nuts, dried fruits, and similar products are available. I usually visit when I’m looking for feta cheese or Greek-style yogurt.

Overall, it’s a solid choice. That said, I’ve had some issues with their yogurt, which is often left on the shelf close to its expiration date. On the plus side, their Fage yogurt is the most affordable I’ve found locally. Since my mom enjoys many of their dips and spreads, I often pick up snacks here when she’s visiting.

Aside from the yogurt, one warning concerns their canned tomatoes. They stock a lower-quality brand with a strong metallic flavor that can spoil your meal.

Her sofa from Gene Sane arrived, bringing her the happiness we anticipated. Several months earlier, she and I visited Gene Sane to select fabric for a sofa and a chair. While the fabric wasn’t cheap—some choices were genuinely exquisite designer materials—I’m confident some alternatives could be found elsewhere at a lower price. Nevertheless, their customer service throughout the entire upholstery process was exceptional. In fact, my parents had two sofas and three chairs reupholstered there.

Living in an Oakland condo with a ridiculously small elevator created a challenge for my parents when it came to my grandma’s exceptionally long sofa. To overcome this, Gene Sane went the extra mile by bringing the sofa mid-upholstery to the building just to confirm it would fit in the elevator. Such dedication to customer service is truly commendable. Fortunately, the sofa fit, but their contingency plan was to upholster it in two parts that could be flawlessly joined inside the apartment. This level of expertise is typical of upscale NYC shops, and although it wasn’t necessary, it was reassuring to know they had that capability.

They also demonstrated careful attention to detail by perfectly aligning all the stripes on every cushion, both front and back. These thoughtful touches genuinely make a meaningful difference.

Penn Mac offers an outstanding selection at its cheese counter, though it often gets quite crowded. For more personalized service, it’s best to visit during quieter times, such as weekday afternoons. They also provide an extensive range of dried pastas, and their bulk olive oil balances quality and price well. The fresh pasta display is equally attractive.

However, the heavy foot traffic makes Penn Mac less convenient for regular grocery shopping. Since I usually do my weekly shopping in the Strip, I find I can navigate other Italian or Greek wholesalers much more quickly—often in the time it takes just to get through Penn Mac’s entrance. Unless I’m seeking a specific cheese that’s hard to find elsewhere, I typically skip Penn Mac and choose Sunseri’s or Stamoolis Bros, both of which are less crowded and offer a similar variety.

Not long ago, while standing in line and chatting on my cell phone, the deli counter guy playfully teased me—those deli men always manage to amuse me. Honestly, their wit alone makes the trip to the store worthwhile. Beyond their humor, though, it’s the food—glorious food—that keeps me coming back. I visit the Macaroni Company weekly, and it never ceases to impress. While you wait, the deli staff offer samples of meats and cheeses, and the store features an extensive selection of bulk foods, high-quality meats, Italian cheeses, a fill-a-bottle olive oil station, fresh pasta, and bulk spices. Truly, this place is charming (or “loverly,” if you appreciate Eliza Doolittle).

On weekends, the store becomes packed like sardines in a can, and I’m fairly certain many customers are tourists. Still, that doesn’t diminish its appeal. That was a long sentence—though not nearly as lengthy as some of the old-fashioned books I’ve read.

Ultimately, the Macaroni Company feels like a little slice of Italy blended with Pittsburgh flair and plenty of fun.

They provide a respectable selection of cheeses, sauces, and pastas, along with a modest but adequate bread and produce section. While most online reviews have been positive, I feel the need to share my less than satisfactory experience.

When it comes to the pasta, exercise caution. You may end up paying a premium for noodles that fall apart immediately upon hitting boiling water. It’s important to know exactly what you’re buying or to avoid those options altogether.

Generally, the cheese counter staff have been knowledgeable and accommodating whenever I asked for advice on cooking or pairing cheeses. However, on my most recent visit, I told a regular employee that I was preparing Mexican food for friends and was looking for a cheese suitable for queso. Before I could finish, as soon as I mentioned “Mexican,” he gave me a sharp glare and said that although I might assume he was Mexican, he was not. Then he walked away to get a drink of water, leaving me standing there. Perhaps he was having a bad day, but it certainly didn’t improve mine. In the end, I bought my cheese from a shop down the street. I’m uncertain if I’ll return, or at least I’ll try to be helped by someone else next time.

As I ventured further into the store, I quickly found exactly what I was seeking: CHEESE! The environment felt somewhat chaotic—messy, sweaty, and clearly overdue for a thorough mopping. Despite this, I didn’t feel the urge to leave immediately, which is always a good sign.

Customer service truly deserves a perfect 5 out of 5. We were there because my husband suddenly felt nostalgic for Spain and wanted to prepare a variety of mini bocadillos with different meats and cheeses. Since we had already picked up the meat nearby, the Macaroni Co. was the ideal spot to find a wide selection of cheeses. The woman who assisted us was fantastic—patient even with a long line—and immediately suggested cheeses that would pair beautifully with our meats. Her extensive knowledge of cheese varieties was impressive, and I could have listened to her discuss the history of cheese all day; she made it genuinely engaging. My husband, who is known for being indecisive, couldn’t settle on a favorite cheese.

As for the food, I’d rate it 4 out of 5. We sampled at least seven cheeses, and while I didn’t enjoy any (I’m simply not a cheese person), my husband loved every single one. We also searched for Rustic Italian or any hard-crusted bread. Although it’s not the store’s fault, there really should be a sign that says, “Please do NOT touch the bread unless you’re buying it!” I saw at least three people squeezing the bread with dirty hands to test its softness, which was rather off-putting. Why anyone thinks that’s acceptable is beyond me! If you must squeeze bread, at least do it through the packaging—just don’t handle it directly. This was the primary reason I gave 4 stars instead of 5, along with the overall lack of cleanliness.

Each year as Christmas approaches, we uphold the cherished tradition of traveling to Pittsburgh to soak in the festive atmosphere. The Strip District is always the heart of our visit, with PennMac as our top destination. The cheese and olive room moves me every time—just thinking about it brings tears to my eyes. I make sure to stock up on jarred sauces that are reliably fresh, flavorful, generously sized, and reasonably priced. We also filled the car with loaves of bread, and the striking display of salted fish for the Feast of the Seven Fishes was a true highlight.

The most memorable part of our trip, however, occurred in a cozy, slightly worn room lined with massive canisters of homemade wine and small tasting glasses. Initially, I worried I had walked into a private staff gathering, but a friendly employee reassured me that customers were welcome to sample. Though hesitant at first to try the unlabeled wine, it turned out to be wonderfully warming and comforting. While the wine wasn’t for sale, the tasting provided a perfect refuge from the biting cold and a pleasant opportunity to connect with fellow shoppers.

With our bounty packed for the journey back to Ohio, we left feeling content and fully immersed in the Christmas spirit.

I usually enjoy their fresh pasta and the wide variety of cheeses they offer. The service is typically excellent, but today was a definite exception. At the cheese counter, I encountered the rudest woman. Later, when I went to the fresh pasta station, the woman there was downright unfriendly. Even though they don’t close until 4:30, she was already covering the pasta at 4:00. When I asked if it was too late to buy pasta, she rolled her eyes and said, “Uh yeah—we’re putting it away right now.” A simple yes or no would have been much more courteous. I replied, “Ok, thanks anyway.” Then, as if she suddenly reconsidered, she asked in a very rude tone, “Well, did you want something??” Needless to say, I walked away. Pennsylvania Macaroni Company truly needs to improve their customer service. It’s clear she despises her job—if that’s the case, she should find another one! If I didn’t drive so far to get there, I wouldn’t have bothered writing this review. Every January, I usually purchase three months’ worth of cheese for my family, but I won’t be doing that anymore.

I fully endorse this place. I’ve trusted Penn Animal Hospital with my pup’s care since he was just three months old. Now at nine years old, despite my frequent travels, I wouldn’t entrust anyone else with his vaccinations or wellness checkups. I even make special trips back to Pittsburgh just for his veterinary care.

Yesterday, we had a minor emergency when I noticed my dog limping and his paw seemed painful. Without hesitation, I took him directly to Penn Animal Hospital. We waited only about ten minutes before being seen. The veterinarian was excellent—completely unfazed by my dog’s large size, which matters a lot to me, even if it doesn’t to others. Though big, my dog is a gentle teddy bear who adores people far more than other animals. At nine years old, he still behaves like a two-year-old—joyful and energetic. The doctor was patient and attentive, thoroughly addressing all my concerns, which made the experience very reassuring.

Regarding a previous reviewer’s comment about record-keeping, it’s true they still use paper files rather than electronic records, but their documentation is meticulous.
