I keep my own records as well, but once when I needed to board my dog and couldn’t find my paperwork, I called Penn Animal Hospital, and they promptly faxed the necessary documents to my workplace. So yes, they do have a fax machine. My only concern is that paper records could be lost in a fire or flood, but that doesn’t lessen my trust in this hospital or stop me from continuing to bring my dog here.

This place doesn’t measure up to Mike and Tony’s or Big Greek Gyro in Market Square, and I won’t be returning. Only accepting cash was inconvenient, and the staff, who aren’t Greek chefs, came across as somewhat condescending. The $5 gyro sandwich was mediocre at best, with just a few tomatoes added and a lackluster sauce. The fries, costing $2.50, were undercooked. When I asked for ketchup, I was told to find a table with a bottle. It was a plain bottle filled with mystery ketchup—definitely not Heinz, which feels like a major oversight in Pittsburgh. I also had to track down silverware and straws myself, which you’d expect to be included with the meal.

Drinks run about $2 with no free refills. A sign warned that refills cost 50 cents and that taking one without paying counts as stealing and could lead to prosecution. Alternatively, you can purchase a drink from their cooler for $1, but these are generic juices or water—the kind you’d find at a dollar store for 25 cents or less.

The tables were noticeably dirty, which was disappointing. Despite that, I was surprised by the number of customers, so it seems to be a regular hangout for some. They offer daily specials, but for me, quality and flavor matter most—and on that front, I’d give them a C.

Yelp showed this place on Smithfield near 4th, but it appears to have closed since all we found there was a 7/11 and a Subway. Instead, we came across Zorba’s on the corner. With the cold weather, neither of us wanted to wander around looking for food, so the outdoor menu advertising specials caught our eye and we decided to give it a try.

My husband ordered the buffalo chicken salad, the Wednesday special, while I chose the gyro salad, which came with pita bread. His salad was huge—loaded with fries, plenty of chicken, and lettuce. He picked balsamic dressing, which I found unusual, but he enjoyed it. The fries were hot and crispy, and the chicken had a mild spice, though it was somewhat dry.

My salad was just as large but mostly lettuce. At first, I thought the lamb meat was scarce, but it kept appearing, almost like the miraculous loaves of bread Jesus fed to the hungry. Still, I was disappointed by the lettuce quality—I really dislike those large, crunchy pieces near the root because they’re bitter no matter how much dressing you add.

The main reason I’m giving this place only 3 stars is because of my salad. The lettuce was bitter and crunchy, and the gyro meat arrived lukewarm instead of hot. After about five minutes, the chilled dressing made the meat cold. On top of that, the dressing was bland and insufficient for my large salad, so I had to pay 75 cents for extra. It was frustrating to pay more for additional dressing that lacked flavor.

Inside, there’s plenty of seating, but it’s basic—simple tables and chairs spread out, nothing fancy or photo-worthy. It felt like a cheap cafeteria, which I wouldn’t mind if the food were better, but I wasn’t impressed by either my gyro meat or my husband’s chicken. Maybe they had an off day, so I’m not ruling this place out just yet.

P.S. Bring cash only!

As someone who isn’t typically a coffee enthusiast, I initially found the experience a bit overwhelming. Thankfully, the friendly staff made navigating the choices much easier. A knowledgeable coffee specialist approached me and suggested a blend that genuinely sounded delightful.

On a mission for a friend passionate about pumpkin coffee, I went straight to the coffee expert and said, “must. have. pumpkin.” He immediately understood and introduced me to his signature “harvest blend”—a handcrafted mix of cinnamon, hazelnut, and pumpkin. The aroma and description were so enticing that I trusted his recommendation without hesitation.

Afterward, I turned my attention to the tea wall, stocked with a wide variety of loose leaf teas—definitely more my preference. I spotted a Christmas blend that sounded fantastic, but unsurprisingly, it was sold out just weeks before the holiday. So, I chose some Vanilla Creme Stash tea instead and promised myself to return for a deeper dive into their tea selection.

For anyone exploring the Strip District, there’s also a full coffee bar that I’m confident matches the quality of their impressive beans and teas. The store offers everything you might need for your coffee or tea cravings. If you enjoy either, this spot will surely suit your taste. As the Terminator famously said: I’ll be back!

China Rose is, without a doubt, my favorite tea—not only is it visually stunning, but its flavor is genuinely delightful! I’m also a big fan of the Apple Caramel Almond, especially because of the charming halved almonds that add a nice touch. The milk oolong tea is a bit on the pricey side, but its uniquely exquisite buttery popcorn flavor is hard to find elsewhere. With such a wide selection of coffees and teas, it’s easy to spend hours savoring the aromas and deciding which blends to bring home. They also sell teapots and infusers, perfect for experimenting with different brewing techniques for your loose leaf teas. The prices are impressively reasonable—about two ounces of loose leaf tea or coffee costs just a little over a dollar. The shop itself is cozy and can feel a bit cramped when busy, but once the crowd thins out, you can relax and truly enjoy everything at your own pace. This place is definitely worth a visit—you won’t regret it!

The service at Lidia’s was satisfactory, but the food didn’t leave a memorable impression. You know how sometimes waitstaff joke around, and if your table isn’t into that vibe, you expect them to pick up on it and switch to a more professional tone? My experience was the opposite. My small office group gathered to celebrate a coworker’s farewell with drinks and good spirits. Although the waiter remained courteous and professional, he didn’t quite connect with our more relaxed, personable energy. I didn’t deduct a star since it wasn’t a major issue, but it did slightly affect my overall impression. In fact, the waiter’s demeanor stands out more vividly in my memory than much of the food.

As for the food, I would avoid the tiramisu—it’s mostly cream with barely any cake. On the positive side, the atmosphere is excellent; it’s clear they put significant effort into the interior design. The menu isn’t especially vegetarian-friendly but isn’t overly restrictive either. Lidia’s serves refined traditional Italian cuisine without feeling pretentious or predictable. Still, I have no desire to order the daily special pasta trio again, nor am I inclined to try other dishes from the menu. After some reflection months later, I lowered my rating from four stars to two. I genuinely wanted to enjoy this place, but it just didn’t resonate with me.

The wine list is the true highlight at Lidia’s. While they offer an expensive reserve selection, there’s also a solid assortment of reasonably priced, quality bottles and plenty of wines available by the glass.

The ambiance and decor were as delightful as always, though this year the chairs at our corner table sank so low that we joked about needing telephone books just to reach the table. I usually go for one of the special salads paired with the gnocchi in duck ragu—a dish that reliably impresses with its perfectly cooked gnocchi and rich, flavorful sauce. This time, however, I opted for the fall prix fixe menu featuring Winter Squash. The ravioli, drizzled with balsamic, was a pleasant surprise. For my main course, I chose the quail with apples and squash, and the glaze was especially memorable. Dessert truly exceeded expectations, showcasing creme fraiche and pumpkin ice creams, caramel sauce, and pumpkin fritters. We also enjoyed a couple of $28 bottles of wine; while not exceptional, they were solid, affordable choices that paired well with the meal. Everyone in our party was pleased with their dishes, and we definitely plan to return.

On a Sunday evening, my companion and I dined when the restaurant was moderately busy. We quickly noticed our server seemed distracted, forcing us to flag down another waiter just for more water. Meanwhile, my diet coke sat empty for over thirty minutes without a single offer of a refill.

The salmon was flavorful but drenched in so much olive oil and garlic that the plate was slick and greasy. The pasta tasting was odd—one dish had a strange, almost foot-like flavor, while another tasted like something I could easily prepare at home with a bottle of Prego sauce. The mushroom ravioli in olive oil was the highlight, yet it too was overwhelmed by excessive oil (see the pattern?), making me scrape some off before eating.

In the end, we skipped dessert. The food was merely average, the service fell short, and the overall experience left much to be desired. I won’t be returning.

My experience was mostly positive, though my entrée didn’t quite live up to expectations. I chose the pasta trio, but the broccoli pasta was watery and seemed to be seasoned only with salt. The ravioli wasn’t to my liking—the cheese had a strong, pungent aroma that I found off-putting. The linguini was decent but also somewhat watery. On a brighter note, the butter served with the bread stood out, offered in three flavors: crunchy sugar, apricot, and strawberry.

The appetizer selection was solid, featuring a flavorful Caesar salad, cured meats, and a good variety overall. The soup, however, was bland to me, although the all-you-can-eat option was a nice bonus.

Desserts truly stole the show. I enjoyed the cookies, tangerine panna cotta, and tiramisu—since the tiramisu disappeared quickly, I’d recommend grabbing it as soon as you spot it, even if you’re not quite ready for dessert. There was also a brownie-like treat that was especially delicious. Unfortunately, the almond cake lacked the moistness I had hoped for.

My boyfriend’s gnocchi with duck was excellent and generously portioned. At $24 for one entrée plus unlimited appetizers and desserts, it’s a pretty good value. That said, this isn’t exactly the spot you’d choose for a casual weekend brunch.

The salad, along with the breadsticks and sea salt-crusted bread, was quite satisfying. Unfortunately, the main dishes my girlfriend and I ordered didn’t meet our expectations. The pasta trio initially sounded enticing, but learning that nearly every version contained mushrooms was off-putting. Lidia’s seems to be an Italian restaurant trying too hard to be inventive, rather than embracing the traditional Italian fare, which is sadly scarce on the menu.

My girlfriend played it safe by choosing the lasagna bolognese, but it ended up more like a heap of overly salted meat. There were barely two sheets of pasta and just a few tablespoons of sauce. Dry lasagna is truly disappointing; if she had wanted mostly meat, she would have simply ordered that. After all, lasagna is meant to highlight the pasta.

I opted for the halibut with polenta, but the polenta was so bland I might as well have eaten my napkin, which had more flavor. The dish was topped with San Marzano tomatoes, olives, and capers, but the sauce was thin and watery. What really frustrates me is when chefs overcomplicate fish dishes. The halibut should be the centerpiece, yet it was buried beneath so many onions and capers that I had to rummage around to find it. The fish itself was good, but the portion was tiny, and the rest of the plate was underwhelming.

On a brighter note, the desserts were outstanding. We enjoyed the tiramisu and the Semifreddo di Cioccolato e Caramello, which combined milk chocolate and caramel ice creams, chocolate cake, toasted meringue, and crushed toffee.

The interior was definitely chic—perhaps those light fixtures would have been a more satisfying choice than the lasagna! Overall, Lidia’s feels like a Pittsburgh spot trying too hard, offering portion-controlled dishes that ultimately miss the mark.

After checking Yelp, we decided to try Lidia’s for dinner. The restaurant, located just off the Strip, has a clean and inviting atmosphere. Unfortunately, that was the highlight of the evening for me. Although the dining room was nearly empty, we were seated and then ignored for about 15 minutes. A bread basket was brought to our table, but the bread itself was disappointing. When our waiter finally appeared—looking like a Mafia Don—it still took another 10 minutes before our drinks arrived.

For my meal, I ordered the grilled octopus on a bed of potatoes, accompanied by an heirloom tomato salad, both appetizers. The tomatoes were underripe and lacked acidity, resulting in a bland flavor. There was no salt or pepper on the table, nor was any pepper offered. The octopus was tender and fresh but lacked seasoning.

My husband chose the salmon, which he found acceptable but slightly overcooked—nothing memorable. The third person in our party opted for the pork porterhouse, which was flavorful and enjoyable.

Based on other Yelp reviews, we planned to try the strawberry panna cotta for dessert, but it was sold out by 7:30. We settled for cookies and tiramisu instead. Overall, we left feeling disappointed by both the service and the quality of the food.

The moment you step inside, the elegant atmosphere is striking—with towering ceilings, immaculate white tablecloths, and a staff that carries a reserved demeanor. Yet, beneath this polished exterior, the restaurant functions as a family-style establishment cleverly disguised as fine dining. Our group, consisting of six adults and two young children, arrived just before the dinner rush and were allowed to wait indoors. I had hoped for complimentary appetizers, but unfortunately, none were offered.

At exactly 5 p.m., we were seated, and the dining room quickly began to fill up, confirming that arriving early was a smart move. We ordered five pasta trios, while I opted for the Zuppe di Pesce, a seafood stew. The pasta was satisfying—not outstanding, but certainly a good value at $20. For about $7 more, you can add a Caesar salad and dessert. What makes this place unique is that each day the chef prepares three distinct pasta dishes for the trio, each served by its own dedicated attendant. The meal starts with a generous sampler of all three pastas, which is more than enough for the first round. After that, you can request any combination of the pastas for additional servings. While I’m not sure if it’s officially all-you-can-eat, even the biggest eaters in our group were content after their third plate.

Though there is a children’s menu, our kids eat very little, so we asked if they could share some of our pasta instead. The servers were very accommodating, bringing extra plates so everyone could share comfortably. My wife ordered the pasta trio with salad and dessert; the Caesar salad was excellent—she shared some with me—and the tiramisu was arguably the best we’ve ever had. My Zuppe di Pesce was fantastic, especially for seafood lovers.

Overall, I’d describe this restaurant as a more refined and sophisticated version of Olive Garden—which, to me, is definitely a compliment.

If you’re seeking the ultimate dish, this place delivers three irresistible pastas served in a never-ending skillet—nothing else even comes close. Honestly, what other pasta spot can compete? Olive Garden, or “the OG” as I call it, can’t hold a single noodle up to this gem!

Each visit feels like a fresh adventure. I’ve never encountered the same pasta twice; there’s always some quirky, unfamiliar shape making an appearance, and whenever they announce its name, I’m left completely baffled. But the true highlights are the sauces. Oh, those sauces! Whether meaty, sweet, zesty with lemon, or rich and buttery, the variety seems endless. I’ll never forget the moment I first fell head over heels for this place—thanks to their extraordinary pumpkin ravioli. Pumpkin ravioli, you’ll forever hold a special place in my heart! (Picture me gazing wistfully out the window, like a scene straight from a movie montage.)

If, for some reason, pasta isn’t your thing (though I can’t imagine why), you’re still covered. I once attended a party here featuring a three-course meal. We began with a Caesar salad that was perfectly lemony—just how I like it. For the main, I chose the fillet, and it was absolutely to die for! I was genuinely surprised by how satisfying a non-pasta dish could be. Dessert was a light, fluffy tiramisu—pure heaven. As a bonus, we left with a goodie bag containing Lidia’s Eggplant Pasta Sauce. I tried it a few days later, and it was fantastic—a sweet, slightly spicy red sauce featuring eggplant instead of the usual meatballs. Such a refreshing twist!

The atmosphere is just as memorable. Large tinted windows offer a view—admittedly of a parking lot—but inside, the vibe is cozy and intimate. Dominating the center of the space is a breathtaking glass Chihuly chandelier. It’s simply stunning. Honestly, ditch the OG and give this place a try—you won’t regret it. And yes, they definitely serve free breadsticks!

Before this visit, we had only been to Lidia’s for a wine tasting and hadn’t yet tried their food. We began with a flavorful Fritto Misto featuring housemade sausage and apple. Though we initially worried the apple might overpower the dish, it actually enhanced it nicely.

For our main courses, my wife ordered the gnocchi with braised duck ragout, while I chose the Osso Bucco di Maiale. The Osso Bucco was generously portioned, and while I found it satisfying, it didn’t leave a lasting impression. We took some home. My wife, however, thoroughly enjoyed her gnocchi, so next time I’ll likely opt for a pasta dish myself.

The wine list was extensive, and we shared a lovely bottle of Chianti from the special Valentine’s Day selection. Lidia’s is certainly a great choice for a romantic evening, and we’re looking forward to returning soon.

The moment you step inside the restaurant, its enchanting atmosphere immediately draws you in. Despite the spacious layout, the space feels cozy, warm, and inviting. The designer’s bold yet sophisticated flair is evident in the carefully chosen details and tasteful splashes of color. I was genuinely eager to begin my meal!

I started with the polipo—grilled octopus—which was tender and bursting with flavor, thanks to a zesty vinaigrette. The real standout, however, was the osso bucco: a braised pork shank resting on a bed of barley risotto. Succulent, richly seasoned, and incredibly tender, it truly stole the spotlight. My companion’s hearty mushroom soup and flawlessly grilled salmon were also quite satisfying.

For dessert, I chose the budino di nutella, or Nutella pudding. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite live up to expectations, coming across as a bit too heavy and rich. Did I really say that? Lesson learned—maybe. Probably not.

Service was impeccable from start to finish—we never had to wait, and our dishes arrived promptly. Given the quality and generous portions, the prices felt very reasonable. Honestly, I left needing a looser belt! Lidia’s is definitely a place I’ll be returning to.

The atmosphere left a stronger impression on me than the service or the food—not because they were poor, but simply because they didn’t quite meet my expectations. Although we had a reservation, it was initially missing from the system. When it finally appeared, we were placed on the “wait list.” Eventually, we were seated promptly, but at a table tucked away from the lively main dining area, wedged between the bar and the kitchen.

The wine list was impressive, offering many selections by the glass. Our server recommended an excellent dry white that I thoroughly enjoyed, but I was disappointed when there was none left for a second glass. The alternative he suggested didn’t compare to the first.

At times, the waiter seemed a bit overwhelmed, likely because he was also acting as a bartender—a vantage point our table’s location afforded us. Sometimes our used plates sat for a long time, while at other moments, like when no one asked if we wanted refills on the “Pasta Trio,” the plates were quickly cleared away.

The bread was superb, served with flavorful spreads. One companion ordered the octopus appetizer and declared it the best he’s ever had, which is notable given his adventurous seafood palate. My son and I shared the Caesar salad, which was quite good—was that a hint of mustard in the dressing? Delightful!

For entrees, my two friends chose the “Pasta Trio.” They enjoyed their meals but found the portions inconsistent and the refills less enthusiastic than expected. My grilled salmon was tasty but a bit fatty, which was a new and slightly odd experience for me. The Yukon gold potatoes and green beans with whole grain mustard sauce on the side were absolutely delicious.

Desserts rounded out the meal nicely. We shared a pumpkin mousse and an amaretto cake, dividing them three ways for a sweet conclusion to our evening.

Even after visiting Salt of the Earth, I still wholeheartedly award Lidia’s a perfect 5-star rating. Despite either Jordan or me having worked there at some point, it remains one of the few places we both eagerly choose to dine. Whenever we crave Italian cuisine that genuinely captures the warmth and authenticity of homemade family recipes, Lidia’s is undeniably our top pick.

Not long ago, we stopped by the bar for drinks and appetizers, an experience that never fails to delight. We enjoyed the Fritto Misto—crispy fried vegetables and calamari in a delicate batter, paired with Lidia’s famous dipping sauce. She truly is the queen of sauces! Since it’s impossible to visit without sampling their renowned pasta trio, we also ordered the appetizer-sized pasta-tasting platter, which was absolutely phenomenal.

Our favorite time to visit is definitely for their Saturday or Sunday brunch, which I genuinely believe is Pittsburgh’s best kept secret. For $24.99 per person, you start with a complimentary Bloody Mary or Mimosa, followed by a basket overflowing with scones, donuts, and breads served alongside sweet butters. Then, you head to the antipasto tables, stocked with vegetables, egg frittatas, meats, salads, and soups—a true antipasto feast that encourages creativity, just as the chefs do! Afterward, you select your brunch entrée—whether it’s the Pasta-Tasting trio, Filet & Eggs, or Salmon. To finish, you indulge at the dessert table, featuring tiramisu, Italian cookies, mousse, and more.

I often receive brunch recommendations, but none come close to topping Lidia’s. Brunch is served Saturdays and Sundays from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. Just be ready for the inevitable food coma afterward!

We arrived a little early for our reservation and were seated right away, which started the evening off nicely. The dining room was busy, yet the noise level was pleasantly subdued. If you’re dining with elderly guests, you can request a table downstairs since there doesn’t seem to be an elevator; however, I personally prefer the upstairs seating for its charming view overlooking the dining area.

Our meal began with the Lobster Arancini, which were perfectly prepared—no trace of crunchy or undercooked risotto. The only issue was that there were just three pieces for our group of four, and their small size made it difficult to share evenly.

For our mains, the gnocchi with duck ragu truly stood out: rich but not too heavy, and the gnocchi melted in the mouth. The Zuppa di Pesce impressed with a balanced broth that wasn’t oversalted, despite the abundance of shellfish. There was also a subtle Sherry wine note, and I counted seven or eight different types of seafood in the dish.

Service was both attentive and efficient, allowing us to finish three courses in just over an hour. All in all, Lidia’s remains one of my favorite Italian restaurants in the city.

I’ve enjoyed watching Lidia on TV and trying many of her recipes, and having spent time in NYC, I’m quite familiar with and admire Bastianich’s restaurants. One of the most memorable meals I’ve ever had—though those moments are rare—was at Del Posto. To me, the Bastianich name stands for integrity, passion, and a sincere dedication to exceptional Italian cuisine.

So, when I visited this location, I couldn’t help but wonder: is this really the same team behind it? The experience was completely lackluster and disappointing, as if no one cared about the quality or the overall dining atmosphere. I came for brunch and ordered the pasta trio and antipasti table. It was clear the ingredients were below par, and the dishes seemed mass-produced, missing both flavor and thoughtful care.

At $25 per person, you’d expect a lot more effort. Don’t they care about their reputation and good name? Apparently not. This place feels like a sellout—merely exploiting the name in a setting where culinary standards aren’t as demanding as in NYC. To top it off, the service was underwhelming. Truly a shame.

Overall, the experience left me somewhat disappointed. When we arrived for our reservation, it took quite a while before anyone greeted us, even though the restaurant wasn’t busy. Initially, we were seated outside, but the outdoor seating was right next to the street, which was uncomfortable. Fortunately, they quickly moved us indoors without any issues.

After ordering drinks, there was a long wait before they arrived. I chose the pasta trio special, attracted by the chance to sample three different fresh recipes. Unfortunately, I only truly enjoyed one of the dishes—though I understand the selection changes—and I only asked for a refill of that particular one. My sister ordered the seafood Alfredo, which she said was good. As for my parents’ meals, I can’t even remember what they had because nothing stood out.

While the service was adequate and the food acceptable, I mostly felt unimpressed and thought we paid quite a bit for a rather lackluster meal and overall experience.

I’m awarding Lidia’s brunch a well-deserved five stars. We had a reservation for five at 11:30 a.m. on a Sunday, and the restaurant was pleasantly quiet. The spacious dining room with lofty ceilings created a bright, inviting atmosphere. The staff were friendly and attentive, and importantly, they didn’t rush us out after we paid—a refreshing change.

Make sure to come hungry! Some standout items included the freshly squeezed orange juice in the mimosa, the rosemary and sea salt bread served with sugar butter, and the lemon scone paired with sugar butter as well as apricot and strawberry spreads. I also really enjoyed the fried cauliflower from the antipasto selection. For my main course, I chose the grilled octopus with potatoes, onions, string beans, olives, and pickled onions. The salty seasoning was perfect, and the octopus was tender and cooked just right. The pistachio and ginger mini cookies were my favorite dessert, and the coffee was brewed nicely.

That said, while several dishes were impressive, many others were just average. Overall, Lidia’s brunch felt more focused on offering a broad variety than on exceptional quality. One thing is certain—you won’t leave hungry, and if you do, you probably didn’t order well! They also make splitting checks easy, which is always a plus.

Certainly! Here's a revised version that enhances pacing and clarity while preserving all core opinions and experiences:

My husband and I have been loyal fans of her cooking show, so we were genuinely excited to experience her restaurant firsthand. Unfortunately, that excitement quickly turned into disappointment. Maybe dining there on a holiday was our mistake, but the real issue lay with the restaurant’s blatant cost-cutting, which they executed in the worst way possible: serving FLASH FROZEN FOODS. The menu was limited, with only a few options, and although the $48 per person price tag seemed steep, we hoped the quality would justify it. Sadly, it did not.

The first course was a fried ball purportedly filled with lobster. Instead of any lobster flavor, all we could taste was the overwhelming taste of an overworked fryer—disappointing right from the start. Eager for the next dishes, we were served a Caesar salad and a shrimp with spaghetti squash. The salad was just okay, but the shrimp were particularly underwhelming—tiny frozen ones that might look appealing breaded, but served plain, appeared sad and unappetizing, as if they’d never even seen the ocean, which I strongly suspect is true.

When the main entrée arrived, we still held onto hope despite the hefty $48 price tag. My husband ordered the tuna, which was an absolute joke. The most maddening part was that it was labeled “pescado,” yet there was no real pescado in sight. We could have tolerated a small piece of fresh tuna, but instead, we received an average slab of flash-frozen fish with pre-made grill marks—thankfully, the chefs didn’t have to do the grilling themselves. My pasta trio was merely okay; nothing about it suggested freshness or high quality.

The only bright spot was the service. Our server was excellent—he clearly recognized from our expressions that we weren’t pleased with the food and wisely didn’t ask for feedback. Throughout, he was attentive and professional. After enduring a frozen, uninspired dessert or finger food, we finally received the bill. With a glass of wine, a cappuccino, tax, and tip, the total came to $150. Save your money and opt for Spaghetti Warehouse instead—you’ll at least know what to expect. Lidia, YOU OWE US MONEY!

We began our experience at the bar, enjoying the exceptionally flavorful fried chickpeas while waiting for the rest of our party. Once everyone arrived and we were seated, we placed our orders. My brother, sister, and I all opted for the three-course meal, while the rest of the family chose individual dishes.

The pasta dishes quickly stood out as the favorites overall, with the lamb chops being the only other dish that matched their quality. Both my sister and I ordered the ricotta gnudi, served as large, flavorful spheres—though I would have preferred smaller, gnocchi-sized portions. My brother selected the burrata, which was tasty but quite substantial, and his fiancée enjoyed the Caesar salad, noting its very generous portion.

For the main courses, the clear highlights were the gnocchi, the pasta tasting trio, and the Agnello (lamb chops). I chose the Saltimbocca alla Romana, which offered wonderful flavors but was unfortunately overcooked. My sister’s sausage dish was just average and didn’t quite live up to the expectations we had for a restaurant owned by Lydia. The lasagna, too, fell short of what we had hoped for.

Dessert-wise, the gelato trio was the best option. The tiramisu and upside-down rhubarb cake were enjoyable as well, though the rose gelato was a disappointment.

Our experience was absolutely outstanding! The staff we interacted with were warm, knowledgeable, and remarkably efficient—always available to help but never overbearing, which really speaks to their excellent training. Every dish we tried was delicious, from the crisp salads to the inviting antipasti. For my main, I went with the gnocchi and duck ragu, which was flawless—though I did find the portion a bit on the generous side! My partner’s chicken livers with polenta were just as impressive.

We sampled several desserts from the array on offer, and each one was a delight. The roasted half peaches with crumble topping were especially memorable, but the olive oil and lemon cake with sugar-coated blueberries was another highlight.

This visit was so enjoyable, it made us wonder why we don’t come here more often. After such a memorable experience, we’re definitely planning to return more frequently.

I used to avoid any restaurant if I saw children nearby, but that attitude has completely shifted. Before I share my thoughts on the brunch, I have to praise their baby-friendly amenities! The bathroom featured a nearly private changing station, well-stocked with wipes and a cozy seating nook—truly impressive. Even better, they provided a cradle-style bed where our baby, who’s definitely no angel, slept peacefully. When he wasn’t napping, he happily played there, allowing us to relax and enjoy brunch with our adult friends without constantly watching or entertaining him. A big thank you to Lidia’s for these thoughtful touches—they won me over immediately.

Now, onto the brunch itself: it was outstanding. The bread with three sweet, buttery spreads was my favorite. My mimosa was authentic, not just orange juice with a splash of champagne. The buffet was mostly vegetarian—about 90%—and never looked empty because the staff continually replenished it with fresh dishes. I chose the manicotti for my entrée but also sampled my friend’s pasta trio, which was delicious. And the dessert selection? Absolutely heavenly.

Overall, we had a fantastic experience and will definitely return.

Lidia’s was a major disappointment for me. The atmosphere and service were satisfactory—no issues there—but the food fell well short of my expectations. It felt more like a chain restaurant experience, similar to Carrabba’s or Olive Garden, rather than a place with refined culinary standards. The bread arrived soggy, the salad greens and dressings were overly salted, the pasta sauces greasy and careless, and the generous portions were simply plopped onto dirty plates smudged with greasy fingerprints. To make matters worse, I spent the entire meal shooing flies away from our table.

This left me genuinely perplexed. At Joe’s restaurants, there’s a clear sense that each ingredient is carefully chosen and the dishes are presented with true attention to detail. I anticipated that same level of care at Lidia’s. It made me question whether Lidia herself frequents this location or is even aware of the food’s quality. This seems to be a recurring issue with celebrity chefs—when they’re involved in many ventures and aren’t present regularly, the quality often suffers.

Unfortunately, I will not be returning to Lidia’s.

The food met the expectations set by our previous visit and was quite enjoyable. However, the service did not quite live up to the same standard. On a Monday evening, with the restaurant about half full, we were passed around between servers despite our original server still attending to us. The explanation of the 3-course special was incomplete, leaving us unsure about what was included or which options were available, although all the expected items did arrive.

We also faced difficulties with basic requests like extra cheese for the pasta tasting trio and the second glass of wine that came with the special. When we couldn’t finish all the food, we asked for it to be packed to go. Three of us received our leftovers, but the half portion of the secondi from my wife’s meal—something she had been looking forward to enjoying the next day—was forgotten. We only realized the missing takeout box the following morning.

Perhaps the staff was having an off night, but this experience will definitely affect my decision about returning. Overall, the food was good, but the service was somewhat disappointing for a restaurant of this caliber.

To celebrate my parents’ 50th wedding anniversary, I flew in from Texas with high hopes and chose Lidia’s as the venue. I was genuinely excited. Our party of eight was seated around a round table that felt quite cramped. Five of us ordered the Pasta Trio, which was undeniably the best fettuccine and ravioli I’ve ever tasted—the pasta was fresh, and the flavors truly exceptional.

Unfortunately, the experience took a disappointing turn when we requested seconds. After a long wait following our initial plates, I was served only a spoonful of fettuccine—barely enough for a few bites. Our drinks, aside from water, were refilled just once. I ended up switching from iced tea to water—not by choice, but because my tea glass had quietly been topped off with water before I noticed.

Adding to the frustration, I was repeatedly bumped by waitstaff maneuvering between me and a temporary wall set up for a large birthday party. Thankfully, I know I can find excellent pasta with far better service elsewhere. I truly wish I could say otherwise, but I won’t be returning and wouldn’t recommend this place—unless perhaps for lunch or a quieter evening. Honestly, if Lidia herself saw the service at her own restaurant, I’m sure she would be horrified.

This restaurant tries to present itself as a cozy spot for a leisurely sit-down dinner, but unfortunately, the food didn’t quite meet that expectation.

I began with the Calamari appetizer, shared with a friend, and then chose the recommended Pasta Trio for my entrée. As a calamari lover, I’ve had better at similar places. Here, the calamari was bland and lacked freshness—the batter wasn’t crisp or crunchy, and the sauce tasted watered down. The Pasta Trio, which offers three types of pasta with an "all you can eat" option, was equally disappointing. Since it was recommended, I expected more, but overall, the meal fell flat.

My friend, who usually finishes her plate so thoroughly it looks like she never ate, left some of her Chicken Cacciatore uneaten. She isn’t picky, so that really highlights her dissatisfaction with the dish.

The flavors reminded me of Olive Garden’s American-Italian fare, but honestly, I’d pick Olive Garden any day—their food tastes better and costs less.

Service was mediocre at best. Our water glasses were not refilled consistently. While I wasn’t bothered since I drink slowly, some friends kept searching for water, which distracted them from enjoying their meal. The Pasta Trio is supposed to be "all you can eat," with staff returning to refill plates. Several of us waited for a third serving that never came. The servers didn’t ask if we wanted more and quickly cleared our plates without giving us a chance to request another helping. A few of us left still somewhat hungry, resulting in a grumpy ride home.

Considering the price, I expected better quality. Even if the cost matched similar restaurants, the food was underwhelming. Sadly, from the cuisine to the service, our overall experience was disappointing.

This place urgently needs major renovations. The projector screens are outdated and of poor quality, and although there are a few large rear projection TVs, not a single HDTV is available. TVs are scattered throughout the venue, but they all look grimy and old, with snowy reception on every screen.

The biggest problem is that only six games are broadcast simultaneously across the entire expansive bar. Sports Rock has numerous main bar islands, booths, and pub tables, each featuring its own TV. While that sounds promising, what’s the point of all those seats if only six games can be shown at once? It’s absurd, especially given the size of the place and the huge popularity of college football. I went there to watch a game airing on basic ESPN, and it wasn’t even on. So basically, I could have stayed in my hotel room to watch it instead of coming to this “sports bar”? Give me a break.

The food is just as disappointing. The nachos are no better than what you’d find at 7-11, and the sandwiches are completely flavorless. Service was slow and clearly understaffed. I’m not sure if there’s been a recent ownership change or something else, but something felt off, and they were obviously unprepared for football season.

I do feel bad because the staff were genuinely kind and apologetic, but that doesn’t change the fact that even if they had been showing my game, I would probably still prefer to watch it in my hotel room.

Sports Rock completely missed the mark on the four essentials every sports bar should have: ESPN, nachos loaded with all the fixings, decent beer specials, and big screen TVs.

When we arrived, I felt hopeful seeing that each table had its own TV. Of course, we ended up at one that didn’t work. Even worse, while several out-of-market games were playing, the Virginia Tech game was nowhere to be found. We politely asked for the plain old ESPN channel—no ESPN U or 360, just the regular one. Their excuse was they only had six receivers. That’s understandable, but then why was I stuck watching Maine versus Iowa? To make matters worse, when an attractive girl approached the bar, the bartender switched to the Georgia game within minutes.

The food was a total disappointment. The nachos were absolutely disgusting, my wrap leaked oil and who knows what else, and the fries were dreadful. The only relief came from dipping the fries into the nasty nacho cheese, which somehow made them slightly more tolerable.

At $4.75 a beer, the cost really adds up over a three-hour game. The service was terrible, and honestly, I think I’d get better reception on a TV with rabbit ears. Overall, this place was a major letdown. I will say, just as we were about to leave for an Irish bar that actually had ESPN, I spotted the Hokies game playing way back in a corner. Took them long enough.

If you’re ever in Pittsburgh and want to watch ESPN, here’s my advice: grab a Primanti Brothers sandwich and a six-pack, then watch the game in your hotel room. Don’t waste your money sitting there watching Maine versus Iowa on a tiny TV with awful reception.

The staff, clad in mini referee shorts, fitted striped shirts, and tennis shoes, strike a youthful and appealing balance without going overboard. Although the bar offers plenty of televisions, the grainy screens desperately need an HD upgrade to improve the viewing experience. They mainly attract a football crowd on fall Saturdays—a definite plus—and since most games are broadcast, we had no trouble watching the ones we wanted.

Our server was lively, friendly, engaging, and efficient. She flawlessly handled our drink orders, quickly connected with us, provided a helpful list of recommendations for our upcoming night out, and overall did an excellent job. I had no complaints about my early morning vodka sprite with lime, and my husband’s beer was consistently refilled without delay.

A friend ordered a burger and fries, both served hot, fresh, and delicious—I even snagged a bite. The bar is spacious with ample seating, perfectly suited to our needs. It’s a straightforward sports bar—nothing more, nothing less.

With a few updates, this spot could truly shine. For what we were looking for, though, it was perfectly adequate, and I have no major complaints.

If you’re seeking a classic sports bar atmosphere, this place delivers with a lively crowd and walls lined with TVs. Inside, there are three bars and ample seating options, including booths equipped with personal screens, standard tables, and larger arrangements for groups. Outdoor seating is also available for those who prefer fresh air. For entertainment, you’ll find arcade-style sports games, electronic dartboards, several pool tables, and what looked like a couple of small stages.

The TVs are fairly standard—mostly projection screens with average picture quality. I didn’t check if the regular TVs were HD. A notable feature is the wall of jerseys showcasing names like Ripken, Namath, Mario, Selanne, Montana, McGwire, and a few others I couldn’t quite identify. When we visited, they were setting up for a Hold ’Em tournament, which apparently happens every Tuesday, though I’m unsure how it operates since preparations were still underway as we left.

We ordered wings and beer. The beer was reasonably priced at $4.75 for 23 ounces, and the wings were flavorful, offered in several varieties. Our waitress was young and attractive but somewhat slow and a bit dense. The other waitresses, dressed in tight shirts and short shorts resembling referee uniforms (as others have noted), were also pleasant to watch as they moved about.

Conveniently located near “The Strip,” right next to the Heinz Sports Museum and the Hampton Inn, this spot is easy to reach. We walked from there to Mellon Arena in about 20 minutes. If you want a straightforward sports bar to watch the game, this place fits the bill—just don’t expect anything beyond the usual.

This place fully embraces frat house chic, with a mishmash of worn-out, fourth-hand furniture, flickering fluorescent lights, and, oddly enough, Turkish news blaring on the big screen TV—seriously, what’s going on there? Finding the spot is a real hassle, especially after dark, so keep your GPS handy. Once you locate the building, you have to enter a code (mine was 0002) just to get into the lobby at night. From there, you take the elevator and press “M” for mezzanine—no signs pointed us in the right direction, and the elevator wouldn’t let us select any other floors without a security badge, so we had to figure it out through trial and error.

The moment we stepped off, my friend was ready to bail because the vibe felt pretty sketchy. But I’m glad we stuck around, because the food was genuinely impressive. I ordered the meat lover’s pizza, piled high with pepperoni, sausage, ham, and bacon—it was fantastic. My friend chose the Lamb Shish Kabob, seasoned with some kind of magical spices—flavor fireworks in every bite. It also came with a sesame seed flatbread that was just as delicious.

The location—upstairs, “over the river and through the woods”—and the atmosphere definitely leave much to be desired, but the food more than makes up for it. I deducted one star for the sketchy feel, but the meal was a total win. If this place relocated to a nicer, street-level spot, it would absolutely dominate.

Describing this place as just "hard to find" really doesn’t capture the full challenge—especially if it’s dark and you’re unfamiliar with the area. Still, the pizza crust genuinely impressed me; it’s delightfully flaky and flavorful. As someone who values a solid crust, I’d compare it to a soft Boboli—pleasantly easy to chew without irritating your mouth. I chose the Ephesus Pizza topped with lamb skewers (large, $16.00). Though it’s a white pizza with minimal toppings besides the lamb, they generously piled on 8 or 9 small skewers that were tender and full of flavor.

The setting, however, is a major downside. The restaurant is hidden on the mezzanine level (second floor) of a financial building. When I arrived, the main exterior doors were locked, but a nearby group entered a code to open a side door—an odd experience. Inside, I was immediately confronted by a stairwell cluttered with scattered trash cans. The pizza and sandwich joint itself was in disarray—bread crates stacked on the floor and trash bins overflowing. The bathroom was a filthy mess, caught in the middle of construction.

All this made me hesitant to eat there, unsure about the freshness of the food and the kitchen’s cleanliness. I’m not overly picky, but I do expect a basic level of hygiene. The place should look and feel clean and safe; only then can I truly enjoy whatever they serve. When your first impression is grimy and unkempt, that discomfort hits hard before the food even reaches your mouth.

That said, I do enjoy the pizza. I’d only recommend this spot to my pot-smoking, beer-drinking, party-loving friends because I’d be worried about how others might judge the establishment—and, by extension, how they might judge me and my tastes.

Honestly, even giving two stars feels generous. After completing a half marathon, my friends and I were eager for a quick meal to feed two starving toddlers and five adults. With positive Yelp reviews and the restaurant delivering within a mile, we expected our order to arrive quickly.

When we called, we confirmed they delivered to hotels. I pointed out, “It’s right by the Consol Energy Center, where the Penguins play,” thinking any local would recognize the area immediately. Despite this, we ended up repeating the hotel name four times—a clear early warning.

An hour passed with no pizza, so we called back. The person assured us the delivery driver was “on your street right now, two minutes away.” Yet, twenty minutes later, the driver called saying he was on his way, and then another ten minutes went by before he called again asking for directions. When the pizzas finally arrived, they were cold, the cheese had hardened, and the slices were wildly uneven—some enormous, some tiny—not the neat, uniform cuts we expected.

I felt bad for the driver, who explained his GPS had been stolen that morning. Still, despite our best efforts to clarify the location, the whole experience was a disaster. Hopefully, next time will be better.

I ordered two personal-sized pizzas along with spicy fries, fried zucchini, and onion rings. While the pizzas were genuinely tasty, the sides were disappointing—bland and overcooked.

The main reason for my one-star rating is the multiple health code violations I witnessed. For instance, a Red Bull can was left on the pizza dressing station. The woman who took my payment was also assembling a pizza and didn’t wash her hands afterward; she just went straight back to preparing the food. On top of that, she had long, yellowed nails and wasn’t wearing gloves while handling the pizza, which was quite off-putting.

To make matters worse, she stepped outside for a cigarette break right in front of the restaurant and, upon returning, blew smoke into the dining area.

Yelp lists the price range as $$, but I won’t be coming back. If what I saw at the front of the house reflects their standards, I’d rather not imagine the conditions in the kitchen. I don’t think my assessment is unfair—there were simply too many violations for me to feel comfortable.

5 stars. The buzz from vendors and shoppers in the Strip District about the enormous "RoethlisBurger" immediately drew me in—I had to see it for myself. Peppi’s has a dive bar vibe that fits just right. The flat top grill sits just behind the front counter, while the back seating area, decorated with Steelers memorabilia, adds a cozy atmosphere.

Since I wasn’t very hungry, I chose "The Phantom," a cheesesteak loaded with grilled mushrooms, onions, and a fried egg. My friends ordered a mushroom cheesesteak and the famous #7, the "RoethlisBurger." Each sandwich is a full foot long and comes with typical toppings like lettuce and tomato.

Although The Phantom was smaller than I expected, the flavors melded perfectly. My only gripe was wanting a bit more meat. After some online research, I learned all their steak subs contain only a quarter pound of steak.

We anticipated the RoethlisBurger to be much larger based on the window photo, but camera angles can be deceiving. It’s a blend of chopped burger and sausage, topped with American cheese and a fried egg.

Overall, I would have liked faster service—since some people who ordered after us received their food first—and a bit more meat in the sandwiches. Still, I’m definitely planning to return to try the RoethlisBurger again, now seeing it as a genuinely tasty sandwich rather than just a wild food challenge.

Peppi’s subs almost leave me speechless—almost. You simply have to try a Peppi’s sandwich; no excuses, even if you’re not hungry. Here’s a surprising fact: I can now unhinge my jaw and swallow things whole, something I never thought possible until Peppi’s came into my life. Nursing a hangover? Peppi’s seems to have some kind of magical HEALING POWERS that will set you right.

Since we’re among friends, I’ll be honest: I’m not a fan of Primanti’s. Saying that feels almost like admitting you didn’t like The Godfather, but it’s true—I’m just not into Primanti’s, and Peppi’s is definitely my favorite “Pittsburgh” sandwich.

I’ve enjoyed Peppi’s at the North Side, Dahntahn, and Strip District locations, and every spot delivers. I always order the Italian and can’t get enough of the generous dressing they pile on. And now, at just 9:30 AM, I’m already craving Peppi’s again. Damn.

Do yourself a favor and go eat at Peppi’s. This isn’t hype—it’s greasy, flavorful, and absolutely worth it.

I held a party at this venue last night, and I was genuinely impressed with the banquet facilities—they’re outstanding. We began with an assortment of hors d'oeuvres, and the lamb lollipops stood out as a highlight; they’re truly essential for any event here. In contrast, the lobster rolls didn’t make much of an impression, so I’d recommend skipping those when choosing your menu. The crabmeat stuffed mushrooms were also delicious and worth including.

For the entrees, we chose the filet and crabcake dinner. Although I’m usually hesitant about mass-produced filets, these were cooked to perfection. The crabcakes were packed with jumbo lump crabmeat and contained almost no filler, which was a pleasant surprise. Throughout the evening, Dante, the banquet manager, was exceptionally accommodating and ensured everything ran smoothly.

If you’re considering this venue for your event, I suggest booking the Symphony A and B rooms on the second floor; they offer a beautiful view of the North Shore and PNC Park. While the venue maintains strict food and beverage minimums, if your group is large enough (my party was about 50 people), you’ll receive a complimentary room and may even have the coat check fee waived.

Drink prices are reasonable, and they’re happy to accommodate requests for specific liquors. The hotel itself is stunning, with spacious rooms and very comfortable beds. Remember to ask for a room with a river view. As for parking, I recommend avoiding valet, since the $25 fee is rather high for Pittsburgh.

Drawn in by the glowing reviews and the promise of sophistication, I arrived genuinely excited for my two-night stay. The front desk generously upgraded me to a spacious room with a stunning river view, which unfortunately was one of the few positives. The rest of the room was disappointing: the desk phone was completely useless, the bedding uninspiring, and an incessant buzzing noise from the bathroom forced me to keep the door shut. To add to the frustration, the toilet failed to flush properly.

The service was equally underwhelming. From the start, I noticed my platinum upgrade hadn’t been honored. After contacting the front desk, they assured me they would check availability and call me back. They followed up by sending a bellman with new keys, but he simply handed them over and left without offering any assistance with moving my belongings. Later, while awaiting a FedEx delivery, I checked the tracking and discovered the hotel had rejected my package. After numerous calls to FedEx, the front desk, and the sender, the doorman finally delivered it hours later. Clearly, the hotel should have verified deliveries before refusing them.

To the hotel’s credit, the manager reached out with an apology and offered to send an amenity or a bottle of champagne to compensate for the inconvenience and my delayed checkout. I declined, but shortly after, hotel security knocked loudly on my door, demanding to know why I hadn’t yet vacated the room. That was definitely an unexpected surprise.

I usually choose Renaissance Hotels for their reputation as upscale, contemporary properties, but this location missed the mark entirely. The atmosphere felt stuffy and uninspired—more medieval than Renaissance, to be honest.

When my coworker, a Marriott rewards member, suggested this hotel, I was happy to take their advice—and it turned out to be a fantastic choice. The building’s age lends it a distinctive charm, sophistication, and character that sets it apart. From the moment we arrived, the décor caught my eye, with the grand staircase in the foyer quickly becoming a favorite feature. The location is unbeatable—just a short walk from restaurants and shopping, with the stadiums conveniently located across the river.

During our stay, we were pleasantly surprised by a special event hosted by the hotel for rewards members. This complimentary evening featured a prime rib carving station, homemade short rib pierogis, an open bar, a sushi bar, and a generous selection of desserts including cookies, brownies, and pastries. Every dish was delicious.

Our room was spacious, spotless, and included several modern updates, although the shower could have used some maintenance. The view from our windows, overlooking both the city and the river, was spectacular. The staff’s hospitality stood out; the check-in attendant was friendly, professional, and attentive, and every employee we encountered was warm and genuinely seemed to enjoy their work.

After returning home, I realized I had left my eyeglasses behind. Housekeeping found them and promptly mailed them back to me, arriving within just a few days.

Given the reasonable rates, excellent accommodations, and prime location, I truly can’t imagine staying anywhere else when visiting Pittsburgh.

Paying over $200 per night, I expected a bit more from our stay. My wife and I booked a king "city view" room, though calling it a city view is generous—the attached photos clearly show this. The lofty ceilings were the room’s best feature, giving the modest space a more open feel. Unfortunately, peeling wallpaper and chipped paint near the door were noticeable flaws that kept the hotel from feeling truly outstanding.

That said, the location was excellent. Being in town for a game at PNC Park made the convenience unbeatable. Service during both check-in and check-out was reliable and efficient.

Overall, I wouldn’t say this hotel is any better or worse than the Omni William Penn. While it offers a better location, the quality of the rooms and service is about the same. Next time, I’d simply choose whichever provides the better rate.

Although I grew up in Pittsburgh, this was my first stay at the Renaissance during an out-of-town wedding visit. The rooms were spotless, and the beds were exceptionally comfortable—a definite highlight—though the bathroom showed some wear. At check-in, there was confusion: my soon-to-be father-in-law had reserved three rooms and wanted all charges consolidated on his card to earn reward points, but the front desk staff struggled to accommodate this. Later, the same employee billed each room separately instead of charging the designated card, causing a minor billing issue the next morning. We're fairly easygoing, so it wasn’t a major problem, but the four-day hold on funds during travel was frustrating. Considering the room rates, I expected better-trained staff. The hotel itself is stunning, with elegant architecture, but unless you’re truly set on staying here, I would probably explore other options in Pittsburgh. To me, it just doesn’t seem worth the price.

There are a number of advantages at this venue. The covered walkway connecting the Westin to the Convention Center stands out, making it easy for guests to avoid getting wet during rain or to escape the stifling heat and humidity—especially helpful if you’re staying at the Westin. Once inside, the convention center impresses with its wide corridors and spacious halls, as well as an abundance of clean, well-kept restrooms. On one side, there’s also a balcony that overlooks the Allegheny River, offering a serene view and a comfortable place to enjoy some fresh air.

However, there are drawbacks to note. To get from the Westin walkway into the convention center, you have to take a slow elevator up or down a level, which is a bit of a hassle and could have been avoided if the walkway had started at the Westin’s third floor. Parking is also an issue—the area is quite expensive. While that’s expected in a city, you’ll need to walk several blocks to find parking that’s less than ten dollars a day.

I live in Bloomfield near the Children's Hospital, and despite the rain, I took my moo moo pie on a 25-minute trek down to Bow Wow (or whatever it’s called) to check out their doggie daycare and gather some basic information. When I arrived, soaked from the downpour, no one was there to greet me. Upon asking for more details, the woman on duty dismissed both me and my dog with a clear attitude. She showed little interest in offering any thorough explanations, responding curtly with “We do this, we do that.” Frustrated, I ended up leaving while she was still speaking.

I don’t usually write negative reviews, but if you choose to prioritize animals over people, that’s your prerogative—still, I deserve some respect. Her demeanor basically said, “I don’t know you, and I don’t care unless you’re paying for our services.” If that’s the impression you want to give, I’ll pass. It was a complete waste of time.

This hotel didn’t quite live up to my expectations and won’t be in my top three choices going forward. Here’s my assessment:

The location is definitely a strong point. Self-parking is available at the Greyhound Bus garage just a block away, costing between $5 and $13 per day depending on the weekday or weekend. Being within walking distance of all the sporting venues is a real convenience. Plus, there’s an excellent restaurant called Tonic right across the street, though it’s not affiliated with the hotel. The gym and indoor pool are also notable highlights.

However, there are several drawbacks. The standard room rate is quite steep. Parking at the hotel itself costs $20 per day with no in-and-out privileges, which felt overpriced. Our room had a persistent unpleasant odor that never went away. Housekeeping started knocking as early as 8 AM and would continue repeatedly if you didn’t hang the privacy sign. The hotel staff lacked the friendly and welcoming demeanor I’d expect from a Westin. The Fish Market, the hotel’s restaurant, was expensive, had limited snack options, and the service was disappointing. The walls were incredibly thin—we were woken by noises from the neighboring room, including someone using the bathroom, which was quite unpleasant. Being located right next to the convention center also means heavy traffic and plenty of annoying crowds.

One last note: we booked the hotel for $70 a night through Priceline, which is a reasonable deal for a 4-star property—you’d likely get either this hotel or the Omni at that price. If you can tolerate the issues I’ve outlined, it might work for you. Otherwise, I’d recommend spending a bit more elsewhere.

Last night, my companion and I arrived early—around 6:00 P.M. for our usual Friday date night—and were promptly seated in a back room. This area featured two large, elongated tables alongside several smaller tables for four. One of the large tables was already occupied by about 20 people, creating an overwhelmingly noisy environment. The room lacked any soundproofing on the walls or ceiling, which only amplified the din. We even saw guests at a four-person table get up and leave without placing orders. Adding to the disruption, many young children were running around, frequently obstructing the waitstaff—who, I must commend, provided excellent service.

We began with two Ketel One on the rocks, but when we tried to order a second round, we were told they had already run out—at just 6:15 on a Friday evening. For our meal, we shared a Waldhorn salad, which was quite enjoyable. Both of us then ordered the sauerbraten with spaetzle and red cabbage. Unfortunately, the meat was dry, and the spaetzle neither looked nor tasted authentic. From our experience, spaetzle are dumplings pressed through a sieve, but what we received resembled doughy noodles in both appearance and flavor.

Being a fan of Black Forest cake, I took a slice home hoping for a treat, but it was bland, with the fruit filling feeling like mere filler. This dessert was described as “homemade.”

The owners are said to be culinary-institute trained, but we find that hard to believe. Having dined at restaurants operated by culinary-institute graduates before, the food never tasted like this. We simply cannot understand the rave reviews or how culinary-institute graduates—if that claim is true—could serve fare of this quality. While taste is subjective, this experience was disappointing for us.

Originally, we planned to pick up take-out from a mid-range chain and eat in our room. However, when I spotted Waldhorn on the list, my love for German cuisine and the affordable prices convinced us to give it a chance, despite the glowing reviews seeming almost too good to be true. That decision led to one of the most unforgettable dining experiences we've ever had.

The staff greeted us warmly, showing impressive knowledge and attentiveness, and offered excellent recommendations for both beer and appetizers. We started with a Warsteiner Dunkel for him and a Spaten Oktoberfest for me, accompanied by a Gebackener Ziegenkäse appetizer. The pastry was wonderfully light and crisp, while the goat cheese, spinach, and sun-dried tomato filling remained surprisingly delicate even after dipping it in brown gravy and sour cream.

For our main courses, my partner chose the Hausgemachte Maultaschen "geschmelzt"—pasta stuffed with meat and spinach, lightly coated with sautéed onions and beef broth. I ordered the Wienerschnitzel but wasn’t thrilled with the fries and broccoli served alongside it. Fortunately, our server cheerfully swapped those sides for spaetzle and red cabbage.

Every bite was flawless. The spaetzle was incredibly light—truly the best I’ve ever tasted—and the red cabbage was beautifully prepared. The Wienerschnitzel melted in my mouth. His meal was a bit lighter but still satisfying and delicious.

All of this came at a very reasonable price: two beers, an appetizer, and two entrees totaled just $50 before tip. Now I’m annoyed it’s so far away!

I’ve always been a committed Costco shopper and moved away from Sam’s, but recently I decided to revisit BJ’s—and I was genuinely impressed by the changes. The last time I visited their Independence location, about eight years ago, I simply browsed without buying anything. However, after a friend showed me her new BJ’s card and described how much the store had evolved, I thought it deserved another chance.

I’m really glad I gave it a second look because BJ’s has made some significant improvements. They now offer smaller portions, so you’re not forced to buy an entire case of lettuce or a large side of beef. They also have a deli counter where you can order just one pound of sliced meat instead of three. Their brands and fresh meat cuts differ from Costco’s, which impressed me enough to purchase a membership.

What stood out most was the ability to buy a small salad mix for $2.59, rather than a large bag that spoils if not used quickly. The fresh meat I’ve tried has been excellent, and their wine prices are attractive, though the selection changes weekly and can be somewhat unpredictable.

While BJ’s isn’t as large as Costco, it’s definitely worth the membership fee. The self-checkout lanes were a big convenience, with no waiting at all. If it’s been a while since your last visit to BJ’s, I’d recommend giving it another try—they’re clearly refreshing their image!

BJ’s functions like a warehouse on steroids—the shelves soar close to the ceiling, and the store surpasses a typical Wal-Mart in size. While you can pay a 15% surcharge for a one-time visit, the $50 annual membership clearly offers better value. They run specials and promotions, but these discounts aren’t available year-round.

Their selection includes nearly everything you might need. Although it may not fully replace your local grocery store, buying in bulk here can lead to significant savings. Some two-packs come at roughly 50% higher prices than single items at Harris Teeter, but many other products are competitively priced with Wal-Mart.

The pet food section stood out to me, especially when I found a 50-pound bag of the same dog food I usually buy at Petsmart for $10 less.

Considering the warehouse deals and gas prices that are better than other nearby stations—though still above South Carolina’s rates—I decided to join as a member. I definitely plan to return to BJ’s.

My overall experience was fairly average—I’ve definitely had better seafood elsewhere. The biscuits were the highlight of the meal. Despite it being a busy Friday night, we were seated quickly, and the server was satisfactory.

However, the seafood was somewhat disappointing. It arrived slightly undercooked and drenched in butter. While I enjoy butter, too much can spoil a dish. The shrimp were very small, and the lobster tail was equally tiny.

The price felt steep, especially since we ordered two children’s meals. The kids’ mac and cheese was simply boxed Kraft, which seemed a bit absurd at $5.99. It’s frustrating that kids’ menus rarely offer more than chicken fingers and mac and cheese. Some children have adventurous palates and would appreciate more authentic options.

I might come back for lunch to savor the biscuits again, but I’ll probably skip dinner here next time.

The portions were generous, and the food quality met expectations, but the service was seriously lacking. After our server handed over the bill, she took a full 15 minutes before casually returning to collect it along with our credit card. Another 10 minutes passed before she finally brought back the receipt for me to sign. Because of her slow pace and inattentiveness, what should have been a straightforward meal stretched to an hour and a half—twice as long as necessary. To add to the frustration, I never received a soda refill. All of this happened during a quiet period, as we arrived around 4:30 PM on a Saturday.

As for the food, I enjoyed the Admiral’s Feast so much that I brought half of it home. My wife was also pleased with her Crab Feast. The Cheddar Bay biscuits stood out as a highlight and helped compensate for some of the other shortcomings. If I find myself craving them again, I’ll likely just call ahead and pick them up.

I truly hope our server never visits a zoo—I’d hate for her to get dizzy watching the tortoises amble along at their slow pace. As for me, I won’t be returning to this location.

We were greeted by two courteous servers, and the ordering process went smoothly without any problems. I chose the Bar Harbor and asked for some Cajun seasoning to boost the flavor, which turned out really well—I have no complaints there.

At the same time, my wife’s grandmother ordered steak and lobster, requesting her steak be cooked medium. Unfortunately, it arrived well done, and to our surprise, the lobster was raw. I can’t understand how that happened, especially since steak and lobster are prepared separately. She sent it back, but by the time her meal was returned, we had already finished both our main courses and dessert. Honestly, how does it take that long to cook a medium steak? It doesn’t! By then, she had completely lost her appetite.

When the bill came, the server told me the manager had comped her meal due to the mistake, so we wouldn’t have to pay for it. However, they then handed her another bill, insisting she was responsible for payment after all. I can’t make sense of that, but in the end, she ended up paying for the meal the manager promised would be free.

Toward the end of our visit, the servers basically disappeared, leaving everything chaotic and disorganized. The overall quality of the establishment took a steep dive. The only bright spot? The cheese biscuits—they were absolutely incredible! Everything else, however, was a complete letdown.

During a recent family dinner, our discussion unexpectedly focused on my dad’s enduring passion for dining out, with Red Lobster as his top choice. I’ve always seen Red Lobster as the seafood equivalent of fast food, so it’s rarely my preferred spot.

However, this visit pleasantly surprised me. Unlike previous disappointing experiences at other Red Lobster locations, this time everyone left satisfied and happy. We arrived in separate cars, and the first thing I noticed was how far the handicap parking spots were from the entrance. My parents parked there, and the walk to the front door was quite challenging for them. Perhaps the layout is designed to encourage some pre-meal activity? I’m not sure, but thankfully the weather was beautiful.

Inside, the staff greeted us warmly, their cheerful smiles and genuine friendliness creating a welcoming atmosphere. Within about fifteen minutes, we were seated. Dad ordered his usual Admiral’s Feast, I opted for the lobster pizza (watching my calories), my wife chose a pasta dish, my mom went with the stuffed flounder, and the kids stuck to fries.

Each dish was delicious—perfectly cooked and served promptly. Dad even remarked that this was the best Red Lobster he’s visited in a long time.

The total bill was $101 for six people, which seemed quite reasonable to me. I would definitely recommend this location.

Jason's Deli provides a quick and straightforward dining experience: you order and pay as you arrive, and your meal is promptly brought to your table. The menu offers a solid selection of classic deli favorites you’d expect.

However, a glaring flaw in their service stands out. The staff seem completely unaware of the freeloading happening around them. While I’ve never taken advantage myself, it’s common to see customers freely helping themselves to the salad bar and taking as much cake as they want. It’s puzzling why anyone would pay for a fountain drink when the cups are conveniently placed right next to the dispenser.

My younger brother especially loves Jason’s Deli because of the candy displays and specialty soft drinks served in glass bottles. We’ve lost count of how many times we’ve had to check his pockets, either sending him back or making him pay for the drinks he’s casually walked off with.

Despite all this sneaky behavior happening right under the staff’s noses, Jason’s Deli remains a simple, dependable spot where you really can’t go wrong.

I wanted a genuine deli sandwich—not just another Subway—so I decided to try this place. For $10.00, I received a 6-inch meatball sub on a white bun, accompanied by Lay's potato chips, a pickle spear, and a regular soda. Unfortunately, the sub wasn’t any better than Subway’s. It felt like a complete waste of my time and money. I could have had the same meal elsewhere (without the pickle) and enjoyed a wider selection of chips.

Their menu is extensive, but I have no idea how their soups, salads, or other dishes compare. I couldn’t even find a list of bread options, which made navigating the menu frustrating. Overall, the food quality didn’t make the effort worthwhile.

UPDATE: At a friend’s recommendation, I returned for lunch on Tuesday (11/1). This time, I ordered the chicken club salad and a cup of Southwestern Chicken Chili—both were quite good. My total was $14.90. Since the food was decent but not exceptional, I’m raising my rating to 2 stars. Still, it remains far too expensive for what you get.

Jason’s food is genuinely delicious—no complaints there. However, the to-go experience is a completely different story and often quite frustrating. About once a month, the entire office decides to order from Jason’s for lunch, and naturally, I’m the one responsible for managing everything.

When I first found out they offered delivery, I thought, “Great, right?” Unfortunately, that wasn’t the case. There’s an $8 delivery fee that they conveniently don’t mention over the phone, which feels unfair. On one occasion, when the money collected at work didn’t add up, I had to call back for an itemized list of sandwich prices—and only then was I informed about the delivery charge. They waived it since it wasn’t disclosed upfront, but seriously, $8 to deliver just one mile? That’s a hard pass from me. I’m not going through that again.

Now, I place all orders by phone and pick them up myself. But out of roughly 20 orders, not once has everything been correct. Salad dressings get left out, menu items go missing, and sometimes items don’t even appear on the ticket. Requests for extra pickles? Usually ignored. It’s an ongoing uphill battle.

Because of all this, I’ve learned to thoroughly check every item before leaving. My advice to anyone picking up a to-go order? Do the same.

Like I said, the food is really good—but honestly, ordering a few sandwiches and salads shouldn’t be this complicated.

Rey—with an “E”—clearly stands out as the most competent and attentive employee, warmly greeting customers as they arrive, exactly as it should be.

Reflecting on my visits, the previous one went fairly well except for one major problem: the service was painfully slow. Even with an appointment, I ended up waiting an hour and a half just for an oil change.

Sadly, this latest visit showed little improvement. Despite having an appointment and the shop being busy, the service pace remained sluggish. What’s even more troubling is that the oil change warning light on my dashboard never turned off afterward. Doesn’t that imply the oil change wasn’t actually done? The last time I was there, that light went off right after the service was completed.

Adding to my frustration, the sticker placed on my windshield to indicate the next oil change wasn’t updated and had the wrong mileage written on it. Overall, this experience left me quite dissatisfied.

I can’t quite understand why emergency room visits take so long. Watching ER on TV, it never seems this slow. In my slightly delirious state, I look around and see the staff moving at a snail’s pace. Honestly, there’s no real urgency here. At this point, why not rename the EMERGENCY room to “Step right up to the pain, misery, and sickness spectacle”? Because this is truly ridiculous.

Here’s how this saga unfolded:

- 6:20 pm: Began yelling and waiting.  
- 8:28 pm: Still waiting; took a photo of Levine’s Children’s Room.  
- 8:35 pm: Still waiting; snapped a picture of the door we’re stuck waiting on for our name to be called.  
- 9:03 pm: Finally called—woohoo!  
- 9:23 pm: Still waiting; just learned the doctor hasn’t even entered the room yet. It feels like a theme park ride—one large room, then around the corner, and more waiting.  
- 9:37 pm: Doctor arrived, but the waiting continues.  
- 11:36 pm: Still here, still waiting.  
- The sun is nearly up!

Is there a doctor in the house, anyone?

Now, at 12:15 am, we’re finally heading out. If you need an emergency room, I recommend Presby in Matthews—the wait was half as long, and the people we met at the pharmacy had far better experiences than we did.

—NCFoodGuy

When my daughter first hurt her wrist, we went straight to the ER for an x-ray to make sure there was no fracture. The wait was short, and every staff member we interacted with was welcoming and attentive, which made the experience much smoother.

We returned for her wisdom teeth extraction, with the oral surgeon overseeing all the preparations and offering thorough pre-op instructions. We arrived on time, completed the insurance paperwork, and she was seen quickly. The procedure went well, allowing her to go home the same day.

I've also accompanied a family member and a neighbor to the ER when they suspected they were having heart attacks. On both occasions, the staff responded promptly, taking them back immediately after they showed cardiac symptoms. Each time, the team was compassionate and supportive, and I was able to check in on the patients.

Every visit has shown me a hospital that is consistently spotless and never crowded. These experiences have convinced me that this is a well-managed facility that delivers excellent care. Having a full-service hospital close by is a major advantage, and I see no reason to travel downtown to the main hospital.
