This evening, my wife drove me to the emergency room due to intense pain from a kidney stone. We arrived around 10 pm, and after registering, I waited about half an hour before my vitals were taken. Then, I was moved to a smaller waiting room where I stayed until 1 am. At that point, I informed the nurse that I was leaving. She told me I was third in line for a treatment room. I likened the situation to arriving at Firebird’s at 7 pm on a Saturday and enduring an endless wait for a table. She agreed I would likely be waiting several more hours, which was simply unacceptable.

Throughout this experience, the nurses and staff were exceptional, but the delay in seeing a doctor was downright exasperating. They offered to provide a note for my employer if I stayed as long as necessary, but since I’m self-employed, that held no incentive, and I made this clear. Next, they wanted to start a saline drip and have me consult with a doctor. Fortunately, I had a CT scan within the first hour of waiting—that was definitely the swiftest part of the entire ordeal. That was the only bright moment in an otherwise disappointing evening. To give credit where it’s due, Cynthia, the nurse who started my IV, did an outstanding job. Still, the rest of my experience made it evident the ER desperately needs to revamp its triage system.

For reasons that completely baffle me, CMC-Pineville insisted I arrive a full hour early at the main entrance. The only positive aspect of this early arrival was that it guaranteed ample surface parking and an entirely empty main waiting area, which was somewhat comforting.

The MRI waiting room was furnished with wide chairs, some equipped with circular tables attached to their left armrests. The walls were painted in soft blue and olive green hues. A 47" LG TV was prominently mounted in the center of the wall behind the check-in window. Additionally, a small alcove offered a coffee maker and bottled water.

While seated behind a column, the technician seemed oblivious to my presence and did not survey the entire room. I had to move closer to the door and wait for her to come out again. The MRI machine was a 2006 GE model. Unlike many MRI machines that emit somewhat melodic sounds, this one caused my body to vibrate—an unusual and unsettling sensation.

Up until that moment, my experience had been quite positive. However, things quickly deteriorated when it was time to inject the radioactive contrast. The MRI technician and another staff member attempted the injection but ended up collapsing veins in both arms. When they suggested trying my hands, I declined and requested a butterfly needle in a forearm vein instead. Their response was to insert the needle into my left wrist, and as the contrast was pushed through, it burned painfully along the vein. I will never have another MRI at this facility. Perhaps they anticipated negative feedback, since I have yet to receive any survey requests for input.

Sam the Cooking Guy is one of my favorite online shows, and his Cedar Plank Salmon looked absolutely breathtaking. Inspired by that, I decided to get cedar planks myself. Instead of ordering online for $10 to $34.99 or picking them up at Walmart or similar stores for about $15, I chose to follow Sam’s advice and visit a lumber yard—or at least something close to it.

When I arrived, I went straight to the wood section and asked the staff for untreated cedar wood. He directed me toward a variety of woods. After I explained my plan, he actually suggested I just go to Walmart. No thanks! Instead, he showed me some 6-foot cedar boards. I grabbed one and asked if he could cut it into 12-inch planks. He did, and I was out the door.

The total cost for 6 feet of cedar wood, cut into six 12-inch planks, was just $2.76. So, rather than spending $10 to $35 on two 12-inch planks, I paid only $2.76 for six. WINNING!!! (And yes, I took pictures.)

At first, I was quite anxious, but the service here was far better than what I experienced at the Northlake location. Although David's usually doesn’t carry my size, the staff genuinely listened and understood that I had already spoken with the bride and received approval to choose a dress different from the one on her registry.

What really stood out was that no one suggested I “eat more” or buy a larger dress to alter—both options felt completely impractical. They treated me with sincere care, and I was in and out within about thirty minutes. This included trying on the dress I wanted in their smallest size (a 2), and their alterations specialist even paused her work to come pin me up and confirm it was indeed too big.

On top of that, I avoided any traffic, which was definitely a bonus.

They sold me on lofty promises and presented the whole process as flawless, but the reality was a letdown when I went to pick up my dress. The staff at the entrance were noticeably rude, insisting I sign a form to claim my dress before even allowing me to look at it. When I refused to sign without seeing the dress first, the woman at the front stayed cold and unhelpful. Then, without warning, another employee told me to grab my dress and follow her to the back, which only made my frustration with their attitude worse.

By the time I got to the back, I was shaking and almost in tears from how stressful the situation had become. When I opened the bag, I was instantly disappointed—the dress was covered in wrinkles, and not one staff member offered to help me try it on to make sure it fit. This was hands down the worst experience I’ve ever had, especially considering I brought them business. The dress was expensive, and, on top of that, all seven of my bridesmaids also bought their dresses from this store.

I simply cannot recommend the David’s Bridal in Pineville. Their corporate office really needs to improve staff training and customer service. To make matters worse, the person who originally sold me the dress isn’t working there anymore.

I am fully determined to report this establishment to the corporate office. Our family’s very first takeout experience quickly became our last. I was shocked to see the cashier handle the register and then place lids on tartar sauce containers without washing their hands or wearing gloves, despite frequently touching the register.

While our order was being handed over, I noticed a line cook eating with bare hands—no gloves at all. The unsanitary behavior was glaringly obvious. I asked another employee to get the manager’s attention, but she froze, acting as if she didn’t know who the manager was. Eventually, I made eye contact with the manager, who seemed to acknowledge I was right before heading into the kitchen, likely to inform the cook he had been caught.

The manager himself appeared unkempt, wore no name tag, and gave no indication he was in charge. I insisted on a full refund—I refused to waste my money there. When I asked for his name, he bluntly replied, “Mr. Rapport.” That’s

The pizza was supposed to come with olives and tomatoes, but when it arrived, it was nearly buried under a layer of onions, with only a few small pieces of olives and tomatoes sparsely scattered. It looked more like an onion tart, and my children refused to eat it outright. Adding to our frustration, the waitress forgot to bring our tea and water and never refilled our drinks, so we had to get and manage those ourselves.

On a different occasion, my daughter wanted to celebrate her birthday dinner there with some friends. We made reservations months in advance and even called the day before to confirm. However, when we arrived, the staff seemed confused and didn’t acknowledge that we were waiting. They eventually escorted us inside but tried to seat us in a booth that was far too cramped and had a large tear in the seat—completely unacceptable. We finally secured a table large enough for everyone, but the service remained inconsistent throughout.

As for the food, nothing was particularly impressive. It tasted like Chef Boyardee or frozen dinners. While serving family style might be a nice idea, it felt awkward when dining out with friends.

During our last visit, four of us went, and three ended up sick for several days afterward. Two required emergency room visits for IV treatment, and one had to see a doctor for Phenergan. After that experience, there’s no chance we’ll be returning.

We still enjoy Buca and think it’s worth visiting if you haven’t yet, but I’m less enthusiastic about recommending it as strongly as before. The most obvious change is the portion sizes—they’ve clearly shrunk, almost as if caught in Dr. Evil’s shrinking ray. While smaller servings have become more common, the reduction here feels especially significant, likely because Buca’s prices have always been on the higher side. Although the warm, inviting atmosphere remains, the smaller plates make the experience less satisfying overall.

Value has also taken a hit. The flavors remain consistent, but the flashy new menu seems designed more to encourage spending than to offer the simple, straightforward options Buca once provided. Even the staff now seem more focused on upselling rather than maintaining the relaxed, family-style service that used to be a highlight. Altogether, it just doesn’t feel the same anymore.

I visited Carolina Place around 1:30 pm, drawn by its reputation as Charlotte’s top Italian restaurant.

To begin with the positives, I ordered the baked rigatoni with meat sauce and spicy Italian sausage, and it truly impressed me. If you appreciate bold, spicy flavors like I do, this dish exceeds what you'd typically expect from a chain. The lunch portion was huge—definitely more than I could finish.

Unfortunately, that’s where the positives end. The service was unexpectedly poor, even though the restaurant wasn’t busy and it wasn’t late in the lunch hour. I also found the dinner prices quite steep for Southern Italian pasta dishes, especially considering the Charlotte location. Their “family dining” concept seemed more focused on easing the kitchen’s workload than enhancing the customer experience.

For me, a satisfying dining experience involves sampling a variety of dishes—not just facing an overwhelming mound of carbs.

Buca di Beppo stands out by fully embracing the flashy, extravagant spirit of Italian-American culture. From the moment you arrive, statues wrapped in Christmas lights set a festive tone, while inside, quirky photos of nuns playing in the ocean add to the vibrant, larger-than-life atmosphere.

Your journey to the table is anything but ordinary. It winds through the kitchen—where you’ll find a booth table—and then passes the Pope Room, a party space centered around a somewhat eerie wax bust slowly rotating on a dais.

Meals are served family style, with a "small" plate more than enough for two to three people. The food consistently impresses; I especially enjoy the baked pasta dishes, garlic bread, and hearty salads that can easily serve as a meal on their own. This is definitely a spot to visit only if you’re truly hungry.

The sole Charlotte location is in Pineville, which can be a bit inconvenient to reach. Still, whenever I’m nearby, it’s a fantastic place to stop in!

Buca di Beppo provides a truly unique dining experience—at least from what I’ve encountered, no other restaurant quite matches it. This Italian venue specializes in family-style meals, where each dish is meant to be shared among your group. So, when dining with two to four people, ordering just one or two dishes usually satisfies everyone. Since I’m somewhat particular about my food, I typically prefer having my own plate rather than sharing.

Unfortunately, the service during my visit was disappointing. Our server appeared indifferent and lacked enthusiasm for his role. Although he agreed to split the bill among the five of us, there was a drawback: one person ordered an alcoholic drink, and the cost of that beverage was divided across the entire group.

One unique aspect of the experience is that when you’re seated, they lead you through the kitchen, which even features a table where guests can dine. Honestly, that was the only positive part of my visit.

I called at 6 p.m. to ask about reservations for that night and was told they were accepting them, but only for 7:15 p.m., not 7:00. We reserved a table for four at 7:15 and arrived early at 7:10. We were informed they’d call our name once the table was ready. When I checked again at 7:25, they said they were behind schedule with several parties ahead of us. Our name was finally called at 7:46, after seating four tables of four and one table of six. Anyone can take a reservation, but actually honoring it—that’s what really matters, right? (UNHAPPY)

The food was underwhelming: a small salad shared among the table, two dinners divided among four people, a side of pasta with a meatball, a $12 bottle of wine, and two desserts. Nothing memorable, especially not for nearly $150. Around us, five or six “birthday/clapping” celebrations created an Applebee’s-like atmosphere. The waitstaff were friendly, efficient, and attractive, but honestly, I’d rather have a slow, unattractive server if the food were better. No rush to return anytime soon.

For quite some time, I thought the exterior of this restaurant looked somewhat flashy. Still, after being around for years, I finally decided to try it with some friends who were celebrating a new job. Our bread and drinks arrived promptly, accompanied by olive oil and balsamic vinegar for dipping.

We started with the mixed green salad, adding Gorgonzola and prosciutto on the side. When I think of mixed greens, I usually picture mesclun, arugula, frisée, and similar leafy varieties. While I wouldn’t expect those particular greens at an Italian restaurant, I was puzzled by the label "mixed greens" here. The only mix I noticed was iceberg lettuce and red cabbage, with maybe five olives and three pepperoncinis scattered throughout. The prosciutto and Gorgonzola were generously portioned, but the prosciutto looked burnt and resembled prepackaged bacon bits. Overall, the salad was just average.

For our main course, we chose the large spicy chicken rigatoni. This is where the meal really fell short. The chicken and peas didn’t taste fresh, and the sauce was thin and lacking depth and flavor. It simply didn’t live up to the authentic experience I had hoped for.

The service was adequate, but next time I’m craving Italian, I’ll probably skip Buca.

Our group of seven ended up with a bill close to $200, despite not ordering any alcoholic drinks, which felt quite pricey. The food was fairly average overall. The family-style portions are the main feature here. For instance, when you order spaghetti and meatballs, you receive a large bowl of pasta accompanied by just two or three meatballs, each about the size of a softball. The meatballs were disappointing, and dividing them among the group was awkward. I would have preferred 8 to 10 smaller meatballs to share.

The atmosphere is cozy and distinctly Italian. While it doesn’t quite capture the authentic feel of Boston’s North End, it’s clear the restaurant puts in a solid effort.

One suggestion for the restaurant: consider relocating the dumpster. It sits prominently in the parking lot near the main entrance, and when the wind shifts, unpleasant odors drift over—definitely not the best impression when arriving or leaving.

Returning an item without a receipt can be frustrating at many retailers, but at least they politely inform you upfront that any refund will be based on the lowest recent sale price. This policy is clearly communicated from the start. At the K—hopefully unrelated to the Bruces we treasure here in Crown Town—you must first provide your ID, address, and phone number before they even disclose what compensation you might receive for your discounted merchandise. After that, you’re left wandering the aisles in a daze, hoping to find something else to buy. Alternatively, you could simply donate the card to someone in need and let them handle it.

If you decide to browse this store, don’t expect the bright, well-lit, or recently updated atmosphere typical of other retailers aiming to attract customers. Instead, outdated flat-screen monitors—stands and all—are awkwardly hung from the ceiling in an attempt to look modern. There are no fancy boxes, just bare computer screens suspended overhead, not even powered on. Really? Had I stopped by before the holidays, that gift card would have ended up in the red kettle out front—if they’d have accepted it at all.

Years ago, I discovered that Taco Bell in the US doesn’t serve fries—a fact that became apparent when my group unintentionally upset an employee by ordering fries supreme. It genuinely felt like we were violating a cherished family tradition by requesting ground beef and cheese on fries instead of nachos.

Unlike in Canada, combos here come with a taco rather than a side. So, if you want nachos supreme, you have to ask for them specifically.

On the plus side, prices in the US are noticeably lower, a common trend across fast food chains nationwide. For example, a Gordita combo costs about $5 here, compared to over $6 in Canada.

This location stood out for its dependable service and quick food delivery. They offer three different Doritos taco varieties, and I’m hopeful Canada will add this selection to its menu soon.

Finally, kudos to the person who swapped a Doritos taco into a Gordita—a smart move that resulted in an absolutely delicious combination!

The item arrived damaged, which I was willing to overlook, but the handling of the situation was quite unsatisfactory. At first, I was told I’d have to wait an extra month for a replacement, but later I was informed it would arrive a week earlier. Before delivery, I was notified of an error and that the only remaining piece was also damaged. I even contacted another Haverty’s location to ask if they could sell their floor model as the other store had, but they declined.

On July 4th, I decided to cancel my order and purchased furniture from a competitor to furnish two rooms in my new home. Unfortunately, my cancellation and refund were never processed. When I called Haverty’s on Friday to check the refund status, they advised me to call back on Monday. When I did, I was told it still hadn’t been handled. Finally, I connected with someone who processed the refund that day.

Overall, this was a very frustrating experience. Although my salesperson was excellent and I liked the products, I would not do business with this company again because of the complications caused by this single issue.

After reading the reviews, I felt hesitant but decided to try it since the meal was complimentary. I arrived around 4:45 for an early dinner and noticed roughly five groups waiting in a crowded lobby, yet no staff were visible—the hostess station was completely unattended. The only employee I saw anywhere in the restaurant was the bartender.

After waiting about five minutes, a young woman finally came over and asked how many were in our party. When I responded, “Two of us, but is there a wait?” she informed me, “Yes, at least 10-15 minutes.” Looking around, I observed many more empty tables than occupied ones. As David K highlighted, while I understand the importance of shifts and seating protocols, customer service and the impression guests receive should always come first.

Worried about what the rest of the experience might entail, I left before being seated. Based on other reviews, it seems I didn’t miss much. Ultimately, the problem appears to stem from poor management. When a manager can’t effectively run the business, it’s unfair to blame the employees.

This store offers a wide variety that caters to all kinds of animals. When I urgently needed an aviary specialist from Banfield Vets, their traveling setup was somewhat inconvenient for me. The selection of bird toys for larger birds is also rather limited. However, their bird food and treats are impressively diverse, and the dog treat section stands out with options far beyond what you'd typically find at Walmart or neighborhood grocery stores.

My petite 10-year-old Chihuahua weighs just 3 pounds—about the size of a soda can with legs—and has very few teeth left. The training reward treats are perfectly sized for her tiny mouth and soft enough for her to chew comfortably.

After exploring every section of the store, I can confidently say that each area is well-stocked, no matter what you’re seeking. Being able to bring my pets inside makes shopping here even more enjoyable. The staff is always friendly and attentive, ensuring every visit is a pleasant experience.

I usually shop at the Matthews Best Buy, the former Circuit City location, which tends to feel a bit more crowded. On this visit to a different branch, I immediately noticed the absence of the usual greeting from the security guard at the entrance—a small but familiar gesture that’s standard in Matthews but missing here.

The employee in the video game section was very knowledgeable and answered all my questions effortlessly. Since my cousin was undecided about making a major purchase, we spent quite some time trying out the Kinect demo. I’m similarly indecisive, though I usually just pick what I want and leave. Buyer’s remorse often follows, but I’ve learned it’s best to go home and enjoy your purchase instead of hunting for better deals elsewhere—a scenario that frequently happens with Best Buy products, in my experience.

The Apple section at this store really stood out—so sleek and shiny, it practically dares you to splurge on things you likely can’t afford without taking out a small loan.

Among all the Best Buy locations my family frequents—from Wilmington to Johnson City—this one is by far the worst. Normally, I avoid writing negative reviews, but after three separate frustrating incidents here, I’ve reached my breaking point.

It all started last year when I bought a new laptop to replace my four-year-old device, also purchased at Best Buy. Despite their assurances, the Geek Squad wiped my old laptop clean without informing me beforehand, causing me to lose a significant amount of important data. Then, they repeatedly told me both computers were ready but kept contacting the wrong person. Each time we arrived to pick them up, the computers weren’t prepared—this happened three times—leading to a maddening cycle of wasted trips and time.

A year later, the same issues reoccurred. After waiting 45 minutes for them to locate me in their system—despite having paid extra for a one-year plan they couldn’t find six months in—I received no notification to collect my computer, even seven days after they said it was ready. When I finally made the trip, it still wasn’t ready. Their response? “Oh, huh, I don’t know what happened there!”—without so much as an apology. A call three days later revealed it was ready at that moment, only for me to discover the Geek Squad had improperly installed it from the start, causing the problems.

This store clearly shows a lack of respect for customers and appears staffed by individuals who can’t follow simple instructions or correctly dial a phone number. The entire experience has been utterly infuriating.

After a quick visit to The Home Depot in the shopping plaza across from Carolina Place Mall, I decided to check out Best Buy to see if they carried what I needed. Usually, I depend on Amazon and prefer to avoid in-store shopping whenever possible—even though I work in designing big box retailers. This time, it was a spontaneous decision: the weather was nice, I wanted to walk off lunch, and Best Buy was right nearby.

The store was clean and featured the familiar layout typical of Best Buy. A young woman stood mid-aisle, seemingly ready to assist customers. When I asked her about a wireless router, she directed me toward the computer section. Confident in my knowledge of what a router looks like, I quickly located them without needing help from the few staff members present. I then compared prices and examined packaging, having already researched online and knowing exactly what I wanted.

Finding the Netgear router, I used my Amazon price check app and discovered it was priced the same at Best Buy as on Amazon. That sealed my decision. I also checked two higher-end models I had in hand, and their prices matched Amazon’s exactly—demonstrating that Best Buy was offering competitive pricing.

Although it was a Sunday shortly after church, the store seemed well staffed. At checkout, I approached a friendly, efficient young woman. We exchanged a few words while I searched through my wallet for my debit card. Given my limited patience for shopping, this visit turned out to be unexpectedly smooth and pleasant.

What keeps me coming back to Bruegger’s is their Jalapeño Cheese specialty bagel—chewy, cheesy, spicy, and absolutely delicious. Sometimes I have it with just cream cheese, other times as a breakfast bagel with egg, but more often I pile on hummus, veggie cream cheese, and plenty of fresh veggies.

That said, I find the prices at Bruegger’s a bit steep. The hummus sandwich I enjoy costs about $5, which feels pricey for what you get. It used to be offered as a full menu item, but now I have to order each ingredient separately, which seems to push the cost higher.

Although it’s a fast food spot, most of the staff are young and often seem distracted or confused—especially when I ask for hummus, which might be an unusual request. What I really want is a genuine smile, some politeness, and a bit of enthusiasm when I hand over my hard-earned money.

Finally, the decor and cleanliness leave something to be desired. The space could definitely benefit from a refresh to brighten the atmosphere and make it more welcoming.

When I read reviews, I usually focus on the negatives to avoid those places and help others do the same. However, this location clearly deserves my full five stars—if I could, I’d give it six. The staff consistently impress with their politeness, friendliness, attentiveness, and efficiency. Their team remains notably stable, which assures me that no matter the day or early morning hours (weekends included), I’ll receive the same excellent product and service. They’re never understaffed.

The bagels here are unmatched, both locally and across the entire Bruegger’s chain. While the “thank you baker” routine can feel somewhat rehearsed, this spot genuinely earns the gratitude of both employees and customers.

A minor irritation is having to wait in line for a quick bagel and to-go coffee while others place elaborate dine-in orders—though this mostly happens on weekends. Thankfully, the self-serve coffee bar helps save time and eases the process for everyone.

I live roughly equidistant from several Bruegger’s locations and occasionally visit others, but I’m almost always disappointed—especially at the Park Road store, as I’ve noted in another review. Maybe I’m slow to learn, but I’m grateful that at least one location gets it absolutely right.

Because this mall is well outside my usual routes, getting there is pretty inconvenient and feels like a bit of a hassle. The constant traffic congestion in the area only adds to my frustration, which is a shame considering the parking lot is genuinely one of the best in the city.

Even with the trouble of reaching it, the mall delivers a solid mix of stores for everyday shopping, though the prices aren’t all that competitive. Overall, it’s a typical mall, and that works just fine for me. There’s almost always a steady stream of visitors, both inside and out, and the outparcels are nearly always full. It’s rare to see empty stores, and the surrounding blocks are often buzzing with activity—something I find genuinely impressive.

Unlike Concord Mills, where new buildings seem to pop up constantly, this mall opts to repurpose older structures, which I really appreciate. Still, setting aside some space for better infrastructure would go a long way in easing the persistent traffic issues.

The mall immediately grabs your attention with its spotless exterior and meticulously maintained grounds, while the interior is just as immaculate. What strikes me as unusual, however, is the presence of FIVE department stores. Americans clearly have a strong affinity for department stores, a stark contrast to Canadian malls where two is typically the limit, and even Sears is struggling to survive.

Even more striking is the heavy concentration of sportswear shops. If you were blindfolded and brought here, you'd likely assume that everyone in Charlotte exclusively wears hoodies, basketball shorts, and Nikes.

Aside from the sportswear outlets, the mall includes the familiar chain retailers like Aeropostale, Victoria’s Secret, and XXI. Several restaurants are directly attached to the mall, with a few more scattered throughout the parking lot. The food court keeps things straightforward, featuring a frozen yogurt spot, McDonald’s, and Chick-fil-A.

In my experience, even when the food is satisfactory, poor service can completely ruin both the meal and the overall visit. That’s exactly what happened when my coworker and I stopped by Applebee’s for the Pick n’ Pair lunch special. The hostess seated us without a single greeting—and to make matters worse, she also served as our waitress. Sarcasm fully intended.

She took our drink order and then disappeared. Several minutes passed before she returned with the drinks and asked if we were ready to order. I chose the Fiesta Chicken Chopped Salad and the New Chicken Tortilla Soup.

I truly don’t understand how it can take so long to serve soup and salad, especially with only two other tables occupied during a late afternoon visit. It definitely shouldn’t consume half of my lunch break. For those of us seeking a brief escape from the office for some peace during the workday, every minute counts.

When the food finally arrived, with only a few minutes left, I hurried through it. The salad was spicy, and the jalapeño dressing was flavorful. The chicken tortilla soup was mediocre—it could have used more chicken and a stronger kick.

Overall, the experience was dreadful. The service was terrible, and the food was just passable. I won’t be returning to this location anytime soon.

When we arrived, Gary greeted us and asked what we were seeking. I mentioned that we were interested in both rings. He showed me a few choices that might complement my ring, and one caught my attention. However, when he asked if he could start the purchase paperwork, I declined, explaining that we were just beginning our search and wanted to explore further options. When we asked about men’s rings, Gary simply directed us to the men’s section without offering any guidance or details, leaving us to browse on our own.

As we looked through the men’s wedding bands, another salesperson approached, but we informed them we were just browsing. Soon after, a woman named Amber came over. Although Kevin wasn’t interested in assistance, I asked for her help. Amber was fantastic—she showed us various ring styles and provided detailed information about each. She even offered to write down the details on a card so we could remember which rings caught our interest. Amber returned to my section to note the options and suggested another ring that matched even better than the one Gary had shown. Friendly, eager to assist, and genuinely engaged, Amber’s support was crucial in helping us understand what to look for at other stores.

We give Gary one star and Amber five stars. Ultimately, we chose not to return because we found rings we loved more at another store that better suited our budget.

I felt uneasy about entrusting my ring to strangers, especially knowing it might be away for some time. Despite this, the staff were exceptional, maintaining their courtesy even during technical difficulties. My two-star rating stems from one specific part of my experience.

Since my fiancé bought the ring as a surprise, I wasn’t supposed to know its price. While some couples may choose rings together, I believe most grooms select them as a surprise or gift. To resize my ring, they had to send it off and replace it with a completely different ring—same design, but one that fit properly. When the cashier printed the receipt and gave me a copy, I felt quite uncomfortable. Seeing the exact amount spent on my engagement ring struck me as somewhat inappropriate. Perhaps this is standard procedure, but it didn’t feel right to me.

That said, I genuinely appreciated the politeness and professionalism of the staff, and the store offered a great selection. It was just a little unsettling to have the price revealed so plainly.

Our server, Derek A. (the tall, bald gentleman), frankly fell short of expectations. He didn’t mention any specials, was slow to refill our drinks, and never offered additional breadsticks or salad. After what felt like an endless wait to get a to-go box and our bill, he loudly complained to someone right behind us about how he couldn’t catch a break and struggled to pronounce my name. Honestly, that’s not something that should be said within earshot of a customer.

On a brighter note, the portions were generous and the entrees flavorful. However, the breadsticks arrived lukewarm—definitely not what we expect from Olive Garden—and no extras were offered.

Overall, the experience was disappointing. Maybe Derek was having a rough day, but I would recommend requesting a different server. Everyone else seemed excellent, and it’s clear that a server’s attitude greatly influences the dining experience.

This visit was prompted by a gift card, though I typically eat here only once or twice a year, knowing the food isn’t truly authentic. They currently offer a 2 for $25 deal, which sounds reasonable at first, but the portions are noticeably smaller than their regular entrees. The special includes unlimited salad and breadsticks, but the salad is just plain iceberg lettuce, and you choose either a small appetizer or dessert to share. The price feels fair, but it would be better if they clearly noted the reduced portion sizes.

Unlike LR’s review, I’ve almost always taken leftovers home from OG. This time, however, after finishing the salad and breadsticks, I ate the entire entree. Unless they recently reduced their portions, the servings were definitely skimpy and had only a modest amount of chicken. The smoked chicken was merely passable.

Our friend opted for the unlimited soup, salad, and breadsticks dinner option (which costs $3 more at dinner), but her experience was marred by a less-than-warm waitress who removed two breadsticks from her table before she was finished. It’s baffling why a server would do that, especially when breadsticks are part of the meal. To make matters worse, the spicy sausage soup she ordered was mostly broth.

Overall, the food was underwhelming, and there are better nearby options where you won’t wait 45 minutes for a table. For genuine Italian cuisine, I recommend local spots like Libretto’s up the road or Portofino’s on Park Rd. These restaurants feature real Italian chefs preparing dishes—not corporate kitchen creations—and offer better value for your money.

If authentic Italian fare is what you want, it’s worth the five-minute drive to Libretto’s or ten minutes to The Carolina Bistro.

OG’s refreshed menu genuinely impressed me, and I’m excited to share my experience! It had been a while since my last visit, mainly because I’d grown tired of ordering the same dish repeatedly. But when my parents came to town and suggested dining there, I decided it was definitely worth giving it another try.

We started with the Moscato, which I appreciate since OG always offers a tasting before you commit to a full glass. Even better, they now serve a glass and a half—a welcome bonus! The Moscato itself is sweet, fruity, and crisp, easily one of my favorites.

For our starter, we selected the lasagna fritta—Parmesan-coated lasagna pieces fried to a golden crisp, served atop Alfredo sauce and finished with Parmesan cheese and marinara. It was an excellent way to begin the meal! The hot, crunchy lasagna blended perfectly with the sauces and cheese, and I’d wholeheartedly recommend this dish.

We also savored the Zuppa Toscana, a hearty soup featuring spicy sausage, russet potatoes, and cavolo greens in a creamy broth, served alongside a fresh salad. For our main courses, we sampled the Tour di Mare, which includes three small portions: creamy shrimp Alfredo, shrimp scampi fritta (a new dish of lightly fried shrimp tossed in garlic and white wine sauce), and Bucatini with meat sauce. The shrimp scampi fritta truly stood out—the distinctive blend of flavors was delicious. The Bucatini pasta, thicker than spaghetti yet equally flavorful, was another fantastic choice.

Our server was exceptional, and the food was superb. I’m definitely looking forward to returning and exploring more of their new menu offerings!

Situated just across from Carolina Place Mall and next to a Red Lobster, this restaurant tends to be quite busy during peak hours—weekends especially are best avoided if you want to skip the wait. I arrived around 5:30 pm on a Monday and was fortunate to be seated immediately. As I ate, the dining room gradually filled up. My server was friendly and attentive, consistently refilling my drinks without any reminders.

I chose the $12.95 special, which includes a choice of soup or salad, an entrée, and a small dessert. The salad was a classic iceberg blend with assorted onions, which I enjoyed, especially since the dressing was flavorful and the salad refreshingly cold—just how I prefer it. I also ordered a basket of five breadsticks for myself and found it difficult to resist eating them all. They were soft, warm, and quite tasty.

For my main course, I went with the bucatini in meat sauce. It was decent—not exceptional or the best Italian-style dish I’ve had, but it did the job. The dessert was a small cake layered with strawberry sauce (I can’t recall the name), and it was acceptable—reminded me of something from the prepared foods section at Harris Teeter. It offered a sweet conclusion to the meal.

Overall, the staff was polite and attentive without being intrusive, and the food was solid, meeting my expectations. It was perfectly satisfactory.

We usually avoid chain restaurants, especially with so many excellent local options nearby. However, since we had a gift card, we decided to try this place for dinner.

We arrived around 6 PM and were seated promptly. By the time we left, the lobby was packed with people waiting for tables. Both of us ordered a glass of the house red wine, which was reasonably priced and surprisingly flavorful for a house pour.

For our meals, I chose the soup and salad combo featuring pasta fagioli soup, while my husband selected the lasagna primavera from the lighter side of the menu, filled with spinach and vegetables. The breadsticks and salad arrived as expected—the breadsticks were delicious and hard to resist having more of. My soup was quite good, and my husband’s lasagna was even better. That said, we couldn’t help but laugh at how small the lasagna was. It made sense, though, since making a “light” lasagna isn’t easy. To give you a sense of scale, it was about the size of half a deck of cards in all dimensions, topped with just three small pieces of grilled chicken. Even though we usually share meals and are accustomed to smaller portions, this was unexpectedly tiny. Still, he ate it without complaint because it was flavorful.

We usually skip dessert, but when the waitress stopped by, my husband ordered the pumpkin cheesecake—perhaps because he was still a bit hungry or craving something sweet. It was excellent: a generous slice that disappeared in about five minutes.

Overall, the experience was decent, but we likely wouldn’t return unless we had another gift card.

Chain restaurants aren’t usually my go-to for reviews, but after attending a surprise birthday party here, I felt compelled to share what happened. My friend had set up a reservation, but when we arrived, it wasn’t in their system—possibly she’d contacted the wrong branch. Regardless, I’m not holding that against the staff. They acted quickly and managed to set up a table for us with little delay, which I appreciated.

As soon as we sat down, though, an overwhelming odor struck me. I turned to my friend to see if he noticed it, and right away he said, “wet dog!”—exactly what I was thinking. The smell was awful, reminiscent of dirty rags or something that hadn’t been cleaned properly. While we waited for the rest of the group, we ordered breadsticks and were told that birthday dessert would require an extra charge. Seriously? That felt like unnecessary penny-pinching. The breadsticks themselves were bland—no garlic, no real flavor—which was a letdown.

Once everyone had arrived, we went ahead and ordered our meals. I chose the Bruschetta Salmon. When I asked the server for his thoughts, he honestly admitted he hadn’t tried it in ages, but mentioned most customers seemed to like it. I appreciated his candor. The salad came out quickly, but after that, the pace slowed considerably. We ended up waiting quite a while for our main courses.

When my dish was finally served, it was disappointing. I discovered two bones in the salmon and decided to stop eating at that point. The risotto pasta underneath was far too heavy, the salmon was on the tough side, and the toppings felt like a mismatched blend of several recipes. Meanwhile, some in our group still hadn’t received their food, which prompted the manager to come over, offer his apologies, and comp several meals. He even offered to cover the birthday guest’s dessert, which was a considerate gesture.

Dessert ended up being the best part. I ordered the chocolate tuxedo mousse cake and genuinely enjoyed it, and everyone else seemed happy with their desserts too. In the end, the only reason this place is getting 2 stars instead of 1 is the service. Our waiter was friendly and personable, and the manager handled things well. Still, I wouldn’t return here in the future.

BuonAppetito! Even though the parking lot was full, we were delighted to be seated in under 10 minutes. Our server was attentive and knowledgeable, and our appetizer arrived within 8 minutes of placing our order.

A recurring and somewhat puzzling issue for me concerns the olives in the salad. Despite the restaurant’s name highlighting olives, the large salad bowl contained only two. If you want more, you must specifically ask, which strikes me as rather unusual. This has been consistent every time I’ve visited.

I thoroughly enjoyed the flavorful spaghetti with meat sauce. My husband opted for the seafood Alfredo but found it just average and wouldn’t order it again.

The tiramisu was delightful, and the coffee arrived fresh and piping hot. Aside from the olive shortage, we had no other complaints.

Every time I step into this place, I know exactly what to expect—the endless soda (cue mock gagging), the familiar décor, and that distinctive, almost enchanting aroma in the air. But honestly, the real reason we keep coming back is the service. Could there be any other explanation? Maybe the ribs, though I’m still unsure if I’ve overcome my strange aversion to touching my food. Yes, I admit it—I’m not a fan of handling my food, and I’m putting that out there on the Internet.

That said, it’s truly the service that keeps us returning. From the moment you walk in, past the kitchen, and back again, this place somehow nails it. It’s surprising—after all my years of paying attention to these details, I never imagined Tony Roma’s would impress me like this.

We also always end up laughing during our visits. Like the other night, when an overly enthusiastic waiter was vacuuming the floor right in the middle of dinner service with a broken battery-powered vacuum. We asked him to stop—not once, but twice. Can you believe it? It got so funny that when my friend dashed out with one of the vacuums pretending to clean, his brother jumped up, ready to snatch it from the waiter, not realizing it was actually his own brother goofing around.

Try Tony Roma’s—you won’t be disappointed. I especially enjoy their soups and salads. And yes, despite everything, I do touch my food.

This was my first time visiting, so I wanted to sample their food before bringing him along to dine in. The young woman who delivered my order—likely the hostess, judging by her attire—approached with a stern, almost unfriendly expression. She asked if my name matched the one on the to-go receipt, which it did. Without smiling and displaying a noticeably cold demeanor, she then requested the coupon. I handed it over and even left a tip—I always tip, even on complimentary meals, having worked as a server for two years at Red Lobster. Her frosty attitude genuinely made me feel terrible, as if she resented me for using the company’s coupon despite the tip.

I ordered the steakhouse burger because I was craving a good burger while pregnant, accompanied by fries. Unfortunately, the fries were chewy rather than crispy and lacked seasoning. The burger itself was flavorful but carelessly tossed into the box. Overall, the customer service was quite disappointing. This was my trial visit, and now I’m certain I won’t return or bring my husband along.

After visiting numerous auto repair shops across Charlotte, I can confidently say Carolina Tire stands out—even though they aren’t the cheapest option. Their pricing is clear and fair, with no hidden fees beyond the initial quote. They also provide thoughtful extras like complimentary roadside assistance with oil changes. It’s evident the team takes real pride in their work, treating it as a true career rather than just a job.

Consistency matters a great deal to me. Whether I’m there for an oil change or a repair, I always receive reliable, hassle-free service. Carolina Tire consistently meets this expectation. Their waiting area further improves the experience, featuring a children’s play space, a large TV, and free Wi-Fi to keep you comfortable throughout your visit.

The only drawback is their location, which isn’t convenient for walking to nearby malls or dining options. They do offer rides to Lynx if needed, but there aren’t many other amenities nearby.

Overall, I’m a big fan!

During my lunch break, my car broke down, so I stopped by AutoZone to purchase the part I needed. I asked how soon they could start the repair and how long it would take. They assured me they could begin "immediately" and that it wouldn’t take much time. About 30 minutes later, they brought my car into the shop, and an hour after that, the repair was finished.

When it was time to settle the bill, they initially charged me $212 for two hours of labor. I questioned this because the car had only been in the shop for one hour, and I had been there a total of 1.5 hours. They then adjusted the charge to a flat fee of $99.07. If that’s their standard rate for an hour’s work, I find it steep—especially since the job shouldn’t have taken that long. This experience has convinced me this will be my first and last visit.

Adding to my frustration, they pulled my car to the front and left it running while we discussed the bill. I plan to share this disappointing experience with everyone I know.

Update: The owner called to apologize and asked me to call back to get a full refund. He also credited my account with a complimentary oil change. I did call for the refund but probably won’t return, as the location isn’t convenient for me. I only stopped there because I needed a repair that day and they were nearby. This all happened on 9/27/2011.

This team genuinely aims to keep labor fees fair while offering highly competitive prices on parts. They stand firmly behind their warranty. For example, after my timing belt replacement, I noticed a noisy idle a few months later, and they promptly fixed it at no extra cost. Unlike many other shops, they avoid adding fees for minor services. At the Subaru dealership and Woodies, I was charged $75 to $90 just for an inspection. In contrast, when I asked Tread Quarters to replace a couple of lights along with brake repairs, they completed everything without increasing the bill. They stick to their estimates and charge only for the actual time worked, even if it’s less than expected. This approach sharply contrasts with Woodies, where I was billed the full quoted price despite them working on my car for only half the estimated time.

While washing my car today, I noticed a deep scratch running around my wheel. From my experience at a custom wheel and tire shop, I know this damage usually happens when a technician forgets to remove the wheel weight before dismounting or installing a tire after a repair. Mistakes do happen, but at my previous job, any technician who caused damage would always inform the customer. Unfortunately, that wasn’t the case at Tread Quarters in Pineville.

When I returned to point out the damage, the same young man mentioned in Aaren H’s negative review flatly denied their work could have caused it and instead suggested I probably curb-rash my wheel. Seriously? It felt like he took my complaint personally. He said he would file a claim, but I have yet to hear anything from the company. On top of that, he mentioned this damage doesn’t affect his hourly pay or anything at the shop.

I have never encountered such poor management before. This treatment is completely unacceptable, and I won’t hesitate to share my experience with everyone I know about the terrible service I received at Tread Quarters in Pineville.

Last summer, when I brought my dog here, I honestly felt a bit uneasy about leaving him behind. However, the staff’s genuine kindness and compassion made a big difference—they truly soothed my nerves, and I appreciated how attentively they addressed my concerns. While I was away, they sent me a photo of my dog to reassure me, and I could even check on him through a playtime webcam, which I found very thoughtful.

The facility also offers some lovely extras, including additional playtime, doggie ice cream treats, and even bedtime stories—yes, bedtime stories! I found that absolutely endearing. When I returned to pick him up, he was so happy I genuinely thought he was smiling. Their overnight rates are quite reasonable compared to other local options, and I’ve brought him back several times since.

Best Friends sweetens the experience by providing a complimentary first night, which is a great perk—I’m always glad to save a little money. They also include a report card when you pick up your pet, which is just too adorable. Even though I’ve moved away, I wouldn’t hesitate to bring my dog here again and wholeheartedly recommend their services.

The boarding process was smooth and efficient, with the staff consistently courteous and approachable. However, I was quite upset when I picked up my two dogs after four days. Both had a strong, unpleasant odor, and one was matted with feces on her underside and had a cut on her back right leg. Once outside, they acted as if they hadn’t been walked all day—immediately veering off the sidewalk to urinate and defecate, which is very unusual since I usually have to walk them for quite some time before they relieve themselves.

I appreciated receiving a photo of my dogs during their stay, along with a report card. Yet, the report indicated their bowel movements were normal, even though both had diarrhea as soon as I took them home. While the facility itself is pleasant and the staff are friendly, I was clearly disappointed by the condition of my dogs when I picked them up.

From the moment the person arrived to pick us up and showed us where she would be staying, the constant barking was so overwhelming it nearly brought me to tears and gave me a pounding headache. She was trembling, and although I almost wanted to back out, we were pressed for time. It genuinely felt like my dog was being sent to doggy hell. The staff seemed distracted and never took the time to explain her daily routine or whether the dogs were taken outside for potty breaks. I’m assuming they simply relieve themselves in their cages, which is both revolting and deeply disappointing.

We dropped her off at 4 pm on Saturday and were told pick-up was only allowed Sunday between 3 and 6 pm, with the first night supposedly free. However, we were charged for two nights, which was confusing and frustrating. Ultimately, we paid $37. I never received any pictures of her, and when I asked, my requests were mostly ignored.

I much preferred Ironton Boarding, where they warmly greet your furry friend, maintain a calm and well-organized facility, and charge only $22 a night. Their staff is genuinely friendly and always happy to see you, plus the dogs get time to run in a large outdoor play area. I will NEVER bring my dogs to Best Friend Pet Care again!

My dog Coop has been a regular here for four years, and each visit he arrives with the same enthusiasm as on his very first day. The ladies at the front desk know him by name, crouch down to his level, hug him, and shower him with affection and praise. Coop is truly treated like royalty at this place. He adores doggie day camp and enjoys a two-bedroom suite with bedding so sumptuous that I wish I could rest there myself. Before I come to pick him up, he’s pampered with a bubble bath, a paw-icure, and a tidy trim. When I arrive, Coop greets me with a warm hug and a glowing update from the staff, who always tell me how well behaved he was and eagerly anticipate his next visit. “Best Friends” isn’t just Coop’s best friend—they’ve become mine as well, because they care for him just as deeply as I do!

I went through severe financial difficulties with my business and could no longer afford to keep my dogs. When I reached out, their policy was clear: no payment, no dogs—which I accepted. However, they then accused me of abandoning my dogs. They refused to return them or consider a payment plan. Instead, they shipped all three dogs away and won’t disclose their location.

While I understand their need to recover money, they sent us to collections, gave my dogs away, and insisted the contract we signed permitted these actions. Now, they claim they have no idea where the dogs ended up. Over time, I spent thousands with them, especially since I was covering the costs for multiple dogs.

What truly frustrates me is that if they intended to send my dogs away, they could have simply handed them over to me and worked out a solution. They never informed me beforehand—I only found out after the dogs had been shipped off. I was forced to give one star, and only because it was mandatory.

I’m genuinely frustrated by how this store keeps piling on extra fees. My husband went out to find something special for me and did an excellent job. However, after selecting the earrings, he was informed that there’s an additional charge for the earring posts. Seriously? How are the posts not included with the earrings when you’re already spending a significant amount? It just doesn’t make sense.

Then there was the necklace he gifted me, which turned out to be a bit too long. When I returned with the receipt to exchange the chain for a shorter one, the employee told me I’d have to leave it there, wait until the next day, and pay a fee to have it shortened. Paying for a gift you received feels completely unfair. Most jewelers rely on customers buying surprises for their loved ones, and they won’t always get the size exactly right.

Fortunately, the two employees who helped my husband and the one who assisted me generously waived the earring post fees and adjusted the chain immediately at no cost. Honestly, it’s the staff and the jewelry itself that saved this review from being a one-star.

After these experiences, I’m even more inclined to support local mom-and-pop jewelers. I don’t appreciate the extra charges and hassle that seem embedded in the process here. Jared’s has become too large and corporate, losing sight of nurturing genuine relationships and customer loyalty. I don’t remember Jared’s being like this before, but I’ve heard they acquired Zales, and much has changed.

It’s unfortunate because Jared’s jewelry is beautiful and the employees are kind, but the overall shopping experience has lost its warmth and, in my opinion, is now tarnished.

I’ve never experienced customer service this bad! We purchased a Groupon for a tire rotation and fuel injection service, scheduled an appointment, and arrived 10 minutes early—only to be told they were running an hour behind. Before leaving, I called to check if any cancellations might let me get in sooner, but Tasha, who answered the phone, didn’t mention the delay at all. If she had, I would have waited 45 minutes before making the trip. Instead, I ended up waiting nearly three hours, which is completely unacceptable. Then, at checkout, she tried to charge me $3.52 for "shop materials." Having worked in a shop myself, I know a couple of shop towels don’t cost that much. So, I grabbed my keys and walked out. My next step is to contact Groupon about this shady operation.

I felt completely swindled when I took my car in for a NC inspection. While waiting, I overheard loud disputes coming from the service area, which was quite unsettling. After about 35-40 minutes, the manager, Will, came out and told me my car had failed inspection because I needed new tires—even though another employee had earlier assured me the tires were fine. When I pointed this out to Will, he simply said, "well, they won't pass for NC." I chose not to buy any tires and took my car to a nearby shop, where it passed inspection with no tire issues.

Later that afternoon, the actual state inspector for this Tire Kingdom approached me to apologize. He explained that my car, including the tires, was perfectly fine to pass. However, his boss, Will, had ordered him to fail my car in order to pressure me into buying tires. The inspector refused because it would have been dishonest—a fact that also explained the yelling I had heard earlier. He said he couldn’t continue working knowing I had been deceived. Although he is the certified inspector, it was Will—who lacks certification—making the decisions. I have to commend the honest inspector despite the clear corruption of the manager.

I filed a complaint with Corporate and have had several conversations with someone there. They admitted Will was wrong and shouldn’t have acted that way. Yet, Will remains the manager at that location, so BEWARE! I was exploited just so Will could push tire sales. What does it say about a company that keeps someone like him in charge?

One final warning: I visited the Better Business Bureau website to file a complaint. You might want to check the reviews about this company there before deciding to do business with them.

We’ve visited this IHOP location several times and found their breakfast to be consistently excellent. The coffee is always fresh and piping hot, the pancakes come out warm and fluffy, and the orange juice strikes the perfect balance—not too tart or too sweet. I’ve never encountered anything unusual in my food, and the staff remain polite and attentive throughout.

That said, a word of caution about the non-breakfast menu. Just this past weekend, I took my daughter and grandmother for a quick, affordable lunch after church. Grandma ordered coffee and a Belgian waffle, which she thoroughly enjoyed. My daughter chose the baby cakes kids meal and ate most of it. Unfortunately, I picked the chicken fried steak with mashed potatoes and corn—and that was a mistake. The chicken fried steak was so tough it was nearly inedible; after a few bites, I gave up. The mashed potatoes tasted stale, as if they’d been sitting out all day, so I left them after one bite. The corn was the only part of my meal that was actually good. By the time we got home, I had to make myself a sandwich because I hadn’t really eaten at IHOP.

As mentioned, this location really shines when it comes to breakfast, which makes sense for an IHOP. Both my daughter and grandmother were happy with their meals. My advice? Stick to the breakfast menu and avoid the other options—you’ll have a much better experience.

If you’re near Pineville, make sure to visit this charming little shop—a true hidden gem stocked with everything you could want. Among their offerings is my go-to ready-to-cook Marusan pan-fry yakisoba noodles, which I depend on and seldom find elsewhere in Charlotte. Though small, the store is well-stocked with all the essentials needed to prepare sushi at home. You’ll find an extensive selection of tsukemono, tea, okake, miso, wakame, kombu, and nori, along with sweet treats like Pokki, gummies, pounded rice red bean pastries, Japanese bread, and a generous variety of packaged snacks. Walking through the aisles feels like a nostalgic trip back to Japan, with many items I haven’t seen since my last visit.

The shop is spotless, and the staff are among the kindest Japanese people you’ll ever meet. I truly appreciated their patience as I asked plenty of questions—even those I thought were a bit silly, such as which sauce to use for homemade yaki-onigiri. With prices slightly lower than other Charlotte stores, the drive out here is definitely worth it.

Curling is often called “chess on ice,” but that comparison misses the mark since chess demands far greater precision in piece placement. A better analogy might be “shuffleboard on ice.” Regardless, the sport is certainly enjoyable to watch and play.

Recently, the Charlotte Centre Curling Club opened its doors to new members and hosted its first Learn to Curl event at the Pineville Ice House. About twenty enthusiastic participants showed up, joined by a few instructors and local TV personality Larry Sprinkle, all eager to dive into the game.

The ice is treated with tiny droplets of water that create a textured layer, causing the 42-pound granite stones to curl as they slide. Players focus on maintaining their balance while pushing the stones forward, then sweep vigorously to guide them along the intended path. Much of the session was dedicated to building stability and mastering the delivery of the stone down the rink.

I spent a good amount of time on the ice myself. During my one successful throw, Larry’s enthusiastic sweeping sent him tumbling onto his backside. On another attempt, I didn’t even get that far—I nearly knocked over the camera. Hopefully, I won’t be billed or sued for almost taking out a local celebrity!

The feature is set to air on April 9th, so I’ll be keeping an eye out. Meanwhile, a highlight video is already online, including the moment I sent Larry Sprinkle crashing to the ice.  
http://www.wcnc.com/on-tv/Larry-learns-that-curling-is-year-round-90346659.html

The public skate sessions here are disappointingly short and overpriced. I attempted to rent skates three times, but none of the pairs were fit for use. The first pair had laces roughly stitched together from two different skates, and the blades were so dull and rounded they resembled battered butter knives. The second pair was somewhat better, but the left blade was bent about 10 degrees to the right, making skating impossible. The third pair showed slight improvement but remained completely unusable. This wasn’t an isolated experience—everyone in our group of seven encountered the same issues. It was clear that all the skates had been neglected and mistreated, with no sharpening or maintenance for quite some time.

Because of these problems, we decided to switch to Extreme Ice in Indian Trail. Although it requires a bit of a drive, the entire operation is professional from start to finish. They provide brand-new skates, longer skate sessions, and a pro shop that caters to all skaters—not just hockey players.

At first glance, the Ice House might seem like an ordinary rink, but their dedication to keeping the ice pristine truly stands out. Their skate sharpening service is noticeably better than that of the “other” Charlotte rink, which is especially important if you’re renting skates. Still, if you have your own skates, I’d recommend bringing them. I understand many people don’t, but rental skates feel like slipping into someone else’s shoes—and since skates are stiff and unforgiving, some discomfort is almost inevitable.

What really impressed me was how attentive and knowledgeable the staff were. I enjoyed chatting with them and even met a few people from my hometown. The only downside is the rink’s limited space. I realize that’s a tough problem to fix, but coming from Minnesota, where hockey is deeply embedded in the culture, the Ice House feels a bit cramped compared to what I’m used to.

Despite the three-star rating, I genuinely appreciated my time at the Ice House. The atmosphere is cozy and welcoming, and I have to say, I love the smell—while some might wrinkle their noses, to me, nothing compares to the scent of hockey. I wholeheartedly recommend the Ice House as a great spot for a date, a family outing, a fun place for kids, or a fresh experience for anyone lacing up skates for the first time.

If you’re new to ice skating in Charlotte, the Pineville Ice House (PIH) is one of the best options. With a $5 entry fee and $2.50 skate rentals, it’s an ideal spot for families, birthday parties, groups of friends, or anyone seeking a fresh twist on the typical roller rink experience—except here, it’s all on ice.

I’ve been to PIH several times, including once with a large group for a game of broom ball, which definitely lives up to its “[dangerous]” reputation. Picture players in everyday clothes, no skates, wielding broom-like sticks as they try to hit a ball into the opposing team’s goal—mostly focused on staying upright and avoiding crashing into the boards. In this game, balance matters more than scoring, unless you count dodging a concussion as a win. To be clear, this isn’t a criticism of ice skating itself, but rather a warning about the reckless and somewhat foolish game of broom ball.

For anyone wanting to improve their figure skating skills, PIH is a solid place to start. Just be sure to check their website first, as public skating hours can be oddly specific. Dress warmly, watch out for the kids zooming around, and always fall with your hands closed—losing fingers is definitely not part of the fun.

I’m no Michelle Kwan, but having spent a fair amount of time on the ice, I found this rink somewhat lacking. We arrived right as the open skate session began (be sure to check their website for the schedule). The entry process was simple: walk in, pay $10 for admission and skate rental, then pick up your skates at the next window.

That said, I was quite disappointed with both the ice surface and the rental skates. The ice felt rough and was clearly overdue for resurfacing. The rental blades were very dull—yes, they’re rentals, but sharper edges would have made a noticeable difference. I also wished they had set up cones to separate casual skaters (those simply cruising laps) from the more advanced skaters attempting spins and jumps. From my experience at other rinks, this arrangement really improves the experience for everyone. Additionally, a better understanding of skating etiquette would be beneficial—I had to dodge people skating the wrong way multiple times.

On a positive note, they serve beer and wine! Had it not been so early, I would have gladly enjoyed a drink. The staff I encountered were friendly enough.

Since Pineville Ice House faces little competition, they likely don’t feel much pressure to make improvements. If you’re in Charlotte and want to skate, this will probably be your go-to spot.

Having written hundreds of reviews, I’ve learned the importance of sharing honest experiences with companies that significantly affect our daily lives—and Fairpoint Communications certainly fits that description. When they took over Verizon’s local phone service in my area, it quickly became clear how poorly they perform. To be blunt, it has been an absolute fiasco.

Once Fairpoint took control of my home landline, billing quickly turned into a nightmare. After my office relocated to Portsmouth, it also became their client. Then, without warning, our landlines completely stopped working, leaving customers with a message stating our number was no longer in service. Even after this was fixed, the lines failed to roll over correctly, and billing was consistently inaccurate. To make matters worse, our internet connection was so unstable that rebooting the DSL modem up to 15 times a day became routine.

Customer service offered little comfort. Representatives often apologized, but the problems persisted. Calling back about the same issue frequently resulted in two completely different answers. The frustration grew so intense that two employees in my office broke down in tears. This is far from an isolated case—most people and businesses I know in New Hampshire and Maine who rely on Fairpoint face similar struggles.

Recently, my company switched providers. Fairpoint did everything possible to delay the transition, but it eventually went through. After the new provider spent a few hours at our office, everything began working flawlessly.

To Fairpoint’s leadership: you clearly took on more than you could handle. Whoever made this decision was either misinformed or simply indifferent. I sincerely hope you are penalized out of existence. As for New Hampshire’s Public Utility Commission, I honestly have no idea what your role is—maybe that deserves its own review.

I rarely give one-star ratings—this is only my twelfth out of 500. I won’t even get into the unresolved billing issues here, but if you’re looking for a phone company in Northern New England, avoid Fairpoint at all costs.

This company took on substantial debt to acquire Verizon’s outdated landline network, yet since hedge funds assumed control, they have consistently refused to invest in necessary upgrades. As a result, both business and residential customers across the region endure frequent and prolonged outages.

We’ve relied on their business DSL service for three years but have never experienced a single uninterrupted month. Daily “routing issues” have become a persistent and frustrating problem. Their customer support is largely ineffective, offering little more than the standard scripted apology: “I’m terribly sorry for your inconvenience.”

The situation has only worsened following their recent union-busting efforts. Here in Vermont, we earnestly hope our public service regulators will take strong, decisive action against this blatant corporate exploitation. We are exhausted by out-of-state companies making promises they clearly cannot or will not fulfill.

My best friend flew in from New Jersey for a visit, and we planned a girls’ day at this spa, both opting for one-hour hot stone massages. Having experienced massages in NJ, NY, and California, we arrived with high expectations. Unfortunately, the experience was disappointing for several reasons.

Right from the start, we were greeted by a very kind woman who neither spoke nor understood English. Regardless of our questions, her answer was always a simple "yes." For example, when we asked if the spa pools were hot or cold, she responded with "yes." I asked again if they were hot and received the same answer. However, when we tested the water, both pools were ice cold. We eventually found the hot tub ourselves, only to discover the jets pointed straight upward, causing a huge mess and making it impossible to sit in front of them to relax muscles. It was absurd.

The hallway from the pools to the locker room felt so sterile it resembled a hospital corridor.

My massage was entirely focused on the stones. My very nice therapist repeatedly placed and removed hot stones for 50 minutes but never actually performed any massage. I waited, expecting the real massage to start, assuming she was warming up my muscles, but it never happened. Then the session ended. Meanwhile, my friend’s massage did include genuine massage work.

The tranquility room was another letdown—an open space right off the showers, lacking any peaceful ambiance. There was no soft lighting, no blankets (and I was quite chilly), nothing to make it feel like a special place for quiet relaxation.

All this so-called indulgence came with a staggering $175 price tag. I haven’t felt this ripped off in a long time. If you expect to be pampered and enjoy a truly special experience, avoid this place—unless you don’t care where your money goes.

As a professional in the salon and spa industry, I was eagerly looking forward to some pampering and booked a body wrap, massage, shampoo blow-dry, and manicure. Brenda, who performed my body wrap, was absolutely incredible—the only service I genuinely appreciated. Unfortunately, my massage with Tym fell short of expectations. I clearly explained that I’m on my feet all day and have back issues, asking him to concentrate on my back and avoid my feet. Instead, he spent about five minutes on my back and devoted the rest of the session to my legs and feet. To make matters worse, he bluntly mentioned that one leg was shorter than the other and suggested I get it checked out, which came across as quite rude and could have been expressed more tactfully.

The woman who did my blowout was very kind, but when I left, my hair was still damp at the roots and the ends were frizzy. For $40, I expected a far better finish. Since I get manicures weekly, I only needed a buff and polish, but I upgraded to include a massage, thinking it would be worthwhile. Had I known the “massage” was merely lotion rubbed onto my hands, I wouldn’t have paid the extra fee. Honestly, the ladies at the mall do a better job.

Overall, I’m quite disappointed with the services here—Brenda’s body wrap was the sole bright spot. Perhaps my standards are higher as a fellow service provider, but if I’m spending $420 next time, I’ll definitely choose a different place.

From the moment you enter, the decor and amenities create a warm, inviting ambiance. As a frequent business traveler, I highly appreciate the spacious, spotless, and comfortable rooms. The large desks provide plenty of room to organize work materials, and the televisions cleverly embedded in the mirrors add a unique touch. Friendly and attentive staff further enhance the overall experience. During warmer months, the outdoor pool offers an ideal place to relax. The hotel’s prime location is a clear advantage, with numerous restaurants and shops just a short walk away. Guests can enjoy complimentary coffee and tasty cookies throughout the day, and it’s refreshing that wakeup calls come from real people rather than automated systems.

That said, a few drawbacks stand out. The fitness room is quite limited, featuring only two exercise machines. The business center feels somewhat outdated, especially due to the slow printers. The lack of an on-site bar or restaurant is also noticeable. While the complimentary continental breakfast is enjoyable, it remains fairly standard for this type of offering.

These minor issues keep the hotel from reaching a five-star rating, though most appear to be franchise-wide concerns rather than unique to this property—except perhaps the business center. Despite these imperfections, I would gladly stay here again.

While traveling with two girls, I needed extra towels. When I asked the housekeeper in the hallway, she told me, "I need a towel from you to give you a towel, but anyway, we don’t have any extras, so I can’t assist." Frustrated, I took matters into my own hands and went down to the fitness center to grab two towels myself. Passing the housekeeper with the towels in hand, we exchanged a look, and I slipped by with a small chuckle.

We also encountered what another reviewer mentioned—a flying beetle in the room. Fortunately, I was able to handle it myself.

The bistro setup was another disappointment. Instead of the complimentary coffee Courtyard used to offer, you now have to purchase coffee from the bistro, which I really dislike.

For those loyal to Marriott, I believe Fairfield Inns offer better value. They’re just as comfortable, with beds and pillows that meet our standards— which is what really matters. Plus, breakfast is free, and Fairfield Inns tend to be newer properties.

I needed a room near the airport for an early flight and, relying on my previous positive experiences, I booked one. However, the moment I walked in, I was confronted by a woman named "Chrystal"—who refused to provide her last name—wearing a scowl that immediately brought to mind the worst DMV encounters or the grimace of a prison inmate. Assuming she might be having a rough day or difficult circumstances, I chose to smile rather than leave right away—though in hindsight, walking out would have been the wiser choice. Chrystal looked as if she had just found something truly disgusting in her lunchbox.

Trying to ease the tension, I mentioned that we were Rewards Members, but it did nothing to soften her hostile glare. After an excruciatingly awkward minute of interaction, I voiced my dissatisfaction with her attitude and asked to speak with her manager. She insisted no manager was available and handed me a card for someone else who was also unreachable. Later, I discovered the person named on the card wasn’t even the actual manager. So Chrystal was not only unpleasant but also dishonest—seemingly intent on spreading misery through her toxic demeanor.

Employees like Chrystal are almost certainly why this Marriott holds the lowest Yelp rating of any Marriott in the state. Whoever is responsible for hiring here clearly needs to provide basic training, as they are completely negligent.

In short, this Marriott’s abysmal rating is well deserved.

Meeting Kyra at the front desk was a highly frustrating experience—her demeanor was unexpectedly rude and unwelcoming. As soon as I mentioned my Platinum Marriott Rewards status with 1,100,000 points, she became defensive and confrontational, insisting I was only a silver member. Even after showing my credit card, license, and platinum rewards card, she failed to enter my information into the system—a fact I only discovered later.

The room itself was deeply disappointing. The carpet was filthy, lint balls littered the bed, the bathroom sink was completely clogged, and there were no extra towels, soaps, or shampoos—only a single tiny bar of soap. When I called downstairs to report these issues, the person who answered informed me that my name wasn’t even registered for the room. It was evident that Kyra neglected her responsibilities; she didn’t input my platinum rewards card, my name, or my credit card details. Instead, she charged another flight crew member’s credit card for both rooms, which is entirely unacceptable.

With just a nine-hour layover, I lacked the energy to argue, but I will never stay here again, nor will my fellow crew members. I plan to warn others so no airline or corporate crews end up at this dump of a hotel. I’ve stayed in rundown motels that were better maintained. Out of the hundreds of Marriotts I’ve visited, this Charlotte Courtyard Marriott stands out as the single dreadful exception. Between the rudeness, inaccurate system entries, filthy conditions, and lack of upkeep, this place deserves a zero—00000.

This hotel is situated just outside the airport boundary and offers a shuttle service, though I opted not to use it during my stay.
