I arrived close to midnight and was promptly welcomed by a friendly clerk who recognized my Platinum status. After processing my credit card, they handed me two room keys and gave clear directions to my room—everything went smoothly.

Inside the room, I noticed two cleanliness issues. While lying down, I felt something crunchy beneath the sheet, which turned out to be a previous guest’s luggage tag that had somehow been washed with the bedding. Although both the tag and sheet were clean, it was an unexpected oversight. The next morning, I found a bar of soap left in the shower by another guest that housekeeping had missed. This was a bit unsettling—what else might have been overlooked? Despite these slip-ups, I chose to let them go, understanding that perfection isn’t always guaranteed.

The room was comfortable, and aside from a noisy group that arrived shortly after me, the atmosphere remained quite peaceful. I left early in the morning, well before the vacuum cleaners started their rounds.

It’s worth noting that Courtyard hotels do not provide complimentary breakfast. If that’s important to you, Fairfield or SpringHill might be better options. I prefer Courtyard because it generally attracts more business travelers and fewer families, meaning fewer chances of hearing children running down the hallways.

Would I stay here again? Given the unbeatable location near the airport and just off I-85, I believe I would.

Just a short walk from the bustling uptown core and before you reach the pricey stadium parking lots, this modest greasy spoon quietly holds its ground. Inside, the faded booths and vintage wallpaper immediately hint at its long history. I even spotted a "Best of Charlotte" award from 1995—hard to believe that was 16 years ago!

The menu is simple and classic, featuring hot dogs, burgers, BLTs, sandwiches, fries, onion rings, and other familiar favorites. This matches well with a kitchen equipped with a two-basket deep fryer, a griddle, and a fixin’s station. Their hot dogs are the highlight. Ordering one "all the way" means it arrives topped with mustard, ketchup, chili, onions, and slaw. For an extra 50 cents, you can add half slices of American cheese beneath all those toppings. Not a bad deal for a two-dollar dog.

If you’re looking to veer off the usual uptown path, feel like putting dietary rules aside for a bit, and don’t mind keeping some Tums handy along with a pack of gum for later, this spot is definitely worth a visit.

While scrolling through Yelp, I noticed no reviews under the exact name on the sign—JACKSON'S JAVA COFFEE HOUSE. Later, curiosity prompted me to check again on my computer, where I found reviews for JACKSON'S JAVA instead. This made me wonder if they’re actually the same place or just a cleverly named knockoff, similar to the McDowells versus McDonald's joke from Coming to America.

Since I work nearby, I decided to stop by a few months ago. My first visit featured a new “rookie” behind the counter. Then, about two weeks ago during my second-to-last visit, I placed an order and waited, all while noticing customers coming in flashing what looked like VIP cards. I was intrigued but didn’t ask about the fuss—I don’t visit often enough to be that curious. It seemed like some kind of secret coffee society.

My most recent visit (not my last ever, just the latest) was for a Chi Tea, which was pretty good. The service remains consistently friendly, quick, and straightforward. Prices are reasonable, though the space can feel a bit cramped when busy.

Give it a try! And if you’re feeling bold, ask about that mysterious card... ekk ekkk ekkkkkkkkk!!!

My stay here was a bit of a mixed experience, starting with the bathroom, which was genuinely frustrating—much like many other hotels. There’s no countertop space around the sink, and the outdated separate hot and cold knobs made adjusting the temperature unnecessarily complicated. The shower pressure was adequate, but the lack of any shelf or ledge to place shampoo, soap, or a washcloth was a glaring design flaw. To make matters worse, the toilet paper holder is awkwardly positioned behind you, making it difficult to reach. Overall, the bathroom’s layout, design, and decor left a lot to be desired.

The room itself felt quite dim, lit only by a few faint lamps scattered about. Although a desk was available, its shape was uncomfortable, with a wooden piece digging into my legs. On top of that, you have to unplug one device just to plug in your computer, which felt like a short-sighted and frustrating setup. Since I was there for work, I didn’t get a chance to try the breakfast or visit the bar, but these room issues made working in the space both challenging and unpleasant.

Parking added another layer of hassle. You must park in a public lot behind the hotel and have your ticket validated by staff to avoid paying at the lot, yet you still pay Dunhill $12 per day for parking. The system is inconvenient, and once I forgot to get my ticket validated, I ended up paying more than if I had just paid the garage directly. Clearly, it’s a poorly managed process.

On the positive side, the bed was comfortable, the room was quiet, and getting around was straightforward. As a business traveler, I’d still prefer a Fairfield Inn or Holiday Inn Express over this hotel, but it’s not far behind.

We arrived at 3:30 pm, only to find that our room wasn’t ready despite the check-in time being 3 pm. The bed, advertised as queen size, was actually a full size—a difference we know well since we recently upgraded from a full to a queen at home. Adding to our disappointment, the mattress was overly soft and the bed frame felt unstable, resulting in a restless night that made our seven-hour drive home even more tiring.

Throughout the night, the wall-mounted air conditioning unit emitted a bright blue glow, and there was no way to turn off the light without shutting down the A/C completely. This forced us to choose between an uncomfortably warm room or the constant bright light.

The room itself was small but adequate. While I understand downtown hotels often don’t offer great value for the price, based on our experience, we cannot recommend this hotel.

It’s been over two years since my last meal at McNinch, yet the memory remains remarkably vivid. I have to agree with Bill—this place truly stands out. In 2008, my partner and I chose McNinch to celebrate Valentine’s Day, fully committing to the experience with a personalized menu and carefully curated wine pairings. Following their instructions exactly, we arrived early to enjoy champagne and tour the charming home-turned-restaurant on Church Street.

What followed was an extraordinary culinary journey lasting more than three hours. We were completely captivated by the exquisite food and wine pairings, all served with impeccable service. Each course was thoughtfully crafted, highlighting a wealth of local ingredients. Our server’s impressive knowledge enriched the evening, sharing engaging details about the origins and vineyards of each wine.

Opting for the wine pairing allowed us to savor a unique and intriguing glass alongside each of the seven courses. Living nearby in the Fourth Ward certainly made the evening more convenient. McNinch House offers a truly special setting for a memorable meal. While the price is steep, it’s absolutely worth every penny. Even two and a half years later, I still find myself reflecting on that dinner. Our total was about $400, including the wine pairings, seven courses, and tip—a splurge, but a perfect choice for celebrating an anniversary or milestone.

I expected a four-star dining experience, but it ultimately didn’t live up to that standard. The service was warm, relaxed, and clearly delivered with pride, yet it fell short of that elevated level. I hesitate to leave a negative review because the staff genuinely seemed kind. The venue’s historic charm is undeniable, but charm alone doesn’t make it a four-star establishment. Thoughtful touches like vintage china, chilled forks, and traditional service were present, but some details—worn bathroom rugs and neglected landscaping—detracted from the overall impression, leaving the atmosphere feeling somewhat rough around the edges.

The pear salad was enjoyable, but the mushroom soup arrived cold. The main course was the biggest letdown: undercooked pork alongside a tough steak. While the sweet potato purée was flavorful, it was the only standout taste on the plate. The pork was raw in the center—not just mine, but others’ as well—and although I’m comfortable with some pink, this was clearly inedible. Since it was a customer event, no one wanted to complain, but if I had been dining alone, I definitely would have sent it back.

Dessert was a typical banquet-style flourless chocolate cake, and no coffee was offered. That might have been an oversight by the event planner, but I would have sincerely appreciated it.

Overall, it was a pleasant outing, but it didn’t live up to the glowing reviews or the price. I suspect they perform better with regular service than when managing a banquet for 40 guests.

He was a regular at Alexander Michael’s when he lived in Uptown, but this was my first visit—so you could say I finally experienced it myself. The restaurant is quietly tucked away from the towering Uptown skyline, nestled in a peaceful residential neighborhood. Without prior knowledge, you’d likely pass right by, mistaking it for just another house on a calm street. There are no large signs outside, and the exterior gives little hint of the lively atmosphere inside.

Once inside, however, the place was bustling. We were lucky to be seated immediately in a cozy, crowded room that felt like an English or Irish pub. The dim lighting and the casually dressed patrons, mostly in their 30s and 40s, created a mature and welcoming vibe—quite different from the usual Uptown bar scene.

We started with a Woodchuck Cider—sweet, bubbly, and refreshing—a nice surprise since not every spot offers ciders. Our server struck the right balance: attentive enough to take our orders and check on us when needed, but never intrusive. I ordered the blackened catfish, while my partner went for the honey chicken. Both dishes were delicious. My catfish, served with spicy black beans, had just the right Cajun kick. The portions were perfect—not so big as to be overwhelming, but enough to leave us satisfied.

All in all, it was an enjoyable outing, and I look forward to returning to this new find. The only minor disappointment was missing the chance to see the infamous pole mentioned on the back of the menu. Located in the women’s restroom, it’s apparently caused quite a few bruises—quite a funny detail!

This spot can easily be overlooked if you’re not already familiar with it. Inside, it doesn’t provide the cozy, welcoming atmosphere you might expect; the lighting is somewhat dim but still sufficient for comfortably reading the menu and having a conversation. The service was dependable, with prompt refills, though we experienced a fairly long wait when asking for the bill.

For my meal, I chose the buffalo chicken sandwich with Cajun fries. Unfortunately, the buffalo chicken didn’t meet my expectations—I usually prefer it saucier and more flavorful. The sandwich felt heavy on the chicken and bun but lacked enough seasoning. In contrast, the Cajun fries were a definite highlight, served in a generous portion that I genuinely enjoyed.

We also tried the nachos, which my special lady friend enthusiastically approved. Although the use of flour tortilla chips seemed unusual at first, it ultimately turned out to be a smart choice. I’m looking forward to returning for some drinks and to sample more items from the menu.

The place hums with vibrant, inviting energy, and the food generally satisfies. Contrary to another reviewer’s remarks, I found the beer selection quite noteworthy. They offer a broad range—from mainstream “goat piss” and Irish brews to options tailored for dedicated beer lovers, including local, national, and international varieties. The Gaelic ale from Asheville particularly caught my attention.

The nachos were definitely a highlight. Although I’m not fond of flour tortillas, the flour tortilla chips paired perfectly with a generous heap of peppers, beans, tomatoes, olives, cream, and tender chicken pieces.

Regarding the Honey Chicken pasta, it was just average. The chicken was juicy and flavorful, but the pasta itself leaned a bit too sweet for my palate. I believe a sharp, tangy feta would have balanced the sweetness more effectively than the somewhat bland Parmesan it was served with.

I’m considering coming back to try other dishes—like their hefty half-pound burgers—to see if they might win me over and turn me into a loyal fan.

If you live nearby, this spot will likely become a frequent go-to thanks to its straightforward, expertly prepared dishes and carefully curated beer selection. When I tried the chicken pita, I was genuinely impressed—the chicken was perfectly cooked and seasoned, served with a warm, hearty pita. Choosing beans as a side satisfied my extra protein craving without giving in to the usual temptation of fries.

The restaurant’s charm is evident in small details, like the note on the back of the menu explaining the beam in the ladies’ room—a quirky feature that often surprises unsuspecting guests. They also share some history of the house, providing engaging reading while you wait for your first drink.

My only minor complaint is the TV in the dining area. While many may be used to eating in front of a screen at home, it somewhat detracts from the overall atmosphere for me. The low ceilings create a cozy vibe, but if you’re hoping to enjoy plenty of natural sunlight on a lovely day, this probably isn’t the best choice.

In a city dominated by sleek, contemporary buildings, the historic and charming homes here offer a refreshing change of scenery. From the moment we stepped into this pub-style restaurant and bar, we were promptly welcomed and seated. I chose a cider on tap—one of my favorites—along with a side salad and the “What it is” dish. To my surprise, the salad stole the show; their homemade dressings were clearly fresh and flavorful. On the other hand, the “What it is” left me somewhat underwhelmed. While I’ve enjoyed many excellent pasta dishes, rotini has never been my preferred choice. The dish was heavily seasoned with dried herbs, which I find less appealing than fresh ones, and the chicken was coated in a strong Cajun spice that didn’t quite suit my palate. Still, I’m open to returning and trying something other than pasta, as I tend to be a discerning critic when it comes to Italian cuisine.

The biggest frustration of the evening was the rushed service. It felt as though the server or chef was in a hurry, which wasn’t what I wanted—I had hoped to relax and savor my meal, not be hurried through in less than 45 minutes. My main course arrived while I still had half of my salad uneaten, and the salad itself was served less than a minute after I ordered it. I understand the space is small with limited seating, but there was no wait for a table, and last I checked, this wasn’t a fast food establishment.

I’ve been to this charming neighborhood spot about five or six times now, and I can confidently say that every visit to Alexander Michael's has matched the exceptional quality of my very first. When my date and I arrived, we were pleasantly struck by the contrast between the warm, quiet, and unhurried summer evening outside and the cool, softly lit, lively atmosphere inside. We were quickly seated at a cozy table just behind the bar.

My date opted for the chicken pita with fries, which I photographed, while I chose the crawfish bake—also captured in a shot. The bake was a delightful blend of shrimp pasta and seafood casserole, creamy and cheesy without feeling too heavy. My date absolutely adored her pita, and after tasting a few bites myself, I can vouch for its genuine flavor. Both meals were truly excellent!

I’m genuinely a fan of this elegant, intimate gem in Charlotte. To me, Alexander Michael's serves refined, all-American bar fare with a sophisticated twist. If you haven’t experienced it yet—GO! And if you have, definitely GO AGAIN!

When my best friend and his boyfriend visited during the holiday season, we decided to stop by this tavern for a quick meal. Even though it was after 1 PM, the place remained surprisingly busy, likely due to its cozy size. Thankfully, we found some open seats at the bar.

The lunch menu offered a tempting variety of options, making it hard to choose. In the end, I went with the burger and Cajun fries, though the grilled cheese was a close second—definitely something to try next time!

Our meals arrived promptly, and I was impressed by the generous size of the burger—wow (pun intended)! The fries were plentiful as well. The burger was juicy without being messy, and the bun from Nova’s Bakery was a fantastic addition. A tip: you’ll want to cut this burger in half! I finished every bite—it just felt right. I couldn’t quite finish the fries, but they were hot, crispy, and seasoned with just the right amount of Cajun spice—enough to add a kick without overpowering the flavor.

The staff were genuinely friendly, chatting with us regularly and ensuring our glasses stayed full while we enjoyed our meal.

Though the prices are a bit on the higher side, the hearty portions made the $9 price feel reasonable to me.

I’ll definitely be back!

This inviting local American pub truly deserves its positive reputation. The interior boasts a dark, vintage charm, featuring bead-board wainscoting, a tin ceiling, and walls adorned with timeless prints that create a warm and welcoming atmosphere. Despite it being a Tuesday night well past typical dinner hours, the place was lively and buzzing with energy. The host—likely the "Ken" mentioned in previous reviews—greeted me warmly and quickly seated me in a snug corner booth, providing an excellent view of the entire pub. Throughout my visit, my waitress Traci was attentive and flawless in her service. Clearly a cherished neighborhood establishment, it attracted a diverse clientele, making for enjoyable people watching.

I genuinely appreciated my experience at Alexander Michael’s, though I must admit the food was good rather than exceptional. The spicy crab soup had a pleasant flavor but lacked the heat I was expecting, while the 4th Ward Beef Stroganoff delivered a classic taste, but its sauce was too thin to properly coat the meat, rotini, or ribs.

Although my business travel habits usually discourage dining at the same restaurant twice, if I ever craved comforting food in a lively setting, Alexander Michael’s would definitely be near the top of my list.

Nestled in uptown’s historic 4th Ward, this charming spot stands out as a true hidden treasure. Whenever I bring friends from out of town, they quickly embrace its cozy, inviting atmosphere and the neighborhood’s timeless appeal.

The food here is genuinely impressive. The spicy crab soup is a must-have—whether you order it by the cup or bowl, it leaves a lasting impression. If you’re just in the mood for a light snack or aren’t very hungry, the fried pickles consistently satisfy. Another highlight is the London Broil, enhanced by a flavorful marinade. It’s served sliced as a dinner entrée or transformed into a sandwich for lunch, each accompanied by a perfectly matched side.

When the dining room fills up, the bar serves as a reliable alternative. It features a rotating selection of local craft beers and is staffed by bartenders who truly know their craft, providing consistently excellent service.

Parking can be a bit confusing due to unclear signage, but there’s a lot less than a block away between Graham and Pine where you can park for two hours without a permit. And if you’ve had a few too many drinks and need a cab, the staff at A Mike’s will gladly point you to a spot where you can leave your car overnight.

Our Valentine’s Day visit to Al Mike’s was genuinely enjoyable, thanks to its warm and inviting atmosphere. Since seating is strictly first-come, first-served—even on holidays—we arrived early to secure a table. We started with two beers and a generous order of potato wedges topped with bacon and cheese, which I found absolutely delightful, though I’d skip the tomatoes next time. For my entrée, I chose the Buffalo Chicken Sandwich with Cajun Fries, while my husband went with the London Broil Sandwich. Both dishes were quite satisfying, and I would readily recommend either. We didn’t have dessert this time, so I can’t comment on that. Our server was attentive and thoughtful, bringing a to-go box before I even asked. I’d suggest Al Mike’s as a great spot for visitors, casual after-work drinks, or a romantic dinner. The tavern-style décor, soft lighting, and lively crowd create a cozy ambiance, and it’s clear the neighborhood holds this place in high regard—it’s consistently busy, much like other beloved Charlotte favorites. Enjoy!

This used to be one of my favorite hangouts years ago. I vividly recall the dim lighting, decent food, and, of course, the infamous pole in the ladies' restroom. So when Melissa and I recently debated where to eat on a chilly winter evening—and knowing this was her regular spot—I suggested Alexander Michael’s.

Parking here is always somewhat tricky. Luckily, we found a spot a short distance down the road on a side street. Still, the darkness outside felt a bit unsettling, making me wish for a buddy system—grabbing a friend, holding hands, and walking together like grade school kids. Inside, the ambiance matched the cold night perfectly, with flickering candles and tables placed close together. We were seated quickly, but that was about the only service we received. The waitress wasn’t rude, yet she was mostly absent. For a small establishment like this, attentive service to every table should be the norm.

The food was mediocre at best. I ordered the London broil sandwich with a side of soup, forgetting that the “crab” soup was made with imitation crab—a label that really shouldn’t be allowed. The sandwich had plenty of meat, so I mostly ate that; it was tender enough but rather bland. At $9.50, I couldn’t complain too much. After all these years, the menu feels limited, somewhat overpriced, and overall lacking a certain spark in both the food and the service.

I’ll give it another chance someday, though probably not anytime soon.

I would have much preferred dining elsewhere—somewhere with more than just two legal parking spots within a five-block radius. One of those limited spots was already taken by the restaurant’s so-called mascot: a weathered pickup truck that has somehow avoided tickets for twenty years.

Although this place was highly recommended as an exceptional “seasonal” restaurant, it left me wanting to call and ask which season could possibly justify serving cold, unappetizing “smoked” quesadillas. I also found myself questioning when, if ever, it’s appropriate to serve a tuna melt that’s warm on the outside but cold in the center. The waitress seemed genuinely surprised that anyone would expect their tuna melt prepared any other way.

About two-thirds through our meal, we were asked to settle the bill because their computer system apparently requires them to halt all service and open a new tab at that exact time.

In the end, the menu offered nothing noteworthy—just overrated pub fare.

I arrived expecting a quaint spot ideal for drinks and light appetizers, but the food was disappointing. The spicy crab soup contained no crab meat and lacked any real heat. Instead of being creamy, it had a gelatinous texture—definitely not something I would recommend.

My London Broil was served medium well, despite my clear request for medium rare. At first, I thought there might have been a mix-up, but the waiter quickly confirmed my order was correct. They took it back and returned it on the rare side, which I prefer. Unfortunately, by then my companions had already finished eating. The meat was so tough that I gave up after a few bites—nothing memorable.

Parking can be tricky. There’s a lot a couple of doors down from the restaurant, along with some street parking if you arrive early enough. That won’t be an issue for me, though, since I don’t plan to return anytime soon.

Overall, I don’t understand the hype. While the place has a cozy vibe, it feels more like a neighborhood bar than a true destination for a quality dinner.

We arrived about 10 minutes before closing but were warmly welcomed by the staff despite the late hour. With us was a woman who had lived in Charlotte for many years and insisted we try the sweet tea. That made perfect sense—authentic Southern sweet tea is what I call "diabetic coma sweet," exactly how I like it. The sweet tea lived up to its reputation, and I ended up drinking quite a bit. We even joked that she should just leave the pitcher with us. She thought we were crazy, and honestly, we were—crazy for sweet tea!

For my meal, I chose the original pita burger, a burger served inside a pita with some kind of Greek-inspired sauce, I believe. Whatever the sauce was, it was flavorful and delicious. The fries were plain, seasoned only with salt. I felt that a touch of seasoning salt might have added some extra zest and character. The onion rings seemed cheap and were just average; to me, they tasted as if they lacked any seasoning.

Overall, the service was exceptional, especially given our late arrival. The food was tasty, the price was reasonable, and the sweet tea was fantastic!

Having dined there before, she warned me to prepare for what might be the best meal I’d ever have. Reluctantly, I have to admit she was right. As many others have pointed out, valet parking is essential—unless you happen to know a perfect hidden spot nearby.

The food was truly exceptional. I was unsure which steak cut to choose, but my server recommended his favorite. While I can’t recall the exact cut, it was beautifully presented and cooked to perfection. We shared two sides from a new menu that hadn’t yet been printed during our visit. One was a phenomenal scalloped potato dish, but my favorite was the creamed corn with tasso ham. I loved it so much that I jotted down the ingredients, hoping to try making it at home someday. Though I haven’t attempted it yet, and I’m sure my cooking will come close, I’d much rather enjoy it at Morton's.

For dessert, I couldn’t resist the molten lava cake, which is apparently their signature dessert—and with good reason. It was amazing! If only I hadn’t been so full from the fantastic steak and sides (excuse the alliteration!), I might have finished every bite.

All in all, I WILL be returning to Morton's, and I truly hope that creamed corn remains on the menu!

For our evening out, we chose a nice top paired with jeans, not realizing Morton's hostess would disapprove of our attire. After checking in with the woman at the front, the man who escorted us to our table made a dismissive comment, “Oh jeans I see...,” which made both my girlfriend and me feel uneasy and uncomfortable throughout our entire visit.

The drinks were lackluster, and while the steaks were acceptable, they failed to leave a memorable impression. Although our waiter was personable and we appreciated his warmth, it wasn’t enough to overcome the poor initial impression we had.

At a restaurant of this stature, I expected a higher standard of service. When patrons plan to spend over $150 on dinner, it’s essential to make them feel welcomed and comfortable. Due to this experience, I have no intention of returning to Morton's and have shared my disappointing encounter with everyone I know.

While seated at the bar, I noticed a man in grimy jeans and a t-shirt so intoxicated that he actually toppled off his stool, and I ended up collecting the stools for him. Realizing the situation wasn’t improving, I chose to leave before placing any order. Once outside, I called the manager to express my disappointment that they had continued serving this man until he was completely wasted and unable to leave on his own. He apologized and invited me to return after the man had left.

When I came back, the man was still staggering around outside. I went back inside, where Rich, the manager, apologized again. I took a seat at the bar, and he offered to buy me an appetizer and a drink, which I accepted. Unfortunately, the bartender never returned to take my drink order, so I decided to leave. The manager was still outside handling the situation with the intoxicated man and the police. As I exited, he noticed me, and I shook his hand, saying thanks anyway.

When things go wrong, HOOTERS does serve a decent chicken wing, but honestly, I would have preferred my Filet and Broccoli. Oh well.

We were genuinely impressed by the steaks, aged for four weeks. My husband chose the porterhouse, and I went with the NY strip—both arriving perfectly cooked to a flawless medium rare. To accompany the meal, we ordered mushrooms in au jus, which complemented the steaks beautifully.

Before our main dishes arrived, fresh butter was served alongside a warm boule of bread, its aroma enhanced by toasted onion baked on top. We also shared the Morton's salad, consisting of crisp greens tossed in blue cheese dressing and topped with egg and anchovies. The generous portions made sharing effortless.

For dessert, my husband selected the molten hot lava chocolate cake, paired with vanilla ice cream and caramel sauce. It was prepared to order when we placed our steak requests and was decadently rich in chocolate. He finished the meal with a tawny port, which I sampled and thoroughly enjoyed, though I was too full to have my own.

Seated comfortably in the circular booth, we savored both the food and our conversation. The attentive service from our waiter and maitre d’ elevated the entire experience, making it all the more memorable.

Dean and Deluca serves as a notable example of this type of establishment. Matt’s, ideally located right on the green and just a short walk from Trade and Tryon, offers a warm and inviting atmosphere. Their burgers, hot dogs, milkshakes, and hand-dipped ice cream stand out, and it’s one of the few uptown spots where you can actually find a corn dog. The combo deals are impressive, and seeing Matt behind the register provides a comforting reminder that family-run businesses remain strong.

That said, the fries don’t quite meet my expectations—they often come out limp and greasy. The food pickup process can also be a bit awkward. While your number is called and retrieving your order is straightforward, the small, cramped area for straws, napkins, and drink lids frequently becomes congested. When several people try to access these items at once, it quickly turns into a frustrating bottleneck.

Matt’s Chicago Dog enjoys a prime location—close enough to the convention center for convenience, yet nicely distanced from the busy crowds. I appreciated the pleasant stroll along the park on the way there and was thankful to have a companion familiar with the area.

Ordering went smoothly thanks to the polite and attentive staff. They noticed our convention badges, asked where we were from, and even recognized some group members who had visited the day before. I chose the two corn-dog combo, while others picked the hot dog and burger combos. The fries arrived piping hot and perfectly seasoned. Our corn dogs offered the ideal mix of crispy golden crust and flavorful sausage. The burger and hot dogs disappeared so quickly that I didn’t get a chance to hear anyone’s feedback. The ketchup supply on the table was somewhat low, but since we arrived just after the lunch rush, that was understandable.

Before leaving, I returned for a Diet Coke refill and noticed a short line at the register. When the cashier saw my cup, he kindly motioned for me to go ahead, saving me from waiting behind others placing orders. That considerate gesture pleasantly surprised me, and I truly appreciated it—more places should adopt that practice.

A previous reviewer had mentioned some confusion about picking up baskets near the utensil station, but during my visit, a young woman brought out the food, calling numbers and waiting for the right person to respond. This method seemed far more efficient than having customers collect their own orders.

All in all, I would confidently recommend Matt’s Chicago Dog to anyone nearby.

Just a short walk from the Green, this spot offers a refreshing escape for anyone stuck in a cubicle all day craving some sunshine. The menu is refreshingly simple, featuring hot dogs, burgers, and sandwiches. While the variety might seem a bit overwhelming at first, I haven’t come across a single sandwich or dish that disappointed me. Upon arrival, you join the line, place your order, and then wait—either for your meal to be served at your table if dining in or for your number to be called if you’re picking up.

The dining space is small and cozy, typical for many uptown spots, but they make efficient use of the area with plenty of seating. Finding a table can sometimes be tricky, but turnover is quick, and you always have the option to take your food outside to enjoy on the Green. One standout element is a mural on the wall that cleverly tricks you into feeling like you’re outside on the street rather than indoors. Kudos to the artist for the impressively realistic glass reflections on the windows.

Though I haven’t yet tried a Chicago dog here (gasp!), every other dish I’ve sampled has been consistently solid, so I’m confident their Chicago dogs hold up just as well. It’s not Chicago, but this place definitely stands its ground.

For more than three years, I’ve relied on this Starbucks as my dependable caffeine haven. Although parking nearby is notoriously awful—a fair complaint—it honestly doesn’t bother me. The place does get crowded and busy during peak hours, but that only adds to its character. What really sets this spot apart is how the baristas remember my usual order—a grande Misto with non-fat milk—and often have it ready before I even reach the counter.

The recent renovation caused some inconvenience since I went without my regular workday coffee fix for 10 business days. During that time, I had to endure dreadful Keurig coffee at home or make a miserable trek from Gateway to N. Tryon in sweltering heat. Frankly, I’d rather suck on a damp, frayed towel than walk six city blocks in 95-degree weather just for a decent cup of coffee. Before the remodel, the cramped layout was the biggest frustration. Between 8-10 a.m. and 2-4 p.m., it was so packed you couldn’t move without brushing against someone, and then you’d have to wait ages for the person ahead to finish stirring their elaborate drink. It was genuinely aggravating.

Fortunately, the renovation brought a significant upgrade. There’s now a cozy seating nook in the back, and the entire space feels bright and welcoming with a rustic charm. Then there’s Sarah, the shift manager—a pint-sized smart-ass (which I adore) who runs a tight ship but still makes every customer feel like the most important person in the room. The whole staff is friendly and fantastic, but Sarah really shines.

Not every Starbucks is created equal, but this location suits me perfectly. That’s my take.

My visit to this place had one clear positive: the atmosphere. It’s a laid-back sports bar with pool tables and plenty of flat-screen TVs. Beyond that, things quickly went downhill. The bartender was an absolute disaster. I don’t say that lightly, especially since I’ve worked behind a bar and understand how hectic it can get or why someone might deserve a bit of leniency. But this was genuinely poor service. We sat at the bar with only a handful of other customers around, so it definitely wasn’t busy.

We told her we planned to eat and asked for menus. My fiancé ordered a Sunset Wheat beer on tap. We weren’t paying close attention as she poured, but when he took a sip, he immediately recognized it as Sam Adams instead. Mistakes happen, sure—but when we looked at the taps, those two beers weren’t even close to each other. After she vanished multiple times, we flagged her down when she finally returned. She apologized and tried pouring the correct beer but only managed half a glass, promising the rest was on its way.

That “soon” stretched into a full fifteen minutes. When she finally came back, she rushed off again before we could say we were ready to order food. We were starving! Eventually, we caught her again and placed our order. Thankfully, we did, because the food took forever to arrive. By the time it finally came, we were absolutely famished.

I ordered the Mahi Mahi over rice, and honestly, I wouldn’t have finished it if I hadn’t been so hungry. The fish was dry, and the seasoning was so overpowering it completely masked any real flavor. I get that it’s a sports bar, but I’ve worked in sports bars that served excellent fish dishes. If it’s not going to be good, it shouldn’t be on the menu.

After flagging down the bartender one last time, we finally received our bill. We’ve decided we’re done eating here, though maybe we’ll stop by just for drinks sometime.

Having lived in New York, I’m accustomed to the confidence that late-night dining options are almost always available. Unfortunately, that assurance didn’t carry over to this part of Charlotte. We spent about 20 minutes wandering through dimly lit, deserted streets before finally finding the Fox and Hound Smokehouse.

Though Charlotte may lack a wide variety of eateries, it more than makes up for it with exceptional value. Fox and Hound perfectly illustrates this—a sports bar featuring pool tables and numerous big-screen TVs.

We enjoyed Budweisers for just $2.50 and Cosmos for $4—if I remember correctly, these prices are valid Monday through Thursday. Deals like that are rare in New York. The wings, priced at 35 cents each, came with five marinade options and were quite flavorful.

My girlfriend and I chose to split some wings and share the Field of Greens salad, which included greens, tomato wedges, Monterey Jack and Cheddar cheeses, cucumbers, roasted corn, peppers, onions, and bacon bits. I added blackened chicken to mine, which was a crucial addition. The service was reliable, and our waitress was very knowledgeable.

Conveniently located near several popular downtown spots, this venue is a dependable option for a night out. The food is quite enjoyable, with appetizers like pretzels and mini dog sliders being my usual choices. Trivia nights often bring us here, though they tend to run long since each question is paired with a song, and there are over 20 questions in total. Despite the lengthy format, we managed to secure second place and received a modest discount on our bill.

A word of caution about the downstairs beer taps: they seem to have dirty lines. After ending up with a couple of skunked beers, we switched to bottled drinks instead. The venue offers pool and darts, but the pool table rental is about $12 an hour, which feels somewhat pricey, especially with roughly 10 tables sitting empty. Lowering the price might attract more players; personally, I’d rather spend that money on extra drinks. There’s also a Landshark ring toss game and darts available for additional entertainment.

Overall, it’s a solid place to relax and hang out in Charlotte.

Despite having visited Uptown many times, Fox and Hound had somehow gone unnoticed—likely because Rock Bottom Brewery, just across the street, dominates the scene. Arriving around 2 p.m., parking was a real challenge. With the DNC in full swing, most spots were off-limits except for a few street spaces. After circling four times, we finally secured one.

Inside, the atmosphere was uncomfortable—like a movie scene where a lively bar suddenly goes silent and everyone stares before resuming their activities. Normally, this wouldn’t be an issue, but when both the waitress and bartender joined in the silence, it became genuinely awkward. We settled into a booth and waited to be acknowledged. We waited, scanned the room, and waited even longer. Eventually, we noticed the bartender but saw no waitress or anyone else moving about. Unsure whether sitting at the bar would have gotten us noticed or if we should have, like schoolchildren, raised our hands for permission to speak, we felt completely ignored. A simple smile or greeting from the bartender would have made a significant difference.

After 14 minutes, a waitress finally approached and asked if we needed more time to review the menu. Seriously? There were only three other parties in an otherwise empty restaurant. The food was flavorful and arrived promptly, and our drinks were refilled regularly without us needing to ask. Still, first impressions matter. No matter how flawless the service was afterward, being blatantly overlooked when it was obvious they saw us left a sour impression.

Reading other reviews, it’s clear we’re not alone in this experience. It genuinely felt like we were deliberately snubbed. For the first time ever, we left without tipping. Ironically, the only courteous person was someone cleaning in the next room—someone who didn’t even serve diners. I will not be returning.

It had been quite a while since I last stepped into Ri Ra’s, and I was genuinely surprised by how closely it still mirrored the pre-fire version. There’s a distinct charm here—and in many pubs—that immediately puts me at ease. During my visit, the game seemed to frazzle the staff a bit, but their dedication was clear. I also appreciated the refreshing absence of TVs cluttering every corner of the venue.

The food truly shines on weekends when Irish brunch is offered. I tried the Irish Benedict for the first time—though it was quickly claimed by someone at my table—and it included rashers, a thick, ham-like meat. While the dish was solid overall, the potato cakes definitely stole the show. I’d gladly return on a non-World Cup weekend just to enjoy that again.

The Bloody Mary was fairly average but came garnished with a massive pickle spear, which is hard to fault.

For me, Ri Ra’s is at its best during quieter moments when friends squeeze into a booth and chat about Ulysses. Still, it’s clear that the sports bar atmosphere is what truly keeps the place thriving.

This visit definitely took place well before the fire—so long ago it almost feels like it predates fire itself. The venue looks fantastic, as if it had never closed its doors.

We came together for a GUYE—or more precisely, a UYE—organized guerrilla-style by Dirty Dave, so it wasn’t exactly an official event. Then again, when are these ever truly official? Unfortunately, it coincided with the World Cup, and Ri Ra was nearly at full capacity—in a way that was far from ideal.

At first, things seemed promising. Our group—Dave S., TR P., Julia S., Michael E., and a few others—secured a spacious booth right at the entrance to the action, keeping us away from the typically noisy back area. That changed when they turned the volume way up. LOUD. REALLY LOUD. I understand wanting to be heard, but it completely drowned out everything else.

After that, service simply disappeared. Having worked in busy environments, I’m no stranger to occasional delays, but this was far beyond normal. Part of the issue seemed to be our server, who spent a significant amount of time on the phone outside the bar—not just outside her section, but literally out on the street. Probably because she couldn’t hear inside with the volume so blasted. Why she was on the phone during her shift is beyond me.

She was friendly, the food was good, and the venue itself was pleasant, but the overall experience could have been so much better. The menu descriptions sounded incredible, but the dishes didn’t quite live up to the hype. Maybe the endless waiting contributed, or maybe the food just wasn’t that great.

And the sweet tea? I wouldn’t recommend it. Skip it and opt for something alcoholic instead.

My friends and I usually arrive just as dinner ends and the bar shifts into its evening rhythm, which often lets us avoid any cover charges, if they’re even enforced. The cozy upstairs area truly enhances the atmosphere.

That said, the service was somewhat disappointing. Placing our drink orders felt unnecessarily slow and drawn-out. As the crowd grew, it seemed our server favored certain groups—perhaps based on their attire or anticipated tips. While this was just my perception, it was quite noticeable. When it came time to settle our tabs, we had to repeat all our drink orders since she hadn’t been keeping track.

The outdoor deck upstairs is a great spot during the warmer months. However, with the indoor smoking ban now in place (which is definitely a plus), the deck sometimes turns into a bit of a smokers’ refuge.

I’d say this spot offers authentic Irish pub fare—though, to be fair, I’ve never actually been to Ireland, so take that as you will. The other menu options, especially from the small sandwich area, are quite disappointing. The Ri Ra sandwich shop may be convenient for most bankers working uptown, but convenience is truly its only advantage. The sandwiches come with a steep price tag yet are surprisingly sparse when it comes to fillings—meat and cheese, specifically. They’re generous with shredded lettuce, but that’s about the extent of it. To make matters worse, the chalkboard menu that appears full of sandwich choices is often cut by half or more because many items are out of stock.

If I were you, I’d skip the sandwich counter and head upstairs to the balcony for lunch when the weather is nice. Their shepherd’s pie is genuinely flavorful and costs roughly the same as one of those disappointing sandwich combos.

As for the bar itself, it’s a fairly uninspiring experience. During busy times, grabbing a drink, holding a conversation, or even catching your breath downstairs can be a hassle. But hey, you’re in Uptown—what else would you expect? It’s only marginally better than what the Epicenter offers, and not by much.

If you’re seeking a spot that hits every mark, this is it. McSorley’s Dark is served on tap in half pints—exactly how it should be, no debate necessary. Ask for Colman’s mustard, and it’s promptly brought to you; on top of that, the staff kindly provided malt vinegar for my fries (or “chips,” if you prefer) without me even mentioning it. These thoughtful details come together to create the perfect chip-eating experience.

The food impresses with bold flavors and generous portions. I thoroughly enjoyed the beer-battered fish and chips, while the pork chop with broccolini and a potato cake looked fantastic—I’ve heard it tasted just as excellent. When it comes to drinks, the Cragganmore single malt stands out. It’s $12 a pour, yes, but as my favorite scotch, it’s worth every penny.

The staff are genuinely warm and cheerful. We booked a Friday night table through OpenTable, and although they warned our exact reservation time might not be guaranteed, our table was ready when we arrived—even with walk-in guests waiting.

Honestly, with McSorley’s, Colman’s, and malt vinegar on the table, what else is there to say?

Ri Ra offers a polished, stylish take on the Irish pub vibe I adore—an inviting place that truly feels like home. Give it a shot; it might just change how you view Uptown.

The sandwich line was quite long, so we decided to go inside the restaurant to sit and place our order. Both the hostess and server provided excellent service. When we arrived on a Monday at lunchtime, the place was fairly quiet. While a few customers came in during our visit, it never became crowded. My boss opted for the soup and sandwich combo and described it as delicious. I chose the Irish stew paired with a Caesar salad, both rich in flavor. I especially enjoyed that the stew featured lamb and had a pleasant cracked pepper kick. A colleague swore by their macaroni and cheese, though I didn’t try it myself. Tempted by the fish and chips, I might give it a shot on my next business trip. There are plenty of local restaurants I haven’t explored yet, and I’m eager to check them out before heading home.

The food here usually meets expectations, and their beer selection is genuinely impressive. I was celebrating a significant milestone with coworkers, and our big boss generously covered the tab—a thoughtful gesture! We started the evening with a variety of appetizers and plenty of beer before moving on to our main courses.

However, my entrée arrived last, and when it did, I literally asked, “Where’s the beef?” My braised short ribs were almost all bone, with very little meat clinging to them. The small amount of meat present was tough and chewy. As a foodie, I was genuinely stunned that the chef would serve a dish like this. Did he think I was some kind of Irish Wolfhound meant to gnaw on bones?

Still hungry, I had to go home and eat something else—because as a meat lover, getting nearly no meat was truly disappointing. I reached out to management but haven’t heard back yet. Honestly, I’m not expecting a response, but I felt compelled to express just how awful this meal was. Thankfully, the excellent beer helped ease my frustration.

Despite my dissatisfaction with this particular dish, RiRa continues to serve the best Fish and Chips in Charlotte and offers an outstanding beer selection. Keep in mind, this one-star rating applies solely to the beef short ribs and nothing else.

I’ve been to this place twice and generally enjoyed the food, although the quality can be uneven. Some dishes really stand out, while others don’t quite hit the mark.

For example, the Baked Goat Cheese ($10.95) is an appetizer that’s a bit pricey but genuinely flavorful. Despite being just a starter, I enjoyed it so much I could have eaten a larger portion. It’s definitely worth ordering.

On the other hand, the Publican’s Reuben ($10.95) was somewhat disappointing. It’s priced the same as the appetizer, yet the bread was soggy and it lacked the crispness and tang I expect from sauerkraut. The meat was dry and bland, so the sandwich didn’t quite satisfy.

My friend chose the Fish & Chips Regular portion ($13.95). He thought they were tasty but wished they were crispier, and the batter didn’t quite suit his taste.

On my first visit here with a group, I tried the Guinness BBQ Burger ($10.95), which I really enjoyed. The onion rings and Guinness BBQ sauce on top added great flavor.

Overall, the food is decent and the atmosphere pleasant. I’d likely return, but I’ll pass on the Goat Cheese next time.

After some consideration, we chose Ri Ra, and my experience was consistently enjoyable. Michael, our bartender, was a true delight—attentive and quick to offer thoughtful recommendations. Though I wasn’t very hungry, having already eaten dinner, I still wanted to try something, so I went with the potato and leek soup, which was rich, creamy, and flavorful.

For drinks, I selected the Jameson Rose. Its vibrant pink hue pleasantly surprised me—it was a fun and unexpected twist! I also sampled the $6 beer flight, which included Guinness, Harp, Smithwick’s, and a blend of Harp and Guinness called the Half and Half. It felt like excellent value with a solid selection of quality beers.

My cousin really enjoyed her nachos but ended up sending back a cocktail. She had ordered a drink so rarely requested that Michael had to check the menu to remember how to make it. Considering the description and my cousin’s very picky palate, I didn’t fault him at all.

Overall, I had a fantastic time at Ri Ra and might just start going out more often.

Ri Ra’s, an Irish bar located downtown Charlotte next to Prohibition, features two moderately sized rooms and a fairly spacious interior. My group stopped by to meet some friends, but I left feeling disappointed. After paying what I felt was an unwarranted $5 cover charge, I stepped inside and was immediately reminded more of an Ivy League fraternity party than a relaxed bar. The patrons, dressed in suits, sport coats, and even tuxedos, felt out of place given the bar’s casual atmosphere.

The overall ambiance struck me as somewhat pretentious, and I experienced several unpleasant interactions throughout the night. The DJ, who was genuinely skilled, played loud house music. While I normally would have enjoyed it, the crowd that evening seemed indifferent, and dancing appeared almost discouraged. Although I don’t believe these few negative moments represent the entire venue, on this particular night, Ri Ra’s fell short of my expectations.

From the moment you enter Ri Ra, the elegant yet soothing atmosphere makes a strong impression. Much of this authentic charm comes from the bar and furnishings imported directly from Ireland. It’s an excellent place to relax and enjoy a meal. Although the stools weren’t the most comfortable, this didn’t significantly affect our overall experience.

The food truly impressed. While the menu isn’t large, the options are reliable. I chose the Lamb Roast Pie, which was outstanding, featuring a flavorful goat cheese and potato bake on top. My wife, who is quite particular, selected the Hot and Smoky burger and thoroughly enjoyed it. The fries stood out for their crispiness and satisfying crunch. For dessert, we tried the Crème Brûlée, but I wasn’t overly impressed—it was cold at the bottom, and the caramelized top wasn’t quite right.

Service was just as commendable. Our waitress was attentive and accommodating without being intrusive. Our meals arrived promptly and were served exactly as ordered.

Overall, we had a pleasant evening with delicious food and a welcoming atmosphere. Ri Ra definitely earns my recommendation!

I’m honestly amazed this place has stayed a staple for so many years! Around 16 or 17 years ago, when I worked in Bank of America’s flagship tower, it was one of my favorite hangouts. It was absolutely *the* spot to hit after work on weekends—and truthfully, I found myself there often during the week too, LOL!

Recently, I was wandering the neighborhood with Tim—my old Ri-Ra companion—and we decided to stop in for a couple of beers and some appetizers to revisit old memories. To my surprise, the place looked just as it did the last time we visited! They even still have bartenders who came straight from Ireland—how cool is that? LOL!

The only downside was the patio being closed; we were told it only opens during specific evening hours. I had really hoped to enjoy my usual Harp’s Lager outside in the sunshine, so that was a bit disappointing. Still, we had a fantastic time overall.

Even with so many new venues popping up nearby, I’d probably come back here just for the nostalgia. If you haven’t been yet, I definitely recommend checking it out!

I ordered a portobello mushroom burger—yes, I know it’s not a typical Irish choice, but please don’t judge. When my meal arrived, I was surprised to see not a portobello patty, but simply a heap of sliced mushrooms on the bun. Naturally, I asked the server why the patty was missing. He explained they had run out of portobello patties and substituted sliced mushrooms instead. I told him I didn’t want that and requested an alternative. He agreed, took the plate away, and went to place a new order.

Afterward, I called over the manager to explain the situation. When I shared my side, he said, “Well, the server told you we were out of portobello patties and that you agreed to the sliced mushrooms.” What?! I corrected him, saying I had no idea they were out until the sliced mushrooms arrived. My wife confirmed this as well. Despite that, the manager firmly backed his server. I reiterated that I neither knew about nor consented to the sliced mushroom sandwich, and the server never mentioned running out of portobello patties.

I then asked how he planned to make things right—perhaps with a complimentary meal or some goodwill gesture. He refused, insisting I was aware of the situation, which simply wasn’t true. The only concession he offered was to comp the original portobello mushroom burger. Thanks, I suppose.

I’m not someone who nitpicks to get a free meal. Having worked in the restaurant industry for years, I would expect a manager to try to resolve the issue and maintain good customer relations, even if he doubted my story. But no—he sided with his server, left me dissatisfied, and now I won’t visit on my own. My wife enjoys the place, so I’ll return with her—but only reluctantly.

If you arrive late or on weekends, be prepared to pay a cover charge. In my opinion, an Irish pub shouldn’t require cover fees—it really takes away from the authentic atmosphere I’m looking for. Honestly, it’s quite disappointing.

That said, the decor, interior, and layout are genuinely impressive. The narrow space perfectly captures the classic Irish pub ambiance, and the bar feels authentically traditional. Overall, the setting is very inviting.

Arriving early and settling at the bar creates a pleasant vibe, while the patio provides a charming spot to enjoy the evening. However, weekend nights are a different story—the crowd tends to be a disappointing mix, so I’d recommend avoiding those times.

As for the food, it’s just adequate. If you’re there late, have paid the cover, and need a bite, it will do. But if you’re not at Ruí Rá and feeling hungry, there are far better options nearby.

Try: A neat Tullamore Dew  
Avoid: Weekend nights

On my first visit, I opted for the classic Reuben, expecting a reliable choice. Unfortunately, the sandwich was barely edible—the corned beef was tough and leathery, making it very hard and chewy. To add to the disappointment, the sandwich was quite small. At $9, I expected much more. The Rose Sauce lacked the bold flavor I had anticipated, leaving the sandwich underwhelming.

The service was inconsistent. One young woman behind the counter was friendly and engaging, but the other two staff members appeared detached and aloof, as if they’d rather be elsewhere.

The only redeeming aspect was the Keogh's Dubliner Irish Cheese and Onion Potato Crisps imported from Ireland. However, if this place depends on packaged chips to boost their meals, their future seems uncertain.

In total, a small sandwich, chips, and a 20oz Diet Coke cost me $14 with tip—far too expensive for a subpar meal. I won’t be returning. Not recommended.

To recap my visit: the clear standout was the dark and stormy cocktail, which is quickly becoming my favorite. Unfortunately, everything else was rather disappointing. The burger, known as the 704, was just average, as were the fries, and honestly, I can’t even remember if it came with pickle chips. The dessert was the biggest letdown—bread pudding arrived cold and rock hard. Even though it was drenched in caramel sauce, it didn’t improve the dish. When the waiter asked how everything was, I answered honestly and could tell he was surprised. Seriously, if you don’t want the truth, don’t ask. I stayed polite but noted the dessert was mediocre at best and questioned why it was served cold—bread pudding should always be warm, right? To add to my frustration, the waiter lost points for trying to clear my plate twice while I still had more than half my meal left, and he even took away my girlfriend’s drink while she was still sipping it. It’s nice to have a late-night spot in uptown, but unless someone else wants to go, I don’t plan to return.

What really stood out to me was that lunch was still being served at 3:30, which perfectly suits my habit of eating late thanks to my job allowing me to sleep in. For parking, the Hearst Tower lot is absolutely the best choice—they validate your ticket, so just remember to bring it inside.

The venue felt cozier than I expected, with a wonderfully relaxed, mellow ambiance. Warm lighting hung above the tables, blending beautifully with the medium-toned wood and soft white bulbs encased in frosted glass, creating a genuinely inviting atmosphere. Although it was empty when we arrived, I can easily imagine it filling up between 11:30 and 1:30, so plan accordingly. Calling ahead seemed both popular and wise during our visit.

We started by sharing crab ragoons and Asian fresh rolls. The crab ragoons completely stole the show—they were superb. The fresh rolls were tasty, but I wasn’t a fan of the sauce; it reminded me of a thick Indian fig sauce, and the duck sauce didn’t complement it well either.

For my main dish, I chose the General Tofu. I feel like I’m echoing Elizabeth’s review, but honestly, it was flawless. HOLY MOTHER, THIS WAS PERFECT. The tofu was fried just right—not overly crispy nor soggy underneath. I requested extra spicy sauce, and they nailed it! Plus, you get to select your vegetable—I picked broccoli, cooked to that rare perfect balance between mushy and firm. The spring roll served alongside was delicious too; there’s something unique in it that makes it hearty yet light—I have no idea what it is though.

The service was attentive, warm, and accommodating. The space felt intimate yet casual, and the food was exceptional. That’s a definite WIN WIN WIN in my book! Enjoy!

Soho is a dependable choice that serves hot, hearty portions faster than many drive-through lines. My husband and I met for lunch just after noon, and by 12:30, we had finished eating and already had the check. The service was notably prompt and courteous—friendly yet efficient—they clearly know how to keep things moving smoothly. During our meal, three different servers checked on us, and after our plates were cleared, another stopped by to confirm our order had been placed.

My husband usually opts for the sweet & sour chicken, which consistently looks well prepared, though I haven’t tried it since it’s not my favorite. This time, I chose the Thai Curry Shrimp ($6.99). The curry sauce leaned more toward Indian-inspired flavors—sweet and rich with turmeric—and while it may have come from a bottle or package, it remained flavorful, mildly spiced, and enjoyable. The dish included generous chunks of vegetables, and they certainly didn’t skimp on the shrimp. The brown rice was chewy and satisfying, and the spring rolls arrived piping hot and crispy, freshly fried.

While it may not be the most authentic international cuisine you’ll ever experience, Soho is a solid option when you’re pressed for time and mindful of your budget. One final tip—be careful with the address! Although the city lists it on Tryon, the actual entrance is on College. I spent several minutes wandering up and down Tryon between 5th and 6th with no luck before calling my husband, who guided me to the nearby street.

In a neighborhood where most restaurants serve dinner only on Saturdays, this spot stood out as one of the few vegan-friendly lunch options. Unfortunately, my main dish—a mix of tofu, vegetables, and wide rice noodles—lacked flavor. Although it looked vibrant and came in a generous portion, the taste didn’t match its appealing presentation. I ended up heavily seasoning it with chile and soy sauces to make it more enjoyable. The tofu spring rolls appetizer was similarly disappointing.

On the bright side, the service was prompt, and with some effort, the meal was salvageable. I suspect the meat dishes might be more flavorful, as my companion didn’t seem bothered—though she is polite, so it’s hard to say for sure. The large portions were definitely a plus, giving me enough to eat again later, which was helpful since I planned to spend the night drinking with limited vegan options nearby.

Overall, Soho Bistro might suit most diners, but it just didn’t quite hit the mark for me.

Champions at the Marriott City Center lands somewhere between memorable and mediocre, delivering the essentials without truly standing out. If you’re hoping to catch a game, you’ll find plenty of TVs spread throughout the venue. Interestingly, when we arrived, every screen was tuned to the same game. We asked the bartender to switch a couple over to the Olympics, and she did so right away. So, whether you get to watch your preferred broadcast largely depends on the bartender—though, isn’t that usually how it goes?

The menu offers a broad range of options. While nothing is gourmet, the bar food holds up well, and the portions are massive! I ordered cheese fries, but what arrived was a huge plate of waffle fries piled high with cheese, scallions, tomatoes, and ground beef—almost like a nacho platter.

When it came to beer, the bartender didn’t just list the selections; instead, she directed us to a display across the room where you pick your favorite. That was my least favorite moment of the evening, especially since the service had been solid up to that point. Had I been ordering, I might have pushed back. My friend, however, glanced and ordered without hesitation.

The ambiance is dark, with rich wood tones and dim lighting, definitely giving off a “guy’s bar” vibe. From the outside, it might look empty, but a quick peek inside reveals a decent crowd, as we noticed every time we stopped by.

Sports bars aren’t usually my first choice for grabbing a beer, but if sports are your focus, Champions is worth checking out. Just be sure the bartender knows exactly what you want to watch—it makes the experience much more enjoyable!

The bar and food here feel fairly typical—nothing that really makes an impression. I mostly see it as a convenient spot. If I were visiting from out of town, staying upstairs at the Marriott, and needed a quick meal or a relaxed place to unwind, it would do. That said, I’m only giving it 2 stars because there are many better options nearby. With so much competition around, you’d expect them to refresh the menu and update the decor.

My best experience was during a Sunday brunch my family hosted over our wedding weekend. On that occasion, the food was excellent and the service flawless, but that clearly isn’t their usual standard.

If it’s raining and you have nowhere else to go, it might be worth stopping by. Otherwise, you’d likely find a better meal just by walking half a block in any direction.

Oh, the relentless complainers! Honestly, this spot isn’t as dreadful as some claim. While it’s certainly not remarkable, it’s understandable why it’s not the worst choice when your only alternative is the Hooters right across the street. On a typical weeknight, the atmosphere was fairly subdued. I ordered an appetizer and sampled some local craft beers—pleasantly surprised by their quality, something like Mecklenburg Brewery or a similar label. I settled in for a peaceful evening, reading while half-glancing at the sports game playing softly in the background.

That calm didn’t last long. Around 8 pm, the bar began filling with the uptown, displaced New Yorker banker crowd—the stereotypical good old boy Bill Brasky type—and the noise level noticeably increased. Since the bar is essentially one large island, I unfortunately chose the side they clearly favored. Thankfully, my server noticed my unease and kindly informed me I could take my drink anywhere on the hotel premises.

I also ordered a quesadilla, which arrived within just three minutes. It definitely seemed pre-made. It wasn’t bad, but you should expect something between fast food and made-to-order.

I planned to catch a movie at the Epicenter and wanted to grab a quick meal nearby. Since I hadn’t been to Champions before, I decided to try it instead of Hooters.

When I arrived, I waited by the hostess stand for about five minutes, but no one came to greet or seat me. Meanwhile, more customers arrived and started lining up behind me. Eventually, a waitress taking orders at a nearby table told us we could sit wherever we wanted. I chose to head downstairs because the upstairs was crowded with kids.

Downstairs, I sat at a table and waited another five minutes, but no one came by. I then moved to a booth just a few feet from the bar, yet still no one noticed me. The server in that section seemed more focused on watching a college football game with some patrons. Frustrated, I moved to the bar, where the bartender promptly brought me a drink and took my order.

I ordered the classic burger with bacon, lettuce, and tomato, along with a side of fries. The food arrived fairly quickly, and both the burger and fries were delicious. I have no complaints about the food or the bartender. However, the atmosphere felt quite dark and stuck in the ’90s. For instance, there’s a mural featuring LeBron James alongside David Robinson and BJ Armstrong. While I understand LeBron’s presence, Robinson and BJ? Shouldn’t more current players like Kemba Walker and Al Jefferson be featured instead?

The bill was reasonable—just over $10 for a solid burger, fries, and a Pepsi with refills. I might stop by again if I’m in the area and craving a good burger, though I’m also curious to explore other nearby options.

Happy Yelping!

The recently refreshed rooms offer a tidy and inviting atmosphere, while the hotel’s restaurants and bars consistently provide a solid dining experience. Staying true to the familiar “Marriott practical” approach, the accommodations include all essentials for a smooth trip, whether business or leisure. The workspace is thoughtfully arranged with plenty of outlets, though internet access still incurs a daily fee of $12.95. The bed linens are notably soft, and if you’re fond of them, you can purchase them through the in-room catalog. Bathrooms are stocked with Bath and Body Works products, and each room features an HD flat-screen TV and an iPod dock. However, I was somewhat surprised by the absence of a mini-bar, which I had expected as a Marriott standard—so no Pringles or beer during this stay.

What truly raised my experience to a 4-star rating was the exceptional service. From check-in onward, everything went smoothly: my reservation and room keys were ready upon arrival, and staff kindly lent me an umbrella to face the snowstorm outside. Every interaction with management and staff was met with a warm greeting, and room service even went the extra mile by rushing back downstairs to get a straw when my Bloody Mary arrived without one. Throughout my stay, everyone remained consistently courteous and attentive.

A minor drawback is the thinness of the walls between rooms. I spent the night next to a couple celebrating Valentine’s Day quite vocally and repeatedly. Even with the TV on, their enthusiastic enjoyment of the king-sized bed was impossible to ignore—it was clear they made the most of their time.

Despite this, Marriott’s consistent quality across all facets makes it a dependable choice. I will certainly stay here again the next time I’m in the “Queen City.”

The lobby features a wonderful restaurant, and the staff are genuinely hospitable. Despite this, I can only rate the place 2 stars. Why? As a business traveler, like many others passing through this town, the wireless internet has been a major source of frustration. Honestly, I need a moment to collect myself because it’s simply dreadful.

Charging per device feels unfair, especially since most guests carry several gadgets, but that’s not my main concern. The real problem is having to reconnect to the Wi-Fi every three minutes on my iPad, which drives me completely insane. If this were a leisure trip, I might be less bothered. However, reliable internet access in my room is vital when traveling for work. Since I’ve never had connectivity issues with my device before, I’m confident the fault lies elsewhere. Over the past two nights, I’ve spent more time refreshing or waiting for the connection than actually getting any productive work done online.

If you want a quick and straightforward sandwich, The Sandwich Club’s efficient assembly line makes it a dependable choice. Expect your sandwich and chips to total nearly $10 at checkout, so don’t be caught off guard. While waiting, the tempting array of chips, parfaits, drinks, and cookies is hard to resist—a clever marketing tactic.

What truly stands out here is the extensive customization. Think of it as the Starbucks of sandwiches: the menu offers a wide selection of mustards, spreads, and toppings, and they generously pile meat onto the bread, just like a classic deli.

The fillings are fresh and flavorful, with bread sturdy enough to hold everything together. My favorite is #27, the signature Sandwich Club, which combines BLT and chicken salad, finished with a dash of dijon for extra punch. It’s a hearty meal, likely around 800 calories once you’ve savored every bite.

For a more substantial option, their “cutlet” sandwiches—fried chicken filets served in sandwich form—are a highlight. The Chicken Parm and Popeye’s choices are especially tasty.

Since this isn’t a sit-down spot, I won’t focus on service. The staff hustle through the lunch rush, and I’m happy to cut them some slack—they’re running a business, not hosting a social event.

Overall, The Sandwich Club is a reliable destination for sandwich lovers. I’d confidently rate it 4 out of 5.

Sushiya Japan is tucked near the second entrance off Providence in the Arboretum, right beside the Qdoba/Chili’s corner. Although I had noticed it a few times before, it never truly made an impression on me until recently. When I finally stepped inside, I was immediately struck by the ambiance. The hardwood floors and soft lighting created an unexpectedly upscale and modern atmosphere for a restaurant in this part of the Arboretum. The dining area was quiet, with only two couples seated at side tables.

Our server quickly took our drink orders, which arrived shortly after. Soon after, we placed our food orders. Most of my friends and I chose the California Roll sushi, which was reasonably priced at $4.25 for eight pieces. The presentation was appealing, and the service was impressively fast. Throughout our visit, our waiter stayed attentive, frequently checking in on our drinks and meals.

As for the sushi itself, I found it just average. Since it was my first time trying sushi and I’m not particularly fond of the typical California Roll ingredients, this was not surprising. Among my friends with more sushi experience, opinions were mixed—some enjoyed it, others did not. The salads were flavorful, and the other dishes my friends ordered, especially the meat options, were well received. My total bill, including sweet tea with generous free refills and the sushi, plus tip, came to about $8.

What really sets this place apart is the outstanding service, which is why I plan to return—actually, I’m heading back tonight. Next time, I’ll definitely try something different. Given the price, Sushiya Japan is a solid choice and clearly stands out among the Arboretum’s other eateries.

I was the only customer in the restaurant throughout my entire visit, which honestly made me feel somewhat uneasy. After being seated, I was served a complimentary salad that was decent but drowned in far too much dressing. I then ordered the onion soup and egg rolls. The soup was mostly broth with a few onions and lacked the rich onion flavor I had anticipated. The egg rolls tasted as though they were frozen.

For sushi, I chose a roll recommended by the waitress, but it arrived drenched in an overpowering mango sauce that forced me to send it back. No alternative was offered, yet I was still charged $13.95 for the roll after eating only two pieces. When I questioned the server about the charge, she firmly insisted she had clearly described the dish and that I had ordered it—an explanation that caught me off guard. I shared my disappointment and told her to handle it as needed. She disappeared and returned with an older woman. They removed the roll from the bill but did so with a distinctly unpleasant attitude.

While I appreciate that they took the roll off the bill, the overall experience left much to be desired, so I’ll be sticking to my usual favorite spots.

I’ve faced plenty of careless dry cleaners—missing buttons, unraveling seams, and uneven hems have ruined so many cherished garments. That’s why finding Rosa and her team at Eden Cleaners has been such a relief. They treat my clothes with the same careful attention I give them, and that means everything.

For all my needs—alterations, hemming, dry cleaning, pressing—Rosa is my trusted choice. While their prices are a bit higher, the convenience of their Uptown location and consistently outstanding quality make it worthwhile. Parking is easy: just pull into the garage, enter “650” on the keypad, and someone lets you in through the back door—couldn’t be simpler.

I haven’t tried their dry cleaning delivery in Uptown myself, but I’ve heard good things. Over more than three years, only twice have my items come back less than perfect, and both times Rosa promptly offered free repairs. The staff is always efficient, professional, and cheerful whenever I visit. Rosa has remembered my name since 2007 and often asks if I’ve been working out more—she truly stands out.

If you want your favorite clothes handled by people who genuinely appreciate them, Eden Cleaners is the place to trust. They’ll take excellent care of both your garments and you.

I have been a customer at this dry cleaner for about a year. Although the staff isn’t particularly warm, they are polite enough. Parking is conveniently located right outside the store, but spots are limited, so I usually visit during less busy times.

One experience, in particular, left an impression on me. I brought in my white winter coat with a coffee stain and asked if they could treat it. When I picked it up, the stain remained. The owner insisted there was nothing more they could do, saying, “I tried everything.” While I was disappointed, I didn’t push for a refund.

Because I cared about the coat, I decided to tackle the stain myself. I sprayed it with Shout and ran it through a cold wash cycle. To my surprise, the stain disappeared completely, and after air-drying, the coat looked flawless again.

If I can remove such a stubborn stain at home, it’s hard to understand why they couldn’t achieve the same. Despite their assurances, it’s clear they lack expertise with tough stains. Eden is fine for routine cleaning, but when it comes to difficult spots, I’ve learned not to rely on them.

Attracted by the impressive seafood options on the menu, we decided to give this restaurant a try. However, when we arrived around 8pm on a Saturday night, the nearly empty dining room immediately felt a bit strange. One of the highlights was the mojito I ordered—it was genuinely refreshing. For my main course, I chose the seabass, but it didn’t leave much of an impression. The restaurant is clean, and the food is decent, though I wouldn’t consider it a top pick for a Saturday night out. That said, if you do visit, be sure to watch for our waiter. He was incredibly cool and absolutely hilarious! I can’t remember his name, but if you spot someone who looks like Dave Chappelle, you’re in for both a meal and some fantastic entertainment.

I met a friend for a semi-business lunch and didn’t get the chance to sample their house-brewed beers. They serve Kaliber but don’t offer their own non-alcoholic brew. The back of the lunch menu highlights an impressive array of beverages—11 martinis, 4 margaritas, and many more—clearly indicating a fully stocked bar.

After reading previous Yelper reviews, I chose the Goat Cheese and Hummus salad. It arrived with a generous scoop of hummus—at least a cup, possibly more—layered beneath a dressed salad and served on sliced flatbreads.
