The portion was substantial, but the hummus was sharp and flavorful, with just the right hint of garlic to be delicious without worrying about breath at the office. I might have preferred a bit more goat cheese, but that’s a minor quibble given how good it was overall.

My friend opted for grilled chicken topped with cheese, accompanied by fries. While their dish was tasty, I clearly won the food contest!

Overall, it was a very enjoyable experience, and I’d gladly return if I’m back Uptown.

When we tried to order a pitcher of IPA, the waitress interrupted, questioning whether we genuinely liked IPAs and if we understood what we were ordering. I assured her that yes, I enjoy IPAs and am fully capable of ordering a beer like an adult. A more thoughtful way to handle it would have been to say something like, “Our IPA is distinctly hoppier than others; is that okay with you?” Despite this, we went ahead and ordered a pitcher for our group of six, with four of us sharing one beer each. Shortly after, she informed us the beer had a high gravity—claiming it was 9%—and warned that if anyone had more than three drinks, she’d need to identify the designated driver and might have to cut people off. This comment made everyone uncomfortable, especially since the menu actually listed the beer at 5.7%. After that, none of us wanted to order another round. Later, when our chili arrived, the waitress mentioned the green onions looked unappetizing and that she wasn’t comfortable serving them. By then, I was pretty grossed out. Couldn’t she have simply said they were out instead of sharing something so unpleasant about the kitchen? It really killed my appetite. Thankfully, the food was good, but the service alone was enough to deter me from returning.

The menu at this place is impressively extensive, which can be both exciting and a little intimidating. It’s a definite advantage if you know exactly what you want, but for someone like me who tends to be indecisive, it can feel overwhelming. With such a wide range of options, you’re almost guaranteed to find something you’ll enjoy—if not, maybe you’re not human! Luckily, a friend recommended the fish tacos, so I decided to try them. They came as a hard taco wrapped inside a soft one, filled with melted pepper jack cheese and all the classic taco toppings. It was absolutely delicious. The spice level was a bit strong for me, but since I’m sensitive to heat, don’t let that put you off.

I also want to praise the server for being very accommodating. Because I didn’t want the usual rice and beans that come with the meal, she kindly deducted a few dollars and charged me just for the tacos.

Rock Bottom’s reputation for beer is well earned. Their selection was impressive, and after trying a few, the Brown Ale quickly became my favorite.

Although the place was bustling when we arrived, our food came out promptly, and the service was excellent. The restaurant was clean as well.

If I’m ever back in Charlotte, this spot will definitely be on my list to visit again. I highly recommend giving it a try!

I’ve been to Rock Bottom several times for weekday lunches and twice for dinner. Since lunch tends to get crowded, I recommend arriving just before noon or around 12:45 p.m. to avoid the rush. Finding a seat for dinner has always been easy, and the service is consistently reliable.

The menu is quite extensive, offering a wide variety of food and beverage options. I enjoyed the fish tacos, but the chicken piccata was rather average—I had to scrape off the extra sauce, and the green beans served alongside were overcooked and mushy. On the brighter side, the french fries were quite good.

Where Rock Bottom falls short for me is the pricing. It feels a bit steep for this kind of casual dining, similar to places like Applebee’s or Outback. Parking uptown can also be a bit challenging. Overall, if other uptown restaurants are full, Rock Bottom is a dependable choice, though don’t expect anything extraordinary.

I’ve been to Rock Bottom several times before, usually finding their pizza decent and their microbrews adequate—nothing spectacular. The location and atmosphere have always been pleasant, though. So, when I spotted the Oktoberfest menu insert this time, I was genuinely excited. I’m a big fan of German cuisine and Oktoberfest beers.

The German Burger, with half a pound of meat topped with cabbage, mushrooms, Swiss cheese, and ketchup on a fresh pretzel bun, sounded like a sure winner. Unfortunately, it was a major letdown. It tasted like a bland meat patty—completely lacking flavor or any excitement—just dull and uninspired.

The Oktoberfest Sampler Platter included a "Knackwurst" corndog that reminded me of Pronto Pups from northern state fairs—not bad, but annoyingly cold in the center. The fried corned beef and cabbage bites were fairly tasty, though they felt more Irish than authentically German. The platter also came with a fresh Bavarian pretzel and a variety of mustards, which was a nice touch.

As for the beer, Rock Bottom boasts their Oktoberfest as full-bodied with a classic sweet flavor, an award-winning, rich toasted malt profile, and a subtle crisp hop finish. Honestly, if I could curse here, I would. I just don’t understand how this beer is toasty, malty, or award-winning. It’s basically Budweiser with a splash of caramel coloring—lacking any real personality or depth. The finish was completely tasteless, which, oddly enough, was almost a relief.

All in all, I’m just glad a mediocre meal only set me back sixty bucks. If I wanted truly good food, I’d probably need to take on a second job.

Our group of about 10 was thoughtfully seated in a spacious corner at the back, a considerate gesture given the busy Saturday night crowd. Unfortunately, that was the only positive aspect of our evening. From start to finish, our server’s pace was noticeably slow. While I hesitate to mention his name here, unsure if Yelp allows it, his sluggish service was impossible to overlook.

I ordered the honey dijon chicken sandwich with fries. The fries arrived lukewarm and bland—nothing impressive. The sandwich itself was disappointing; it’s surprising how grilled chicken, cheese, bacon, and honey dijon sauce could be so poorly assembled. The bottom bun was completely soggy, and the overall flavor lacked impact. Our birthday guest requested a medium-well steak but was served one nearly raw inside, forcing her to send it back. That said, some members of our party did enjoy their meals.

Service was lacking throughout the night. Several of us waited quite a while just for drink refills. After nearly 20 minutes—or possibly longer—we had to flag down our waiter to request the checks. Even after handing over our credit cards, it took him nearly another 10 minutes to return with them.

We suspect he deliberately slowed his pace, aware that an 18% gratuity would be automatically added for our large party. I seriously considered crossing out the 18% and leaving 10% with a note explaining the service didn’t warrant the full tip, but ultimately, I chose not to.

All things considered, we definitely will not be returning.

This place can be quite unpredictable. On some evenings, you'll enjoy exceptional dishes and attentive service, while on others, the experience falls short. The menu reflects this inconsistency too—shrimp and grits and stuffed chicken truly stand out, but the pizza is best avoided. Beer lovers tend to have a more consistent experience here, as the house-brewed beers often surpass the food in quality. The Southern Flyer pale ale, in particular, is a favorite among fans of that style. Visiting this spot is somewhat of a gamble since both the food and service can vary. Still, you can reliably count on a well-crafted, locally brewed beer, which is sometimes exactly what you’re after.

My initial visit didn’t leave much of an impression, but I was open to trying again. To prepare, I carefully combed through Yelp reviews to pinpoint the most recommended dishes. Despite this, the old house—or restaurant—clearly needs some renovation. Judging by the crowd when I left, they seem to have the resources, yet the place still feels rundown. The staircase wobbles, and the overall atmosphere is tired and outdated—not quaint or charming.

We arrived as a large group and were fortunate to have Ivy, an exceptional server who was both attentive and kind. Unfortunately, the food fell short of expectations. Our hosts generously treated us to nearly every appetizer, starting with fried oysters that tasted like they had been cooked days earlier and reheated in a microwave. The fried green tomatoes seemed frozen and barely cooked—still cold inside and very bland. The New Orleans-style barbecue shrimp came in tiny, salad-sized portions, drenched in the same sauce served with every other dish, including the gumbo.

I won’t go into more detail, but suffice it to say, I don’t anticipate returning anytime soon. It will probably be another ten years before I consider giving it another try. Thankfully, the company was wonderful, which made the experience somewhat tolerable.

The gumbo was a major disappointment, tasting like the roux had been burnt and completely lacking salt. To avoid another letdown, I chose the blackened chicken, assuming it was a safe option, but it was just as bland and unseasoned. None of the dishes, including the chicken, had basic seasoning like salt or pepper. This was easily the blandest and most overpriced meal I’ve had in the city. For my toddler, I ordered the Little Gators chicken strip meal, and the fries were the only part that was somewhat enjoyable. The service didn’t improve the experience; from the hostess to our server, Brandon, everyone seemed distant and unenthusiastic. Although it was a Tuesday night and we arrived at 5:30, a bit of warmth would have made a difference—especially considering I spent $123 on four entrees, four alcoholic drinks, and a kids’ meal for such a disappointing dinner. If they had charged us for the untouched cup of gumbo, the bill would have been even higher.

What truly sets this place apart is the lively nightly music, excellent drinks, and inviting outdoor patio. The old house exudes a warm, cozy atmosphere—like stepping into a cherished elderly relative’s home, but even more welcoming. Overall, the food was satisfying, with appetizers standing out: the BBQ shrimp sauce paired perfectly with the bread, and the crawfish ceviche offered a well-balanced mix of flavor and heat.

That said, my gumbo was somewhat disappointing—bland and lacking depth—though my dad enjoyed his portion. The shrimp and grits were fairly average; the shrimp was underseasoned, and the sausage casing was tough. My sister, who often orders this dish, mentioned it didn’t taste quite the same this time, though she did like the grits. On a brighter note, the blackened catfish I tried was juicy and flavorful. Desserts were pleasant but nothing remarkable. I also found the prices somewhat steep.

One notable drawback was the restroom: the paper towel dispenser was broken, and no alternative drying options were available. While this might be beyond their control, having a backup would certainly be appreciated, as it was quite frustrating.

All in all, this spot remains a reliable choice for appetizers, live jazz, and cocktails.

Although I arrived about 20 minutes late for my reservation (yes, I’m that person), they quickly seated us despite the busy Friday night. Without any hassle or questions, they simply guided us to an open table as if we’d arrived right on time. Traveling with our 3-year-old son, we all breathed a collective sigh of relief once we were comfortably settled.

At first, I wasn’t sure what to order, so I browsed photos on Yelp. While everything looked tempting, the Shrimp and Grits immediately caught my attention. This wasn’t the usual dish—they had given it a flavorful Cajun twist with a rich creole sauce. The shrimp offered a distinctive smoky flavor that perfectly complemented the meal, while the Andouille sausage delivered a bold kick that tied the whole dish together.

For dessert, we chose the Tollhouse Cookie Pie. I had never tried anything quite like it before. It was delicious, though we both felt it could have used more chocolate chips. The walnuts added a nice extra texture and flavor.

We visited this restaurant only once and wisely made a reservation in advance. Upon arrival, the atmosphere felt cozy and inviting—a charming home thoughtfully converted into an elegant dining space. Valet parking was available, adding convenience. The hostess promptly seated us on the second floor, and by fortunate chance, live jazz music was playing that evening, bringing a lively energy to the room.

During restaurant week, the menu offered a varied selection of entrees as part of a three-course meal, paired with a glass of wine of our choice. We began with a perfectly portioned cup of seafood gumbo, served at an ideal temperature and filled with scallops, shrimp, and vegetables.

For our main courses, we chose Diane with Chicken and Fresh Fish, specifically blackened tilapia. Both dishes were well prepared—the tilapia topped with flavorful ingredients, and the Diane chicken accompanied by a medley of vegetables and rice. There was also an option to add shrimp to the chicken. All the food arrived warm.

To finish, we selected the Key Lime Pie. While I don’t recall every detail, it’s hard to go wrong with such a classic dessert. Our server was polite and attentive, checking in regularly and ensuring our meals were served promptly. The price during restaurant week seemed reasonable ($$), though outside that period, it would be a bit pricier ($$$). The restrooms were clean and well maintained as well.

Sometimes the chicken ends up a little greasy, and the fried livers and gizzards turn nearly rock-hard. Yet, on those rare perfect days, this place serves some of the best fried chicken and fried livers/gizzards you’ll find nearby.

I’ve been coming here since I was a kid, thanks to my dad, and the liver snacks have always been a favorite of mine. While indulgent and far from the healthiest option, when cooked properly, the liver stays tender inside with a satisfyingly crispy crust. Although the gizzards are often overcooked, I’ve enjoyed some genuinely outstanding ones on occasion. The chicken is consistently well-prepared, boasting crispy skin that’s pure, artery-clogging bliss.

What I appreciate most is the super meal deal for about five dollars, which comes with sides. That’s usually my go-to order, and you really can’t go wrong with classic sides like mac and cheese and okra.

If you ever find yourself near Chicken Box, the first thing that will likely catch your eye is the sea of cars tightly packed around the lot—that’s exactly what drew me in on my first visit. The parking area was so congested that two staff members were posted outside to direct traffic. After spotting a glowing Yelp recommendation, I placed my order while still parked. By the time I pulled up to the window, my meal was already prepared and waiting.

Honestly, this is hands down the best fried chicken I’ve ever tasted. It perfectly captures the heart of both comfort food and soul food. Their chicken dinners come with a generous selection of sides—biscuits, hush puppies, savory collard greens, and mac and cheese—which makes it nearly impossible to pick just one. It’s truly remarkable, especially considering I’ve only been twice! The place is always bustling and full of energy, so you have to be a bit assertive to place your order, but trust me, it’s absolutely worth the effort.

Love.

He was really looking forward to eating there, though at first, I felt a bit uncertain because of the plain exterior. Thankfully, a friend encouraged me to give it a try, and I’m truly grateful for that recommendation. Despite its understated appearance, Chicken Box truly stands out for its exceptional food. The fried chicken, chicken tenders, and other breaded dishes all have flawless crispness and perfect seasoning. The cornbread strikes just the right balance of sweetness and simply melts in your mouth.

My favorite has to be the fried chicken livers—they offer an ideal crunchy coating on the outside, seasoned beautifully, while the liver inside remains tender and melts effortlessly without being overcooked, which is so important. The sides are equally impressive. The cole slaw provides a satisfying crunch with a subtle sweetness, and the potato salad is so delicious that I can’t quite explain what makes it so special; all I know is I never leave a single bite behind.

I’ve sampled about ten different sides, from greens and yams to fried okra and broccoli casserole—the list seems endless. The only real challenge at Chicken Box is deciding what to order because everything looks and tastes so inviting! Whenever we ask my son where he wants to go, he always shouts, “Chicken Box!” And honestly, I couldn’t agree more!

I really wanted to fall for this place—I was hoping to avoid the awkwardness of clutching Price’s iconic white box like some kind of bandit while walking down the street. All I craved was to sit down and truly savor my meal, dammit! Unfortunately, that just isn’t going to happen here.

This spot is undeniably a dive, but it offers a broad and varied menu. We ordered two white-piece chicken meals with two sides each, and my son chose the 10-piece wingettes. Our sides included mac and cheese, mashed potatoes with gravy, fried okra, sweet potato casserole, and hush puppies. The mac and cheese was genuinely delicious, and the okra was just as satisfying. The sweet potatoes came in chunks—a welcome change—with syrup replacing the usual streusel topping. The hush puppies were classic: dense, hefty little bites, nothing groundbreaking but fulfilling.

Then came the mashed potatoes—ice cold. Seriously, think about that. Why weren’t they fresh? Why weren’t they piping hot, especially drenched in a very peppery gravy (a bit too peppery for me, and I actually love pepper)? The chicken was salty and crunchy but overcooked. The wings were tiny, fried like the larger pieces, and arrived without sauce—just peppery. Since my kid enjoys spicy food, I hope they didn’t tone it down for him, which sadly happens all too often.

Honestly, I’m guessing the cook was more interested in watching the game on a lazy Sunday afternoon around 4. Maybe on any other day or time, this place shines, but on this particular day, it was dry, salty, and just plain meh.

That’s not what I want. I want chicken still sizzling, grease popping off that crunchy skin that makes your eyes roll back. I want a fresh biscuit or roll, coleslaw, tots—all packed up and ready to go. I’d even awkwardly huddle in the car, trying not to make a mess while I eat. I want Price’s.

It had been quite some time since my last visit, and I was genuinely eager to enjoy their fried chicken, mac & cheese, and collard greens once again. When I pulled into the parking lot, a large sign hanging from the roof immediately caught my eye, proclaiming that the original owners had returned, though the restaurant was now under new management. Sadly, I must say the original owners have really undone what was once an exceptional spot.

Inside, the massive menu board that once proudly featured a wide selection of outstanding soul food sides was completely gone. It seems the new management is trying to replicate Price’s by offering only mediocre coleslaw and subpar tater tots. The biggest disappointment, however, is the fried chicken recipe—it’s clear it has been changed.

Does anyone know where the previous managers have gone? I truly miss their homemade cooking because this new Chicken Box Cafe just doesn’t live up to what it once was.

After finishing my yoga class just before noon, I headed to the market with about $24 in cash. The space was cozy, hosting around fifteen vendors. As expected at a typical farmer’s market, the selection included fresh fruits and vegetables, farm-raised hormone-free chicken and red meat, baked goods, incense, and handcrafted arts and crafts.

I spent my entire budget and left with three cucumbers, a handful of bite-sized plums, oversized scallions, five potatoes, two fried pies, pecan coffee cake, a mini fruit pie, peaches, homemade butter garlic herb biscuits, and several beefsteak tomatoes. Although there was a vendor selling loose tea, I ran out of money before I could explore their offerings.

I did wish there had been a wider variety of leafy greens, especially since many are currently in season. While the overall assortment didn’t match some other markets I’ve visited, the prices were reasonable. Farmer’s markets focus on supporting local producers, and as an advocate of the slow food movement, I’m simply glad that Noda has one!

*Arriving later in the day, a couple of hours before closing, helped me find better deals.

If you’re hoping for a genuinely enjoyable way to spend your time, this place might leave you disappointed. During a birthday party with about seven guys, someone collided with me at full speed without slowing down, sending me crashing directly into the wall. When an employee came over to reposition my kart, he chose to make a sarcastic remark about the kart having brakes. I explained I was already using them—that was the exact problem. Meanwhile, several guys in my group hit the wall just as hard or even harder and were all asked if they were okay. I, however, received no such concern. Another woman in our group injured her neck and had to sit out the rest of the event, yet no staff member offered her any assistance. This is simply what I observed; maybe it was an off day.

From this experience, it became clear to me that this venue doesn’t seem particularly welcoming to amateurs or female participants. The price is steep, but I’m still awarding three stars because the karts and tracks are in decent condition. For serious competition and championship-level racing, this location is about as good as it gets. Still, I don’t see myself returning just for casual fun.

Having visited go-kart tracks in LA, Boston, and Vegas, I can confidently say this facility is the worst I’ve encountered. Unlike those other venues, which all included a crucial feature—a dedicated safety or training staff member, or at least a safety briefing video—this place lacks any of that. Instead, the process is reduced to registering on a computer, paying, and then aimlessly searching for where to put on your track suit, completely unguided. There’s no one available to advise you on what to wear or where to go next.

After finally locating the track, you wait in line to drive, but once again, there’s no instructional video or explanation of the rules. You simply climb into your kart and start racing. I might have overlooked these lax safety procedures if my brother and I hadn’t been yelled at by the manager or owner while on the track. His exact words were, “WHERE ON PLANET EARTH CAN YOU STILL DRIVE WITH YELLOW LIGHTS FLASHING?”

If stopping at yellow lights is mandatory, that rule should be clearly communicated before the race begins. For context, the yellow lights were on due to a crash. We slowed down as we approached the crash site, exercising caution only where necessary. That’s when the manager started yelling, completely ruining the experience. We were left stunned, wondering where that sudden outburst originated.

Overall, this place falls far short of the professionalism and quality I’ve experienced at K1 or F1.

I arrived around 8 pm on a busy Saturday night, though perhaps I had set my expectations too high after such an excellent first visit. Unfortunately, the customer service this time didn’t meet that standard. The front desk attendant seemed distant and unwelcoming. Shortly after I arrived, a mother with three children came in for her first visit and asked straightforward questions about registration and pricing, only to be clearly dismissed.

I’m unsure whether the staff aren’t given breaks or if they’ve grown too comfortable with the many regulars, but two of the three front desk employees were eating behind the counter. Meanwhile, one of the two staff members on the track was casually pacing back and forth, snacking from a takeout tray, which felt unprofessional.

I really wish there were clearer guidelines about which age groups and skill levels are appropriate for racing alongside adults. A girl who appeared to be around 12 to 14 years old joined our race for the first time and definitely created a safety risk. Though I consider myself only moderately skilled, she was weaving all over the track, forcing many drivers to brake suddenly and nearly collide with her as she consistently stayed in the middle lane. She likely completed only about three laps compared to the usual seven to nine, making her presence a serious hazard.

My boyfriend paid for two games, but I chose not to stay for another. We’ll be returning (no refunds), hoping for a much better experience next time.

If you're new to tattoos, the window booth offers a fantastic vantage point to admire the artistry during gallery crawls. Meanwhile, seasoned tattoo fans can enjoy the shop’s open, social atmosphere while getting inked. Just next door, the Baku Art Gallery showcases canvas pieces by several tattoo artists, highlighting their creativity beyond skin art.

With over thirteen years of tattoo experience across five different artists, I consider this studio one of the most relaxed and inviting I’ve encountered. Its easygoing vibe provides much-needed comfort during what can sometimes be an uneasy process.

The talented team covers a broad range of styles—from old school traditional and Japanese to black work and more—ready to bring your designs to life or create a unique, lasting piece. I’ve had the pleasure of working with Matt Terry, whose skill truly stands out, and I’m eager to have Joey ink me soon.

Nathan Fish designed a tattoo for me that I genuinely love. I came in with an image I found online for inspiration, and Nathan skillfully brought it to life, incorporating every detail I requested. The final piece exceeded my expectations, going beyond the original reference I brought.

What truly distinguishes this shop, though, is the people. Building a connection with my tattoo artist is something I deeply value, yet it was missing during my first tattoo experience at another studio. This time, I brought my best friend Winnie, who had her tattoo done by Travis Lakeman, and hers turned out fantastic as well. Throughout the entire process, both Nathan and Travis made sure we felt comfortable and at ease—something essential when you’re spending hours under the needle.

Additionally, every artist here embodies true creativity. Their artwork is showcased at their workstations and in the attached gallery, offering an authentic glimpse into their talent and artistic vision—precisely what tattooing should celebrate.

From beginning to end, the experience was exceptional, and the pricing is very reasonable—they definitely don’t overcharge. I will absolutely return for more tattoos and wholeheartedly recommend this shop to anyone seeking quality ink.

Though full payment for the 50-person event had been settled months in advance, the caterer persistently requested additional funds right up to the wedding day, compounding an already exorbitant cost. The Basic Cake clause in the contract remained vague and was never properly clarified. Despite the bride submitting the schedule well ahead of time, the catering staff repeatedly approached the family throughout the evening, continuing to ask for it.

Adding to the disappointment, the staff cut the cake before the couple’s special moment and served it during the toast. The food was served cold, and while the presentation looked appealing, the portions were noticeably inadequate. Rolls arrived without butter, and salt and pepper were entirely missing; when requested, the staff claimed that offering these condiments would offend the chef.

Although the team was scheduled to arrive by 2:30 PM, they did not show up until after guests began arriving at 3:45 PM for the 4 PM ceremony. Overall, this experience was utterly disgraceful. I will neither use this caterer again nor recommend them to any clients or professional associates.

Charlotte Airport offers a broad range of dining options, combining quick-service outlets with sit-down restaurants to suit diverse preferences. If you want to unwind with a drink and a smoke before your flight, Chili’s is the place to go. The airport also features spacious bookstores stocked with knick-knacks, snacks, magazines, and various other retail shops. Wait times are typically short, and the staff remains consistently friendly.

Let’s be honest—being stuck at an airport due to a delayed flight is frustrating, but it’s a common experience for nearly every traveler. If you’re seriously rating this airport just one or two stars, you probably haven’t yet had the “pleasure” of dealing with airports like Raleigh, Nashville, Mobile, Birmingham, or New Orleans, to name a few.

After nightfall, this airport becomes eerily deserted and ghostly quiet. If you’re lucky, you’ll be hauling a heavy computer bag through three full concourses, desperately searching for someone to help—holding onto the faint hope that maybe, just maybe, there’s another flight. Spoiler alert: there isn’t. The empty terminal almost seems to mock your hopeful optimism. If fortune favors you, you might end up staying at the Ramada for $59.

Charlotte-Douglas, clearer and more visible signage would make a major difference. Those white rocking chairs hardly ease the confusion, especially since you’re a US Airways hub and I needed their support. My ticket printout promised assistance in any concourse, but that proved to be completely false. While the white rockers and wi-fi are pleasant perks, they hardly make up for everything else.

Among the many airport USOs I've visited, this one truly stands out. Although it doesn’t have showers or beds like some others, its genuine lounge atmosphere more than makes up for it. The main area features plush leather recliners facing a large flat-screen TV, and if the programming doesn’t suit your taste, there’s a separate room to retreat to. For internet access, three computers are available. Opposite a pair of spacious round bar tables, a counter offers complimentary snacks such as sodas, hot dogs, baked goods, and more. Gamers will enjoy a dedicated corner with two small TVs set up for PS2 and Xbox, while families traveling with toddlers can make use of a thoughtfully arranged playroom.

Whenever I have a layover, this USO is my go-to spot to relax, whether or not I’m traveling on official Army orders. Since volunteers typically staff the facility, I make it a point to sign in and show my support. The USO welcomes both military and civilian visitors, and you can access it on the second floor, where extra seating is usually available—especially when the main floor is crowded.

Charlotte airport has a distinct rhythm, quickly shifting from bustling to nearly empty in minutes. Our flight arrived just after 9pm, and after a quick meal at Tequileria, we headed to the USO. When we returned downstairs shortly after 10pm, nearly all the shops and food court had already closed. In just ten to fifteen minutes, the airport went from lively to eerily quiet—almost like stepping into a twilight zone episode.

I also appreciate how conveniently clustered the shops and dining options are here. Although the walk to our connecting gate was a bit lengthy, the moving walkways made it feel much shorter. Honestly, I’d gladly choose to pass through Charlotte again just to spend a few moments relaxing in those rocking chairs.

Premier status grants you Star Alliance privileges, letting you skip the hassle of changing planes in Phoenix. While on the ground, the airport surprisingly offers an enjoyable experience. Check-in staff are consistently courteous, and TSA agents efficiently guide travelers through security with a friendly, helpful demeanor, all contributing to the terminal’s leafy, refined atmosphere. Inside, you can savor solid Carolina BBQ—don’t miss the combo with Brunswick stew—and unwind in a cozy atrium featuring an open bar and an excellent beer selection. For an even richer experience, head to the Concourse D/E retail strip to find the North Carolina wine bar. Yes, a genuine wine bar. There, knowledgeable attendants offer generous, personalized tastings of impressive Yadkin Valley wines that hold their own nationally. For $7, you receive a guided tasting complete with insights into the grapes and wineries. After choosing your favorite, buy a full glass for another $7 and settle into a rocking chair just outside, watching the steady stream of frazzled travelers glide by on the moving walkways. Take advantage of the free, though sometimes overloaded, WiFi to post reviews like this and enjoy a brief moment of calm—until you hand over your boarding pass and become packed like sardines in the belly of an overcrowded, undermaintained plane.

I arrived with modest expectations but was pleasantly surprised by my experience at the airport. While there’s a decent variety of dining options, every place I tried had long lines—something that seems unavoidable. Despite numerous staff hustling behind the counters, their presence didn’t make the wait any shorter. Most food choices were the usual uninspiring chains—not particularly exciting, but typical for airports. Still, I was glad to see that most facilities were clean and well-maintained.

What really stood out was the exceptional cleanliness of the terminals and gates. With some spare time, I wandered through much of the airport. A memorable highlight was spotting a US Airways plane sporting the vintage PSA livery, complete with the iconic smiley face on its nose. Although I’m not a fan of US Airways, that sight stirred a strong wave of childhood nostalgia. I remember PSA only flying planes with engines mounted on the tail and wings set far back, so this wasn’t entirely accurate—but it was still a charming nod to the past.

The gate staff also impressed me with their friendliness and helpfulness. I observed them assisting many travelers and was genuinely struck by how smoothly they kept things moving, even for bumped and standby passengers, all while remaining courteous.

The biggest disappointment was the restroom situation. While bathrooms are available, they’re spaced far apart and aren’t particularly clean—a noticeable and unfortunate contrast to the otherwise spotless airport environment.

This airport truly earns its “walking airport” nickname because of the considerable distances between concourses. If your gate is at one end, expect a lengthy trek to reach it. Passenger traffic varies throughout the day, ranging from crowded to nearly empty depending on the time. Personally, I’ve never faced long security lines, though that might just be good luck. When checking in, I usually choose the self-service kiosks, as they’re typically faster than staffed counters—provided you’re not checking bags.

Parking is a significant drawback here. There simply aren’t enough spots, especially during busy travel periods, and the daily fees can be quite steep once you find a space. If you can, arranging a drop-off is a smarter alternative to leaving your car parked.

Charlotte Douglas won’t impress with its shopping, dining, or customer service, but on the plus side, it won’t add unnecessary hassle or complications to your trip.

Navigating CLT for passenger pick-up and drop-off is easy, thanks to both covered and uncovered parking options offered at reasonable rates. The airport is a solid choice for those with layovers as well. While you’ll find the standard Starbucks locations, I recommend taking the opportunity in the afternoon to enjoy a local Carolina brew—Carolina Blonde is my top pick. If you spot an available white rocking chair, take a seat; these spots have plenty of nearby power outlets and provide complimentary, seemingly unrestricted Wi-Fi.

One of the standout conveniences at CLT is the ability to use any security checkpoint, giving you access to all concourses from A through E after screening—a feature that’s uncommon at most airports. Although there are some moving walkways, walking between concourses can be quite a trek, so keep an eye out for electric carts. The higher-numbered E gates, especially, are a significant walk from the central atrium. After several trips out to gate E32, I’ve joked that it might have been easier to just walk the entire distance!

Keep these practical points in mind: Rental car counters are located offsite, so you’ll need to board your rental company’s shuttle. Smoking lounges aren’t available inside the secure area, so you’ll have to exit and follow the posted signs. Out front, you’ll see the statue of Queen Charlotte Mecklenburg with her arm extended, holding her crown. At the C security entrance, there’s an “elite” lane open to all elite-status passengers, not just those flying with US Airways. Currently, CLT doesn’t provide CLEAR or PDA boarding passes. Also, expect significant ATM fees if you use a machine not associated with your own bank.

The humidity hits you as soon as you step off the plane. While the airport gets quite busy during peak hours, finding your way around is still fairly easy. I appreciated the complimentary WiFi, and the food court tables placed right next to power outlets made it convenient to charge devices while eating.

Dining options are typical airport fare, including Chili’s Too!, Burger King, and Cinnabon. It’s odd how Cinnabon seems almost exclusively found in airports. For a more regional choice, Bojangles’, a Southeastern fried chicken chain similar to Popeyes, is available.

Overall, the airport lacks much personality or distinctive charm. I also experienced a lengthy delay on the runway, though that may have been a one-time occurrence. My connection was from L.A. to Fort Lauderdale.

No matter your destination within CLT airport, expect to trek at least 20 minutes—often longer. The layout is genuinely frustrating. That outdated “spokes off a hub” design, once functional decades ago, now results in cramped, overcrowded corridors. This issue is worsened by people who seem completely oblivious to their surroundings, abruptly stopping right in your path and forcing you to weave around them. Just when you believe you’ve avoided every obstacle, an electric cart speeds by and clips you—it felt like the 27th time for me.

The concourses feel worn and congested, with barely any air conditioning to provide relief from the heat. Food options mostly consist of fried fare or the tempting aroma of BBQ. At least the NASCAR restaurant served a decent breakfast.

What truly stands out is the staff. Whether airport personnel, TSA agents, airline representatives, or restaurant employees, their warmth and eagerness to help are impressive. A simple smile and a “thanks much” earns you excellent service. Their kindness was especially appreciated when our Delta flight faced maintenance issues—they promptly rebooked us on USAirways, arranged a direct flight to Denver, and upgraded us to first class.

The rocking chairs in the atrium add a pleasant touch. With nine hours to kill, it was the perfect spot to relax, recharge laptops, and play drinking games—take a sip every time you spot someone in a straw hat or see an electric cart roll by.

CLT airport is known for its easy navigation, thanks to its spotless condition and simple layout. However, a few insider tips can make your visit smoother—such as avoiding the slow-moving security line caused by 26 teenagers who refuse to remove their gaming devices. Parking is another highlight, with daily rates near $6 and long-term parking around $4 per day (thanks to Bill F. for that useful tip!). As someone from Chicago, I can say that’s an excellent bargain.

Once inside, it’s wise to choose your security checkpoint carefully. Seasoned travelers usually prefer checkpoint A since it tends to move fastest and is often filled with experienced business commuters. While any checkpoint provides access to your gate, be ready for a longer walk if your flight leaves from Gate E.

Faith D. made a valuable point about the moving sidewalks: while they’re convenient, if you’re standing still, kindly step aside to let others pass. If you have extra time, take a stroll through the charming shops and eateries spread throughout the terminal, along with numerous conveniently placed ATMs. And don’t forget to try the gelato stand—they offer genuinely delicious treats.

Overall, I genuinely enjoy this airport. Hats off to the QC!

Every time I arrive in Charlotte, especially on flights like STL to PHF, I often find myself rushing through multiple terminals to make my connection. While the plenty of moving walkways connecting the gates should help, nothing annoys me more than being stuck behind a family of four blocking the entire path or someone slowly wandering on the left side. Honestly, people: just like when driving, pass on the left and keep to the right. It’s clear that many travelers here—unlike those holding everyone up—are pressed for time.

I don’t have much to say about the food and drink options, though the selection seems reasonably good. On a positive note, when a flight was canceled back home, US Airways handled the situation very well. They arranged accommodations at a nearby hotel—I can’t recall the name—and covered both my transportation and lodging for the night. Kudos to them.

I’ve always been genuinely fascinated by airport architecture and enjoy unraveling their layouts. It’s especially interesting to watch how an older airport like Charlotte-Douglas expands and adapts over time to meet the changing needs of its city. As a reliable international hub, it’s large enough to offer flights to nearly any destination. However, while being a US Air hub provides certain advantages, it also tends to make flying in and out of Charlotte fairly expensive.

I’ve consistently appreciated Charlotte-Douglas’s well-organized long-term parking, which I often rely on during business trips. Yet, during my most recent visit, all the long-term lots were closed, forcing me to use the daily lot instead. Although it’s not much farther, the added hassle of driving around searching for a spot increased the stress of having to leave ample time for check-in and security.

Within the past year or so, the airport introduced new body scanners, but this technology has sparked some controversy. I felt somewhat uneasy about the images displayed and who might be viewing them, but I still went through the scanner on my last trip. Hopefully, there won’t be any negative health effects—if there are, I’d likely opt for the pat-down instead.

Charlotte Douglas Airport provides several parking options to accommodate different preferences. The most affordable choice is the long-term lots, priced at $4 per day and including a shuttle to the terminal. If you prefer to park closer, nearby lots and garages charge $6 daily and also offer a quick, three-minute shuttle ride. Alternatively, parking across the street costs about $16 per day and allows you to walk directly to the terminal. When returning, look for shuttles outside baggage claim on the middle island—white buses labeled “Long Term A,” “Long Term B,” or “Daily” will take you back to your vehicle.

Inside the terminal, ticketing is located on the upper level. During busy periods, heading toward the ends of the terminal for security screening can save you time. Checkpoint A usually sees lighter traffic, while Checkpoints D/E are often nearly empty, helping you avoid long lines and delays.

Beyond security, the central area features a food court, ATMs, a few shops, and the well-known rocking chairs. If you have time and need to charge your devices, outlets are conveniently located nearby. For dining, the Carolina BBQ is worth a try. While it may not be the best in town, it’s a better choice than most fast-food options—don’t miss the fried pickles!

Coffee lovers will find Starbucks on both sides of the central area and near Gate C. The US Airways lounge sits between Gates C and D/E, with entrances on either side for easy access.

If someone is picking you up, have them wait in the Cell Lot. Once you notify them, it’s usually just a two-minute wait before they arrive outside baggage claim.

Overall, Charlotte Douglas stands out as one of the more pleasant airports you’ll visit. If you have some extra time, take a leisurely stroll, browse the shops, or simply relax in a rocking chair and watch the world go by.

I’ve passed through Charlotte airport countless times, though it’s never been my final destination. On one occasion, I was stuck overnight due to missed connections and air traffic delays in Philly—an experience I’d rather avoid. The airport is quite large, with all international flights departing from Terminal D and smaller regional flights operating out of Terminal E. Since most of my travel involves PHX, my US Air domestic flights generally leave from Terminals B or C.

If you land at the far end of Terminal B and need to connect to a regional flight in Terminal E, be prepared for a fairly long walk. Although people movers are available, the distance can still feel like a real trek for some travelers.

One feature I appreciate is the white rocking chairs in the central area—they add a calming touch as I speed past on the people mover. I haven’t taken the time to sit in one yet, but they certainly look inviting.

There’s a spacious US Airways club lounge, but if you’re traveling internationally, keep in mind it’s not an Envoy lounge, so it’s smaller than the one in Philly. Still, it offers a comfortable place to relax with pleasant views.

Throughout the airport, there’s a good variety of dining options, plus a Body Shop store. This is especially convenient when I’m heading back to PHX, as I can purchase items over 3oz to carry on—a definite plus.

This airport stands out with its pristine, well-maintained environment and straightforward layout, enhanced by conveniently placed flight information screens throughout. My check-in process was flawless, thanks to TSA staff who were notably gentle and considerate, ensuring my comfort at every step. Although the security line involved the usual lengthy wait common at international airports, once I passed through, finding my gate was effortless.

Getting around the airport was quick and hassle-free, aided by the Enterprise shuttle, which ran frequently every five to ten minutes. While I didn’t personally use the pick-up or drop-off zones, they seemed to operate efficiently, and my shuttle navigated them without any problems.

All in all, the airport’s simple design, modern amenities, and attentive customer service combined to provide a pleasant experience. I would gladly choose to fly through this airport again.

Whenever I leave from Charlotte, I usually stick with daily parking since it’s only six dollars per day—unless my trip is on the longer side, in which case I look into other options. If Uptown is where you’re headed, expect to pay a flat taxi fare of twenty-five dollars.

While I haven’t had to make a connection through Charlotte, I appreciate how straightforward the airport is to get around. Its smaller, more compact setup is a refreshing difference compared to the overwhelming sprawl of airports like ATL, LAX, ORD, or JFK. The terminal itself has a welcoming vibe, and all the white rocking chairs scattered around make for great spots to relax before boarding.

Security is the standard annoyance—no better or worse than what you find at other airports. I typically show up about an hour before my flight unless I want to grab breakfast at Salsarita’s, where the cheesy breakfast quesadilla is a fast-food favorite that gets my travel day started off right.

A consistent frustration, echoed by many travelers, is the lack of available outlets—a complaint that seems to be true for most airports. (Seriously, why does adding permanent charging stations or power strips seem so complicated?)

If you run into a long wait at security, remember that all three checkpoints—A, B, and C—lead into the same central area. You can switch to a shorter line if you see one, but depending on your gate, this might mean a longer walk.

This trip clearly showcased both the airport’s strengths and weaknesses. On my return, severe thunderstorms caused numerous flight cancellations. While my flight was unaffected, long lines stretched throughout the E concourse as many passengers faced delays.

The airport’s compact layout makes navigation generally straightforward, but expect some walking since there is no automated tram system connecting the concourses yet. I recommend allowing at least an hour and a half for layovers, especially if your luggage is yellow-tagged on an inbound express flight and you need to walk to a mainline concourse.

There is a wide selection of food, dining, and shopping options that may even surpass the quality found at nearby ATL. Still, despite these advantages, I remain hesitant to use CLT frequently due to my growing frustration with US Airways, which is beyond the airport’s control.

Charlotte is a frequent layover for travelers, as most people aren’t actually from the area. If you have a connecting flight, you’ll often get dropped off at one end of a concourse and need to hurry to the far end of another, usually with just 17 minutes to make your next flight—that’s the reality of the airline industry these days. Even if you’re not connecting, you’ll probably end up at the remote end of the E concourse, almost as if preparing you for the long walks that come with future transfers. The distance can seem significant, but it’s simply part of navigating the airport.

Despite this, the overall process is manageable. Security lines typically move efficiently, and parking is straightforward, with some of the lowest daily rates found in the garages. There’s also a convenient cell phone lot, so you can wait comfortably for your loved one’s arrival and easily pick them up at baggage claim when they’re ready.

During a recent layover at Charlotte-Douglas (CLT) airport, I expected a few basics that most travelers rely on today: friendly airline staff, reasonably priced and satisfactory food options, and—most importantly—conveniently located power outlets for charging devices. Unfortunately, CLT fell short in all these areas. After being bumped from one flight and needing to catch another, the staff seemed aloof and only somewhat willing to help. Food choices were limited unless I was prepared to walk across the terminal, and what was available in the C concourse was mediocre at best, lacking anything memorable. While the beer was acceptable, $8 for a local craft brew felt pricey. The biggest frustration was the near absence of visible electrical outlets—they seemed almost deliberately hidden.

On a brighter note, the expansive panoramic window at the far end of the concourse overlooking the runway offered a peaceful spot to relax in a rocking chair while watching planes taxi and land.

Overall, CLT isn’t a bad airport, but it certainly needs updates to meet the expectations of today’s travelers. It lacks the sleek atmosphere of JFK’s Terminal 5 and doesn’t quite reach the standards set by PHL.

After enduring eight grueling months in Charlotte, I can confidently say that flying out of this airport was just as intolerable. The restrooms are consistently filthy and constantly reek, no matter the time or season. Rude staff, especially those from US Airways, frequently act as if they’re doing you a favor. Back in 1997, a cockroach even crawled out of my Pizza Hut box. The dining options are dismal—a monotonous lineup of soulless corporate chains. If you live here, you’ve likely grown used to it. The airport is perpetually overcrowded at all hours, offering barely any space to move.

The parking situation only worsens the frustration, particularly if you reside in this corporate-driven city. Charlotte mandates the use of their parking lots, with no private alternatives available. Your only choices are to compete with other corporate employees for a spot or pay an exorbitant fee for valet parking.

I harbor a deep grudge against both Charlotte and this dreadful airport.

Most of my flights are with Air Canada and United, but every now and then—usually after missing a connection—I’m rerouted through US Airways and end up at Charlotte airport. In contrast to my typical layovers in Chicago, Washington, or Newark, I find Charlotte refreshingly smooth and hassle-free. Its compact layout means navigating the airport is quick and straightforward, so there’s hardly any stress. Although moving walkways are available, they suggest not using them if you have a stroller. The variety of dining options, from fast-service counters to full-service restaurants, is inviting and there’s always something appealing to eat. Flights typically run on time here, so that usual domino effect of delays just doesn’t seem to happen. Over time, I’ve really come to appreciate Charlotte’s airport.

Since I’ve only ever connected here, I can’t comment on the check-in or security areas. Still, every visit has been positive. The restrooms are a particular highlight—attendants keep them impressively clean and stocked with mouthwash and other small amenities. If you’re traveling with young children, the family restrooms are a thoughtful and welcome convenience.

CLT offers a warm, welcoming atmosphere that feels just right, even though it doesn’t provide the wide dining variety found at larger airports. Its charm is enhanced by friendly staff and the presence of cozy rocking chairs for a bit of relaxation. Clear signage makes navigating between areas easy and hassle-free. While the food options aren’t outstanding, they are certainly sufficient—my favorite is Jamba Juice, which I highly recommend.

The D terminal stands out as the newest and most polished section, featuring spacious gates, a rum bar, an ale house, and a gourmet grab-and-go food area. In contrast, the other terminals have very limited seating near the gates, often pushing travelers into the walkways and blocking both foot traffic and motorized carts—an all-too-common frustration.

What else can I say? It’s an airport—I’ve encountered both better and worse. Overall, when a direct flight isn’t available, I make it a point to have a layover at CLT.

I’ve passed through this airport many times during both domestic and international layovers. The layout is relatively straightforward, but expect to walk quite a bit between terminals, so comfortable shoes and a suitcase with smooth-rolling wheels are essential. Most terminals are connected by walkways, which means shuttles aren’t necessary, but you will spend a fair amount of time on your feet.

The central hub that links several terminals offers a decent variety of dining options. I’ve spent time there on multiple occasions, including a 2005 layover returning from Nicaragua when I watched the Super Bowl at a Chili’s or a similar spot. For those seeking vegan fare, a few choices are available as well.

If you have some extra time after your first or second Bloody Mary, there are several decent shops to explore. While this airport isn’t top-tier, it holds up well regarding ease of navigation, food quality and variety, and overall cleanliness.

Charlotte Douglas International Airport sets itself apart with a tidy, well-organized environment—a pleasant change from many other airports. Most retail areas have been updated, embracing the popular "mall-like" ambiance that travelers now expect. Thanks to the classic hub-and-spoke layout, with terminals radiating from a central hub, navigating the airport is straightforward. At its center lies the central court, where a mix of dining and shopping options await, along with a distinctive row of white rocking chairs—interestingly positioned with their backs to the people-mover walkways. People-watching here is genuinely enjoyable; during peak hours, the space feels lively without ever becoming overwhelming.

Terminal E, the newest addition, boasts a sleek, contemporary atmosphere. International travelers departing from Charlotte will pass through this terminal, which appears to offer a broader selection of stores, though each terminal has some retail options.

Parking is refreshingly simple, offering hourly, daily, long-term, and remote lots. The farther you park from the terminal, the more you save. Shuttle buses run frequently between parking lots and the terminal, easily spotted and clearly marked unless you arrive very late. After hours, I’ve found that asking airport staff for guidance on the correct shuttle is the best approach. Just remember your parking location—long-term lot one and long-term lot two are quite different.

For those seeking extra convenience, terminal-level valet and business valet services are available. While dropping your car off right at the terminal is undeniably convenient, the business valet option is puzzling—it’s actually located farther than remote parking and still requires a shuttle ride. They offer oil changes and car cleaning for an added fee, but the premium cost doesn’t seem warranted. My advice is to skip the business valet.

Overall, CLT is a fairly typical airport, but its modern, clean, and spacious design makes your visit noticeably smoother and more pleasant.

Charlotte-Douglas clearly stands out as my preferred major airport in the Eastern US, and the reasons are obvious. The terminals are bright, spacious, and thoughtfully designed for easy navigation. While the gate waiting areas can sometimes feel a bit cramped, there are more comfortable spots nearby to relax. The airport offers a wide variety of dining and beverage options, enhanced by distinctive rocking chairs that add a pleasant charm. Every time I’ve used the on-site car rental service, the process has been quick and hassle-free. TSA security efficiently manages busy periods, and despite numerous visits, I’ve never encountered any issues. Although the airport isn’t located close to downtown, traveling to and from the city has consistently gone smoothly. The staff at the information booth are genuinely helpful, which is a refreshing change compared to my experiences at Miami or JFK. On one occasion, a significant flight delay caused me to miss a connection, but even then, finding a nearby motel that evening was surprisingly straightforward.

CLT has undoubtedly made significant progress and is clearly investing considerable effort in improvements, although some challenges remain. Having passed through the airport several times, I genuinely empathize with connecting passengers—the terminals’ tree-like branching layout can be quite confusing to navigate. Parking continues to be inconvenient, and the walk to the shuttle stops leaves much to be desired. Still, the recent upgrades to shopping and dining options are genuinely impressive.

Unfortunately, security at CLT stands out as the worst I’ve experienced. Surprisingly, I’ve had better encounters during random bag inspections in Central American countries, despite language barriers. Security lines move agonizingly slowly, and many TSA agents seem to forget that professionalism and authority do not require rudeness. Of all the agents I’ve encountered, only one wasn’t rude or overly suspicious, though she seemed quite new—I hope the demands of the job don’t wear her down.

On a brighter note, the cell phone lot is a valuable feature, offering nearby free parking for those waiting to pick up arriving flights. Additionally, the airport has significantly expanded its number of flights and destinations. If CLT can iron out these remaining issues, the overall experience would be much smoother and more enjoyable.

During my two connections through this airport while flying US Air to the Caribbean, I had notably different experiences. On my first connection, I was lucky to catch an earlier flight at the gate next door, so I barely spent any time inside the terminal. However, my second stop included a three-hour layover, giving me ample opportunity to explore the airport more thoroughly.

Customs and Immigration moved along at a fairly typical pace with standard service. What really stood out was the need to pass through security again afterward. Instead of a traditional metal detector, the airport used an advanced scanning system where passengers stand and rotate during the scan. Having flown frequently through JFK, I can confidently say nothing there matches this near-CIA-level technology, despite JFK handling much heavier security demands.

The most frustrating part was how painfully slow the security line moved because of this system. The process was inefficient, and the staff seemed unusually relaxed, showing little urgency. While this didn’t personally impact me—since I always allow plenty of time between flights—I can easily see how other travelers at this US Air hub might struggle to make their connections. The pace definitely needs to improve.

Once through security, I found a welcoming central atrium furnished with Adirondack chairs—a surprisingly comfortable and pleasant spot to wait. In contrast, the rest of the terminal felt dated, featuring low ceilings and uninspired seating areas. Food options were standard, but I appreciated seeing a Papa John’s instead of the usual Sbarro or Famous Famiglia. The pizza was quite tasty. Had I not been traveling alone, I probably would have tried the tequila-themed Tex-Mex restaurant, which included a bar and seating.

The airport tends to get busy, but never in a way that’s truly aggravating—I’ve never waited more than 20 minutes at security. As others have mentioned, there are three checkpoints, so if the one closest to you looks packed, it’s worth trying another since they usually move more quickly. The TSA agents are generally quite friendly, which is a relief when you’re managing a fussy or talkative toddler through the line.

A downside is the limited variety of food and drink options outside security. Currently, there’s only a Starbucks on the upper level near the departure gates. I understand the airport was designed before security restrictions tightened, which is unfortunate because I genuinely enjoy spending time there and probably would if entry didn’t require a ticket. Still, having a wider selection of dining choices would definitely be a welcome improvement.

And honestly, that Cinnabon aroma—can we talk about it? It’s impossible to miss; you can smell it from across an entire terminal. While I don’t always want to shell out $4 for a cinnamon bun, that irresistible scent pulls me in every time. I suppose it’s a better temptation than the stale breath smell on a plane!

The airport’s bright, airy atmosphere is truly noticeable, and I genuinely appreciate that I don’t have to walk long distances to reach the terminal. The striking statues welcoming visitors to the Queen City consistently brighten my mood.

However, the lack of restaurants or bars where I can relax with family and friends while waiting for frequently delayed flights is a major disappointment. Although security screenings are an unavoidable part of travel, they clearly need significant improvement. TSA agents here often come across as rude and overly aggressive, even compared to those in other major cities. The continued presence of bathroom attendants feels outdated—a relic from the fifties that is long overdue for modernization. Additionally, Charlotte struggles to attract enough airlines or foster sufficient competition, resulting in too few direct flights. Unless I’m willing to add four extra hours to my journey, US Airways remains the only direct option to London. For an airport aspiring to be an international hub, that’s quite disheartening.

Only one of the two parking lots was open, which forced many drivers to park along the curbs due to the lack of available spaces. To make matters worse, the shuttle bus was cramped and unbearably hot, clearly revealing that the airport isn’t prepared to handle such heavy traffic.

My wife and I usually prefer security lines with metal detectors rather than the naked body scanners, but TSA directed us to a line using only the latter. We opted out, leading to a long and unnecessarily drawn-out wait for a pat-down—an experience that was quite frustrating.

After finally passing through TSA, our experience improved. The airport provides ample space, so despite the busy crowds, it never felt overwhelming. The complimentary Wi-Fi also worked very well.

Overall, I’d give this airport 3 stars. However, the parking and shuttle bus issues significantly detracted from the experience. I dislike starting a trip feeling hot and sweaty—that’s exactly how I felt after squeezing onto that overcrowded shuttle.

If you need to walk from point A to point B, don’t expect a quick trip—there seem to be millions of people (okay, a slight exaggeration) crowding the corridors. Thankfully, the airport makes up for the congestion by offering a wide variety of solid dining options, so you’ll have plenty of meal choices.

What truly left a lasting impression on me was the genuine warmth of the staff in the international section. One person even called me “sweetie,” and after spending months abroad, that simple kindness almost brought me to tears—it was deeply moving to be treated with such heartfelt care. From my perspective, customer service in the U.S. is exceptional, and CLT definitely ranks among the best.

The airport itself is fairly compact. I started at the far end of Terminal B and needed to get to Terminal D. Despite the heavy foot traffic, the walk took only about 10-15 minutes, which is quite reasonable. I’m skilled at navigating crowds and tend to walk with a relaxed yet brisk pace, so if you move slower, it’s wise to allow extra time. Fortunately, plenty of small shops line the route where you can pause, browse, and recharge before continuing.

Finally, this airport is an excellent choice for international arrivals. I cleared customs in what felt like seconds (again, a slight exaggeration). While there were many lines, re-entering through security was smooth and well-organized. Of all the international airports I’ve experienced, this one stands out as the best for returning to the U.S. I wholeheartedly recommend making this your preferred airport for international travel whenever possible.

The airport’s atrium initially suggests a pleasant visit, but that positive impression quickly fades once you venture deeper inside or try to leave.

The terminal is spacious and thoughtfully arranged, featuring a variety of amenities—from a sleek wine bar to multiple coffee shops and retail outlets. The ambiance is enhanced by a sushi bar and live piano performances, while the simple, inviting layout includes rocking chairs for added comfort. Cleanliness and openness are consistent throughout, and the free WiFi is notably strong and reliable.

However, as a US Air hub, delays are a frequent frustration—waiting is unavoidable on every trip, and cancellations occur from time to time. Once you enter the concourses, all the appealing features disappear, replaced by worn-down establishments like a rundown Sbarro’s and generic chicken chains. Exiting the airport is just as aggravating; the bus and taxi areas are a confusing mess, and I often find myself in the wrong place when trying to reach the parking lot or hotel. The signage desperately needs improvement.

While the atrium offers some hope for CLT, everything beyond that central area serves as a stark reminder of the drawbacks of flying with US Air. The airport has clear potential, but even dependable free WiFi can’t compensate for its flaws. A refurbishment of the concourses might finally elevate it to a solid three-star rating.

Terminal E is quite a trek to reach. While it offers a wide variety of dining options, expect the usual steep prices. The public areas, including restrooms, are generally clean and well-maintained. The terminals and concourses feel spacious, with free Wi-Fi adding a convenient bonus.

Parking, however, is a significant hassle. To avoid the frustration of searching for a spot closer to the terminal, I consistently choose long-term parking and rely on the shuttle service. Flights departing from Charlotte are outrageously expensive, so I only fly out of CLT when no other direct flights are available.

Over the past twenty years, all my business associates have preferred driving to GSO or Raleigh instead. Flights from those airports are much more affordable, parking is easier, and both check-in and baggage claim processes are less troublesome.

If you expect to leave on time, prepare to be disappointed. The same frustration applies when making connecting flights through Charlotte. Whenever possible, avoid this airport—especially if you have a connection to ATL or other major hubs.

Much of the negative feedback about Charlotte Douglas stems from US Airways’ poor service. Since Charlotte is one of their primary hubs, better performance would be expected, but that rarely happens. US Airways is a far cry from the excellent Piedmont Airlines of the past. They’ll give your seat away if you don’t check in early and won’t hesitate to bump passengers. Whether fair or not, this leaves a poor impression on Charlotte Douglas.

This airport’s overwhelming size made navigating it a truly frustrating experience, feeling much like wandering through a never-ending maze. With my flight already delayed by two hours, I had just 30 minutes to clear customs, recheck a bag, go through security again, and make a dash to terminal B. The international baggage claim moved at a glacial pace, and finding the correct exit was unexpectedly difficult. To make things worse, the distances between customs, baggage claim, security, and the gate were absurdly far apart. Because of all this sluggishness, I barely caught my flight with only one minute to spare.

The service offered no relief either. The staff appeared completely indifferent, moving as if they didn’t care about travelers pressed for time, which made the entire experience far from pleasant.

Regarding delays, this airport used to be dependable in my younger years. However, every delay I’ve faced—about five times annually—has consistently been caused by incoming flights from Charlotte. It seems Charlotte’s air traffic control relies on outdated technology, as taxiing and landing always drag on endlessly.

To top it all off, I was flying US Airways, which only compounded the frustration of the whole ordeal.

Sometimes, you simply have to accept that certain events are beyond your control. Landing on the far side of Charlotte International definitely disrupted our plans. With only 15 minutes to catch the SFO flight, everyone hurried through the already congested terminals. Traveling light, I felt a wave of sympathy for a mother making her way back to California with her two children. I offered to carry her carry-on and helped escort them to the gate. Missing my flight wouldn’t have been a big deal, but if she and her kids had missed theirs—especially on Mother’s Day—it would have been quite difficult. Luckily, we arrived with five minutes to spare. Maybe that was my good deed for the day? Either way, the whole experience gave us plenty to talk about on the flight back to SFO!

The airport was smaller than I expected, but that didn’t bother me at all. Even with my brief visit, navigating the terminal was easy thanks to clear and effective signage. While passing through, I noticed a good variety of dining and shopping options, though I didn’t have time to check any out. On my return trip, security screening was quick and efficient, which I appreciated. The only downside was that the rental car facilities are off-site, requiring a bus transfer—a setup I’m not fond of since I usually prefer on-site rental services. Still, the bus arrived promptly, and the covered waiting area was a welcome relief, especially given the rain when I arrived. Overall, I have no complaints except for the US Airways delay heading back to Philly, but that issue clearly lies with the airline and airport, not with the airport itself.

Charlotte Douglas Airport offers a truly unpleasant experience and could easily be considered the worst airport in the United States. Ladies, be sure to carry cash. While you’re definitely not heading to a strip club, the unsettling vibe in the restrooms might make you think otherwise. With attendants present, all I want is to wash my hands quietly—without being called “honey” or “sweety,” or repeatedly asked for money. I don’t want to rush out, trying to stay unnoticed and feeling like I’m doing something wrong. Paying them just for doing their job? Absolutely not.

If the awkward bathroom situation isn’t enough, brace yourself for unfriendly food service. The staff at every food station seem just as miserable as I do—smiles are rare.

My final advice: wear comfortable shoes and stay alert. You’ll be walking long distances during layovers, and on top of that, watch out for the many carts zooming by—you could easily get knocked down. It’s no surprise that so many travelers struggle to make their connecting flights here!

My flight from Tampa landed conveniently close to the gate for my connecting flight, which was a relief. I quickly made my way to the restroom, though it was understandably crowded. Upon entering the only available stall, I immediately noticed that the hook on the back of the door—intended for hanging bags or purses—was broken. Carrying a large cross-body bag containing my laptop, tablet, phone, and more, I had no choice but to awkwardly hold it on my lap instead of hanging it up, as is typically possible in most airport restrooms.

What frustrated me most about this airport was how cramped the gates and seating areas were, tucked into tight corners. It was difficult to find a spot to sit and wait, and with multiple flights departing simultaneously, lines forming, and the overall chaos, hearing boarding announcements was nearly impossible. To add to the inconvenience, the trash cans in the seating area were overflowing. Travelers tried to discard plastic cups and other waste before their flights, but eventually some spilled onto the floor.

Overall, the experience was unpleasant. I’ve definitely been to far better airports.

Almost every time I visit—about 99.9% of the time—I end up having to lace up my running shoes and dash to the next gate, which is almost never close to where I land. Although my profile only shows two check-ins, I’ve actually been here quite a few times. For example, on a recent trip home, we arrived an hour late at gate B3, which forced me to sprint all the way to gate D7, only to face a delay. Then, we had to move again to gate C13 because the plane at D7 was infested with ants in its cargo hold, having just arrived from Montego Bay, Jamaica. Looking back, the situation was pretty amusing, but at the time, juggling a small yet heavy carry-on while dressed in a cute sundress and flat sandals made it quite challenging. Overall, the airport is very clean and offers a good variety of dining options. Just be prepared to race to your next gate as soon as you arrive!

Living in the Triad, I often choose to drive to Charlotte since PTI offers limited flight options. One thing I really value about Charlotte’s airport is its single-building layout—no trams or shuttles required—which makes layovers and connections much simpler. However, this convenience comes with a drawback: the airport is almost always crowded, and navigating through the steady stream of people can be frustrating. Still, they manage security well, with numerous checkpoints open that keep wait times fairly reasonable.

The food options are standard airport fare—nothing remarkable—but I always make it a point to grab a Cinnabon or Jamba Juice. Both arrivals and departures areas have their issues. The arrivals zone often gets congested as people park in the waiting areas, causing traffic jams and making it difficult to meet your ride. Departures experience similar backups since all airlines share the same drop-off lane.

US Airways is my preferred airline at Charlotte because they fly the routes I need. Their scheduling is somewhat unusual, with four flights departing from the far end of Terminal C within a ten-minute span, which usually leads to some confusion and a bit of chaos. Still, credit is due—out of roughly 30 flights I’ve taken from Charlotte over the past three years, only two have faced significant delays.

I often feel reluctant about Charlotte Douglas Airport, mostly because its close proximity to RDU makes my time there feel almost wasted. Since the flight between the two airports is only about 30 minutes, I’m usually already irritated by the time I arrive. When I have layovers in Charlotte—which frequently involve delays and other complications—I find myself wishing for a wider selection of shops, more comfortable places to relax, and better dining options. Seriously, where is the fresh food? During a recent three-hour layover, I spent nearly 45 minutes wandering around in search of something safe and appealing to eat, only to end up sitting in a sticky, messy area.

That said, the airport is fairly straightforward to navigate and isn’t so large that moving around becomes overwhelming. Because I’ve only had layovers here and never flown in or out initially, I haven’t gone through security and can’t speak to that experience. Still, I hold out hope for a better visit someday—I’ve read other Yelp reviews suggesting it’s possible, but I just haven’t been lucky yet.

During my last trip through the airport, weather delays kept me waiting for several hours. To occupy myself, I walked laps beginning at C Concourse, moving through the central area, and continuing down Concourse A, making full use of the moving walkways. Most shops were closed due to the late hour, but with music playing, I comfortably escaped into my own little world.

I was traveling to Charlotte for a business trip on the Monday after Thanksgiving. Jacksonville was fairly quiet at departure, but Charlotte Douglas was bustling and lively in stark contrast. The agents there clearly take their roles seriously, yet everyone I encountered was polite, and no one was unnecessarily rude.

While US Airways isn’t usually my first choice since I tend to fly west more than north, I will definitely keep them in mind for future trips. Given enough time, a layover in Charlotte wouldn’t be an unpleasant experience at all.

I hadn’t expected the airport to feel as spacious as it did, especially given its relatively modest size. The rocking chairs scattered throughout the terminals created a cozy, welcoming atmosphere that I truly appreciated. The restrooms were immaculate, although the presence of a traditional bathroom attendant felt somewhat outdated and a bit awkward in such a modern setting. Navigating the airport was fairly straightforward, and I enjoyed the variety of amenities, including a Jamba Juice, several sit-down dining options, and a handful of shops to explore.

That said, weaving through crowds at security and while moving between terminals was quite frustrating. The security checkpoint really needs to be moved further back to ease the heavy congestion. Another drawback was the lack of power outlets at my gate, which was inconvenient.
