I also didn’t understand why we had to deplane on the tarmac, especially since the plane was large enough to have a proper First Class section. Staffing was insufficient, too—there should have been at least one person directing passengers at the plane and another stationed at the airport entrance to streamline the process.

Despite these irritations, I was surprised by how much I didn’t dislike this airport as much as I initially expected.

CLT manages to make layovers surprisingly enjoyable, even though air travel itself is rarely comfortable. The airport’s amenities immediately stand out, with free, fast, and reliable wi-fi available throughout the terminal—a major benefit for travelers. The main concourse offers a warm, welcoming atmosphere and is thoughtfully designed to evoke a classic Southern downtown, complete with tree-lined walkways, rocking chairs, shops, and plenty of natural light. Dining options are solid, and the convenience of a Starbucks in every concourse adds to the positive experience.

The one significant drawback is the amount of walking required, since the airport consists of a single, sprawling terminal. If your connecting flight is in a different concourse, expect to walk quite a bit. Still, when time is short, airport staff are always willing to offer a ride.

Overall, CLT turns layover time into a surprisingly pleasant experience if you have to wait.

CLT remains my go-to airport mainly because flying into Columbia is outrageously expensive. Each visit here is smooth and enjoyable, with no significant issues along the way. The parking garage is under renovation right now, so you have to park farther away and take a shuttle, but this isn’t much of a hassle.

Even though the airport is small and cozy, it still offers everything you need at the start or end of your trip. There’s a good selection of hotels close by, and the terminal has a solid range of dining options. Starbucks is available too, for anyone needing their caffeine fix.

The TSA screening is impressively well-organized, which is always a welcome surprise. Staff throughout the airport are genuinely warm and friendly, and that kindness extends to the restaurant employees as well (see my Wendy’s review for details). I really do miss the nonstop flight from Honolulu that US Airways used to run—I’d happily pay extra for that kind of convenience.

Navigating the airport is easy, thanks to clear and visible signage everywhere. Unless Columbia’s prices come down, I’m sure I’ll keep flying out of CLT.

My layover at CLT began with low expectations. Outdated fluorescent lighting, worn carpet, and a frustrating shortage of accessible power outlets made what should have been a simple two-hour wait feel interminable. Then an announcement grabbed my attention: Sunday church services were being held in the Main Terminal “above the Cinnabon”—yes, those exact words were used. Without that invitation to leave the gate, my already unfavorable view of the airport would have stayed firmly in place.

As I moved toward the terminal, several observations became apparent. Some areas clearly hadn’t been updated in years, while others looked well maintained. US Airways unmistakably dominates the airport’s presence. The many rocking chairs scattered throughout noticeably boosted passenger comfort. Also, with all security checkpoints positioned at the front, travelers avoid multiple screenings when transferring between concourses.

Overall, the terminal felt fairly modern, featuring clear signage, moving walkways, a solid selection of shops and eateries, plenty of rocking chairs, and power outlets spread throughout. If you’re arriving, I’d recommend consulting CLT’s vintage-style map online to help you find a snack or a book to pass the time during your layover.

Since April 4, 2009, I’ve relied on Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) for over a hundred arrivals and departures. Occasionally, I’ve also obtained gate passes to escort my daughter through security. One major reason CLT remains a dependable choice for layovers is its wide range of dining options. Whether you’re after an upscale wine bar, a casual burger spot, or a variety of fast food, the airport offers something for every palate. And if Carolina barbecue is what you’re craving but must stay within the secure area, the main atrium features a standout barbecue joint.

When departing, you aren’t limited to a particular security checkpoint—any will grant access to all gates. This is a welcome difference from airports like Newark, where your choice of checkpoint can restrict gate access. Since the line at Concourse A often gets long, it’s wise to check Concourses B or C for shorter waits.

As for airlines, Southwest, United, and Delta operate out of Concourse A, with American Airlines currently there as well, though the merger might cause a relocation. JetBlue and Lufthansa are based in Concourse D.

Some practical tips: rental car agencies don’t have counters inside the terminal, so you’ll need to catch a shuttle from your provider. Smokers should note there are no smoking lounges within the secure zone—you must exit and follow the signs outside. TSA PreCheck lanes are available at checkpoints B and E, while other checkpoints offer “elite” security lanes open to any elite passenger, not just US Airways flyers. For lounge access, there are two US Airways Clubs, and since US Airways has joined the OneWorld alliance, American Airlines travelers with Admiral’s Club privileges can also use these lounges.

Regarding parking, I consistently recommend Park ‘N Go over Business Valet. From my experience, their service is not only superior but also more affordable than the airport’s valet option.

I was fully prepared for a 12-hour layover when I booked my flight, so the wait itself wasn’t a problem. When I arrived at the gate, the overhead bins were completely full, so I went downstairs to baggage claim to pick up my luggage—no issues there. However, after retrieving my bag, an agent informed me that I couldn’t return upstairs to the restaurants because I had technically exited the airport’s main terminal.

I explained that we hadn’t eaten yet and only went downstairs because we were instructed to do so. Her reply was that there was a Starbucks downstairs, which was definitely not the meal I had in mind. Although frustrating, I was willing to accept that.

Then things took a turn for the worse. While I was working on my laptop and eating my sandwich, mice scurried right past my feet—inside an airport! That’s absolutely revolting and completely unacceptable.

Consider this a warning: keep a close watch on your belongings and avoid placing bags on the floor. If I can avoid it, I won’t fly into Charlotte again. And if I must, I’ll just rent a car and drive instead. Shaking my head—one very disappointed traveler.

From the moment you step into this airport, the cattle feed lot atmosphere hits you—the place feels cheaply built, with rickety, uncomfortable seats and a total lack of power outlets. The overall vibe is rundown and clearly second-rate. More often than not, you’ll land at concourse A or B and then face a draining 45-minute trek through crowds of grumpy, discourteous travelers just to reach concourse E. The food options don’t help—mostly greasy fast food and calorie-heavy meals, which seems to be Charlotte’s norm judging by the local waistlines. Honestly, bringing an apple and keeping your layover short is your best bet.

Despite these drawbacks, I still prefer connecting through Charlotte over most other airports. Flights here almost always depart on time, and compared to places like Philly or O’Hare, I rarely miss a connection—which is vital for smooth travel. I do wish they’d add charging stations and replace those awful, uncomfortable seats. At least the free WiFi remains one of the airport’s few redeeming features.

This airport is almost always busy, with US Airways as the main carrier, which leaves me feeling somewhat conflicted. The terminal itself feels welcoming, offering a variety of dining options and plenty of places to pass the time while waiting for your flight. A particularly charming touch is the white rocking chairs placed throughout, giving the space a warm, small-town atmosphere.

Upon my first arrival, I was surprised to learn that I had to descend the plane’s stairs and walk outside before reaching my gate—an entirely new and unusual experience for me. Beyond that, I generally enjoyed my time at the airport.

However, what really caught my attention was the unmistakable rudeness of both the airport staff and locals. This was especially confusing considering how pleasant the town itself is. Everyone I spoke with seemed to harbor a general dislike toward others, which was frustrating and left me feeling unwelcome. It’s hard to comprehend how people can be so unhappy living in such a nice place. It honestly blew my mind, but perhaps I’ll never fully understand people. Coming from Chicago, I can honestly say the folks there were friendlier than anyone I encountered here.

Charlotte clearly claims the runner-up spot—just behind Philly—in the chaos rankings. Navigating this airport felt like a nonstop sprint, with crowds of frantic travelers desperately rushing to catch their connecting flights. My wife, child, and I dashed full speed from gate to gate. When we finally arrived, a woman—whose name sounded like Faseeka? Phasequa? Something similar—told us she had held the flight as long as possible, which was barely five minutes. Yet, the plane was still parked right at the gate, clearly visible through the window. We begged her to let us board, but she insisted the flight was closed and turned away to avoid facing us.

About 10 to 15 minutes later, when we returned, the plane was STILL there. Meanwhile, she kept typing on her computer, ignoring my attempts to communicate. I asked for her name and how to spell it, but she refused and snapped at me, completely disregarding my questions. In the end, we missed a flight that literally sat with its door open for 15 minutes because she wouldn’t let us on. Screw this airport! We then had to endure a five-hour wait for another flight to an airport two hours from our home. Thanks, you cold-hearted woman. I get that your job is veeeerryyyy stressful—sorry to trouble you like that, Faseequa! (Sarcasm)

I was quite surprised by the unfriendly attitude of some staff members. Since it was my first visit to this airport, the unfamiliar layout immediately threw me off. I had never encountered the term “concourses” before, and to add to the confusion, my boarding pass didn’t even show a gate number. Naturally, I approached an employee for directions. She gave me a look that plainly said, “Are you serious?” Assuming she was just busy and hesitant to assist a newcomer, I asked again where I should go. She responded with the same dismissive glare, making it clear she was simply being rude. When I tried to explain and show her that my boarding pass lacked a gate letter, she abruptly cut me off, condescendingly saying, “Concourse A.” Honestly, I was just relieved to be done with her if that’s how she treats first-time visitors.

On a more positive note, the TSA agents checking boarding passes at security were a welcome change—friendly and even engaging in conversation. I thought, “Finally, some decent people.” However, the bag screening proved frustrating. Keep in mind, this was my third airport that day, and I had only packed my laptop, phone, and DS. I had passed through two other airports without any issues or confiscations. Yet here, they searched my bag, claiming I carried some kind of liquid. When they found my expensive face wash, they insisted I surrender it. That was especially aggravating since I had gone through the same type of scanner twice before without losing my face wash.

The next time I have a flight with a layover here, I will definitely choose a different route—even if it costs significantly more.

A few years ago, I ran into some difficulties at this airport, but I’m optimistic that conditions have improved since then. After recently moving to the area, I was pleased to find that daily parking costs just $5. With construction currently underway to expand the parking lots, I’m hopeful the rates will remain steady.

On a recent early morning United flight, the gate agent truly stood out. Her warmth, humor, friendliness, and professionalism made for an excellent start to my day. Over time, I’ve flown US Airways through CLT and experienced a variety of positive, negative, and neutral moments.

Although my time was limited, I noticed inviting lounges and cozy spots to relax, along with decent dining options. The restrooms were clean, and the staff provided clear, helpful directions to the bus stop for long-term parking. The buses ran frequently and offered ample space to accommodate several families and their luggage.

As I moved through the entire airport, it became immediately clear that every terminal was crowded—every seat was taken, and many travelers stood waiting for their flights. Though I’m not sure of the airport’s exact size, the vibrant and bustling environment was unmistakable.

I appreciated that the restrooms were fairly tidy, with attendants keeping sinks dry and consistently replenishing paper towels. To my surprise, there was even a basket of candy—something I usually see only in international airports, not often in U.S. ones.

Most staff members were warm and approachable, and the shop owners were enjoyable to converse with while I browsed. On the downside, the dining options were quite limited. Still, if your layover isn’t long, this likely won’t be a significant drawback.

The airport offers free WiFi, but it took quite a while to connect on both my iPhone and Mac. Additionally, more charging stations are urgently needed, as the few available simply aren’t sufficient for the thousands of travelers passing through.

And yes, as Skye A. emphasized, PLEASE turn on the AC in every terminal! It’s frustrating enough to have a disagreement with the Sbarro cashier, but the stifling heat only intensifies the irritation.

You accepted the position, so perhaps handling pre-packaged food sales isn’t your area of expertise. This isn’t the first time I’ve experienced your unpleasant attitude. At the newsstand just before gate C19, despite a long line, four employees were standing around chatting with you. When I asked if you knew how to operate the register, you admitted you didn’t, instructed another employee to start ringing up purchases, and then walked away. Later, your foul-mouthed coworker complained about how difficult you are and refused to bag the $20 shirt I had just purchased, insisting it wasn’t her responsibility. While I understand life can be challenging, please don’t take that frustration out on customers who are genuinely trying to support your business. To everyone at Charlotte airport, this is exactly why I avoid flying US Air. Your rude demeanor and poor service are significant factors. Despite traveling frequently, I rarely encounter such subpar service anywhere else.

Is it possible that everyone here has completely lost their minds? Let me outline three clear reasons why this place is a total disaster.

First, outlets are supposed to provide power, right? Yet none of yours do. So what purpose do they serve? Because they certainly don’t work as outlets. I tested three different ones on various walls, including the charging station, and not a single one functioned. Truly perplexing!

Second, your courtesy transporters emit a relentless, grating whirring beep. Why on earth? It’s unbearably irritating, though I suppose it somehow fits the overall atmosphere of your airport.

Third, your staff seem completely devoid of energy and enthusiasm. When I went in to buy a protein bar, the woman didn’t make a single bit of eye contact. And when she said “have a great day,” I’m pretty sure she was addressing the magazine rack.

You earn only two stars from me. Please take the time to call an electrician who can rewire all your outlets—every single one. Honestly, it’s crucial.

Additionally, put some effort into properly operating the people transporters. Stop them from spinning wildly, as if the Pope and Gandhi jumped in, started grinding, and then left the alarm blaring for everyone to see.

Finally, reconsider your hiring standards. Look for individuals who might actually manage to crack a smirk at me. Just a smirk—that’s all I ask. I’m not that unattractive… am I?

Charlotte… oh, Charlotte. What a catastrophe.

This airport has never been a comfortable experience for me, mainly because it’s always uncomfortably cold inside, no matter when I visit. The large glass atrium that connects all the terminals is visually attractive and offers a good range of dining options, including Chili’s, Carolina Pit BBQ, Cinnabon, and Tequileria. It would be a nice place to relax and watch planes take off and land—if it weren’t for the persistent chill. I suspect the glass design contributes to the cold, though I can’t be sure.

On top of that, the airport is far from family-friendly. Traveling with an infant is especially challenging since the Family Bathrooms, though present, are nearly always locked and inaccessible. This means I have to change my baby in cramped restrooms, juggling a stroller and diaper bag while blocking other travelers’ paths. It’s incredibly frustrating.

Every time I fly out of this airport, there’s some sort of ticket issue or a major delay. It often feels like I spend more time stuck on a delayed plane sitting on the Charlotte tarmac than inside the terminal itself—which might not be literally true, but that’s how it feels. Being delayed with an infant only adds to the stress.

If you can avoid this airport, I’d strongly recommend doing so. But if you have no choice, be sure to bring socks and a sweater!

What stood out to me most about this airport was the lack of convenient transit options to downtown or nearby areas without relying on a taxi or bus. Unlike other airports I’ve visited, which typically have a rail system offering swift city access—perfect for a 4-6 hour layover that allows you to explore and still return on time—this airport didn’t provide that convenience.

As a food lover, I had hoped to discover some noteworthy dining options. While there are plenty of eateries available, none tempted me enough to spend $20 on a burger and soda. I’m usually not enthusiastic about airport food, but I imagine places like LAX or Newark might offer a more fulfilling culinary experience.

Finding something engaging or entertaining to do was somewhat difficult. On the positive side, mobile phone charging stations were available, which I appreciated. I believe free Wi-Fi was offered as well, though I can’t be certain. Beyond these amenities, there wasn’t much to keep me occupied. Even though I enjoy traveling, airports themselves aren’t my favorite places—I prefer to keep moving.

Overall, this airport ranks above many others I’ve encountered. Given the choice, I’d pick a long layover here over several others I won’t name.

This airport isn’t as large as major hubs like Detroit, Atlanta, or Minneapolis, but it’s still big enough that a tram system would be helpful. During my visit, however, I didn’t see any trams. When my connecting flight was already boarding, the many moving walkways simply weren’t sufficient. To make matters worse, several of these walkways were out of service, and even an escalator wasn’t working. Anyone who’s ever carried a suitcase upstairs knows how uncomfortable that can be.

The restroom had an attendant, but it didn’t feel as clean as other airport bathrooms I’ve used. There were no toilet seat covers available—some airports even offer rotating plastic ones—so this felt somewhat outdated.

On a more positive note, the airport featured a food court and a seating area with rocking chairs, which caught my eye since it was the first time I’d seen rocking chairs in an airport. Although I didn’t try them, it was a small but noteworthy detail worth mentioning.

Though CLT is a smaller hub, it surprisingly offers a wide variety of dining and shopping options. I was eager to try the pit BBQ, but my connecting flight came up too quickly to make it to the food court. What truly impressed me were the airport staff—some of the friendliest and warmest people I’ve ever encountered. It’s uncommon to see a gate agent sincerely apologize for a delay while providing clear, timely boarding updates, yet that’s exactly what happened here.

On the downside, the airport seemed to attract some of the most unpleasant travelers I’ve had the misfortune to observe. I was bumped into multiple times by passengers rushing to their gates, and my family received dirty looks simply for occupying six seats, even though there were six of us. To make matters worse, as we headed to the gate, we witnessed a dog squat right in the middle of the terminal and relieve itself.

Since I was only passing through on a connecting flight, I can’t comment on the security process.

Charlotte Douglas remains busy around the clock, with terminals crowded from the quiet early mornings through the hectic midday rush. Though its large size can be overwhelming, the clear layout and ample shopping options make navigating and finding ways to pass the time relatively easy. Cleanliness stands out as a notable positive. However, while charging stations and Wi-Fi are available, these amenities fall short and would greatly benefit from significant improvements.

The primary issue is the persistent overcrowding. TSA lines often stretch to daunting lengths, corridors become packed with foot traffic, and it’s common to see travelers lingering in hallways simply because there’s nowhere to sit or relax. Food lines frequently become so long and frustrating that I’ve skipped breakfast entirely to avoid them. While expanding the facility might alleviate these problems, such plans seem unlikely in the near future. Overall, Charlotte Douglas is less aggravating than LaGuardia but still falls short compared to many of its peers.

The museum’s most notable feature is its impressive collection of aircraft, ranging from fighter jets and helicopters to bombers, commercial airliners, and smaller recreational planes like Tomcats, Phantoms, and various other F-series models. Visitors have the chance to board three of these planes. During my Saturday visit, volunteers were scattered throughout, eager to lead tours or answer questions. Our guide, who seemed no older than sixteen, impressed me with a depth of knowledge about the planes that far exceeded my understanding of most subjects.

Along one wall, meticulously restored aircraft from both World Wars are displayed alongside exhibits chronicling the transformation of Morris Field into today’s Charlotte Douglas Airport. While the historical context is engaging, it’s truly the planes themselves that command your attention.

For casual aviation enthusiasts, this museum is a genuine delight. However, serious aficionados might find the experience somewhat limited beyond the hands-on access to the restored aircraft. Families will appreciate the friendly, interactive environment and the ample seating available for those who prefer to sit and observe. Overall, it’s a fun, laid-back stop, ideal for spending about an hour. Admission was $11 for adults and, if I remember correctly, around $5 for children.

The aircraft collection here includes a couple of retired fighter jets, several experimental planes, and a well-preserved vintage Piedmont passenger aircraft, but overall, the variety feels quite limited and somewhat disappointing. Most of the aircraft are roped off and inaccessible, with only three or four exceptions where visitors, under supervision, can sit inside a cockpit. Inside the hangar, there are several glass display cases, though the lighting is dim and there’s a persistent motor oil smell—understandable given the setting. While additional aircraft are reportedly displayed outside, access to those is currently restricted due to security concerns.

The main attraction is the US Airways Miracle on the Hudson plane. Although still under assembly as of July 2nd, it is already on display, accompanied by a looping documentary video about the incident. However, what immediately draws attention is the overwhelming presence of corporate logos plastered all over the aircraft—a particularly disappointing detail. Considering the museum’s potential to rival the Smithsonian, seeing such blatant advertising on such an iconic artifact is genuinely upsetting. I sincerely hope the logos will eventually be removed and visitors will be allowed to board the plane. If neither happens, it will be a letdown for the museum, the city, and anyone who paid $11 expecting to experience this historic aircraft as it deserves.

If the Miracle on the Hudson plane isn’t your primary reason for visiting, I’d recommend checking out a local airshow instead. There, you can watch planes in flight, explore static displays without ropes, and perhaps even meet the pilots.

During our trip, my boyfriend and I—both passionate about aviation—made visiting this museum a priority. Although it’s noticeably smaller than the aviation museums in Pensacola and Washington, D.C., it feels more like a heartfelt homage than a typical museum.

Most people know the incredible story of the airplane that safely landed on the Hudson River, and here, you can actually see that very aircraft. On its flight from LaGuardia to Charlotte, it struck a flock of Canadian geese, causing engine failure. The museum also features a documentary that I highly recommend watching; it’s a poignant story that may bring tears to your eyes at times.

I’m naturally drawn to genuine, emotional experiences, and despite the museum’s limited size and exhibits, it leaves a lasting impression and is definitely worth a visit.

One quick tip: if you happen to forget your college ID, don’t worry. Simply log into your student account on your smartphone and show that to receive the student discount.

Located in a single hangar and modest in scale, this museum delivers an unexpectedly immersive experience for aviation enthusiasts. The highlight is the US Airways Airbus A320, which became internationally known after both engines were disabled by a bird strike, leading to an emergency landing on the Hudson River—an event celebrated as "The Miracle on the Hudson" because every passenger and crew member on Flight 1549 survived. As you explore the "Flight 1549" exhibit, take time to watch the documentary; it clearly recounts the flight, the dramatic water landing, and the subsequent rescue. The museum also houses a Douglas DC-3 that once flew for Piedmont Airlines and a DC-7 from Eastern Airlines. For those interested in military aircraft, there are impressive displays such as the Harrier Jump Jet and the F-14. The gift shop, though small, is inviting and features a well-chosen selection of Flight 1549 memorabilia. I thoroughly enjoyed my visit and would eagerly recommend the Carolinas Aviation Museum to anyone with a long layover in Charlotte.

I’m generally not one for most museums, except aviation ones, which I’ve explored quite thoroughly. Since the Carolinas Aviation Museum is named after the state where the Wright brothers’ first flight supposedly took place, I was genuinely eager to visit. However, arriving at 3:30 pm only to find out they close at 4 was a bit disappointing. Still, I paid the $12 admission fee—actually $12.87 with tax, which I hadn’t encountered elsewhere—and went inside.

With just about thirty minutes to spare, I managed to see everything the museum offered: a single, non-air-conditioned hangar housing around fifteen aircraft. The Miracle on the Hudson exhibit took up most of the space. While the story is compelling, it didn’t fully engage me since I wasn’t personally connected to the event.

What bothered me most was the outdoor static display. A few additional planes sit just outside the hangar, but visitors can only view them through a fence. When I asked why, staff cited TSA regulations. It seemed like an easy fix to move the fence to the far side of the ramp, allowing visitors to get closer, as is typical at other museums. After all, it’s a museum, not a zoo.

So, is it worth a visit? Maybe if you’re nearby, have about thirty minutes to spare, and don’t mind the $12 fee. Otherwise, Charlotte offers plenty of other attractions that provide better value for your time and money.

I chose Burger King because it’s one of the few places open early, and I genuinely enjoy their breakfast options. Unfortunately, mediocre service at fast food joints has become so common that it almost seems expected. I find myself wondering how this standard became accepted. When I worked in fast food during my youth, I always aimed to provide excellent service—being quick, knowledgeable, friendly, and attentive. Is that really too much to ask? If success isn’t possible in fast food, then where is?

I stood in line behind just one other customer, patiently waiting my turn. When it came, I stepped forward but had to pause while the employee next to the cashier finished speaking with the previous customer—or at least took a break. After placing my order, I moved aside to wait. Looking around, I noticed chutes full of pre-made sandwiches under warming lamps, while employees gathered in the back chatting. More staff clustered near the register, also engaged in conversation. It seemed no one was genuinely working except the cashier, who appeared to be putting in half the effort. He left his station to fill the first customer’s order, then proceeded to fetch my coffee and complete my order.

Meanwhile, an inconsiderate airport employee behind me “kindly” offered to take my freshly poured coffee so I could get a “fresher” cup. Fortunately, the Burger King employee ignored him and handed me my coffee. The food was decent and still somewhat warm, but isn’t it reasonable to expect staff to perform their duties properly while on duty? Do we really need ten Burger King employees standing around doing nothing while the rest of the team remains idle?

She was so absorbed in a conversation with a coworker while taking my order that she barely acknowledged I was there. When I asked for honey mustard, it was as if my request vanished completely. Still focused on her chat, she handed back my receipt and card without making eye contact or saying thank you. I had to say, "Excuse me," just to get her attention, and she responded with a confused "Huh?" After I repeated myself, she finally said sauces would be available at the pickup counter.

At the pickup station, my chicken fingers were carelessly tossed into a bag and folded shut, with no one asking if I wanted any sauce or offering a single polite word. I had hoped the chicken fingers would be good, but they were dry, tough, and thoroughly disappointing. By then, it was 10 p.m., and with every other food option in the airport closed, I was stuck with this unsatisfactory meal. I definitely regretted my choice and have no plans to return.

How well you remember a night at Scorpio’s often hinges on your sobriety—sometimes the details get a bit fuzzy. Once you get past the irritable ticket takers, you’re greeted by a wave of top 40 remixes. I appreciate that the music isn’t blasted so loud that you can’t hear someone shouting right beside you.

The drinks leave much to be desired: they’re weak and don’t offer much value for the price. Still, it’s worth noting that Sundays feature free well drinks with a $10 cover, and Fridays have free beer on tap, so those specials might be worth taking advantage of.

The real highlight is the dancing. The spacious dance floor is always a treat to watch as everyone lets loose. I particularly enjoyed seeing a twink confidently and effortlessly twerking. No matter the night, I always have a good time—even when I’m the designated driver. Outside, the patio fills with people smoking and chatting, making it a great spot to meet new people unless you’re sensitive to cigarette smoke.

Scorpio’s is a lively venue, especially with its fantastic drag shows that are genuinely entertaining. The crowd is usually diverse, but Saturdays can get wild and “ghetto,” with frequent fights breaking out, so I’d recommend avoiding that night.

From the moment you step inside, you’re met with a vivid, psychedelic mix of saloon ambiance blended with a somewhat tacky Italian flair. The staff—mostly older women—are genuinely warm and welcoming. For nearly sixty years, this place has been serving pizzas, pasta, and Texas toast with garlic bread.

That said, nostalgia can only carry you so far. The food ultimately disappoints, especially given the steep prices. A small two-topping pizza costs around $12, but the crust has a poured batter-like texture reminiscent of Elio’s. The sauce is barely there, and the cheese stretches in an unnervingly artificial way. The $6 "Greek salad" is essentially half a head of iceberg lettuce, oddly flavored diced beets, a light sprinkle of feta, two tomato quarters, and a handful of small olives.

I’ve already given this spot two chances, and while I’m hoping the third visit brings some improvement, it truly feels like the recipes and cooking style haven’t changed in twenty years—and likely won’t anytime soon.

The building’s historic charm and warm, inviting interior immediately catch your eye. Being just a short walk from my home made me genuinely eager to try this place. Unfortunately, after three visits, the food has consistently fallen short of my expectations.

I’ve tried the pizza and two different pasta dishes. The pizza was fairly ordinary, and the lasagna didn’t leave much of an impression. The chicken alfredo was the biggest disappointment—the sauce was so thick it resembled gravy more than a true Alfredo. The bread served before the meal was equally underwhelming, seeming as if it had been taken straight from the bag and simply placed in a basket.

On top of that, the prices don’t seem to justify the quality of the food. Overall, I might stop by Open Kitchen now and then, but unless the menu or pricing improves, I won’t become a regular.

This place is clearly begging for a Chef Ramsey makeover. The passion for cooking has clearly waned, replaced by a heavy dependence on canned ingredients for convenience. Their so-called "world famous pies" are essentially perfectly round frozen pizzas, topped with a single, congealed, tasteless layer of cheese. They look like tiny frisbees covered in cheap pizza sauce and cheese that tastes like it belongs in a school cafeteria. I could only manage one slice out of eight before giving up.

The lunch side salad was equally disappointing—served in a small bowl packed with iceberg lettuce and an absurdly thick inch of Italian dressing. Yes, a full inch of dressing, which felt completely over the top. The lasagna and spaghetti were painfully generic as well. Aside from the charming kitschy décor, the only dish I can genuinely praise is the seafood with béchamel sauce. However, it’s so rich that you can only indulge once every few years without worrying about your heart.

While this might sound harsh, it’s not because I want the restaurant to fail—in fact, I’m rooting for the opposite. I just wish they would breathe new life into their menu with authentic Italian dishes, or even Greek fare, given their heritage! I love the atmosphere, but the food isn’t compelling enough to bring me back, and that says a lot. I wanted to become a regular, but I simply can’t stomach the food. At this point, I’m seriously tempted to call Gordon Ramsey and ask him to save them from themselves.

I wasn’t overly disappointed by my visit. Thanks to a Groupon, I had the opportunity to try appetizers, main courses, wine, and dessert at very reasonable prices, though the food didn’t leave a strong impression.

When the waitress brought out the bread and breadsticks, I was somewhat disappointed since I enjoy fresh bread. Unfortunately, the bread was clearly store-bought, and the breadsticks felt more like bread crackers, packaged in small plastic bags just like typical crackers—hardly something that would entice me to return.

For my entrée, I opted for the lasagna, described as "put back in the oven with extra cheese." While the lasagna itself was acceptable, the heavy cheese and grease didn’t really appeal to me.

With some money left over, we indulged in the pineapple cheesecake. Having never tried pineapple cheesecake before, I now understand why—it was overly gelatinous, and we ended up scraping off the orange-colored "pineapple" topping.

The décor and history of the place were quite interesting, and I do regret not trying the famous pizza. Still, I don’t expect to come back to give it a try.

The moment you step inside, you’re embraced by a warm wave of history and nostalgia. The food is dependable—not the best in Charlotte, but certainly far from the worst. The lunch specials offer the greatest value, with generous portions that often last for two meals. Each special includes a drink and your choice of soup or salad, though the salad is simply a basic bowl of iceberg lettuce.

A must-try here is the cheesy garlic bread, which I always pair with marinara sauce; just be aware that the sauce comes with an extra charge. The main entrees—lasagna, spaghetti, and cannelloni—tend to share a similar flavor. If you’re not a fan of rich, cheesy dishes, the salad options might be a better choice.

What truly distinguishes this place is its atmosphere. Vintage photographs adorn the walls, and original menus are part of the decor. Take a moment to check out the old prices and notice the antique cash register still in use at the front counter.

While not necessarily a destination to seek out, if you’re in the area, it’s worth stopping by for a meal. Usually busy at lunchtime, this restaurant has been a cherished fixture on the city’s west side for over sixty years.

I ordered the chicken Barcelona, which arrived overflowing with canned mushrooms and an unexpectedly generous amount of what I can only call "questionable meat grease." To my surprise, it also came with a side of canned, unseasoned tomato paste—something I hadn’t noticed on the menu. This left me genuinely perplexed—until my girlfriend’s manicotti was served. Her dish correctly included the canned tomato paste but also contained a puzzling addition of canned mushrooms.

It seemed the kitchen had a sudden insight worthy of the great Italian philosophers: “We’ve got a third of a can of mushrooms left, worth about 25 cents, plus a large can of tomato paste with at least 30 cents remaining. Why not just toss these leftover canned ingredients into both dishes and save 55 cents?”

On a brighter note, the frozen cheesy garlic bread was surprisingly tasty!

I’m genuinely astonished this establishment is still operating. Nostalgia seems to be what draws patrons back—those who remember this sanctuary of canned and frozen fare from years past. The clientele appeared, well, distinctly overweight. Perhaps it’s the massive, carb- and fat-laden portions that keep them grazing here. Maintaining such a high BMI definitely requires commitment.

As for my dish, the so-called "meat" consisted of greasy lips and other unappetizing bits. I tried to overlook its appearance and take a bite, but that turned out to be a serious error.

To top off my Food Lion visit, the owner at checkout was downright rude. When my friend and I tried to split the bill between two credit cards, he snapped, “Oh come on. You are killing me!” I fired back, “Yeah, the garbage on a plate you call food is killing me!” He clearly didn’t appreciate that—and frankly, I couldn’t have cared less.

If you’re craving lasagna, the sausage crumbles and marinara here clearly outshine the usual meat sauce. The meatballs, however, can be hit or miss depending on who prepares them. My favorite dish by far is the eggplant parm—it truly leaves an impression. Just a heads-up: the sweet tea is intensely sugary. For those watching carbs, the chicken parm is a dependable choice, though it’s definitely not low in fat. The Barcelona dish is excellent, but be prepared—half a stick of real melted butter is served right on your plate, no substitutes.

All the dressings—ranch, blue cheese, 1000 island, French, and Mama Ks—are homemade, but don’t expect anything fancy or elaborate with your side salad. Both the marinara and meat sauce are crafted in-house as well.

Yes, the restaurant has an old, somewhat dusty vibe, but honestly, can you name another Charlotte spot that’s been open continuously for 60 years and isn’t? If you can, I’ll gladly eat my words. *No pun intended. That’s my take!

Classroom Central invites participation through two main avenues: as a teacher (or principal, etc.) at a school where a certain portion of students qualify for the free lunch program, or as a volunteer—the perspective I’m sharing.

The organization runs smoothly and efficiently. Its L-shaped store, complete with shopping carts, is stocked with essential supplies such as notebooks, binders, die cuts, pencils, pens, lined paper, calculators, and glue—items educators often purchase out of their own pockets to support their classrooms. Thanks to generous donations, ongoing supply drives, and dedicated volunteers, teachers can “shop” here entirely free of charge. The store also offers extras like backpacks, lunch boxes, and a variety of prizes for students.

To ensure fairness, a system limits both the quantity per item and the total number of items each teacher can take, preventing the shelves from being completely emptied each month. Despite these limits, many educators regularly “leave” with around $400 worth of supplies per visit, making this resource invaluable.

In summary, Classroom Central provides outstanding support to teachers and programs already facing budget cuts and other challenges. It’s genuinely hard to find any criticism for such a meaningful and impactful effort.

If you’re looking for budget-friendly home décor, this K-Mart might pleasantly surprise you. They carry knock-offs priced lower than Target or IKEA, though some pieces do feel a bit outdated. Along with the popular Martha Stewart collections, I’ve found a ‘runner’ rug and bedspread that easily pass for department store quality. Their furniture offerings are solid too, so don’t underestimate the style in my living space.

The clothing section, however, is somewhat hit-or-miss. Tucked among Big Bubba t-shirts and overalls, I’ve discovered trendy pieces reminiscent of Gap styles from a few years ago. The young men’s area is especially worth checking out at the end of the season, when utility shirts or metrosexual boot-cut jeans can be snagged for under $15. Yes, really.

Outside of these gems, much of the store feels like filler. If you expect a wide range of sporting goods, shoes, or electronics, you’ll likely find limited options or steeper prices than at other big-box retailers. But if you approach K-Mart like a thrift store—searching for hidden bargains—you might be pleasantly surprised. I’m still torn on whether shopping here is truly frugal or just a bit frivolous, but honestly, who can resist grabbing another inexpensive belt?

I stopped by this McDonald's just after 4 a.m., and immediately, the staff’s indifferent greeting left a poor impression. Their appearance was sloppy, with several employees not even wearing the proper uniforms. My order was mishandled, and instead of preparing a fresh replacement, I suspect they simply swapped the bacon for dried-out steak and shriveled onions, leaving the egg, cheese, and bagel unchanged. When I asked about the wait, the worker said it would take longer, yet my sandwich appeared within 15 seconds.

The other item I ordered—a bacon, egg, and cheese—arrived tough, dry, and cold. After waiting in the drive-thru so early in the morning, I expected three hot, freshly made biscuits and a bagel. Instead, the entire experience was disappointing. They didn’t offer any apology or compensation for the mistake and delay. Honestly, it felt like they were just playing with people’s food.

Breakfast had only just started at 4 a.m., and I placed my order at 4:11 a.m., so I can’t understand why the food was already dry and hard. The staff’s unprofessionalism and lack of care disgusted me to the point where I didn’t even want to meet their eyes. Tired and hungry, I wasn’t willing to wait for them to remake my order.

I don’t usually eat at McDonald's because you generally know what to expect, but this experience was completely unacceptable. You’d have to see it to believe it. The staff here, including management, clearly need much stronger training. There’s no excuse for running a business like this, no matter the location.

The first thing that comes to mind about this place is how utterly "comically awful" the entire experience was. I went there for lunch with some coworkers, and despite the restaurant being nearly empty—only one other table occupied—it still took far too long for a server to approach us, and even longer for our drinks to arrive.

The biggest frustration came when it was time to get the bill. Without any warning or explanation, our server simply walked away. We never received any drink refills or even a quick, “Hey folks, I’m stepping away for a bit.” Nothing at all.

When we finally decided to pay, we went to the counter and told the girl there we wanted to settle up. She just shrugged, shouted back, “COUNTER!” and walked off. No one came out from the back. Eventually, someone in our group flagged down a girl wearing a Pizza Hut shirt to help us.

She pulled up our ticket but then asked for my ID just to pay for a $5 pizza with my card. Honestly, if I were stealing a credit card, I’d find better uses than buying a small pepperoni from Pizza Hut. She swiped my card several times, then abruptly turned and walked off without explanation. Another woman returned with her, shooting me some seriously dirty looks, and asked to try my card again since it hadn’t gone through.

I handed over my card, thinking, I can’t wait to get on Yelp and share this nightmare.

I don’t own a firearm and never feel comfortable shooting or even holding one—my hands tremble and I get queasy. Still, after visiting several gun shops for work, this place truly leaves a strong impression. As Dave S. noted, Hyatt is a highly regarded establishment and ranks among the top 10 largest volume gun dealers nationwide—an employee even printed out an article to confirm this.

The store offers an extensive selection of firearms, prominently displayed on walls and in cases throughout. Every staff member I spoke with was exceptionally knowledgeable, sharing captivating stories about machine guns and the histories of various handguns.

The shop is almost always busy, even on Black Friday when no discounts or sales are offered. What stands out most is the patience with which salespeople attend to each customer, no matter how crowded it gets. The calm and frustration-free waiting by customers truly reflects the deep loyalty this shop inspires.

The airport shuttle is really the only positive aspect of this Days Inn. Breakfast was limited to the usual cereal and pastries, and there were no newspapers available. While the front desk did provide menus from local delivery restaurants, none actually delivered to the hotel when we called.

Noise at night was a persistent problem, with children running through the halls and slamming doors around midnight, yet the staff showed little interest in addressing it. On the plus side, when the Wi-Fi went down, I asked the front desk to restart the router, and they responded promptly. However, being located directly beneath the airport’s flight path means loud noise from planes taking off and landing is common during busy times.

The hotel isn’t especially convenient for accessing I-77, as it’s about six miles away, but it’s manageable if you’re headed that way. Housekeeping was disappointing: we left early in the morning and returned late afternoon to find our room still uncleaned. We had brought our own brand-new soap, assuming it would remain untouched since it was different from the hotel’s, but it disappeared after housekeeping had been through.

Overall, we would not stay at this Days Inn again. The service simply did not justify the price we paid.

We won’t be returning to this hotel the next time we’re in Charlotte. While the gentleman at the front desk was polite and seemed genuinely hardworking, the rest of our stay unfortunately fell short.

On our first night, all the exterior lights were off, and cars drove around the parking lot for hours blasting loud music. The noisy and unsettling atmosphere made it difficult to relax or fall asleep with all the commotion happening right outside our room.

The next morning, when we pulled back the curtains, we noticed a group of sketchy-looking individuals lingering a couple hundred feet away at what appeared to be an “I-95 coach waiting area”—though we had no idea what that was. Their intense stares as we walked to our car left us feeling quite uneasy. We thought about canceling our second night, but a sign in the office stated no refunds after 10 minutes of check-in, so we decided it wasn’t worth the hassle and braced ourselves to stay.

During the day, it became evident this was not a desirable part of Charlotte. The streets were filled with some intimidating people, which only increased our discomfort.

Later that night, upon returning, we found the air conditioning blasting at a chilly 60 degrees. Hoping to warm up in the shower, we discovered the shampoo packets had been replaced with bar soap—an inconvenience since we’d forgotten our own shampoo and planned to use the hotel’s.

Overall, the stay was quite disappointing. I’ll give an extra star to the front desk staff for their kindness and effort, but beyond that, the experience was just bad, bad, bad.

This venue, one of Charlotte’s oldest and most respected spots for punk, hardcore, metal, and rock, boasts a legendary reputation—rumor has it Nirvana once played here. The experience is an intense sensory onslaught. The walls, covered in band stickers and graffiti, document the many random acts that have taken the stage. Inside the cramped, packed room, the sound hits so hard that your ears will be ringing long after the show ends.

In the summer months, the glaring lack of air conditioning—likely a cost-saving move—turns the crowd into a sweaty mess and makes the bathrooms a real test for your sense of smell. The no-smoking policy is also enforced quite loosely.

The PBR tallboys are served ice-cold, something many bands can attest to—I’ve witnessed several performers drenched by beer flying from the moshing crowd. One final tip: bring cash unless you want to risk the unreliable ATM tucked behind the bar.

The cover charge here is typically quite low, and the beer stays affordable, but the sound system? It’s painfully loud! This place bursts with character. Native Charlotteans often cherish it, reminiscing about sneaking in to see Black Flag at 15 back in ’83 or having their first sexual or drinking experiences in the parking lot. Those youthful memories usually overshadow the venue’s clear flaws.

For those of us who arrived in Charlotte later, the experience is entirely different. The bathrooms? Without question, the worst in the whole city. Speaking as a guy, I can hardly imagine what women must endure—hovering over toilets, worried about the unknown germs on the seats. The restrooms are genuinely disgusting. Then there’s the indoor smoking ban. They used to openly ignore North Carolina’s statewide ban (a bartender once joked, “Yeah, like the cops ever come HERE”), but recently they finally enforced it, taking away the one thing I really liked about the place.

That said, don’t get me wrong. If you come with good friends to catch a solid band, you’ll have a great time. It’s just that now, at 41, my patience for shabby facilities has definitely worn thin.

Although my stay lasted only three nights, I’ve firmly decided this will be my last visit here. I didn’t want to move, but the unbearable conditions left me no choice. It’s unclear whether management is simply incompetent or deliberately letting the property crumble while squeezing every last penny. Most of the staff seemed beaten down, and honestly, I don’t blame them. The entire place felt grimy and run-down.

For an entire month, the elevator remained broken and unrepaired, forcing guests to climb three flights of stairs through filthy stairwells. When I mentioned this to a staff member, she admitted she avoided those stairs altogether—and I understood why. Our second-floor room was no better: grimy walls, horrible lumpy pillows, a miserable shower, and black grime seeping from the sink faucet. Just walking barefoot across the floor left my feet dirty. Outside, the security side door was broken and left wide open. To top it all off, they charged us $1.00 per day for an in-room safe we never used. The best view I had of this place was from my rearview mirror as I drove away. Done.

I’m posting this review on Hotels.com as well to warn other travelers about the nightmare I experienced. After my US Airways flight was canceled due to “aircraft maintenance,” I was placed at this Microtel. The attendant apologized, saying it was the only option, and I thought, “How bad can it really be?” Let me assure you—it was absolutely dreadful. Even as a seasoned traveler used to rundown spots and rustic mosquito-net bungalows in Laos, the only way I survived this stay was by drinking heavily and passing out.

Before you even think about arriving, erase any thought of staying here. Be sure to thoroughly inspect your bed for bed bugs immediately. At one point, I saw two police officers escorting a visibly cracked-out prostitute away from the ice machine. Even through my alcohol haze, it was clear something was seriously wrong when the receptionist was arguing with four officers at 2 a.m.

The room itself was repulsive—everything about it looked, smelled, and felt awful. The sheets were riddled with holes, and although the airport shuttle took only six minutes, it ran just once an hour. To make matters worse, it was a smoking room—and I don’t smoke. It’s no surprise that guests who checked in before me checked out after just 15 minutes. When I discreetly asked why, they said they worked for Wyndham and claimed this place was below even their standards.

Take my advice: avoid this hotel at all costs. Please, spare yourself the hassle. That’s all I have to say. Consider yourself warned.

At first, being assigned to a hotel near the airport seemed like a practical solution. However, after reading Yelp reviews describing the place as foul-smelling, filthy, and infested with bed bugs, we hesitated but ultimately decided to take the risk since we had no other options. We called for the shuttle, but despite hotel staff assuring us it would arrive within 15 minutes, we waited outside in the cold for 40. Shivering and exhausted, we returned to the airport seeking alternatives, but none were available. Finally, after another 15-20 minute delay, the shuttle arrived and took us to the hotel.

Upon entering our rooms, one reeked of cigarette smoke and had multiple hairs on the freshly made beds that were clearly not ours. The other smelled somewhat better but had a large beetle crawling on the wall, a spider in the bed, crumbs on the nightstand, hairs and grime in the shower, and hairs and urine stains on the toilet. There we were—five girls stranded at midnight in this disgusting hotel on the opposite coast, with every other hotel either fully booked or outrageously expensive—and United Airlines completely unresponsive. After this ordeal, I will never fly with them again.

To make matters worse, once back in California, we learned someone else had a nearly identical experience last year—she slept in the bed, got bed bugs on her face, and had to visit the emergency room due to the reaction. I wish I could give this place zero stars. It is absolutely DISGUSTING. Avoid it at all costs.

I’ve always enjoyed discovering tucked-away burger and sandwich joints, and this place fits that description perfectly. Though the exterior looks a bit worn, it doesn’t bother me at all. Inside, the décor matches the outside—definitely tacky and lacking real charm. Despite the lack of atmosphere, the spot more than makes up for it with affordable prices and generous portions. For just $4.75, my gyro arrived warm with a side, making for a genuinely satisfying meal. The gyro meat was nestled inside a soft pita, packed with plenty of lettuce, tomato, onion, and a well-balanced tzatziki sauce that complemented the sandwich without overwhelming it—no excessive tang, garlic, or herbs. On the downside, the onion rings were the usual frozen cornmeal variety, so I’d recommend sticking with fries instead. Why is it so rare to find beer-battered onion rings? Overall, this is a dependable, budget-friendly place to grab a meal near the airport—even if, like me, you don’t work there.

It took me a while to recover from the terrible stomach bug I caught after dining here. I paid $10.92 for a small meal—just a salad, water, and a tiny tiramisu—which is outrageously overpriced for such a modest portion. Lunch really shouldn’t cost that much for so little food.

The salad included an egg, which I’m not fond of, so I simply set it aside on a napkin. When the waitress checked on me and I mentioned my dislike for the egg, she neither apologized nor offered to remove it; instead, she just walked away.

The tiramisu was absolutely dreadful, tasting more like a failed banana pudding than the dessert it was supposed to be. If you love tiramisu like I do, I’d recommend going to Olive Garden or SAM’s Club during the holidays instead—you’ll be far better off.

All told, I have no intention of returning.

The staff here are genuinely warm and consistently generous with refills, never making you feel rushed—definitely deserving a solid 4 stars. However, the food is what matters most to me. After dining here 4 or 5 times, I’ve noticed that everything I’ve tried tastes like a frozen meal. Maybe I’m just choosing the wrong dishes? Each time, I’ve gone with one of their daily specials—I’d expect a daily special to be reliably good, wouldn’t you?

For today’s meal, I selected the chicken stir fry. The chicken had grill marks, indicating it was grilled at some point, but it was quite dry. The vegetables were drenched in sauce, almost as if they had been sitting in it for a while before being reheated. The white rice was adequate. The lunch special also included a salad and a piece of bread. The salad was simple, made up of shredded lettuce, a cucumber slice, a tomato slice, and an onion ring.

Since my coworkers often visit this place, I’ll probably return, but when it comes to the food, I have to give it a firm 2 stars.

After arriving late at the airport, we were looking forward to trying their renowned Dirty Rice, Fried Chicken, and all the sides. Unfortunately, placing our order at the drive-through was almost impossible, as the young woman’s voice kept cutting out over the speaker. Thinking it was just a technical glitch, we moved ahead to the payment window.

When we got there, we were told to pay $7 for the supreme meal, even though we had actually ordered the 12-piece chicken with dirty rice—the supreme package with all the fixings. We clarified our order, but the man at the window simply waved us off, called for someone else to help, and walked away. Soon after, a young African American woman came to the window and questioned why we didn’t want the supreme meal box. Every time we tried to explain that we had ordered the family meal, she closed the service window on us. Finally, she slammed the window shut, threw her hands up in frustration, and walked off without coming back or telling us the price. We were left at the pick-up window, completely ignored and confused.

As this was our first visit to this part of the state, the whole experience made us wonder if poor customer service like this is common here. With Disney World thriving nearby, it seems there must be better staff elsewhere. If this is how customers are treated, we will NEVER return to any of your restaurants in this area. The lack of proper training and disregard for patrons means we won’t be supporting your businesses here again.

We’ve all faced the usual wait at fast food places, expecting a quick meal but often ending up disappointed. This particular visit, however, was one of the most frustrating I’ve ever experienced. When I arrived, the drive-thru line was quite long, so I chose to park and order inside for takeout instead. Before going in, I gave a dollar to a homeless man outside, which is common in this neighborhood. Once inside, my annoyance grew as I saw the line was just as long. Here’s a tip: don’t let hunger drive your decisions—that was my mistake that day.

At the front of Wendy’s, only one employee was managing everything. She wasn’t just taking orders; she was bagging food, frying fries, and likely assembling the burgers as well. I waited about 15 minutes just to get my order, when I clearly should have gone to Cook Out down the street or Pinky’s—places where you actually receive your food in under 15 minutes.

When I got home, I made a point to be polite to the girl working because I genuinely felt sorry for her. But upon opening my food, I wasn’t surprised to find it ice cold. The bun was tough, as if it had been sitting out for a while, and the cheese was barely melted. So, not only did I wait 15 minutes, but I also ended up with awful fast food. It’s a real oxymoron, I know—but seriously, come on!

What initially drew me in was the convenient location right off the highway, paired with those iconic 1950s drive-in microphones and ordering booths that lend a nostalgic charm to the place. While the parking lot felt somewhat unsettling due to the sketchy neighborhood, it didn’t significantly affect my experience. I went with the 1/4 Barbecue chicken meal, swapping out the slaw for potato salad and replacing fries with onion rings. I also tried the "Minced" barbecue sandwich, which reflects the traditional North Carolina style BBQ most people expect.

Food Network featured this spot largely because of its retro 50s drive-in vibe and the distinctive way they prepare the chicken—deep frying the pieces before soaking them in barbecue sauce. Although this method is unique, it results in a rather greasy dish. The chicken was just “okay” and not something I’d make a special trip for.

The barbecue sandwich was similarly disappointing. I’m fairly confident the meat wasn’t smoked, as no smoke was visible from the kitchen, and it lacked the smoky flavor characteristic of quality, slow-cooked North Carolina BBQ. While the sandwich was slightly closer to authentic NC BBQ than what I had at Mac’s—which was overcooked and bland—I still wouldn’t recommend this spot for North Carolina barbecue or much else.

After trying numerous eateries featured on the Food Network—many of which come highly acclaimed—I’ve come to a simple conclusion: the food at quite a few of these places is underwhelming. While people often offer glowing compliments to avoid offending the establishments, the truth is the cuisine frequently falls short. These spots seem to earn their recognition more for being local landmarks, having unique qualities, or holding historical significance—which I genuinely admire.

Take BBQ King as an example. It fits all those descriptions, yet the food itself is fairly average. The BBQ lacked smoky depth and richness—I’m quite sure it wasn’t truly smoked. Though I’m no barbecue expert, this simply isn’t quality barbecue.

That said, the regular fried chicken is flavorful, and the fried chicken dipped in BBQ sauce offers an intriguing twist. It’s not exactly my favorite, but I understand how someone raised on it would appreciate it. The service is solid, the cheeseburgers are reliable, and best of all, the prices are very reasonable.

My husband and I, both originally from the East Coast but now living in Utah, always look forward to authentic Southern BBQ when we visit home. This place caught my attention because of its long history—it’s been around for decades. I especially liked that they still use the original ordering system, which helped me picture the restaurant during its prime. The menu is fairly extensive, so there’s something for everyone. The fried chicken dipped in barbecue sauce was the highlight for me—it was so flavorful that I’d return just for that dish.

However, there were a few downsides. The restaurant only accepts cash, so we had to use their ATM, which meant leaving the car at the drive-up and going inside to pay. While some vintage elements are charming, the lack of credit card acceptance felt inconvenient. The person who delivered our food to the car essentially asked for a tip, which I found somewhat rude. The neighborhood also felt a bit sketchy. As for the food, the pork BBQ was mediocre, the hush puppies were greasy—likely from frying too many at once—and the french fries were bland.

Overall, I’d recommend this spot if you’re after the fried chicken, but for your barbecue cravings, you might want to try elsewhere.

The day was pleasant, making it a great choice for a drive-in visit. Although I try to keep an open mind when trying new places, past reviews can sometimes make that difficult. Around noon on a Saturday, I ordered the BBQ plate with fries and slaw. The venue was moderately busy, with about half the stalls occupied. My food took a brief moment to arrive, but not long enough to make me wonder, “Where is my order?”

When the server dropped off my tray, they quickly moved on to the next vehicle without collecting payment. While this felt a bit unusual, it was likely the most efficient way to keep things moving. The pork was finely minced and generously coated in sauce, and the slaw was minced rather than shredded. The plate also included a sandwich bun alongside the fries. I first tried the pork without sauce—it was moist and tender but quite bland. Adding the sauce didn’t improve the flavor; it was bland as well and lacked any smoky notes.

The fries were acceptable—soft and fluffy inside but missing the ideal crispness. The slaw was fresh and crunchy but similarly bland. I’m not overly concerned about the sauce since taste preferences vary and some enjoy spicier options. Still, despite the pork’s tenderness and juiciness, the overall experience was underwhelming. The meal wasn’t bad, but it wasn’t good either. There are definitely better places out there serving much more flavorful BBQ.

After discovering this spot on "Diners, Drive-Ins and Dives," I finally made the trip, despite their closure on Sundays and Mondays. I opted for the BBQ chicken, which the show described as "fried chicken coated in East Carolina-style BBQ sauce." Unfortunately, the sauce was overly thick and sweet, quite unlike the traditional East Carolina style that resembles Tabasco sauce. While this was somewhat disappointing, the fried chicken itself was cooked flawlessly—juicy and just right.

The fries were unremarkable, likely frozen commercial varieties, but they were cooked properly and salted well. In contrast, the onion rings stood out as a definite highlight, especially if you enjoy the cornmeal style. Although cole slaw isn’t usually my preference, the slaw here was fresh and surprisingly flavorful.

One hiccup occurred when my friend ordered a Sun Drop but received a Coke instead, even though the order ticket clearly indicated Sun Drop. We could have used the speaker to correct the mistake, and given our $17.85 drive-in lunch, we probably should have.

The pulled pork sandwich left me wanting more, primarily because it arrived without any sauce—I simply can’t understand why they skip it. On a brighter note, the fried BBQ chicken quickly became everyone’s favorite. Tender, juicy, and boasting a satisfying vinegar tang, it truly stole the show. We ordered both a breast and a wing without any additional charge, and that’s likely what we’ll stick with on our next visit.

The fries were flavorful, though the cheap Hunt’s ketchup didn’t do them justice; they’d pair much better with Heinz. The hush puppies were somewhat bland for my taste—I prefer them with a hint of onion mixed in. The onion rings were the flour variety, but the batter kept falling off, which was frustrating; I definitely favor the crunchy cornmeal style.

Because the restaurant is closed on Sundays and Mondays, we had to wait until Tuesday to finally give it a try. The iced tea was a delightful surprise—already sweetened and genuinely delicious. The cole slaw tasted just like grandma used to make, but the potato salad and roll were fairly average. Fortunately, we had cash on hand since they don’t accept credit cards. We’ll be returning, and after reading other reviews, I’m excited to try the cherry lemon Sundrop next time.

Isn’t it generally expected to tip the person who delivers your food? Maybe that’s just how I see it. As someone living in New Jersey and seeking quality BBQ, I decided to explore Charlotte’s top BBQ spots during my trip south for the holidays. Among the many options, BBQ King caught my eye because it had been featured on Triple D and praised as the best thing the reviewer had ever tasted. Naturally, BBQ King became my destination, and I was eager to try their BBQ chicken.

When we first arrived in Charlotte on a Sunday, BBQ King was closed. So, on the return trip, we made sure to allow enough time to stop by. BBQ King is a classic drive-in with an intercom ordering system, which I thought was pretty cool. What immediately stood out was the limited BBQ selection—mostly burgers, steak, fried chicken, and other typical drive-in fare. Still, I stuck with my plan and ordered the BBQ chicken, adding the minced BBQ sandwich just to be safe.

When the food arrived, I was surprised to find that the BBQ chicken was actually fried chicken smothered in BBQ sauce. That’s when it dawned on me—in the Carolinas, BBQ means pork, like the minced sandwich I had ordered. Unfortunately, BBQ King wasn’t going to satisfy my craving for traditional BBQ. But I had to try it anyway. Taking a bite of the chicken, I found it delicious—the sauce tangy and vinegary, the meat juicy and tender, with a satisfying crunch. I wouldn’t call it BBQ, but it was definitely good! The pork sandwich was decent, though it lacked that authentic smoky flavor. Adding some coleslaw really turned it into a satisfying sandwich.

Would I recommend BBQ King? With full transparency, yes—it’s unique enough to warrant a visit. Would I return? Only if I were with someone who hadn’t been before. As I mentioned, I was on a quest for authentic BBQ, and BBQ King doesn’t quite serve it in the traditional sense.

This drive-in BBQ joint truly radiates small-town charm. When I arrived, a man came out to greet me, and after a brief exchange to confirm my order, I chose the chopped pork sandwich. Coming from Texas, I don’t usually consider North Carolina BBQ to be genuine "BBQ," but as the saying goes, "When in Rome." With that mindset, the sandwich—topped with finely shredded slaw—was unexpectedly flavorful. They also served BBQ sauce on the side, which I genuinely enjoyed. The fries, however, were bland and unremarkable—just average. The real highlight for me was the Coke, which was absolutely fantastic, boasting the perfect tang and flavor. Overall, while it wasn’t the best BBQ I’ve ever had, it was solid for what it was and exactly what I ordered, despite my initial uncertainty about placing the order correctly. If you find yourself in the area, it’s definitely worth a visit.

During my second trip to Charlotte, I made a point to visit this spot after seeing it on the Food Network a few years ago. Noticing several people carrying out boxes when I arrived only confirmed it was worth trying.

The restaurant still looks just like it did on TV, and the food definitely justified the price. We ordered a quarter BBQ chicken served with fries, cole slaw, and a roll, along with a minced BBQ pork sandwich, regular fried onion rings, and a large Cherry Lemon Sundrop soda—all for $16.45.

The car hops were friendly and worked for tips. When one of the retired owners learned we were visitors rather than locals, he came over to chat. While we enjoyed our meal, he asked how we were liking it, and we had a pleasant conversation.

As for the food, I expected the chicken to be crunchier, but it was hot and well-seasoned throughout. The BBQ sauce lacked the vinegary tang I had hoped for, which was a slight disappointment, but overall, the flavors were solid. The Cherry Lemon Sundrop could have had a stronger cherry syrup and lemon flavor, yet it remained refreshing and enjoyable. My sister found her sandwich just average but loved the onion rings, saying they reminded her of a place back in Greenville/Mauldin, SC. Interestingly, that spot was owned by the owner’s son-in-law—small world!

If I’m ever back in Charlotte craving BBQ fried chicken and a classic drive-in vibe, I’d definitely return.

My installation was scheduled for a Saturday morning between 9 and 11 a.m., but the technician didn’t contact me until 2:30 p.m., saying he was the "outside guy" and on his way. When I asked about the earlier time slot, he reacted irritably—I actually laughed when I realized who it was, given he was 3.5 hours late! Despite this, I let him come and at least complete the outside work.

Around 3:30, I called the number provided in my appointment email. A woman answered but was completely unaware of my situation. She tried to transfer me to dispatch, but the call failed. She called me back, and when I requested a supervisor, I was put on hold for 15 minutes. She called again, attempted another transfer, and mentioned there was a "problem" with my order but couldn’t explain the details. After another 20 minutes on hold, I gave up and hung up.

She called one last time, promising to follow up as soon as the department was available—but I never heard from her again. The whole experience was unbelievable. While I’m not thrilled with Time Warner or most of their contracted installation and repair personnel, they usually at least call if they’re going to be late or need to reschedule. This time, they didn’t. DON’T DO IT!

The receptionist who checked me in was evidently unfamiliar with the correct procedure and had to ask for help from three other receptionists. This is frustrating, especially since anyone hired for this position should have received thorough training beforehand. There was a complete lack of communication between the doctor’s office and the contacts department. Initially, the nurse at the office told me that dilation wasn’t necessary. However, when I arrived at the contacts department, they insisted on dilation and sent me back to the office for another part of the exam—all after more than an hour had already passed. Returning to the waiting area, I was surprised to find out they hadn’t even requested that I come back or undergo dilation. Although the original nurse provided the reversal drops, this glaring lack of coordination is a significant problem. Needless to say, today they lost three patients: me and my family. They urgently need to get things sorted out.

During the shampoo, I first noticed a faint tingling on my scalp that didn’t seem alarming. However, by the time I sat in the stylist’s chair, the sensation had escalated into an intense burning. My ears turned a vivid red, and every part of my face touched by the damp hair became severely irritated. It was clear I was experiencing a strong adverse reaction to their exclusive use of Aveda products.

The stylist became genuinely worried and, appropriately, called over the salon manager. Unfortunately, the manager responded with indifference and dismissal, noting that she and other clients had experienced similar reactions. Her only suggestion was that I “take a Benadryl” once I got home. That was the extent of it—no effort to resolve the issue or offer an apology, just a recommendation to medicate.

To make matters worse, I was charged full price for what was clearly a distressing experience. Perhaps they felt this was necessary to cover the cost of rinsing my hair again. Any service professional who disregards the importance of customer care will not be earning my business again.

This was my first session with Kris A., assigned to me as a Junior Stylist after I specifically requested one. From the start, we thoroughly reviewed what I wanted—and just as importantly, what I didn’t want. Despite this clear communication, she essentially refused to give me the layered cut I asked for. To make matters worse, she styled my hair using a round brush, even though I explicitly mentioned that I never use one and dislike that style. I had anticipated a layered, shoulder-length cut to enhance my natural wavy hair, but instead, I left with an outdated look—straight hair flipped up at the ends—that was anything but modern.

Though Kris asked all the right questions, it felt like she either ignored my answers or simply didn’t care, and honestly, I can’t decide which is worse. I started the appointment feeling happy and excited but ended up completely deflated. My hair is now shorter, but that’s something I could have done myself. What was meant to be a special financial treat turned out to be a total waste. I will not be returning.

Families with children might hesitate to choose this spot. However, for a reasonable price, you get a decent pizza freshly made just steps away. The buffet’s biggest draw is its extensive selection—not the quality, as these pizzas aren’t the finest you’ll find. While other nearby pizza buffets usually offer only 3 to 5 options at a time, Cici’s typically features close to a dozen, excluding dessert pizzas.

Besides pizza, the buffet includes pasta (which often looks unappetizing), cheese bread, and a modest salad bar. After finishing their meal, kids or other family members can head to the arcade, watch TV, or even annoy other families—a behavior generally tolerated here, unlike at most other restaurants.

If you haven’t come across McDonald’s, can you really call yourself a local? This particular location, right across from SouthPark Mall, definitely deserves a mention. Thanks to SouthPark’s strict regulations, McDonald’s had to blend seamlessly into its surroundings—and they absolutely succeeded. The two-story brick building is surprisingly charming and fits perfectly within the upscale SouthPark vibe.

I ended up dining here when the Original Pancake House had an hour-long wait. Conveniently situated just across from the mall and directly in front of OPH, this McDonald’s was the obvious choice. Since we wanted breakfast and had shopping plans to keep, waiting wasn’t an option. So, we took the short walk over, placed our breakfast order, and settled upstairs on the second floor. The meal was delicious, as usual, and it was genuinely entertaining to watch the SouthPark crowd from above. When else do you get to look down on SouthPark folks the way they typically look down on you? Ha!

There’s no need to focus on the food—you already know what to expect. What truly surprised me was the player piano downstairs, softly filling the space with soothing quasi-classical melodies.
