Upstairs, accessible via a spiral staircase, you’ll find wi-fi and a large screen quietly streaming cable news at a comfortable volume. Watching people quietly working on their laptops created an unexpectedly calm and manageable atmosphere. Normally, I avoid dining inside fast-food places because the environment tends to be unwelcoming, but this spot offered a refreshing change. Even during a busy lunch rush, I found it quite clean, which contrasts with another reviewer’s opinion.

Getting inside can be a bit challenging since you must cross through the drive-through lane, where drivers don’t seem very mindful of pedestrians. Still, I’d gladly return here to linger for a while—something I honestly didn’t expect.

Before my meeting, I was looking for a quick bite in South Park and noticed most nearby places were slow-paced sit-down restaurants. Wanting something different, I decided to try this spot instead. The staff was friendly, but my order took much longer than I expected to arrive. Rather than rushing, I opted to sit down and enjoy my meal.

While waiting, I overheard employees loudly chatting about heading home and their aching feet—likely during a shift change—but their voices carried from the register all the way to the kitchen, making it difficult to ignore.

Setting the atmosphere aside, the sandwich was heavily coated in mayo, almost as if someone was trying to put out a fire with it. The fries arrived blisteringly hot, which seemed to explain both the delay in food prep and the long drive-thru line. To top it off, they had run out of ketchup packets, so I had to improvise by spreading a large dollop of ketchup on a napkin.

In the end, I suppose you really do get what you pay for.

She was genuinely enthusiastic about Harpers, calling it her “best kept secret, the place I bring everyone!” Her excitement immediately caught my attention, prompting us to try it for lunch. The meal was quite enjoyable overall, but the service was a major letdown—slow is the only way to describe it.

Fortunately, the food exceeded expectations. We started with the house potato chips, a dish my friend had never encountered at any restaurant before—something I found quite surprising. They were served with blue cheese, a blue cheese sauce, and scallions generously sprinkled on top. These chips made an excellent appetizer and set a positive tone for the meal.

For the main courses, we both chose salads: I went with the Oriental chopped salad, while my friend opted for the grilled chicken house salad. Both were fairly standard yet came in generous portions. The dressing on mine was especially flavorful, and the Asian noodles added a satisfying crunch to the greens.

The slow service was most noticeable during checkout. We waited at least 20 minutes just to get the bill and catch the server’s attention. When she finally split the check, it was done incorrectly, resulting in me paying for my friend’s potato-cheddar soup—which, by the way, was very tasty.

Overall, the experience was pleasant. Since it was my first visit to a Harpers, it reminded me of Houstons, a chain from Atlanta. If you’re nearby, I’d definitely recommend giving Harpers a try!

Each time I walk into this place, the familiar aroma—a blend of wood-fired and everyday kitchen scents—immediately takes me back. It remains one of the few dependable spots to dine with my parents. Although their vegetarian options are limited, I appreciate that their veggie burger is homemade. I also enjoy the six cheese penne without bacon, and their pimento cheese dip has consistently been a favorite.

That said, my lunch yesterday was quite disappointing. I wanted something light, but aside from a meatless salad, little on the menu appealed to me. I’m fond of a good bowl of soup, yet Harper’s rarely features a vegetarian option, and yesterday was no exception. Hoping for a suitable alternative, I ordered the spinach quesadilla, expecting it to be more spinach-forward than cheesy—after all, how hard can it be to prepare a decent quesadilla?

It turned out to be a major letdown. The quesadilla was a mess, overloaded with a gooey cheese mixture. The filling was wildly inconsistent: one slice was mostly cheese with just a hint of spinach, another seemed packed entirely with what I’m almost certain was their repurposed spinach dip, and a third contained an unexpected amount of cold, mealy tomato chunks.

As usual, when my dad ordered a small cup of soup, the server’s barely concealed disdain for our modest order was obvious—her sneer was unmistakable.

After this experience, I think I’ll be steering clear of Harper’s for a while.

I used to think of this place as a cozy retreat—a true home away from home—where the blend of brick and wood created a warm, vibrant atmosphere without ever feeling overwhelming. The service was always well balanced: efficient yet unobtrusive. Their American comfort food consistently delivered quality and truly felt worth the price.

Lately, though, things have taken a downturn. The grilled Portobello sandwich I once enjoyed has vanished from the menu. The prime rib portion has shrunk to just 11 ounces, priced at $20, and now includes only one side. Keep in mind, prime rib is naturally fatty—I usually trim about a third—and what remains weighs less than half a pound. To make matters worse, when I ordered fried sweet potatoes, they served frozen, pre-seasoned fries instead of the simple, authentic potatoes they used to offer.

The prime rib was cooked rare as requested, but, as often happens, the chef heavily salted it before cooking, making it impossible to reduce the saltiness. While many might enjoy it that way, what about those who don’t or need to watch their sodium intake?

It’s painfully clear this place has become a franchise, with management cutting too many corners given the prices they charge. Though the venue looks the same, the food quality now reminds me of something you’d find in Orlando, FL.

That brings Texas Roadhouse to mind. Normally, I’m not a fan of their themed spots—with peanuts on the floor and overly cheerful, young servers—but for the same $20, I get a generous 16-ounce prime rib that’s as good or better than Harper’s. It comes with a couple of solid sides—the sweet potato baked from a fresh tuber—and they even include complimentary appetizers. Plus, five-dollar Margaritas or Martinis to enjoy.

Sure, Texas Roadhouse is noisy, crowded with kids, and lacks finesse, but given the current economy, I’d rather spend my money there on beef or smoked pork chops than at Harper’s. Honestly, I never thought I’d say that.

I settled into the bar area and decided to try one of the new interactive tables—definitely a nice upgrade! However, I quickly noticed the menu was much smaller than before. After browsing the options, I finally found my favorite burger and ordered it with fries. I made sure to remind the waitress to keep the fries hot this time, as they had been cold on my last visit—I really wanted to enjoy this meal.

When the burger arrived, it looked different—smaller and less appealing. To my surprise, I could fit the entire burger in my mouth now, which felt odd since it used to be huge and required a knife and fork. Unfortunately, the flavor didn’t live up to my expectations. The cheese wasn’t melting and oozing like before; it was barely noticeable, and the meat tasted fairly bland. I was genuinely disappointed.

In short, prices have gone up while quality has dropped. Looks like I’ll have to find a new go-to burger spot. Booooooo!

At first, I expected this place to be a mix between Chili's and Applebee's, assuming I might leave feeling disappointed or even worse than when I arrived. However, that expectation didn’t hold up. I chose the Sicilian pizza, generously topped with prosciutto and other savory ingredients, and truly enjoyed every bite. My sister went with the Chicago pizza and had no complaints.

One improvement would be to add detailed descriptions of the pizzas on the menu. Without asking the server about the Sicilian’s toppings, I wouldn’t have known what I was ordering. The name "Chicago" pizza is particularly misleading since it usually refers to a very different style. Thankfully, our server clearly explained all the toppings and remained mostly attentive throughout our meal.

Aside from the menu’s lack of detail, my family and I had a pleasant experience overall. I would definitely consider returning.

Harper’s definitely creates a chic atmosphere with its open kitchen, wood-fired oven, and a diverse menu full of tempting options. We were eager to try it and were seated immediately. Our server was friendly and quite amusing, though he didn’t quite meet my expectations for attentiveness. After taking our drink orders, he promised to return shortly—but then we ended up waiting... and waiting... ugh.

On the bright side, the extra time gave us a chance to really dive into the menu, which offers everything from steaks and chicken to ribs, burgers, salmon, and, naturally, pizza.

Here’s how our dining experience went:

We started with the lobster and artichoke dip. It was flavorful, with generous chunks of crab and artichoke, though the portion felt small for the price. Still, it was tasty enough that I’d order it again—just not to share (hehe).

For my entrée, I chose the special Oriental Chicken pizza, topped with chicken, lettuce, wontons, mushrooms, red peppers (which never arrived), and honey ginger dressing. It was just okay. I really enjoyed the crust—thin, crispy, and carrying a pleasant smoky note from the flame grill oven. The honey ginger dressing was nice, but overall, it didn’t quite impress me.

My friends both opted for salmon—one honey glazed, the other blackened—served with mashed red potatoes. That was genuinely delicious! Between the two, my favorite was definitely the honey glazed salmon. It struck the perfect balance of sweetness, enhancing the salmon without overpowering it. Luckily, my friends were generous since I ended up eating about half their salmon. I did share my pizza, to be fair! They agreed the pizza was just okay, nothing spectacular.

I’ll probably return to Harper’s for another try—mostly for that honey glazed salmon!

Though this restaurant boasts deep roots in the South Park neighborhood and a menu with classic appeal, any sense of tradition quickly fades the moment you step inside. The atmosphere takes a hit when a hostess greets you while chewing gum and texting instead of offering a proper welcome. I understand the temptation to check social media—no judgment—but her exaggerated “OMG LOL” and “#LMFAO” reaction to a customer picking up a to-go order was simply over the top.

If you plan to dine in or sit at the bar, don’t let that initial impression completely turn you away. The bar’s touch screen monitors are perfect for anyone wanting to tune out their dining companion—whether that’s you or, evidently, the hostess. Honestly, does anyone really engage in conversation over dinner anymore?

The food is exactly what you’d expect from a mid-tier Americana spot, but the service leaves much to be desired. My salad arrived with a dried-out, crusty chicken breast and no dressing. Attempts to reach a manager were futile; apparently, Tuesday nights are hectic for management, though the hostess seemed unbothered. The veggie burger tastes unmistakably like cardboard, with the bun only adding to that texture—it’s barely tolerable unless paired with tequila. The filet, ordered medium rare, came out medium and was hardly edible. Asking the waitstaff for a refill felt as futile as waiting for a quick response at the DMV.

It’s especially frustrating because I once genuinely enjoyed this place. Now, even with young couples and awkward online daters at the bar letting touch screens fill the silence, the vibe just doesn’t feel right anymore. The ribs are passable, but the sides fall short.

If I were to recommend this spot to anyone, it would be my neighbor who consistently neglects to clean up after their dog or my grandfather, who has lost his sense of taste and isn’t bothered by slow service since he takes forever to finish his soup. I’d definitely suggest calling ahead to check if they’re busy—and avoid Tuesdays altogether.

Before trying this place, I usually check Yelp, and this time the reviews were quite mixed. Still, I figured maybe people just chose poorly, and I wanted a change from my usual Subway routine. The moment I stepped inside, the decor immediately threw me off—it felt like walking into a house of mirrors. Some call this spot a Charlotte institution, but since I’m new here, I can’t vouch for that. What I do know is the interior badly needs a facelift; it gave off a creepy vibe.

I went with the chicken cheesesteak, fries, and coleslaw. If you’re expecting authenticity, this isn’t the place. The cheesesteak was soggy, and the mushrooms were watery. The biggest letdown was the chicken—it reminded me of Steak-ums, just a thin slice resting on a blob of mayo, tomatoes, onions, and mushrooms. There was barely any chicken, and it tasted tough and leathery. The fries were okay but nowhere near as crispy as some reviewers claimed, and they definitely needed salt. Once they cooled and lost their appeal, I didn’t finish them. The coleslaw was drenched in mayo, so I only ate a small portion. The pickle was good, though very salty—but since I’m a pickle fan, maybe I’m biased.

All in all, I probably won’t return. Looking back, I should have just stuck with Subway. Take it or leave it.

Rusty's isn’t about following the latest culinary trends or pursuing Michelin stars. Instead, it focuses on consistently serving hearty, reliable, and satisfying meals every day. From the outside, the place has a simple charm—a few tables shaded by umbrellas, a modest neon sign, and a plain white "Rusty's" sign above the entrance. Just a heads-up: the nearby construction in Quail Corners can sometimes be a bit distracting.

Stepping inside, you’re immediately transported back to the 90s. To your left, the walls are covered with business cards, a cooler is stocked with drinks, a large menu hangs by the ordering window, and the dining area is scattered with plenty of National Geographic magazines. It’s a cozy, no-frills spot that feels just right—welcoming, straightforward, and unpretentious.

The menu features classic deli staples—sandwiches, soups, potatoes, and salads. My wife and I usually stick with our favorite, a double-decker PB&J, though we sometimes try something new. The potatoes come in generous portions loaded with toppings; while they’re not my favorite, they’re definitely worth a try if you’re extra hungry. I have a soft spot for their Reuben—a modest sandwich filled with sauerkraut and Thousand Island dressing. It’s not a towering New York–style pastrami mountain, but it’s simple, comforting, and thoroughly satisfying.

Overall, I truly love Rusty's. It’s a beloved local gem that reliably delivers quality food day after day. Thanks for everything, Rusty's!

After living here for nearly two years, I deeply regret not moving out before renewing my lease. The previous staff was approachable and attentive to daily concerns, but the current management is entirely ineffective, lacking urgency and basic business sense. Since rent payments are mostly automated, their primary role seems limited to conducting tours and signing leases.

Though the model units and common areas appear modern and updated, the apartments themselves still have appliances over thirty years old. When I asked about replacements, I was told that as long as they function, it’s “by design” and they won’t be replaced. Meanwhile, rent increased after the first year despite no improvements to the property.

The resident quality hasn’t improved either, confirming what others have said. Trash and pet waste are scattered throughout, and some parents let their children play in the street, making the blind curves dangerous for drivers. The pool is consistently dirty, the hot tub is broken, and debris floats on the water’s surface.

Maintenance issues are ongoing across the apartments and complex, but repairs are half-hearted and often repeated because problems aren’t properly addressed. The place is infested with bugs, and I seriously doubt pest control fees are used effectively. Walls and ceilings are in poor condition, coated with layers of paint that barely mask the damage—clear signs of temporary fixes. Every month brings a new problem, yet residents aren’t notified when complex-wide maintenance or repairs occur.

Overall, this is a terrible place to live, especially paying over $900 a month for such poor conditions and service. There are definitely better options out there.

We rent a 2-bedroom, 2-bath apartment for $639 per month, which includes pet fees, water, trash, and sewer. Although our unit hasn’t been updated yet, management is actively renovating apartments throughout the complex with modern kitchens and bathrooms. Despite this, our experience has been positive. A major convenience is that every apartment comes equipped with a full-size washer and dryer, making daily chores much easier.

Where you live within the complex greatly influences your experience. We live near the front, where it’s quiet and feels secure. In contrast, residents deeper inside the complex have reported less favorable experiences, which likely explains some of the negative reviews. The community mainly consists of families and younger residents.

The complex offers several pools, a tennis court, and a soccer field. There’s also a fitness center with various equipment, though it’s not the most up-to-date. One frustration we encountered was difficulty obtaining a key for the tennis courts—we never received one during our entire lease.

Staff at Willow Ridge are friendly and generally responsive. For example, it took about a month to replace the linoleum in our bathroom, but smaller repairs tend to be addressed more quickly. Residents are allowed to paint their walls, provided they repaint them to the original color before moving out.

Overall, considering the price, this apartment complex is a solid place to live.

From the very first day he moved in, a persistent leak in the bedroom made itself impossible to ignore, flooding the carpet every time it rained. This issue had clearly existed for quite some time, yet the landlord still chose to lease the apartment. Despite his repeated requests to be relocated, released from the lease, or at least have the leak repaired, each appeal was met with cold indifference or outright refusal. The manager claims repair bids are underway, but TEN MONTHS LATER, the bedroom continues to flood with every rainfall.

During this time, furniture and box springs have been destroyed, including a cherished wooden shelf handcrafted by his grandfather, now warped and beyond repair. Despite these damages, the manager refuses to reduce rent, compensate for lost work hours, or even acknowledge the harm caused. Several days each month, the apartment becomes uninhabitable as fans roar, dehumidifiers drone, and water relentlessly seeps in. To make matters worse, mold has developed in the kitchen due to the ongoing dampness, and a musty odor permeates every room. He is forced to store his clothes in sealed plastic containers just to keep them dry and free from the damp smell.

As this nightmare drags on, I am deeply concerned about his physical and mental health. His financial situation is suffering significantly, and with each passing day, the emotional burden only grows heavier.

My first two visits featured slow but tolerable service, and the food was decent—I especially appreciated the spicy mayo dip. However, today’s third visit took a disappointing turn. While eating my taco salad, I suddenly discovered a clump of hair in my mouth. I removed it, hoping it had simply fallen from my sleeve or shoulder, but it was clearly neither mine (I’m blond) nor my companion’s (she has red hair).

We calmly asked to speak with the manager and explained the situation. He picked up the hair from the napkin and immediately denied any responsibility, claiming that none of the employees had dark-brown hair—despite every staff member I noticed having exactly that. Then he walked away, muttering something to the server that sounded like “wants a free meal.” Afterwards, they charged me $3 for my drink and gave my companion her full bill.

While the incident was disgusting, I understand that mistakes can happen. What truly upset me was the manager’s implication that I was lying. If something like this happened in my own restaurant, I would do everything possible to make it right—not insult the customer. This showed a complete lack of professionalism and respect. We will never return.

El Monterrey falls squarely into the category of Mexican-themed eateries that Charlotte could easily do without—much like a minor league baseball team downtown. From the moment you step inside, a strong sense of déjà vu sets in. This exact setup has been duplicated countless times across the country. The décor is uninspired, with gaudy Budweiser and Corona ads plastered across the walls, mass-produced imitation "papel picado" hanging overhead, and cheap, generic tables and chairs. It almost feels like one owner snapped up all these places and simply swapped the names to create a false sense of variety.

I visited for lunch today with my mother, and the experience was completely unremarkable. The service was prompt and courteous, and the food tasted exactly as expected—neither impressive nor disappointing. One detail stood out, though not in a good way: along with the chips and salsa, they served a small dish of white dip. It had a flavor somewhat like ranch with bacon but carried an artificial note, as if made from powdered ingredients and cream cheese. It wasn’t terrible, but it didn’t complement the other items well.

As for price, considering it’s standard Mexican fare, it felt a bit steep. After 3pm, finding a decent dish under $8 is unlikely. Just something to keep in mind. Overall, dining here feels like grabbing a burger at McDonald’s—you go because it’s nearby and convenient, not because you’re seeking anything memorable.

When there’s a chance of pain or fainting, a compassionate bedside manner is absolutely essential. Throughout the procedure, Dr. Lind and his assistant skillfully combined genuine warmth with professionalism, doing everything possible to keep me comfortable.

The surgery was minor and involved the same toe that had a similar operation years earlier by another doctor—long before Jongeys was established. When I mentioned that the anesthetic used previously had been ineffective, the staff confidently reassured me that anesthetic medications have significantly improved since then. True to their word, the “new medications” were noticeably better. Although I still felt some brief, sharp pains and mild discomfort despite extra injections, it was far less than what I had experienced before.

To support optimal healing, Dr. Lind and his assistant carefully explained the necessary post-operative care to be done at home. The receptionist was also exceptional—warm, friendly, and patient throughout the entire experience.

When I scheduled my appointment, I clearly communicated that my issue involved my ankle, hoping to be assigned a doctor experienced in that specialty. However, upon arrival, the first physician I saw admitted she wasn’t an ankle specialist and asked if I could return later that same day to see someone who was. Although taking off work twice in one day was inconvenient, I agreed and came back.

The second doctor, introduced as the "ankle specialist," examined me but admitted he wasn’t "exactly sure" what the problem was. He suggested several possible causes and administered a cortisone injection to alleviate the pain. Unfortunately, the relief lasted only two days. Afterward, I went to another clinic recommended by a co-worker, bringing my x-rays from Carmel Foot Specialists. This new doctor criticized those x-rays as being of "such poor quality" that no diagnosis could be made, adding that "it’s typical for podiatrists to rely on substandard imaging equipment."

Following his evaluation and review of my symptoms, this doctor ordered an MRI, which finally provided a diagnosis and treatment plan—something Carmel Foot Specialists failed to deliver despite two visits. Meanwhile, I was charged over $500 by them, making the entire experience a frustrating waste of time.

My son was advised to get an orthotic for plantar fasciitis, so we initially chose an affordable option. Unfortunately, that first orthotic failed within a month, prompting us to return it and purchase a more expensive model—over $300—with a one-year warranty. Regrettably, this second orthotic also deteriorated before the year ended and began cutting into my son’s foot. We returned it and asked for a replacement.

At the appointment, Dr. Lind didn’t examine my son’s foot. Despite our explanation that the orthotic was causing discomfort, he dismissed our concerns casually, saying, “I’d like to see you get some more wear out of these.” We were still charged the regular co-pay, and Dr. Lind—whose qualifications I question—sent my son home still in pain without even removing his sock to inspect the injury.

After raising my concerns with the office, I was promised a follow-up call, but no one ever contacted me. Because of this experience, I am submitting a formal complaint to the North Carolina Board of Podiatry Examiners. I strongly urge others to think twice before entrusting their child to this practice. Situations like this contribute to the rising costs of insurance.

I was prescribed a custom-made medication that was supposed to be shipped to me, but after waiting an entire week with no delivery, I called only to find out it hadn’t even been ordered. Although I chose to overlook this mistake, later that same week I experienced severe foot pain. I reached out to Carmel Foot Specialists on Monday and Tuesday, but didn’t receive a return call until Wednesday, which I missed. When I called back later that day, I never heard from them again.

The management at the Park Road office is clearly unprofessional and poorly run. Frustrated by their repeated failure to return calls promptly and unable to reach Carmel Foot Specialists by phone, I went in person to retrieve my records. The visit was deeply disappointing, especially due to the office manager’s unprofessional demeanor. Her parting comment, “Have a Nice Day,” felt sarcastic and was completely unnecessary.

Based on my experience, I strongly recommend finding a podiatrist with a well-managed office. I have never been treated so poorly by any physician’s office. It’s obvious that patients are not valued here—they make you feel unimportant and won’t be there when you truly need assistance. I highly advise seeking care elsewhere.

Whenever I’m feeling unwell, I usually turn to my comfort foods—soup and ice cream. But what truly sets Carmel Family Physicians apart is the exceptional care I receive. As a patient for five years, I can honestly say I’ve never been more satisfied. They’ve supported me through a variety of illnesses, including bronchitis, strep throat, sinus infections, upper respiratory issues, and food poisoning.

The office is conveniently located just off 51 and 485 near CMC, making it easily accessible. Their flexible hours fit well with my busy schedule—they stay open until 8 PM on weeknights and offer walk-in hours on weekends. One of the best perks is how often I’ve been able to call and get a same-day appointment, a rarity at most places I’ve visited. The team comprises highly skilled doctors and physician assistants, and I especially recommend seeing Clint Price—he’s exceptional.

The staff always greets me warmly, the waiting room is stocked with current magazines, and I typically spend no more than 20 minutes there. Overall, I truly appreciate everything about this practice.

Adding my voice to the many who praise Taipei South, I want to share my experience with this spot. I’ve known it for about eight years and have never seen any advertisements—understandably so, as it simply doesn’t need them. Despite its less-than-ideal location, the restaurant thrives, and the reasons are clear. The food consistently offers robust flavors and generous portions, with eggrolls that genuinely stand out as the finest in town. Service is reliably prompt, with staff topping off your drink even when it’s only half full. Impressively, all of this comes at the price of a typical fast food meal.

Although I moved away from that neighborhood three years ago, I still make it a habit to visit about once a month. I haven’t found any Chinese restaurant in Center City that compares; they tend to be pricier, less satisfying, or both.

The only minor downside might be the wait staff’s somewhat brusque manner, which could make some patrons feel hurried. I prefer to see it as efficient service—they work quickly but never pressure me to leave, even if I linger chatting after paying the bill. It seems they recognize that most customers are regulars who know exactly what they want almost immediately upon sitting down.

Taipei South serves food that’s more than just acceptable—it’s genuinely flavorful, offering generous portions at a reasonable price. However, it’s important to recognize this is American Chinese cuisine, not authentic Chinese fare, similar to what you’d find at many Chinese eateries nationwide.

The bigger issue lies with the customer service. While the women at the front aren’t unfriendly—I want to be clear on that—the quality of service is inconsistent. Sometimes orders are taken promptly, drinks are regularly refilled, and meals arrive without delay. Other times, the experience is noticeably different.

For example, during my latest visit, the waitresses spoke very little, which is typical. They provided a small jar of Dr Pepper to make refilling my cup easier, but one waitress then used that same jar to refill another customer’s drink—who was unaware I’d been using it—and returned the jar to my table. This happened well after the lunch rush, around 1:45 with the restaurant about one-third full, yet I still waited 12 minutes just to receive my check and receipt.

Honestly, a bit more warmth and hospitality here would go a long way and significantly improve the overall experience. Perhaps the owners are comfortable with the status quo since the food is good and business steady. Still, it’s no secret that friendly, memorable service is what truly keeps customers coming back. I genuinely hope Taipei South takes this feedback to heart.

Musashi distinguishes itself as one of the rare places in Charlotte where you can enjoy a chilled, pleasantly chewy plate of zaru soba—a welcome break from the city’s relentless summer heat. The sashimi here is consistently among the freshest available locally, and the specials almost always deliver solid value, offering two choices each visit. There’s no need to hesitate over special B; choosing it won’t take away from your dining experience.

For those who enjoy mackerel, you’re in good company—my parents and sister are devoted fans. Personally, I can only enjoy mackerel as raw sashimi, since previous encounters with fermented fish in less-than-appetizing tomato paste still linger in my memory.

The wine list brings a playful element, with whimsically unconventional spellings like “Kabernet Sabigny” that I found genuinely delightful. Still, the restaurant struggles with the familiar service lapses and somewhat somber server demeanor common in many Asian establishments—a contrast that can seem out of place in a city renowned for its sunshine and Southern hospitality.
